en: The Divyāvadāna: Divine Avadānas.
Homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
********** Avadāna 1 ********** 001.000. The Legend of Koṭikarṇa.
001.001. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

001.001. In the village of Vāsava in Parāntaka, there lived a householder named Balasena, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging possessions, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He took a wife from a family of equal status.

He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her. Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and others; he supplicated the deities of the groves, the deities of the forests, the deities of the crossroads, and the deities who receive offerings.
He even supplicated those deities born together with him, those sharing his dharma, and those who were constantly attached to him.
There is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers;
however, that is not so.
001.007. If it were so, every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Rather, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
Which three?
The mother and father are full of desire and have come together;
and the mother is healthy and in her fertile season.
A gandharva becomes present.
Through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
And he remained thus intent on his prayers.

And a certain being, in his final existence, seeking welfare, having grasped the end of the path to liberation, not turned away from nirvana, having no desire for cyclic existence, turned away from rebirth in any state of becoming, and bearing his final body— having passed away from a certain class of beings, he entered the womb of that Prajāpati.
001.014. There are five unique qualities found in certain women:
what are the five?
She knows when a man is impassioned.
He knows when she is free from passion;
he knows the time and he knows the season.
001.015. He knows when the embryo has entered the womb.
001.016. He knows from whom the embryo has entered.
He knows whether it will be a boy or he knows whether it will be a girl.
If it is a male child,
he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a female child, [she remains resting against the left side].
She remained resting on her left side.
Being exceedingly joyful, she announced it to her husband: "By good fortune, noble son, may you prosper!
I have become pregnant."
"And since he remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy.
Overjoyed, he uttered this inspired exclamation: "May I indeed behold the face of a son, long desired by me!"
"May he be born to me, not not-born;
may he perform my duties;
being supported, may he support me in return."
He shall receive his inheritance;
my family lineage will endure for a long time.

And when we have passed away, he will give gifts, whether small or great, perform meritorious deeds, and dedicate the merit, saying: "May this follow those two wherever they go, according to their rebirth."
Knowing that she had conceived, he attended to her as she rested upon the upper terrace, providing her with whatever was required:

cooling remedies when it was cold and warming remedies when it was hot; and food prescribed by physicians that was neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent—food entirely free from the qualities of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces; like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat, never descending to the ground below.
And for him, there was no hearing of any unpleasant sound until the fetus reached full maturity.

After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth. A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad and expansive forehead, joined eyebrows, a prominent nose, and [adorned] with an inlay of jewels.
He was adorned with a fastened ear-ornament.
The householder Balasena summoned jewel appraisers and said to them,
"Sirs, determine the value of these jewels."
"It is not possible to determine the price of these jewels.
It is the nature of things that for whatever cannot have its price determined, a value of ten million is set.
They said, "Householder,"
"The value of this jewel is ten million.

His kinsmen, having gathered and assembled together, performed an extensive birth ceremony for the newborn for three weeks— twenty-one days— and then established his name, asking, "What shall be the name of the boy?"
"This boy was born under the asterism Śravaṇā while wearing an ornament set with jewels worth ten million;
therefore, let the boy’s name be Śroṇakoṭikarṇa."
On the very day that Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa was born, two servant boys were born to the householder Balasena.
He established the name of one as Dāraka.
"He is the protector of another.
Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to play with him, two to cleanse him, and two to bathe him.
He was raised and nurtured by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions.
He grows quickly, like a lotus situated in a pond.
When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing,
as well as to arithmetic, calculation, finger-calculation, sealing, extraction, depositing, entrusting, the examination of commodities, and the examination of jewels.
He became proficient in these eight examinations, an eloquent speaker, and one whose conduct was skillful and effective.
His father had three dwelling-houses constructed: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
He had three pleasure gardens laid out: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
He provided him with three harems: the senior, the middle, and the junior.
He, having gone to the upper terrace of the palace, played, took pleasure, and amused himself with instrumental music performed by women alone.
Meanwhile, the householder Balasena was constantly engaged in agricultural labor.
Koṭikarṇa saw his father daily occupied with such agricultural work.
He said, "Father,
for whose sake are you constantly engaged in agricultural labor? He replied, "Son,"
Just as you, having gone up to the terrace of the upper palace, sport, enjoy, and amuse yourself with instrumental music performed by no men—
if I were likewise to sport, enjoy, and amuse myself in this manner, our wealth would before long undergo diminution, exhaustion, and total depletion.
He reflected: "This exhortation is being made for my very sake.
He said: "Father, if that is so, I shall go."

"I am going down to the great ocean. His father said, "Son, I have such a vast quantity of jewels that even if you were to distribute them like sesame seeds, rice, jujubes, and lentils, they would never be exhausted."
"Nevertheless, my store of jewels would not be exhausted.
He said, "Father, give me leave;
taking merchandise, I shall set out upon the great ocean."
002.029. Balasena, knowing his persistent insistence, gave him permission.

Then the householder Balasena made a proclamation by ringing a bell in the village of Vāsava: "Whosoever among you is able, let him gather merchandise suitable for a voyage upon the great ocean, free of customs duties and without tolls, to travel with Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa, the caravan leader."
Five hundred merchants had gathered merchandise suitable for a journey across the great ocean.
A householder named Balasena reflected: "By what kind of vehicle will Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa travel?
He further reflected: "If it were by elephants..."
Elephants are delicate and difficult to maintain;
horses are also delicate and difficult to maintain;
donkeys are both mindful and delicate.
"Let him go by means of a donkey-cart.
His father summoned him and said, "Son, you must not go ahead of the caravan, nor should you go behind it."
003.004. If the thief is strong, he falls upon the caravan from the front;
if he is weak, [he falls from behind].
He falls behind.
You must travel in the midst of the caravan.
And even if the caravan leader is killed, you must not speak of it to the caravan.
The two, Dāsaka and Kāpāla, were also told: "Sons, Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa must not be released by you under any circumstances."
Then, at another time, Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa, having performed the auspicious rites and ceremonies for good fortune, approached his mother, prostrated at her feet, and said: "Mother, I am going;
look upon me with favor, for I am setting out for the great ocean."
She began to weep.
He said, "Mother, why do you weep?
His mother, her face clouded with tears, replied, "Son,"
"Perhaps I shall see my little son alive once again. He reflected: "I have set out with auspicious rites;
yet she speaks such an inauspicious thing."
Enraged, he said:
"Mother, I have set out for the great ocean after performing the auspicious rites and ceremonies for success;
yet you perform such inauspicious acts!"
"Do you not see the states of woe?
She replied, "Son,
you have uttered harsh words."
"Confess your transgression as a transgression.
In this way, this karma may reach attenuation, exhaustion, and termination.
She then had him forgive her for that transgression as a transgression.

Then Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa, having performed the auspicious rites and ceremonies for success, loaded a great quantity of merchandise suitable for sea travel onto carts, pack-animals, mule-carts, baskets, camels, oxen, and donkeys, and set out for the great ocean.
Wandering in succession through villages, towns, market-towns, hamlets, and cities, he eventually reached the shore of the great ocean.
Having carefully prepared a sea-going vessel, the wealth-bringer set out upon the great ocean.

Carried by a favorable wind, he reached the Island of Jewels. Having examined them again and again, he filled that ship with jewels, just as one fills it with sesame seeds, rice, jujubes, and horse-gram.
003.020. With favorable winds, Śroṇa reached Jambudvīpa with his ship successfully completed its voyage.
003.021. That caravan was made to encamp right there on the seashore.
Then the caravan leader Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa, taking Dāsaka and Pālaka with him, withdrew from the midst of the caravan to a secluded spot and began to calculate the income and expenditure.
Afterwards, he said to that servant, "Servant, go and see what the merchant is doing. He went.
003.023. When he saw Sthorā harassing the caravan, 003.024. he too began to harass Sthorā.
Dāsaka reflected: "Pālaka will cause the caravan leader to be summoned."
Pālaka also thought to himself, "The caravan leader Dāsaka will summon me.
Having caused his caravan to halt for the night, he set out;
he too lay down, overcome by a deep sleep.
That caravan proceeded until dawn.
They asked, "Sirs, where is the caravan leader?"
He went ahead;
having gone ahead, they asked, "Where is the caravan leader?
He came from behind.
Going behind, they ask: "Where is the caravan leader?
He goes into the middle;
having gone into the middle, they ask.
003.029. Since even there he was not found, Dāsaka said, "The thought occurred to me: Pālaka will summon the caravan leader.
Pālaka also said, "The thought occurred to me: Dāsaka will summon the caravan leader."
"Friends, we have not done well in that we abandoned the caravan leader. Come, let us turn back.
They replied, "Friends," and so on.
"If we turn back, we shall all meet with disaster through this improper course.
Come, let us first make an agreement: no one must inform Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa’s parents until the merchandise has been unloaded."
Having made this agreement, they departed.
Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa’s parents heard that Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa had arrived;
they said, "He is coming from behind."
Going behind them, they asked, "Where is the caravan leader? He is going ahead.
They were thus distracted until their merchandise had been unloaded.
Afterwards, they said, "Mother, we forgot about the caravan leader.
One of them came and reported, "Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa has arrived.
Having provided him with a welcoming reception, the two of them went out to meet him, but they did not see him.
Another person came and said, "Mother,
congratulations! Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa has arrived."
Having given him an escort, they went out to meet him but did not see him.
From then on, they no longer placed their trust in anyone.
In the pleasure groves, in their own assembly halls, and in the temples of the gods, they wrote and left behind inscriptions on parasols, fans, water jars, and sandals, saying: "If Śroṇa..."
Koṭikarṇa is alive;
wait briefly, wait quickly!
Then, having passed away and died,
he was reborn from that very place of transition into another distinguished state.
Those two, weeping out of grief, became blind.
Śroṇa Koṭikarṇa, the caravan leader, having been touched and warmed by the rays of the sun, woke up; however, he did not see the caravan, but only a donkey-cart.
He mounted that donkey-cart and set out.
During the night, as the wind blew, it swept away the sand from the road and covered it over.
Those donkeys were mindful; having repeatedly sniffed the scent, they set out very slowly and gently.
The caravan leader, wondering why they were moving so slowly and gently, struck them with his goad-stick.
They became agitated and bewildered, lost their mindfulness, and set out on the wrong path.
Eventually, they entered a certain forest. Afflicted by thirst and with faces distraught, they went along with their tongues lolling out.
Seeing them, compassion arose within him.
He reflected: "If I do not release them, I shall meet with disaster through this unrighteousness.
Who is that heartless being, who has abandoned the world beyond, that would strike their bodies with the goad-stick?"
He released them, saying: "From this day forward, eat grass with uncut tips that have not been trampled;
drink waters that are undisturbed;
and let cool breezes blow upon you from the four quarters."
Having abandoned them, he set out on foot.
Eventually, he saw an iron city, high and imposing. At its gate stood a man who was dark, fierce, and violent, with bloodshot eyes and a protruding belly, his hand grasping an iron club.
He approached him.
Having approached, he asked that man, "O man, is there water here?
But he remained silent.
The man was asked by him, "Is there water in this city?
He remained silent once more.
Then that caravan leader, having entered there, uttered the words, "Water! Water!"

004.029. Śroṇa Koṭikarṇ was surrounded by about five thousand hungry ghosts who resembled burnt pillars, whose bodies were as upright as skeletons, covered with their own hair and body hair, resembling the interior of mountains, and having mouths like the eye of a needle.
004.031. They said, "Caravan leader, you are compassionate."
"Give us water, for we are afflicted by thirst.
He replied, "Sirs,
I too am searching for water."
"From where shall I give you water?
They replied, "Caravan leader,
this is a city of hungry ghosts."
"Where is there water here?
For twelve years now, we have heard the sound 'water, water' from you.
He replied, "Who are you, sirs?"
"By what karma have they been reborn here?
"Śroṇa, the humans of Jambudvīpa are difficult to deceive;
you will not believe me."
"O sirs, I am an eyewitness;
why should I not believe it?
They spoke this verse:
"We were abusive and wrathful; we were stingy and miserly. Not even the slightest gift was given by us, because of which we have come to the realm of the ancestors. (1)
"Śroṇa, go!
You are one of great merit and power.
Have you ever seen anyone who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, emerged in safety and well-being?"
Having set out, he eventually saw that man.
He said to him,
"O gentle-faced one, alas, if you had informed me beforehand that this was a city of hungry ghosts!"
"I would not have entered here.
He was told by him: "Śroṇa, go;
you are one of great merit and power."
"By whom you, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, have emerged in safety and well-being.
He set out.
Then he saw another iron city, high and towering.
005.011. There too, at the gate, stands a man who is Death—fierce, red-eyed, with protruding cheeks, and with an iron club held firmly in his hand.
005.012. He approached him.
005.013. Having approached, he spoke thus: "O man!"
"Is there water here in this city?
He remained silent.
Being questioned by him once more—"O man," [he asked].
"Is there water here in this city?
He remained silent.
Thereupon, he entered and called out the words, "Water! Water!"

He was surrounded by many thousands of hungry ghosts (pretas) who resembled burnt pillars, standing upright like skeletons, covered with their own hair and body hair, resembling the interior of a mountain, and having mouths like the eye of a needle.
"Śroṇa, you are compassionate;
give us, who are afflicted by thirst, some water to drink."
He said, "Sirs, I too am searching for water;
how could I give you water?
They replied, "Śroṇa,"
"This is the city of the hungry ghosts. Where is there water here?
For twelve years now, we have heard the sound 'water, water' coming from your direction."
And he said: "Who are you, sirs, and by what karma have you been reborn here? They replied: "Śroṇa," they said.
"The people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to deceive;
you will not believe me.
He replied, "Sirs, I am one who has seen it with my own eyes."
005.022. "Why should I not believe it?
They spoke this verse:
005.023. "Those who are intoxicated by the pride of health, and those who are intoxicated by the pride of the increase of wealth,"
005.024. And not even the slightest gift was given by him, because of which we have come to the world of the ancestors. //2//
"Śroṇa, go!
You are one who has performed meritorious deeds.
Have you ever seen or heard of anyone who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, emerged alive with well-being and safety?"
He set out.
Eventually, he saw that man and said to him,
"O gentle-faced one,"
"Alas! If you had informed me that this was a city of hungry ghosts (*preta*), I certainly would not have entered here.
He replied, "Śroṇa, go!"
"You are one of great merit and renown.
Have you ever seen or heard of anyone who, having entered the city of the hungry ghosts, emerged alive, safe and sound?
He set out.
005.029. Then, at the time of sunset, he saw a celestial mansion and four apsarases who were beautiful, graceful, and lovely to behold.

005.030. There was also one man, handsome, lovely, and graceful, adorned with armlets, earrings, various garlands, ornaments, and ointments, who was sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying together with them.
He was seen by them from afar. They began to address him:
"Welcome, Śroṇa!"
"Are you thirsty or hungry?
He reflected, "Surely this must be a god, or a nāga, or a yakṣa.
And he said, "Noble sir, I am thirsty."
"I am hungry.
He was bathed and fed by them,
and he remained in that celestial mansion until the time for the rising of the sun.
He was told by him, "Śroṇa, descend;
there will be danger here.
Having descended, he stood to one side.
Thereafter, at the time of the sun’s rising, that celestial mansion vanished;
those apsarases also vanished,
and four brindled black dogs appeared.
006.006. Having cast that man head-first down, they repeatedly tore out his vertebrae and begged from him until the time for the setting of the sun arrived.
006.007. Thereafter, once again, that celestial palace appeared, and those apsarases appeared.
And that man played, took pleasure, and amused himself with them.
Approaching them, he asked: "Who are you, and by what karma have you been reborn here?"
They said, "Śroṇa, the people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to deceive;
you will not believe us.
He replied, "I am one who has seen it with my own eyes."
"How could I not believe it? Śroṇa, in the village of Vāsava, I was a butcher of sheep.
By repeatedly slaughtering sheep and selling their meat, I made my living."
And the noble Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion for me, came and said: "O gentle-faced one, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable.
Desist from this evil, unrighteousness."
"I do not desist because of his words.
Again and again he dissuades me, saying: 'O gentle-faced one, the ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable.'"
"Desist from this evil, unrighteous practice.
Even so, I did not desist.
He asked me: "O gentle-faced one,"
"Do you slaughter these sheep during the day or rather at night?
I replied, "Noble sir, I slaughter them during the day."
He said, "O gentle-faced one,
why do you not take up the observance of the precepts at night?
From him, I took up the observance of the precepts at night.
"Because I undertook the observance of the precepts during the night, through the ripening of that karma, I experience such divine happiness specifically at night.
But as for the sheep that were slaughtered by me during the day,"
As the ripening of that karma, I experience such suffering even during the day.
And he spoke this verse:
"By day, a tormentor of the lives of others; by night, endowed with the virtues of moral conduct."
I am indeed experiencing the fruit of that karma, whether auspicious or evil. (3)
"Śroṇa, will you go to Vāsavagrāma? I shall go.
My son lives there;
he makes his living by slaughtering sheep again and again."
"You should say to him: 'I have seen your father.
He will say: 'The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable. Desist from this evil, unrighteous conduct.'"
"O man, you say this: 'The people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to deceive.
No one will believe you."
"Śroṇa, if he does not believe you, you should say:
'Your father says that beneath the slaughterhouse there is a jar of gold, which was placed there full.
Having dug it up, satisfy yourself with perfect happiness.'"
"From time to time, provide the noble Mahākātyāyana with almsfood,
and dedicate the merit to us by name.
In this way, perhaps this karma may become attenuated, exhausted, and brought to an end."
He set out.
Then, at the time of sunrise, he saw another celestial mansion.
Therein was a single apsaras, beautiful, lovely to behold, and graceful.

And there was a man, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, who was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with her.
Seeing him from afar, he began to address him:
"Welcome, Śroṇa!"
"Are you not thirsty, or are you not hungry?
He reflected: "Surely this must be a god, or a nāga, or a yakṣa."
He said, "I am thirsty and hungry.
He was bathed and fed by him,
and he remained in that celestial mansion until the time for the setting of the sun.
He was told by him, "Descend;
there will be danger here.
Having seen the danger, he descended and stood to one side.
Thereafter, at the time of the sun’s setting, that celestial mansion vanished;
that apsaras also vanished,
and a great centipede appeared.
007.006. She wrapped her body around that man’s body seven times and remained there devouring his brain until the very time of sunrise.
007.008. Thereafter, that celestial palace appeared once again.
Then that apsarā appeared as well.
That man—handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold—played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
He approached him and asked, "Who are you?"
"By what karma have you been reborn here?
He replied, "Śroṇa,
the humans of Jambudvīpa are difficult to deceive."
"You will not believe it.
He replied, "I am an eyewitness;
why should I not believe it?"
He said, "If that is so, I was once a brahmin in the village of Vāsava who committed adultery.
Then the noble Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion for me, came and said: 'O gentle-faced one,'"
"The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable.
Desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma. Despite these words, I did not desist.
Again and again he tried to dissuade me;
yet, in that very same way, I did not desist from that evil, unrighteous practice.
He asked me: "O gentle-faced one,..."
"Do you approach another man's wife by day, or rather at night?
He was told by me: "Noble sir, at night."
He said, "O gentle-faced one, why do you not take up the observance of the precepts during the day? [The other replied:
"I have taken up the observance of the precepts during the day in his presence."
"Because I undertook the observance of the precepts during the day in the presence of the noble Kātyāyana, through the ripening of that karma, I experience such divine happiness during the day.
But as for that act of approaching another's wife at night— "
As the ripening of that karma, I experience such suffering even at night.
And he speaks this verse:
"Infatuated with another's wife at night,"
Throughout the day, I was endowed with the virtues of moral conduct;
indeed, I now experience the fruit of that action, both auspicious and sinful.
"Śroṇa, you will go to Vāsavagrāmaka. There, my son is a brahmin who commits adultery.
He should be told: 'I have seen your father.'"
He said: "The ripening of the fruit of this action is undesirable. Desist from this evil, unrighteous act!
O man!"
"You say this: 'The people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful.
Who will believe me on this, Śroṇa? That which you do not believe—"
He should be told: "Your father, having filled a golden jar and buried it beneath the Agniṣṭoma altar, left it there.
Having unearthed it, satisfy yourself with perfect happiness.
And from time to time, provide for the noble Mahākātyāyana with almsfood."
"And assign the dedication of merit in our names as well;
perhaps by this, this karma may reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination.
Having said this, he set out.
007.030. Eventually he saw a celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
There was a woman there, beautiful, lovely to behold, and gracious, adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments.
At the four legs of her couch sat four hungry ghosts (*preta*) bound there.
Seeing him from afar, she began to address him: "Śroṇa, welcome!
Are you not thirsty, or are you not hungry?
He reflected: "Surely this must be a goddess, or a nāgī, or a yakṣī."
He said, "Noble lady, I am thirsty; I am hungry.
She massaged him, bathed him, and gave him food.
And it was said:
"Śroṇa, if these people seek anything, do not give it to them.
Having said this, desiring to make those beings witness the fruit of their own karma, he entered his celestial palace and remained there.
They began to search for him, saying, "Śroṇa, you are compassionate.
We are hungry;
give us something."
When it was thrown to one, a flood of chaff appeared;
when it was thrown to another, he began to eat glowing iron balls;
when it was thrown to another, he began to eat his own flesh; when it was thrown to another, pus and blood appeared.
She departed with a foul odor.
Śroṇa, you were warned by me;
why did you give this to them?
What does she say?— "This is my husband, this is my son, and this is my daughter-in-law."
"This is my slave girl.
He asked, "Who are you, and by what karma have you been reborn here?"
She said, "Śroṇa,
you will not believe it when I say that the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful.
Since I am an eyewitness, why would I not believe it?"
She said: "I was a brahmin woman in the village of Vāsava.
When the night of the constellations had arrived, I prepared and set out excellent food.
Then, out of compassion for me, the noble Mahākātyāyana entered the village of Vāsava for alms."
008.014. I saw him, pleasing in body and pleasing in mind. Seeing that his mind was serene, I, having conceived a sense of faith, offered him almsfood.
Then this thought arose in me: "I shall inform my husband."
"He will experience great joy.
Having bathed, he returned.
I said, "Noble son,"
"Rejoice! The noble Mahākātyāyana has been provided with almsfood by me.
He became enraged, saying, "As long as nothing is given to the brahmins..."
"Did you give the first alms-offering to that shaven-headed ascetic while the honoring of your kinsmen was not yet being performed?
Having become indignant, he said: "Why does that shaven-headed ascetic not eat the floating chaff?"

His brother Bhavila reflected: "He is exhausted from traveling across the great ocean; I must arrange a marriage for him."
He was told by him: "Brother, tell me, for whose sake—whether for a wealthy man or a caravan leader—shall I request a daughter?
He replied: "I have no need for sensual pleasures."
"If you grant permission,
I shall go forth.
He replied, "When there is no news at our house,"
"At that time you did not go forth; now you go forth for the sake of sensual pleasures.
Pūrṇa replied, "Brother," and continued:
At that time it was not fitting, but now it is appropriate.
Having recognized his persistent insistence, he granted him permission.
He said, "Brother,
the great ocean has many dangers and little enjoyment; many enter it, but..."
Only a few emerge;
by no means should you embark upon the great ocean.
You already possess abundant wealth acquired through righteous means.
If these brothers of yours say, "Let us live together," you must not dwell with them, for they have acquired their wealth through unjust means.
Having said this, he took his attendant and set out for Śrāvastī;
traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
While staying in the park at Śrāvastī, he dispatched a messenger to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having gone there, he informed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, the caravan leader Pūrṇa is staying in the park, desiring to see you, the householder."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada reflected: "Surely he has now come by land, being weary from traveling by water.
He then asked: "O man, how much merchandise have you brought?"
He said, "Whence is his merchandise?
It is he and I, with a single attendant between us."
Anāthapiṇḍada reflected: "It is not fitting for me that I should cause this eminent man to enter with a lack of hospitality.
He caused him to enter with great honor, and had him anointed, bathed, fed, and provided with comforts.
While they were seated in private conversation, Anāthapiṇḍada asked: "O caravan leader," [he said].
"What is the purpose of your visit?
"Householder, for the first time I desire the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, raising his upper body and extending his right arm, uttered this inspired exclamation: "O, the Buddha!"
"O, how wonderful is the Dharma!
O, how wonderful is the well-proclaimed nature of the Saṅgha!
For now, such eminent men as these, having abandoned their extensive circles of kinsmen and relatives, and vast treasuries and granaries, yearn for the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking the caravan leader Pūrṇa with him, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma.
The Blessed One saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approaching, carrying a gift.
Having seen him, he addressed the monks: "Monks, here comes the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with a gift.
There is no such gift for the Tathāgata as this gift of those to be converted.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side together with the caravan leader Pūrṇa.

Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, this caravan leader Pūrṇa desires the going forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
May the Blessed One, out of compassion, grant him the going forth and the full ordination.
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One addressed Pūrṇa the caravan leader: "Come, monk; lead the holy life.

At the conclusion of the Blessed One's words, he became shaven-headed, clad in the outer robe, with bowl and water-strainer held in his hands, and with hair and beard as if shaved only seven days prior, as though he had been ordained for a hundred years.
Thus addressed by the Tathāgata, "Come," he was shaven-headed, his body enveloped in the outer robe.
Immediately his senses became tranquil, and he remained thus, established in the aspiration of a Buddha. //4//
Then, at another time, the venerable Pūrṇa approached the Blessed One. Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the venerable Pūrṇa said this to the Blessed One: "It would be well for me, O Blessed One, if the Blessed One [were to teach] in such a way..."
"May the Blessed One teach the Dharma in brief, so that having heard the Dharma in brief from the Blessed One, I may dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute—
for the sake of which sons of good family, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes, go forth from the home into homelessness with perfect faith."

"Having realized for myself in this very life that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, having attained it and entered into it, may I go forth [with this thought]: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Pūrṇa: "Excellent, Pūrṇa!"
"It is indeed excellent, Pūrṇa, that you speak thus: 'It would be well if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief... [as before] ...until I understand no further existence beyond this.
Therefore, Pūrṇa, listen; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak."

"Pūrṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, dear, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and alluring. If a monk, having seen them, delights in them, welcomes them, becomes intent upon them, and remaining intent upon them, persists in delighting in, welcoming, becoming intent upon, and persisting in those forms, he comes to experience joy."
From delight (nandi) arises joy and gladness;
when there is joy and gladness, there is lust (rāga);
when there is joy and lust, there is the fetter of joy and lust (nandī-rāga-saṃyojana).
"O Pūrṇa, a monk who is bound by the fetter of delight in sensual pleasure is said to be far from nirvāṇa. O Pūrṇa, there are sounds cognizable by the ear,
and there are odors cognizable by the nose."

Tastes are to be cognized by the tongue; tangibles are to be cognized by the body; and mental phenomena are to be cognized by the mind—those which are desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of passion.
And when the monk saw them, as before, it is said that he was "near to nirvāṇa.

However, Pūrṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing, as before, up to being on the side of the bright, which is said to be near to nirvāṇa. By this brief instruction, Pūrṇa, you have been exhorted by me.
"Where do you wish to dwell? Where do you wish to make your home?
"Venerable Blessed One, having been exhorted by this brief instruction, I wish to dwell in the Śroṇāparāntaka regions; I wish to make my home in the Śroṇāparāntaka regions.
"Pūrṇa, the people of Śroṇāparānta are fierce, impetuous, harsh, abusive, wrathful, and reviling."
"023.011. Pūrṇa, if the people of Śroṇāparāntaka should revile you face to face with wicked, untrue, and harsh speech, and should provoke and abuse you, what would you think of that?
Venerable sir, if the people of Śroṇāparāntaka should revile me face to face with wicked, untrue, and harsh speech, and should provoke and abuse me..."
It will occur to me: "Ah, how kind are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka! Ah, how affectionate are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka, who [yet] address me face-to-face with wicked, untrue, and harsh words."
They revile, incite to anger, and abuse with words,
but they do not strike with the hand or with clods of earth.
O Pūrṇa, the people of Śroṇāparāntaka are fierce, as previously described, up to being abusive.
"Full, if the people of Śroṇāparāntaka were to strike you with their hands or with clods of earth, what would you think of that?
Venerable sir, if the people of Śroṇāparāntaka were to strike me with their hands or with clods of earth,"
It will occur to me: "Ah, how kind are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka! Ah, how affectionate are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka, who strike me with their hands or with clods of earth!"
But they do not strike with a staff or a weapon. Pūrṇa, the people of Śroṇāparāntaka are fierce, as previously described, up to being abusive.
If, Pūrṇa, the people of Śroṇāparāntaka should strike you with a staff or a weapon, [you should endure it].
How will that be for you?
Venerable sir, if the people of Śroṇāparāntaka should strike me with a staff or a weapon, it will occur to me: "Ah, how kind the people of Śroṇāparāntaka are!"
How affectionate indeed are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka,
who strike me with sticks or weapons, yet do not deprive me of life in every way.
"Full, the people of Śroṇāparāntaka are fierce, up to being abusive.
Full, if all the people of Śroṇāparāntaka were to deprive you of life entirely, what would you think of that?"
Venerable sir, if the people of Aparāntaka were to deprive me entirely of life,
it would occur to me: "There are disciples of the Blessed One who, being distressed by this putrid body and feeling ashamed and loathing it, even take up a weapon."
They beg even for poison;
they die even when bound with ropes; they even fall from precipices.
"How fortunate indeed are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka!
How affectionate indeed are the people of Śroṇāparāntaka,
who have released me from this putrid carcass with so little difficulty!"
"Excellent, excellent, Pūrṇa!
Endowed with such patience and gentleness, you are capable, Pūrṇa, of dwelling in the Śroṇāparāntaka regions and making your home in the Śroṇāparāntaka regions.
Go now, Pūrṇa!"
Being liberated, liberate others; having crossed over, help others cross; being comforted, comfort others.
"Having entered final nirvana, cause [others] to enter final nirvana."
Then the Venerable Pūrṇa, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
Then, at the end of that very night, in the forenoon, the Venerable Pūrṇa dressed himself, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Śrāvastī and finished his meal, he returned with his bowl after the meal.

Having put away his bedding and seating exactly as he had used them, and taking up his bowl and robe, he set out on a wandering tour toward the country of Śroṇāparāntaka, and eventually arrived at that country.
Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Pūrṇa dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śroṇāparāntaka for alms.
At that time, a certain hunter, bow in hand, was going out on a hunt.
He saw him.

He reflected, "I have seen this ill-omened, shaven-headed little ascetic," and having realized this, he drew his bow back to his ear and rushed toward the Venerable Pūrṇa. The Venerable Pūrṇa saw him.
Having seen him, he turned his upper robe over his shoulder and said, "Good sir,
I am entering for the sake of this insatiable one; strike here!"
And he spoke this verse:
"For whose sake birds wander in the thicket, deer fall into captivity, and men bearing arrows, spears, and lances perish incessantly in battle;
for whose sake the wretched, moving through stormy weather, and the miserable fish swallow the iron hook—for the sake of this belly, which is a mire of evil, I have come here from afar. (5)
He reflected: "This renunciant is endowed with such patience and gentleness;
why should I strike him? Thinking thus, he became filled with faith.
Thereupon, the Venerable Pūrṇa taught him the Dharma.
He was established in the precepts for going for refuge;
furthermore, five hundred laymen and five hundred laywomen were ordained,
and five hundred monasteries were constructed.
And hundreds of couches, stools, small seats, high seats, pillows, bolsters, and square cushions were provided.
At the end of those very three months, he personally realized the three knowledges and became an Arhat.
Having become free from passion for the three realms, he became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by all the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

Then, at another time, the wealth of Dārukarṇin’s two brothers diminished, was exhausted, and came to an end. They said, "That one who resembled Kālakarṇī has departed from our home. Come, let us live together."
He asked, "Which one is that who resembles Kālakarṇī?
They replied, "Pūrṇakaśrī;
she has departed from my house."
"He does not resemble Kālakarṇī.
The two of them said, "Whether it be Śrī or Kālakarṇī, come; let us dwell together."
He said, "The wealth of you two was acquired through unjust means,
whereas mine was acquired through just means.
I will not make my dwelling together with you in one place."
The two of them said, "That son of a slave-girl has crossed the great ocean again and again and acquired wealth, by means of which you boast while enjoying yourself.
What capacity do you have to cross the great ocean?
Thus he was made to feel pride by them.

He reflected, "I too shall embark upon the great ocean," and as before, he eventually set out upon the great ocean. Then that ship was driven by the wind toward a forest of *gośīrṣa* sandalwood trees.
The helmsman said: "Sirs, that which is heard of as the Gośīrṣa sandalwood forest—this is it.
Take from here whatever is of value."
At that time, the Gośīrṣacandana forest was the possession of the yakṣa Maheśvara.
That yakṣa had gone to the assembly of the yakṣas.
Thereupon, about five hundred axes began to be carried into the Gośīrṣacandana forest.
The yakṣa named Apriyākhyo saw about five hundred men carrying axes in the Gośīrṣacandana forest.
Having seen them, he approached where the yakṣa Maheśvara was.
Having approached the yakṣa Maheśvara, he said this to him: "O village chief, you should know that five hundred axes are being carried toward the Gośīrṣacandana sandalwood grove.
Whatever task or duty you have, perform it now.

Then the yakṣa Maheśvara, having convened an assembly of the yakṣas and becoming filled with indignation, stirred up a great fear of a dark storm and set out toward the Gośīrṣacandana sandalwood grove.
The helmsman announced: "Listen, you merchants of Jambudvīpa! That which is heard of as the danger of the Mahākālikā wind—that is this very thing.
What do you think?
Then those merchants, terrified, trembling, agitated, and with their hair standing on end, began to offer prayers to the deities.

Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and the other lords of gods, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, and dānavas—we have fallen into a most terrifying calamity; O Protectors, may you today be free from fear for us. (6)
Some men pay homage to Śacīpati (Indra), others to Brahmā, and still others to Hari and Śaṅkara;
seeking protection from winds, piśācas, and yakṣas, they take refuge in trees and forests upon the earth. (7)
Dārukarṇī remained with little concern.
The merchants said, "Caravan leader, we have fallen into hardship, distress, and peril."
"Why do you remain so indifferent?
He replied, "Sirs, I was told by my brother: 'The great ocean has little to offer in the way of enjoyment and many dangers.'"
"Many who are blinded by craving enter [the ocean],
but few will emerge;
you must not enter the great ocean by any means whatsoever."
"Thus, having treated his words as if they were not words, I have entered the great ocean.
What shall I do now?
Who is your brother? "Pūrṇa."
The merchants said, "Sirs,
he is indeed that noble Pūrṇa, renowned for his great merit.
Let us take refuge in him alone."
With one voice, they all uttered this cry: "Homage to that noble Pūrṇa! Homage, homage to that noble Pūrṇa!
Then, the goddess who was devoted to the venerable Pūrṇa—
She approached the venerable Pūrṇa;
having approached him, she said this to the venerable Pūrṇa: "Noble sir, your brother has fallen into a state of hardship, distress, and peril."
"Pay attention!
He paid attention.

Then the Venerable Pūrṇa entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from Śroṇāparāntaka and sat cross-legged upon the boundary of the ship in the great ocean.
Then that Kālikā wind, as if struck back by Mount Sumeru, turned back.
Thereupon, the yakṣa Maheśvara reflected: "In the past, whatever vessel was touched by the Kālikā wind was cast away and shattered like a tuft of cotton."
"Now, what is the yoga by which this Kālikā wind, as if struck back by Mount Sumeru, has turned back?
He began to look here and there until he saw the Venerable Pūrṇa sitting cross-legged at the boundary of the ocean.
Having seen him, he spoke again: "Noble Pūrṇa!"
"Why do you harass me? Venerable Pūrṇa replied, "I am subject to old age.
Why do you harass me alone?"
"If I had not attained such a multitude of virtues, my brother would have been reduced by you to nothing but a name.
The yakṣa Maheśvara said, "Noble one, this Gośīrṣa sandalwood forest is preserved for the sake of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
What do you think, leader: what is superior, a universal monarch, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha?"
"Noble one, has the Blessed One appeared in the world? "He has.

"If that is so, let what is incomplete be brought to completion. Then those merchants, as if their lives had returned to them, conceived a deep faith in the venerable Pūrṇa; they filled that vessel with gośīrṣa sandalwood and set out.
In due course, they arrived at the city of Sūrpāraka.
Then the Venerable Pūrṇa said to his brother: "To whomsoever the ship arrives as a successful vessel under that person's name, it belongs to him to go there.
You, however, must distribute the jewels among these merchants."
"I shall have a sandalwood palace built for the sake of the Blessed One using this gośīrṣa sandalwood.
He then shared the jewels with those merchants.
Thereupon, the venerable Pūrṇa began to have a palace constructed with gośīrṣa sandalwood.
He summoned the artisans and said to them, "Sirs,
do you take five hundred kārṣāpaṇas every day, or rather, a cat’s paw of gośīrṣa sandalwood powder?
They replied, "Noble sir, [we would take] a cat’s paw of gośīrṣa sandalwood powder."
In a very short time, the Candanamāla palace was completed.
The king said, "It is vast;
it is a magnificent palace."
He became one who had reached the ultimate perfection of all his past lives.
Whatever fragments of bone and powder remained there, he ground them up and applied them as an ointment right there.
And all those brothers forgave one another and were told: "Invite the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, and provide them with a meal.
"Noble sir, where is the Blessed One?
"In Śrāvastī."
"How far is Śrāvastī from here?
"More than a hundred yojanas.
"In that case, let us first look for the king."
"Do so.
They approached the king;
having approached him, they bowed their heads in salutation and said, "Your Majesty,"
"We wish to invite the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, and provide them with a meal;
may Your Majesty grant us your assistance.
The king said, "In that case, it is well."
"So be it;
I shall prepare.
Thereupon, the Venerable Pūrṇa ascended to the roof of the shelter, stood facing the Jeta Grove, and [extended] both...
Having placed his kneecaps upon the ground, scattered flowers, and wafted incense, he had an attendant take up a golden pitcher and began to pay homage:
"O you of pure conduct, O you of most purified intellect, who always perceive the ultimate goal through the application of devotion!"
"O virtuous one, having beheld those who have become protectorless, please show compassion and come. Thus it was said.

Then, through the power of the Buddhas and the power of the deities, those flowers formed a flower-pavilion above; having gone to the Jeta Grove, they remained there like a mass of clouds in the sky. The Venerable Ānanda was skilled in interpreting signs.
With palms joined in reverence, he asked the Blessed One: "From where, Blessed One, has the invitation come?
"From the city of Sūrpāraka, Ānanda.
"How far away, Venerable Sir, is the city of Sūrpāraka?"
"It is more than one hundred and twenty-seven yojanas, Ānanda.
Let us go, Ānanda!
Announce to the monks: 'Whoever among you is able to go to the city of Śūrpāraka tomorrow and eat there, [let him prepare himself].'"
"Let him take a voting stick.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One; having taken a voting stick, he stood before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One took a voting stick.
And by the elder and senior monks.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa Kuṇḍopadhānīyaka, an elder liberated through wisdom, was seated and present in that very assembly. He too began to take a voting stick.
The Venerable Ānanda replied to him with a verse:
"Venerable sir, this must not be eaten in the house of the Lord of Kośala, nor in the palace of Sujāta, nor in the Mṛgāra residence. (9)
"The city of Sūrpāraka is more than a hundred yojanas from here;
one must go there by means of supernatural powers. Remain silent, Pūrṇaka! (10)
He was one liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
Therefore, he had not produced supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
This thought occurred to him: "By me, the entire mass of afflictions (*kleśagaṇa*) has been vomited up, spat out, abandoned, and relinquished."
Thus, being despondent over my supernatural power— which was shared with the non-Buddhist outsiders—
I applied myself with diligence and produced a supernatural power such that, before the Venerable Ānanda could give the voting stick to the third elder,
he extended his arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, and took the voting stick.
Then he spoke this verse:

"O Gautama, neither by physical beauty nor by learning, nor by qualities of power, nor even by powerful mental aspirations, is the state of the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñatva*) attained in this world. (11)

Examined by the various powers of tranquility, ethical conduct, and insight, as well as the powers of meditative concentration, those whose youth has been ravaged by old age become like me—possessors of the six supernormal knowledges. (12) Thus it was said.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this one is the foremost among my monks, my disciples, in the matter of taking the lot for the caityas. Let him be the very first to take a lot; that is to say, the Elder Pūrṇa Kuṇḍopadhānīyaka.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and announce this to the monks."
Furthermore, although I have said, "O monks, you should dwell with your virtues concealed and your faults revealed," nevertheless,
that city is occupied by non-Buddhist heretics.
Whoever among you has attained any supernatural power, [let him display it].
"Therefore, having gone there to the city of Sūrpāraka with her, you must eat.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he announced to the monks:
"Venerable ones, the Blessed One has spoken thus: 'Monks, although I have said that you should dwell with your virtues concealed,' and so on as before, up until: 'having gone there, you must eat.'"
Then King Sūrpāraka had the city of Sūrpāraka cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, adorned with various kinds of fragrant incense burners, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, strewn with diverse flowers, and made beautiful.
The city of Sūrpāraka had eighteen gates.
That king also had seventeen sons. Each prince was stationed at one of the gates with the utmost magnificence.

And at the main gate, by the great majesty of the king, the venerable Pūrṇa, Dārukarṇī, Stavakarṇī, and Trapukarṇī were stationed as the sovereign of Sūrpāraka. Then, those who travel on leaves, those who travel on grass, and those who travel on vessels arrived through supernatural power.
Seeing them, the king said, "Venerable Pūrṇa,"
"Has the Blessed One arrived?
Venerable Pūrṇa replied, "Great King, these are merely leaf-carriers, green-vegetable carriers, and vessel-carriers; the Blessed One has not yet arrived."
When the elder monks had attained various kinds of meditative absorptions and attainments,
he asked again: "Venerable Pūrṇa, has the Blessed One arrived?"
The Venerable Pūrṇa said: "Great King, it is not the Blessed One;
rather, those monks are indeed the elders among elders.
Then, at that time, a certain lay follower spoke this verse:
Some, relying upon lions, tigers, elephants, horses, serpents, and bulls—some upon auspicious jeweled palaces, mountains, and variegated trees, and others upon radiant chariots;
others like clouds in the expanse of the sky adorned with streaks of lightning—prepared to depart with great splendor, as joyful as if going to the city of the gods. (13)
"Some, having pierced the earth, fly upward; others fall from the surface of the sky.
Some even sit upon thrones—behold the power of those possessed of supernatural might! (14) Thus it was said.
Then the Blessed One, having washed his feet outside the monastery, entered the monastery, set his body straight, established mindfulness before him, and sat upon the prepared seat.
As soon as the Blessed One placed his foot in the fragrant chamber with conscious effort, an earthquake occurred in six ways: this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently.
It quakes, it quakes violently, it quakes intensely;
the eastern quarter rises up, while the western quarter sinks down.
The west rises and the east sinks;
the south rises, and...
The north side sinks down;
the north side rises up, and the south side sinks down.
The edges rise up, and the center sinks down;
the center rises up, and the edges sink down.
The earth sinks down in the center.
The king asks the venerable Pūrṇa, "Noble Pūrṇa, what is this?
He replies, "Great King,..."
The Blessed One placed his foot upon the Gandhakuṭī with great effort, whereby an earthquake of sixfold movement occurred.
Then the Blessed One emitted a radiance with the color of golden rays, by which Jambudvīpa was turned into the appearance of molten gold.
Again, the king, his eyes wide with wonder, asked: "Noble Pūrṇa, what is this?
He replied: "Great King, the Blessed One has emitted a radiance with the color of golden rays."
Then the Blessed One— tamed and with a tamed retinue, peaceful and with a peaceful retinue— together with five arhats who were likewise peaceful, set out toward Sūrpāraka.
Then a deity dwelling in the Jeta Grove took up a bakula branch and, providing shade for the Blessed One, followed behind him as he departed.
The Blessed One, having understood her intention, disposition, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, that goddess shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Now, in a certain region, there lived about five hundred housewives.

They saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect. And upon seeing him, great faith arose in them toward the Blessed One.

This is the nature of things: twelve years of practiced tranquility (*śamatha*) does not produce such fitness of mind as the first sight of a Buddha does for a being who has accumulated the causes of roots of merit— just as a sonless man gains a son, or a poor man discovers a treasure, or one who longs for a kingdom receives the consecration of kingship.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the time for their conversion had come, sat down on the seat prepared before the community of monks.
They too, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, knowing their dispositions, latent tendencies, elements, and natures, [taught them] until they realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truths, they uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Venerable Sir, what has been done for us by the Blessed One was not done for us by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by our circle of beloved kinsmen and relatives, nor by the deities, nor by our deceased ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins."
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed;
the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
We have been established among gods and humans as those who have transcended all that is transcended.
We go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
May the Blessed One accept us as laywomen (upāsikās).

Then, rising from his seat and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: "O, would that the Blessed One would grant us something here, upon which we might perform a memorial service!
Thereupon, through his supernatural power, the Blessed One released some of his hair and nails.
By them, a stūpa for the hair and nails of the Blessed One was established.
Then, by that resident of Jetavana, that *bakula* branch was placed upon the pole of that stūpa.
And the Blessed One said: "Blessed One," [she said].
"I am staying here at this stūpa performing service," she said,
and she remained right there. Consequently, some people came to know it as the Ghariṇī-stūpa.
Some call him Bakulamedha, whom even today the monks who pay homage to the caityas still revere.
Thereupon, the Blessed One set out.
Now, in another hermitage, five hundred sages were living.
That hermitage of theirs was well-provided with flowers, fruits, and water.
Intoxicated by that abundance, they considered nothing else.
Then the Blessed One, observing that the time for their conversion had come, approached that hermitage.
Having arrived, he used his supernormal power to wither the flowers and fruits of that hermitage and dried up its water.
The green grass was trampled and the sacrificial altars were cast down.
Then those seers, resting their cheeks upon their hands, remained lost in thought.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed them: "O great seers," he said.
"Why do you remain absorbed in anxiety?
They replied, "Blessed One, you have entered this world as a field of merit for bipeds, yet such is our condition.
The Blessed One asked, "What is it?"
They said, "Blessed One,
may this hermitage, which was once endowed with flowers, fruits, and water, be restored to its former state. "So be it," the Blessed One replied.
Then the Blessed One withdrew his supernatural power, and everything returned to its former state.
Thereupon, they were filled with supreme wonder and directed their minds toward serene faith in the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having understood their dispositions, underlying tendencies, elements, and natures, delivered such a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths;
upon hearing it, those five hundred seers realized the fruit of non-returning and manifested supernormal powers.

Then, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, they said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may we receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may we practice the holy life under the Blessed One.
Thereupon, they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monks; practice the holy life."

At the conclusion of the Blessed One’s speech, they became shaven-headed, clad in saṃghāṭī robes, with bowls and water-strainers held in their hands; though their hair and beards had been grown for only seven days, they possessed the deportment of a monk ordained for a hundred years.
For it is said: "As soon as they were addressed by the Tathāgata with the word 'Come,' they became shaven-headed, their bodies enveloped in saṃghāṭī robes;
with their faculties immediately calmed, they stood thus established through the Buddha’s resolve. (Verse 15)
By applying themselves, striving, and exerting themselves, they—just as before regarding this fivefold group—eventually became those who were to be saluted.
Then the seer who was their instructor said: "Blessed One, by me, in this disguise, a great multitude of people has been deceived."
"I shall first inspire faith in him, and afterwards I will go forth into the religious life.

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the five hundred former seers and the five hundred monks in the shape of a half-moon, departed through the air above by means of his supernatural power and reached Mount Musalaka in due course.
At that time, a seer named Vakkalin was dwelling on Mount Musalaka.
From afar, that seer saw the Blessed One adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as described previously, and beautiful in every respect.
Upon seeing him, his mind became filled with serene faith toward the Blessed One.
Filled with serene faith, he thought: "What if I were to descend from the mountain and approach the Blessed One for an audience?
The Blessed One might pass by out of regard for those to be trained;
what if I were to throw myself down from the mountain?"
He threw himself from the mountain.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are of a nature that does not forget.
The Blessed One received him through his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Then, the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that,
upon hearing it, Vakkalin realized the fruit of non-returning and manifested supernatural power.

Then he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya," as previously described, until: by the Blessed One being summoned with the words "Come, monk," he was ordained, and thus remained, fulfilling the Buddha’s intention.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks who are resolved through faith, namely, the monk Vakkalin.
Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a thousand monks and performing various miracles, arrived at the city of Sūrpāraka.
The Blessed One reflected: "If I enter through one gate..."
"Others will think otherwise; what if I were to enter by means of my supernatural power (ṛddhi) alone?
Thereupon, he descended from the sky above into the middle of the city of Sūrpāraka by means of his supernatural power.

Then the king, the lord of Sūrpāraka, the venerable Pūrṇa, Dārukarṇī, Stavakarṇī, Trapukarṇī, and those seventeen sons, each with their own retinue, as well as many hundreds of thousands of living beings, approached the place where the Blessed One was. Then the Blessed One, followed by many hundreds of thousands of living beings, proceeded toward the Candanamāla palace.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.
As that crowd of people could not see the Blessed One, they began to break down the sandalwood palace.
The Blessed One reflected: "If this sandalwood palace is destroyed..."
"There will be an obstacle to the merit of the donors.
What if I were to create this [stūpa] out of crystal?
Thereupon, the Blessed One created it out of crystal.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the intentions, latent tendencies, dispositions, and natures of that assembly, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained great distinction.
Some produced roots of merit conducive to liberation.
Some attained the stages conducive to penetration; some realized the fruit of stream-entry; and some realized the fruit of once-returning.
Some realized the fruit of non-returning;
some realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions; and some generated the resolve for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.

Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.

Then Dārukarṇī, Stavakarṇī, and Trapukarṇī, having prepared excellent hard and soft foods and arranged the seats, announced the time to the Blessed One by messenger, saying: "It is time; the meal is ready. May the Blessed One now consider it the right moment. At that time, the two Nāga kings Kṛṣṇa and Gautamaka were dwelling in the great ocean.
The two of them reflected: "The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma in the city of Sūrpāraka.
Let us go; we shall hear the Dharma.
Thereupon, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred nāgas and having summoned five hundred rivers, they set out for the city of Sūrpāraka.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of non-forgetfulness.
The Blessed One reflected: "If these two Naga kings, Kṛṣṇa and Gautama, were to come to the city of Sūrpāraka, they would render it uninhabitable."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Accept, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this urgent alms-food from the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Maudgalyāyana, there are five kinds of urgent alms-food for me."
Which five?
The newcomer, the one about to depart, the sick, the attendant of the sick, and the steward of the requisites.
In this context, however, the Blessed One is concerned with the steward of the requisites.

Then the Blessed One, accompanied by Maudgalyāyana, approached the two nāga kings, Kṛṣṇa and Gautamaka. They said, "Pay heed, O lords of nāgas; the city of Sūrpāraka will no longer be our domain. They replied, "Venerable sir, it was through such favor that we came here—that we were not able to cause even the slightest harm to a creature as small as a grain of rice or an ant, much less to the inhabitants of the city of Sūrpāraka."

Then the Blessed One taught such a Dharma to the two Naga kings, Kṛṣṇa and Gautamaka, that upon hearing it, they went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and undertook the precepts.
The Blessed One began to perform his meal.
Each individual nāga thought, "O, would that the Blessed One might drink my water!
The Blessed One reflected, "If I were to drink the water of only one [nāga],"...
"These will undergo change;
a strategic arrangement must be made.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Go, Maudgalyāyana!"
"Bring a bowlful of water from where the confluence of five hundred rivers occurs.
"Very well, Venerable Sir," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One, and having gone to the place where the five hundred rivers converge, he took a bowlful of water.
Having approached, he presented a bowl full of water to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One took it and consumed it.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reflected: "The Blessed One has previously said that these two are performers of difficult deeds."
For, monks, a son’s mother and father are his nourishers, sustainers, and rearers; they are the givers of milk and the showers of the wondrous Jambudvīpa.
Even if a son were to attend upon his mother with one part and his father with the second for a full hundred years, [he could not repay them].

Or, even if one were to establish them in various forms of sovereignty and dominion over this great earth— such as jewels, pearls, beryl, conch-shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, emeralds, musāragalva, rubies, and right-spiraling shells— even by such means,
parents would not have been fully repaid or benefited by their son.

But he who causes his faithless mother and father to undertake, train in, enter into, and be established in the perfection of faith; who [causes them to be established] in the perfection of ethical discipline if they are immoral, and in the perfection of generosity if they are stingy—
To the extent that one encourages, disciplines, settles, and establishes one who lacks wisdom in the perfection of wisdom—
by this much, a son would have performed his duty or rendered service to his parents;
yet, I have not rendered any such service to my mother.
"I shall investigate where my mother has been reborn," he thought. As he began to investigate, he saw that she had been reborn in the world-system Marīcika.
He reflected: "Whose disciple is she to be?"
He beheld the Blessed One. This thought occurred to him: "We have come here from afar;

what if I were to inform the Blessed One of this matter? He then addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it was previously said by the Blessed One: 'O monks, parents are indeed doers of what is difficult for their son...'"
"Regarding my parents:
my mother has been reborn in the world-system Marīcika,
and she is to be converted by the Blessed One."
"Therefore, may the Blessed One deign to discipline her out of compassion.
The Blessed One said, "Maudgalyāyana,
by whose miraculous power shall we go?"
“Blessed One, by my power.
Thereupon, the Blessed One and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana set out, placing their feet upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
On the seventh day, they arrived at the world-system Marīcika.
That noble maiden saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana from afar.
Upon seeing him, she approached him with great agitation and said, "At last, I see my son!
Then the crowd of people said, "Venerable sir, this is an old man who has gone forth."
"And what of this girl?
How can she be his mother?
The venerable Maudgalyāyana replied, "Sirs," and spoke further.
"These aggregates (skandhas) of mine have grown from others;
therefore, she is my mother.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of that noble maiden, gave her a Dharma teaching such that she penetrated the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard it, that noble maiden shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, with the thunderbolt of knowledge, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, she uttered three exclamations as before, until she was established among gods and humans. And she said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, corrupted by many faults, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and I have attained the path to Nirvāṇa.
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure and utterly stainless eye, free from all defects;
I have reached the lovely state cherished by the Noble Ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering. (17)
O Sage, worshipped by Daityas, humans, and gods in this world; free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
whose appearance is so difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes—today your vision has become fruitful.
"I have transgressed, Venerable Sir; I have indeed transgressed.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
Please accept me as a laywoman from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge with deep faith."
"May the Blessed One, together with the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, accept my alms-food today.
The Blessed One accepted the request of that noble maiden by remaining silent.
Then, that noble maiden [saw] that the Blessed One and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana were seated comfortably.
Having understood this, she satisfied and served the Blessed One with her own hands with pure and exquisite solid and soft foods.
When she knew that the Blessed One had finished eating, she removed his hand from the bowl, took a lower seat,
and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One taught the Dharma to her.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was the bowl-bearer for the Blessed One, presented the bowl.
The Blessed One said to him, "Maudgalyāyana, let us go."
“Let us go, Blessed One.
“By whose supernatural power?
“By that of the Tathāgata, the Blessed One.”
"If it is so, then attend to the Jeta Grove.
We have arrived, Blessed One; we have arrived.
Then Maudgalyāyana, his mind overcome with wonder, said: "What indeed, Blessed One, is this supernatural power?"
"O Maudgalyāyana, [the Dharma] is as swift as thought!
Venerable sir, I did not realize that the Buddha-dharmas were so profound, so exceedingly profound. Had I realized it,"
"Even when my body was ground to pieces bit by bit, my mind did not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
what shall I do now that my fuel is burnt?"

Then, monks, having conceived a doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Pūrṇa, by which he was born into a family that is wealthy, of great fortune, and of great enjoyments?
What karma was performed by which he was reborn in the womb of a slave woman?"
"And having gone forth, did he realize arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements?

The Blessed One said: "Monks, deeds were done and accumulated by the monk Pūrṇa; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Deeds were done and accumulated by Pūrṇa."
"Who else shall experience [the result]? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element."
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do actions performed and accumulated— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (19)

033.009. Monks, in the past, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī.
He had gone forth into this teaching and performed the service of the Dharma for the Saṅgha of the Tripiṭaka.
Eventually, it was the turn of a certain Arhat to take charge of the monastery's maintenance.
He began to sweep the monastery,
but the wind carried the refuse here and there.
He reflected: "Let it be for now until the wind subsides.

Then, seeing that the monastery had not been swept by the attendant, he, in a state of intense agitation, uttered these harsh words: "Whose slave-son is this that takes turns with the monastic requisites?"
That Arhat heard it. He reflected: "This man is possessed by the outbursts of passion;
let him be for now."
"Later, I shall inform him.
When his outburst of passion had subsided, he approached him and said, "Do you know who I am?
He replied, "I know; you are one who has gone forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, and I am as well."
He said, "Even if it is so, nevertheless, that which was to be practiced by me after going forth has been done; I am now bound by all fetters.
You have uttered harsh words of speech. Confess your transgression as a transgression."

"May this karma indeed reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total termination. Thus he confessed his transgression as a transgression. Because of that, he was reborn in hell and had to become the son of a slave girl.
He was not reborn in hell;
however, for five hundred births he was reborn in the womb of a slave woman,
even until this present final existence, when he was again reborn in the womb of a slave woman.
Because he rendered service to the Saṅgha,
he was born into a family that is wealthy, affluent, and of great possessions.
Because he recited, studied, and mastered the skill regarding the aggregates (skandha) there, [he has attained this result].
Having gone forth in my teaching, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for actions that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the second story, the Pūrṇāvadāna, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 3 ********** 034.001. The Third Story of Maitreya. 034.002.
When King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, had the ferry-landing constructed for his parents, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī then had a ferry-landing constructed for the sake of the Blessed One.
The nāgas reflected: "Our bodies have fallen into a state of ruin; what if we were to help the Blessed One cross the river Gaṅgā by means of a bridge of hoods?
They then constructed a bridge of hoods.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "O monks, whoever among you is able to go from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī [and visit] Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, the king of Magadha..."
To cross the river Gaṅgā by means of the boat-bridge,
let him cross it by that;
or rather, O monks, let whoever [desires to do so] among the Licchavis of Vaiśālī cross by means of the boat-bridge.
He replied to him: "I too shall cross the river Gaṅgā together with the venerable monk Ānanda by means of the bridge of the nāgas' hoods.
There, some have already crossed by means of the bridge of boats belonging to King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha."
Some of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī crossed by means of a boat-bridge;
the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, crossed by means of a bridge of the hoods of nāgas.
Then, at that time, a certain lay follower spoke this verse:
Those who cross the ocean lake by building a bridge and abandoning the small ponds—those people have indeed constructed a raft; they are wise people who have reached the further shore. //1//
The Blessed One, the Buddha, has crossed over and stands on dry land as a brahmin;
here the monks, his disciples, are bathing and binding together rafts.
"What would one do with a well if there were water everywhere?
Having cut off the root of craving here, whom would one go about seeking? (3) Thus it was said.
The Blessed One saw a certain area of ground that was exceedingly high.
Having seen it, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you wish to see that which is a thousand fathoms high, sixteen fathoms in width, and variegated with various jewels?"
Blessed One, this is the time; Sugata, this is the occasion, that the Blessed One should raise up this sacrificial pillar.
The monks looked on.
