Then the Blessed One touched the earth with his hand—which was marked with the wheel, the auspicious svastika, and the nandyāvarta; webbed; produced from hundreds of manifold merits; and capable of providing comfort to those who are afraid.
The nāgas reflected: "For what reason has the Blessed One touched the earth?"
"As long as you desire to see, so long shall you behold it. Then they raised it up.
The monks began to look at the sacrificial post.
The venerable Bhaddāli, too, was free from anxiety as he sewed his rag-robe.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, take note of the height and circumference of this sacrificial post;
it is about to disappear."
He vanished.
The monks asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, look! The monks are seeing the sacrificial pillar.
The venerable Bhaddāli, however, remained unconcerned and continued sewing his rag-robe.
Is it because he is free from passion, or because he has been previously attended upon?
If it is because he is free from passion,
there are others as well who are free from passion.
"Is it because they have previously attended upon him? Where and by whom was he attended upon?
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is both because they are free from passion and because they have previously attended upon him."
"Where did he perform his service?
"Monks, in the past there was a king named Praṇāda, a friend of Śakra, the lord of the gods.
He was childless and longing for a son; resting his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought: 'I possess a vast accumulation of wealth, yet I am without a son.'"
"Upon my passing, the royal lineage will be extinguished.
Then Śakra saw him and asked, "Friend,
why do you sit there lost in thought with your cheek resting on your hand?"
He said, "Kauśika, I have accumulated much wealth and yet I am childless;
upon my passing, the royal lineage will come to an end."
Śakra said: "Friend, do not remain consumed by anxiety.
If there should be some son of the gods subject to the law of passing away,"
"I shall cause you to accept the state of being my son.
Now, it is the natural law that for a son of the gods who is subject to passing away, five portents appear: his unstained garments become soiled, and his unfaded garlands wither.
A foul odor issues from his mouth,
sweat flows profusely from both armpits,
and he finds no stability upon his own seat.
Then, five omens appeared to a certain son of the gods.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, said to him, "Friend,
take rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of King Praṇāda."
He said, "Kauśika is a source of negligence.
For kings, Kauśika, are prone to many sins.
Lest I, having ruled the kingdom unrighteously, should become destined for hell."
Śakra said: "Friend, I shall remind you.
The gods of Kauśala are heedless and full of sensual pleasure."
"It is so, friend.
Nevertheless, I shall remind you:
by him, rebirth was taken in the womb of the chief queen of King Praṇāda."
On the very day she conceived,
a great cry was raised by a vast multitude of people.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-hued, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, joined eyebrows, and a prominent nose.
His kinsmen, having gathered together, established his name, asking, "What shall be the name of this boy?
The kinsmen said, "On the very day this boy descended into his mother's womb..."
On that very day, a great multitude of people raised a shout. On the very day he was born, a great multitude of people raised a shout. Therefore, let the boy's name be Mahāpraṇāda (Great Shout).
The name Mahāpraṇāda was established for him.

The boy Mahāpraṇāda was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to cleanse him of impurities, two to suckle him with milk, and two to provide him with other specialized requisites.
He was raised and nurtured by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other most excellent and refined provisions.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had become a youth, he was introduced to writing;

then to arithmetic, calculation, finger-reckoning, subtraction, depositing, and placing; and to the examination of commodities, the examination of timber, the examination of gems, the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, and the examination of princes.
He became one who was proficient in the eight examinations, an eloquent speaker, quick in his movements, and wise.

Whatever various arts and crafts there were belonging to those Kṣatriya kings— anointed on the head— who had attained sovereignty, power, and valor over their territories and ruled after conquering the great circle of the earth, [he mastered them all].

Namely: in the training of elephants, on horseback, in chariots, with arrows, with the bow, in marching forward, in retreating, in handling the goad, in handling the lasso, in handling the javelin, in binding with the staff, in binding the feet, in binding the topknot, in shooting from a distance, in shooting at vital points, and in shooting without missing; he became an expert in these five areas, possessing firmness in striking.
It is indeed the nature of things that the name of a son is not yet known as long as his father lives. At a later time, King Praṇāda passed away,
and Mahāpraṇāda was established in the kingdom.
After he had ruled the kingdom righteously for some time, he began to rule it unrighteously.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said to him:
"My friend, I was the one who persuaded you to take up the kingship of Praṇāda."
"Do not rule the kingdom unrighteously;
do not become one destined for hell.
Having ruled the kingdom righteously for some time, he again began to rule the kingdom unrighteously.
A second time Śakra said: "O noble one, I have already persuaded you to accept the status of being King Praṇāda’s son.
Do not exercise sovereignty through unrighteousness."
"Lest you become destined for hell.
He replied, "Kauśika, we are kings who are heedless; being full of pleasure, we forget in an instant."
"Please establish some sign of ours,
so that upon seeing it, we may give gifts and perform meritorious deeds."
"And it is not possible to perform a meritorious act without a cause.
Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave an order to the divine son Viśvakarman: "Go, Viśvakarman, to the residence of King Mahāpraṇāda and construct a celestial circular arena."
"And erect a sacrificial pillar—
one thousand fathoms in height and sixteen spans in girth, variegated with various jewels and made entirely of gold.
Then, by the divine son Viśvakarman, a celestial circular arena was fashioned in the palace of King Mahāpraṇāda, and the sacrificial pillar was erected.
036.012. A divine pavilion, made entirely of gold and variegated with various jewels, rose up a thousand fathoms in height.
Then, by the great proclamation of King [Mahāpraṇāda], a hall for giving was constructed.
His maternal uncle, named Aśoka, was appointed as the attendant of the sacrificial pillar (yūpa).

Then, everyone living in Jambudvīpa, intent on seeing the sacrificial pillar, arrived and, having eaten, gazed upon the pillar and ceased performing their own duties. Consequently, the activities of agriculture were completely cut off.
The king’s taxes and revenues were not coming in.
The ministers brought only a small amount of revenue to him.
King Mahāpraṇāda asked: "Sirs, why is this?"
"Why have so few taxes and levies been brought in?
"Your Majesty, the multitude of people living in Jambudvīpa come here, eat, and behold the sacrificial pillar,
but they do not perform their own religious duties."
"Agricultural activities have been cut off;
the king’s taxes and revenues do not arise.
The king said, "Let the hall of giving be cut off!"
They were cut down by them.
Then that multitude of people, having taken their own provisions and eaten, remained gazing at the sacrificial post and did not perform their own ritual duties.
036.021. Agricultural activities have been completely cut off;
nevertheless, the taxes and revenues do not arise.
The king asks: "Sirs, why is this?"
"The halls of charity have been abolished;
now, taxes and revenues do not arise.
The ministers said, "Your Majesty,"
The multitude of people, having taken their own provisions and eaten, stood gazing at the sacrificial post and did not perform their own duties;
the activities of agriculture were completely abandoned.
Since no taxes or revenues were being collected, King Mahāpraṇāda gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds, and then had that sacrificial pillar floated away in the river Gaṅgā.
What do you think, monks? He who was the maternal uncle of Mahāpraṇāda, named Aśoka—
This very person is that monk Bhaddāli;
it was there that he previously attended upon him.
"Venerable sir, where will that sacrificial pillar go to its dissolution?
"Monks, in a future time there will be humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years.

Among those humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will be a king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four quarters, righteous, a king of Dharma, endowed with the seven treasures."
He shall possess these seven kinds of precious jewels, namely:
the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh.
Furthermore, he shall have a full thousand sons who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

He will dwell having completely conquered this entire earth, bounded by the ocean—free from thorns, free from enemies, without oppression, without punishment, and without weapons—by means of righteousness and moral conduct.
King Śaṅkha will have a brahmin priest named Brahmāyus.
He will have a wife named Brahmavatī.
Pulsing with a portion of Maitreya, she will give birth to a son named Maitreya.
The young Brahmin Brahmāyus will teach the Vedic mantras to eight hundred young Brahmins;
he will then bestow those young men upon Maitreya.
The young brahmin Maitreya will cause eighty thousand young brahmins to recite the Vedic mantras.
Then the four Great Kings, who possess four great treasures—
Piṅgala among the Kaliṅgas and Pāṇḍuka at Mithilā— [will appear].
Elāpatra is in Gāndhāra, and Śaṅkha is in the city of Vārāṇasī. //4//
And taking this sacrificial post, they will present it to King Śaṅkha;
King Śaṅkha, in turn, will bestow it upon the brahmin Brahmāyus;
and the brahmin Brahmāyus will bestow it upon the young Māṇava Maitreya.
The young brahmin Maitreya will also give [his share] to those young brahmins.
Then those young brahmins, having cut that sacrificial post into pieces and distributed them, will divide it among themselves.
Thereupon, the young brahmin Maitreya, seeing the impermanence of that sacrificial post, will, through that very sense of spiritual urgency, take refuge in the forest.
On the very day he takes refuge in the forest,
on that same day, having been suffused with the portion of Maitreya, he will attain unsurpassed knowledge.
His designation shall be "Maitreya, the Perfectly Awakened One."
On the very day that Maitreya, the perfectly awakened one, shall attain unsurpassed knowledge,
on that same day the seven treasures of King Śaṅkha will disappear.
King Śaṅkha, too, surrounded by a retinue of eighty thousand subordinate kings, will follow Maitreya, the perfectly awakened one, into the homeless life.
Furthermore, his jewel of a woman named Viśākhā,

accompanied by a retinue of eighty thousand women, will also follow Maitreya, the perfectly enlightened one, into the homeless life. Then, Maitreya, the perfectly enlightened one, surrounded by a retinue of eight hundred million bhikṣus, will proceed to the mountain Gurupādaka.
There, where the uncorrupted heap of bones of the monk Kāśyapa remains,

the mountain Gurupādaka will open a fissure for Maitreya, the perfectly awakened Buddha; through which Maitreya, the perfectly awakened Buddha, [will see] the uncorrupted heap of bones of the monk Kāśyapa.

Taking him by the right hand and placing him upon his left hand, he will thus teach the Dharma to the disciples: "O monks, this disciple named Kāśyapa was designated as the foremost among those of few desires, those who are contented, and those who advocate the ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa), belonging to that Teacher named Śākyamuni who appeared in the world when the lifespan of beings was one hundred years."
"Since the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, this [Mahākāśyapa] has performed the communal recitation of the teaching.
Upon seeing this, they will be moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking: "How is it that with such a physical form, he has attained such a multitude of virtues?
Through that very sense of urgency, they will realize arhatship.
There will be ninety-six koṭis of arhats who have realized the ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa). And when they attain a state of spiritual urgency (saṃvega),
at that moment this sacrificial pillar (yūpa) shall go to its destruction.
"Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the simultaneous appearance of two jewels in the world?
The Blessed One said, "By the power of their vows.
"In what regard, Blessed One, were those vows made?"

037.029. Monks, in the past, in times gone by, in the Middle Country there was a king named Vāsava who ruled over a realm that was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
037.030. His trees were always in bloom and fruit;
the god sent down showers of rain properly from time to time.
There is an extraordinary abundance of crops.
In the northern region, a king named Dhanasaṃmata rules a kingdom that is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
Even his trees always bear flowers and fruit.
"The King, from time to time, bestows showers of rain correctly;
therefore, there is an abundance of crops.
Then, at another time, a son was born to King Vāsava, with a crest inlaid with jewels.
After performing an extensive birth ceremony for him, the name Ratnaśikhin was established.
At a later time, having become disillusioned by the sight of the aged, the sick, and the dead, he retired to the forest.
On the very day he retired to the forest, on that same day, he attained unsurpassed knowledge.

The name Ratnaśikhin, the Perfectly Awakened One, arose for him. Then, at another time, King Dhanasammata, having ascended to the upper terrace of his palace, was seated surrounded by a host of ministers.
He addressed the ministers: "Sirs," he said.
The kingdom of some other king as well was likewise prosperous and flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people and inhabitants;
the trees were always in bloom and fruit,
and the god sent down showers of rain properly from time to time.
"Is there such an abundance of crops as we have here?
Merchants from the Middle Country, having taken their wares, traveled to the Northern Region.
They said, "Your Majesty, in the Middle Country there is a king named Vāsava."
Upon hearing this, King Dhanasammata was immediately seized with indignation.
Overcome by this indignation, he addressed his ministers: "Gentlemen, equip the fourfold army;
we shall inflict a crushing defeat upon his kingdom."

Then King Dhanasaṃmata, having equipped a fourfold army— consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry— arrived in the Middle Country and stationed himself on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā. King Vāsava heard that King Dhanasaṃmata, having equipped a fourfold army— consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry— had arrived in the Middle Country and was stationed on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having heard this, he too mobilized a fourfold army—consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry—and stationed it on the northern bank of the Ganges.
Then, the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, knowing that the time for their conversion had arrived, took up residence for the night on the bank of the river Ganges.
The Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin then gave rise to a worldly thought.
It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, give rise to a worldly thought,
at that moment the gods, such as Śakra and Brahmā, perceive the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
Then the gods, including Śakra and Brahmā, approached the Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaśikhin.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, they sat down to one side. By the power of their physical splendor, a great and magnificent radiance was produced. It was seen by King Dhanasammata.
Having seen it, he asked his ministers again: "Sirs, what is this great and magnificent radiance in King Vāsava’s realm?
They replied: "Your Majesty, it is a great and magnificent radiance in King Vāsava’s realm."
They said, "Your Majesty,
in the realm of King Vāsava, a perfectly awakened Buddha named Ratnaśikhin has appeared;
Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods approach him in order to see him."
"By that very [act], he has become possessed of a sublime radiance; he is one of great supernatural power and great majesty. This is his majestic influence."
King Dhanasaṃmata said: "Sirs,
in whose realm has such a field of merit consisting of two-legged beings arisen,
whom even the gods such as Śakra and Brahmā approach in order to behold?"
"What kind of harm shall I do to him?
He then dispatched a messenger to him, saying:
"Friend, come!"
"I shall not do anything for you. "You are one of great merit and power,
since within your realm dwells this Jewel-Crested One, the Perfectly Awakened One, a field of merit for bipeds."
"The gods, beginning with Śakra and Brahmā, approach to see you;
however, I shall depart after giving you an embrace around the neck,
so that there may be mutual joy in our hearts."

King Vāsava did not place his trust [in anyone]. He approached the presence of the perfectly enlightened Ratnaśikhin; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly enlightened Ratnaśikhin, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Vāsava said this to the Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaśikhin: "Venerable Sir, King Dhanasaṃmata has sent me this message: 'Dear friend, I will do nothing for you;
having embraced you limb to limb, I shall depart.'"
"In this way, there will be mutual mental joy between us.
Therefore, how should I proceed?
Ratnaśikhī, the perfectly awakened Buddha, said: "Go, Great King."
"It will be auspicious.
Blessed One, should I prostrate at his feet?
"Great King, kings are indeed preeminent in power."
039.004. [The king] should prostrate himself.
039.005. Then King Vāsava, having bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, rose from his seat and departed.
039.006. He approached King Dhanasaṃmata.
Having approached, he fell at the feet of King Dhanasammata.
Then, King Dhanasammata embraced him around the neck, inspired confidence in him, and sent him on his way.
Then King Vāsava approached the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Vāsava said this to the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin: "Venerable sir, for whose feet do all kings prostrate?"
Of the king, the great wheel-turning monarch.

Then King Vāsava, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, the perfectly awakened one, he addressed the perfectly awakened Ratnaśikhin: "May you grant me your consent."

"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept tomorrow's meal at my home. Then King Vāsava, having prepared pure and exquisite hard and soft foods that very night, rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, set out water jars, and [waited] for the Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaśikhin.
He announces the time by means of a messenger: "It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is prepared; may the Blessed One do as he deems it the right time."

Then, in the forenoon, the perfectly enlightened Ratnaśikhin, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached King Vāsava.
Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then King Vāsava, perceiving that the perfectly enlightened Ratnaśikhin was comfortably seated, personally satisfied him with pure and excellent food, both solid and soft.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, with pure hard and soft foods, and having perceived that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl,
he prostrated at his feet and began to make a formal aspiration: "By this root of merit, O Venerable One, may I become a universal monarch (cakravartin)!"
Immediately thereafter, a conch shell was blown.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaśikhin, said this to King Vāsava: "Great King, when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, you shall become a universal monarch named Śaṅkha.
Thereupon, a loud sound, a great clamor, arose.
039.025. King Dhanasaṃmata, hearing the tumultuous noise, asked his ministers: "Sirs, why is this tumultuous noise being heard within the realm of King Vāsava?

They approached him and reported: "Your Majesty, because the Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaśikhin, has prophesied that King Vāsava will attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), the multitude of people is joyful, satisfied, and delighted."
Because of that, a tumultuous noise arose.
Then King Dhanasammata approached where the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin was;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Dhanasaṃmata said this to the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin: "Venerable sir, for whom do all the wheel-turning monarchs prostrate at the feet?
"For the Tathāgata, O Great King, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then King Dhanasaṃmata rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and [approached] where Ratnaśikhin was.

Having bowed with palms joined toward the Perfectly Enlightened One, he said this to the Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnaśikhin: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.
The Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnaśikhin accepted the invitation from King Dhanasammata by remaining silent.

Then King Dhanasammata, understanding that the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin had given his consent by remaining silent, bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin and departed from the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin.
Then King Dhanasammata, having prepared pure and exquisite hard and soft foods that very night, rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, and set out water jars;
he then sent a messenger to inform the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin of the time: "It is time, Blessed One."
"The meal is prepared;
may the Blessed One now do as he deems timely.

Then, in the forenoon, the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to where Dhanasaṃmata was.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.

Then King Dhanasammata, perceiving that the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin and the community of monks headed by him were comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent solid and soft foods.

In many ways, having satisfied and served the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin with his own hands with pure and exquisite foods, both solid and soft, and having perceived that he had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, [the king] prostrated at his feet, pervaded this entire world with a portion of loving-kindness, and began to make a formal aspiration: "By this..."
"By this root of merit, may I become a Teacher in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha.

The Samyaksambuddha Ratnaśikhin said: "Great King, when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, you will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha named Maitreya. By the power of that vow, two jewels shall appear in the world."
The Blessed One said this.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus ends the third [tale], the Maitreya-avadāna, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 4 ********** 041.001. The Story of the Brahmin’s Daughter (Brāhmaṇadārikāvadāna).
041.002. The Blessed One arrived at Nyagrodhikā.
Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Nyagrodhikā for alms.
A young Brahmin girl from Kapilavastu was settled in Nyagrodhikā.
That Brahmin girl saw the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics.

Adorned with a fathom-wide halo, possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides— upon seeing him, this thought occurred to her: "This is that Blessed One, the joy of the Śākya clan,
who has renounced sovereignty from a lineage of universal monarchs, abandoned his vast harem and his abundant treasuries and granaries, and having gone forth, now wanders for alms."
"If she were to accept a portion of groats as alms from me, I would give it to her.
Then the Blessed One, knowing her thought with his own mind, held out his bowl and said, "Sister, if it has been relinquished by you,"
"Let it be poured into this bowl.
Thereupon, her faith increased all the more.
Realizing, "The Blessed One knows my mind with his own mind," she, with intense faith, gave the offering of barley meal to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile,

at that moment rays of light— blue, yellow, red, and white, possessing the colors of emerald, ruby, diamond, beryl, musāragalva, coral, red pearl, right-spiraling conch, stone, agate, gold, and silver— emanate forth.
Emitting rays from his mouth, some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward—

Having gone to those hells— Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, Mahāpadma, and all the hells ending with Avīci—
they descend into the hot hells having become cool.
In those cold hells, they fall down having become warm;
by that, at that very moment, the particular causes of suffering for those beings are allayed.
It occurs to them: "Have we indeed passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth a manifested form (*nirmita*).
Upon seeing that manifestation, it occurs to them: "Indeed, venerable sirs, we have not passed away from here."
Nor were they reborn elsewhere.
Having developed serene faith in that emanation, they exhausted the karma to be experienced in hell and took rebirth among gods and humans,
where they became vessels for the truths.
Those that go upward, having reached the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods,
as well as the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahman, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, and the Ābhāsvara gods—

Having gone to the gods of the Limited Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue, and Universal Virtue realms; the Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Vast Fruit realms; and the Unclouded, Without-Heat, Clear-Sighted, and Beautiful-to-See realms, up to the Akaniṣṭha realm, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
And they speak these two verses:
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha! Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket. //1//
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. (2)
Then those rays of light, having circled the trichiliocosm— the great three-thousandfold world system— followed closely behind the Blessed One as he went.
If the Blessed One wished to prophesy regarding the past,
they vanished behind him.
If he wishes to prophesy regarding the future,
they disappear from the front.
If he wishes to prophesy regarding rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human,
they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
the light disappears into his big toe.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among human beings, [the light disappears into his knee].
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch,
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartirājya*), they disappear into the palm of his right hand. If he intends to prophesy the enlightenment of a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*), [they disappear into his left ear].
If he intends to prophesy individual enlightenment,
they disappear into the circle of hair between his eyebrows.
If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
they disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the circle of hair between his eyebrows.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"A multitude of rays, variegated with thousands of diverse colors, has issued forth from within your mouth."
By him all directions were illuminated on every side, just like the sun as it rises. //3//
And he spoke these two verses:
“Free from rebirth, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme cause for the world.
The Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a reason. (4)

O steadfast one, O Jina-lord of Śramaṇas, having yourself realized this at that time through your own wisdom, dispel the arisen doubt with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words, O bull among sages, for the sake of those listeners who long for it. (5)
"042.025. The Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause.
042.027. Those multitudes of people desire to hear the reason for which the Wise Ones display a smile. (6) Thus [it was said]. The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda; it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. Ānanda, have you seen that brahmin girl?"
"By whom, having conceived a state of serene faith, was this alms of roasted flour given to me?
"I saw her, Venerable Sir.
"Ānanda, that brahmin girl, by this root of merit, shall not go to an evil rebirth for thirteen eons."

"Rather, after passing through successive births among gods and humans, in his final existence, his final dwelling, his final physical frame, and his final acquisition of a self-body, he will become a Pratyekabuddha named Suparṇihita. A report spread all around: "A certain Brahmin girl, having conceived faith, offered a portion of barley-meal as alms to the Blessed One."
She was prophesied by the Blessed One for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
Her husband had gone to the forest for the sake of gathering flowers and fuel.
He heard that his wife had offered a gift of groats to the śramaṇa Gautama.

And having heard that she had been prophesied by the ascetic Gautama for solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi), he became filled with indignation once more and approached the Blessed One. After exchanging various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: "Has the venerable Gautama come to our place?"
"O Brāhmaṇa,
is it true that my wife offered you a portion of barley meal as alms,
and that she was prophesied by you for Pratyekabuddhahood?"
"It is true, O Brahmin Gautama! You renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch and went forth into homelessness.
How is it that you now, for the sake of a portion of barley meal as alms, knowingly speak a falsehood?"
"O Kāśyapa, who would have faith that such a fruit comes from a seed of this magnitude?
Therefore, Brahmin, I shall ask you a question; answer it exactly as you see fit."
"What do you think, brahmin? Have you ever seen any wonderful and marvelous phenomenon?
"Let alone other wonderful and marvelous phenomena, O Gautama;
there is a wonderful and marvelous phenomenon that I have seen right here in this very Nyagrodhika grove."
Listen to that first, O Gautama. In this Nyagrodhikā, to the east, there is a banyan tree after which this place is named;
beneath it, five hundred carts stand without being joined together, not crowding one another.
"What is the size of that banyan tree's fruit? How large is it?
"About the size of a field."
"No, Master Gautama; it is not the size of a blade of *kiliñja* grass,
nor the size of an oil-press wheel,
nor the size of a cartwheel."
The size of a grain-measure basket;
the size of a *bilva* fruit;
the size of a *kapittha* fruit?
"No, Master Gautama, it is not even the size of four mustard seeds.
Who would believe you that such a great tree has grown from a seed of such a minute dimension?
"Whether Master Gautama believes me or not," [he replied].
"This field is not visible [to me].
However, O Gautama, the soil is undamaged, smooth, sweet, and rich; the seed is fresh and well-sown;
and from time to time, the rain god sends down showers."
By that [merit], this great nyagrodha tree was produced.
Then, when this had occurred, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Just as [a seed grows] in a field, you are here before my very eyes, O twice-born one."
Thus, the Tathāgatas indeed have direct perception regarding the ripening of karma. //7//
"O Brahmin, just as you have seen this small seed and yet such a very great tree, so too, O Brahmin, have I seen this: a small seed and yet a vast abundance. (8)
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue from his mouth, covered his entire facial circle up to the hairline;

and he said to that brahmin: "What do you think, brahmin? Would one who, having extended his tongue from his mouth, covers his entire facial circle, ever knowingly speak a falsehood even for the sake of a hundred thousand universal monarchies?"
"No, O Gautama.
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"May my tongue here indeed be a speaker of falsehood, rather than one that speaks with straightforwardness and truth."
Therefore, O brahmin, you should understand that this is not so; for I am indeed a Tathāgata. (9)
Then that brahmin became full of faith.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, gave him a teaching of the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard it, the brahmin shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up in twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry: "I have transcended, O Venerable One."
"I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
Please accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge with deep faith.
Then that brahmin, having rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, rose from his seat, and departed.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
the monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the fourth story, the Story of the Brahmin’s Daughter, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 5 ********** 045.001. The Story of the Brahmin Stuti.
045.002. Now the Blessed One arrived at Hastināpura.

A certain brahmin, seeing from afar the Blessed One adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain, auspicious on all sides, approached the Blessed One and began to praise him with verses:
Golden-hued, pleasing to the eye, a source of joy, endowed with all virtues—the god beyond gods, the charioteer who tames men—you have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of existence. Thus.
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile,
as described previously, [the rays] eventually disappear into the *ūrṇā* between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
“A multitude of rays, variegated with thousands of diverse colors, has issued from within your mouth;
by it the quarters of the world have been illuminated on all sides, just as by the rising sun. (2)
And he spoke this verse:
"Free from rebirth, having abandoned dejection and pride, the Buddhas have become the supreme cause for the world.
The Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile—white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk—without a reason. (3)

O steadfast one, O Conqueror of Sages, having yourself realized that at this moment through your own wisdom, dispel with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words the doubt that has arisen in those listeners, O Lord of Jinas, who long for it. (4)
045.025. The Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, whose steadfastness is like that of the king of mountains rising from the salt ocean, do not display a smile without cause.
045.027. Those multitudes of people long to hear the reason for which the Wise Ones display a smile. (5) Thus it was said.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Ānanda, did you see that brahmin by whom the Tathāgata was praised with a verse?"
"I have seen him, Venerable One.
By this root of merit, he will not go to a state of ruin for twenty kalpas.

However, after passing through the cycle of existence among gods and humans, in his final dwelling, his final physical form, and his final acquisition of a self-body, he will become a Pratyekabuddha named Stavārha."

The monks, having fallen into doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Behold, Venerable Sir, how this brahmin praised the Blessed One with a single verse, and the Blessed One has prophesied his attainment of pratyekabodhi.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now."
Listen to this: how in the past he praised me with a single verse, and I established him in five excellent villages. 046.006. Listen to that!
Pay close and careful attention; I shall speak.

046.008. Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people. 046.009. He was exceedingly fond of poets. In Vārāṇasī there was a certain brahmin who was a poet.
The brahmin’s wife said to him, “Brahmin, it is the cold season.
Go; by speaking some agreeable words to this king, perhaps you might obtain some protection from the cold.
He then set out.
As the king was departing mounted on the back of an elephant, the brahmin reflected: "Should I praise the king, or rather the noble elephant?
Then this thought occurred to him: "This noble elephant is dear and pleasing to all the world."
"Let the king wait for a moment;
first, I shall praise the noble elephant," he said,
and spoke this verse:
"Your body is equal in form to that of Erāvaṇa; you are endowed with beauty and excellent marks.
O great lord of elephants, you are praised as a hundred thousandfold in color and stature, possessing a truly beautiful form. (6) Thus.
Then the king, filled with faith, spoke this verse:
“That lordly elephant of mine, so beloved and pleasing, which brings joy and captivates the eyes of men—since you have spoken its descriptive words, I shall give you five excellent villages. (7)
"What do you think, monks? He who was that noble elephant at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself.
Even then, I was praised by him with this single verse."
And this one was established by me in five excellent villages.
Now, having been praised by him with a single verse,
I have also predicted his attainment of solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi).
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the fifth avadāna in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Story of the Brahmin Stuti.
********** Avadāna 6 ********** 047.001. The Avadāna of the Brahmin named Indra.
047.002. The Blessed One arrived at Śrughnā.
In Śrughnā there lived a brahmin named Indra.
Having attained beauty, youth, and learning, he boasted excessively, saying, "There is no one equal to me.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated on a seat prepared before the community of monks in a certain place, teaching the Dharma.
The brahmin named Indra heard that the ascetic Gautama had arrived at Śrughna.
This thought occurred to him: "It is said that the ascetic Gautama is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
I shall go and see whether he is more handsome than I, or not."

Having gone out, he saw the Blessed One adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides.
And having seen him, this thought occurred to him: "Even though the ascetic Gautama is more handsome than I, he is not taller.
He began to look at the Blessed One’s head, but he could not see it.
He climbed to an even higher place.
There, the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Indra: "Enough, brahmin;
you will only come to exhaustion."
If you were to ascend even to the summit of Mount Sumeru to look upon the head of the Tathāgata,
you would only experience even greater exhaustion and still not see it.
"Moreover, have you not heard that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are beings whose heads cannot be seen even by the world including the gods and asuras?
Furthermore, if you wish to see the physical proportions of the Tathāgata, there is in your house a fire-offering pit; beneath it stands a staff made of gośīrṣa sandalwood."
"Having excavated it, have it measured;
that shall be the measurement of the Tathāgata’s physical frame derived from his father and mother.
The brahmin Indra reflected: "This is a marvel for him; I have never heard of such a thing before."
"I shall go; I shall see.
Having gone with great haste, he began to dig beneath the fire-offering pit.
Everything was exactly as it had been.
He became full of faith. He reflected: "Surely the ascetic Gautama is omniscient;
I shall go to attend upon him."
Filled with serene faith, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then, the Blessed One, knowing his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, gave a Dharma teaching such that it led to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Just as the brahmin Aindra, having shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity—which had risen up with twenty peaks—realized the fruit of stream-entry;
having seen the truth, he said: "I have transcended, O Venerable One! I have transcended!"
"I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
Please accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge with my very life.
Then Indra the Brahmin, full of faith, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One: "If..."
"I would like to have a sacrificial post set up made of gośīrṣa sandalwood," he said.
The Blessed One replied, "Go, brahmin; you have my permission to set it up.
Thereupon, in a secluded and open space, he had that sacrificial post erected with great honor.
And a festival was proclaimed.
Other brahmins and householders, perceiving that it would be for the sake of establishing merit, also established family traditions.
Because the festival was proclaimed by the brahmin Indra with a sacrificial post (*yaṣṭi*), the name "Indra-festival, Indra-festival" (*indramaha*) came into being.
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to where Toyikā is.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One arrived at Toyikā.
And in that place, a brahmin was plowing with a plow.

Then he saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a walking mountain of gold.
Seeing the auspicious mountain of jewels on all sides, he reflected: "If I approach the Blessed Gautama and pay him homage,
there will be a loss of my [karmic] merit."
"If I were to go down and pay my respects,
there would be a loss of merit.
Therefore, what means might there be by which there would be neither a loss of my duty nor a loss of my merit?"
The thought occurred to him: "I shall perform my salutation while remaining right here.

In this way, there will be no neglect of my duty, nor any loss of merit. Standing right where he was with his goad-stick still held in hand, he performed the salutation, saying: "I pay homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "This moment is one that brings about the destruction of existence.
This is a brahmin.
If he possessed such right conviction, knowledge, and vision as this—'I would be saluted by him through this very approach'—"
In this way, he would have paid homage to two perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, in this very spot remains the uncorrupted collection of bone relics of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having very quickly folded his upper robe into four layers, spread it out and said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One sit upon this very seat that has been prepared;
thus this spot of earth will have been used by two Perfectly Enlightened Ones—both by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa and [by you]."
And as for what has now been said by the Blessed One:
the Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
Having sat down, he addressed the monks: "Do you wish [to hear] the time?"
"O Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to show the monks the undisturbed collection of relics of Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having seen it, the monks will develop serene confidence in their hearts."
Then the Blessed One gave rise to a worldly thought.

Now it is the nature of things that whenever the Buddha-Blessed Ones give rise to a worldly thought, at that very moment even creatures as small as ants and termites perceive the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
The nāgas reflected, "For what reason has the Blessed One generated a worldly thought?
They saw that he desired to behold the uncorrupted physical remains of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa.
Thereupon, they raised up the uncorrupted physical remains of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, take note of this sign;
it shall disappear.
It has disappeared."
King Prasenajit heard that the Blessed One had raised up the unbroken mass of relics of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa for the disciples to behold.
Upon hearing this, filled with curiosity, he set out to see it together with his harem, the princes, the ministers, the military commanders, and the people of the towns and countryside.
Virūḍhaka did likewise.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
the seer-ordained Purāṇa,
and Viśākhā, mother of Mṛgāra.

And many hundreds of thousands of living beings, filled with curiosity to see it and impelled by their former roots of merit, set out [to go]. Then, before that [stūpa] had vanished, they heard: "That collection of the bodily relics of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has not been disturbed."

Upon hearing this, they were overcome with pain and dejection, thinking, "Our journey has become in vain. Then, a certain lay follower circumambulated that spot and formed this thought in his mind: "How much merit will arise from my walking here on foot?"

Then the Blessed One, in order to produce a state of freedom from regret in that great multitude of people and having understood with his own mind the thought in the mind of that lay follower, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand gold coins of Jambūnada gold are not equal to the merit of that wise man who, with a mind full of faith, takes a single step toward the shrines of the Buddha. (1)
A certain lay follower placed a lump of clay in that spot and formed this thought: "The Blessed One has elsewhere declared that such is the merit for taking even a single step;
how much merit, then, will there be from this lump of clay?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing his mind with his own mind, spoke:
"A hundred thousand gold *niṣkas* of Jāmbūnada gold are not equal to the merit of one who, with a devout heart, places even a single lump of clay upon a stūpa of the Buddha. (2)
049.012. Then, having heard this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings performed the act of depositing lumps of clay.
Others scattered loose flowers there and formed this mental resolve: "The Blessed One has declared that such is the merit of taking a single step and of depositing a single lump of clay."
"But as for us who have offered these loose flowers, how much merit will there be?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand gold coins of Jambūnada gold are not equal to this."
Whoever, with a mind full of serene faith, should offer a heap of beautiful, loose flowers at the shrines of the Buddha; //3//
Others there constructed a flower-pavilion and formed this intention: "The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of loose flowers;
how much merit will there be for our flower-pavilion?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand loads of Jāmbūnada gold are not equal to the wise person who, with a devout heart, constructs a flower-grove at the shrines of the Buddha. (4)
Others there offered garlands of lamps and formed this thought: "The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of a monastery adorned with garlands;
how much merit will there be for our gift of lamps?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:

"A hundred thousand times ten million *koṭis* of gold from the Jāmbūnada river would not equal [the merit of] that wise man who, with a devout mind, offers a lamp at the shrines (*caityas*) of the Buddha. (5)
Others there offered a perfumed consecration.
Thus they formed this thought: "The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of a lamp;
how much merit will there be for our perfumed consecration?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing their minds with his own mind, spoke this verse:

"A hundred thousand heaps of gold, made of Jāmbūnada, would not equal [the merit of] that wise man who, with a clear and devoted heart, performs a perfumed consecration at the shrines of the Buddha. (6)
Others there raised parasols, banners, and flags.
And having thus perceived the mind with his own mind, he spoke this verse:
"One should worship him who remains [in the world] and also him who has entered final nirvāṇa."
Having equally clarified the mind here, there is no distinction in merit. (7)
050.015. For thus the Buddhas are inconceivable, and the qualities of the Buddhas are also inconceivable.
050.016. For those who have faith in the inconceivable, the maturation [of their merit] is likewise inconceivable. (8)
It is not possible to reach the further shore of the qualities of those inconceivable, unimpeded turners of the wheel of Dharma, the perfectly awakened Buddhas. //9// Thus it is said.
Then the Blessed One gave such a Dharma teaching to that great multitude of people that,
upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained a great distinction. Some generated the resolve for the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvaka-bodhi).
Some were established in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some in unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and some reached the stage of the summit (mūrdhāgata).
Some attained the summits (*mūrdhan*),
some attained the heats (*uṣmagata*), and some attained the patiences (*kṣānti*) that accord with the truths.
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry;
some realized the fruit of once-returning; and some, through the abandonment of all afflictions, realized arhatship.
For the most part, they were established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One would permit it, I would like to have a great festival celebrated here.
"I permit you, householder," [the Blessed One replied].
It was to be celebrated.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada established a great festival;
it became known by the name "the Toyikā Festival."
The Blessed One spoke thus.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Avadāna of the Brahmin named Indra.

********** Avadāna 7 ********** 051.001. Divyāvadāna 7: The Story of the City Beggar Woman (Nagarāvalambikāvadāna). 051.002. Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kośala country, arrived at Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kośala country,
had arrived at Śrāvastī and was staying there in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Having heard this, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, [the Blessed One] remained silent.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow, together with [the Saṅgha]."
"By the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Blessed One had consented through his silence, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada [approached] the Blessed One.
Having rejoiced and approved of what was spoken, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
He went toward his own residence;
having arrived there, he addressed the doorkeeper: "O man, no entry is to be granted to the heretics until the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished their meal."
"After that, I will give it to the non-Buddhist ascetics.
"Very well, Noble One," the doorkeeper replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then, during that very night, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.

Having risen early in the morning, prepared the seats, and set out the water jars, he informed the Blessed One of the time by means of a messenger: "It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems fit. Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, proceeded to where the meal was being prepared for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both solid and soft.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served the Blessed One with pure and exquisite foods both hard and soft, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, with long hair and beard and wearing coarse robes, went from one forest dwelling to the Jeta Grove. He saw that the Jeta Grove was empty.
He asked the attendant: "Where is the community of monks headed by the Buddha?"
He was informed: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has invited [the Buddha].
He reflected: "I shall go; I will partake of almsfood right there."
"I shall attend upon the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Having said this, he went to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Thereupon, the gatekeeper said to him, "Noble sir, wait!"
"You shall not enter.
For what reason?
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has given this command: 'Do not grant entrance to the heretics for the time being.'"
"Once the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished eating, I shall afterwards give [alms] to the heretics.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa reflected: "I have gained great gain; I have obtained what is well-obtained."
Thinking, "The faithful brahmins and householders do not know me as a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas;
I shall go and show favor to the wretched," he went to the park.
There he reflected, "Whom should I show favor to today?"
Meanwhile, a certain female resident of the city, afflicted with leprosy, suffering from pain, and with limbs that had become putrid, was wandering for alms. He approached her,
and she became exhausted from the effort of begging.

She saw the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, serene in body and serene in mind, with a peaceful deportment. She reflected: "Surely I must have performed a service toward such a worthy recipient of offerings, since my present state is of this nature."
"If the noble Mahākāśyapa, out of compassion for me, would accept some rinsing-water from me,
I would give it to him. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing her thought with his own mind, held out his bowl and said, "Sister, if it has been relinquished by you..."
"Let it be given into this bowl.
Then, having developed a serene mind, she gave it into that bowl;
and a fly fell in.
She began to remove it. As she did so, her finger fell into that rinsing water.
She reflected: "Even though the Noble One did not throw it away, it was out of consideration for my feelings."
"However, he will not eat it.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having understood her thought with his own mind, ate while standing right there, leaning against a certain base of a wall in her very presence.
She reflected: "Even though the Noble One has eaten out of consideration for my feelings,"
"By this food, he will not perform the function of eating.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing her thought, said this to that female scavenger: "Sister, rejoice! I shall pass the day and night on your food."
An intense joy arose within her, thinking, "The noble Mahākāśyapa has accepted my alms-food.
Then, having developed a serene mind toward the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, she passed away and was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
She was seen by Śakra, the lord of the gods, as she was offering the gruel, developing a serene mind, and passing away.
But he did not see where they had been reborn.
He began to look into the hells, but he did not see them;
nor did he see them among the animals, the hungry ghosts, humans, or the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
For thus, the range of the gods' knowledge and vision extends downward, but not upward.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he asked a question in the form of a verse:
While the great-souled Kāśyapa was indeed wandering for alms, where did that woman who gave him food find delight? (1)
The Blessed One said:
"Those gods are named Tuṣitas, where all desires are fulfilled; there that woman who gave the meal to Kāśyapa rejoices. (2)
Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Even these humans, who do not have direct perception of merit and demerit, give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Since I am established in the fruit of my own merit through the direct perception of merits, why should I not give gifts?"
"Or am I not performing meritorious deeds?
This noble Mahākāśyapa is compassionate toward the wretched, the helpless, the miserable, and the beggars.
What if I were to provide him with almsfood?"

Having understood this, he built a house in the street of the wretched. He manifested himself as a weaver of no great beauty, wearing a garment of coarse, tattered cloth, with hair disheveled and clad in a hempen shirt, his hands and feet cracked.
Even Śacī, a daughter of the gods, assumed the appearance of a common weaver's wife and began to weave the warp-thread.
And by its side, divine ambrosia was prepared and kept ready.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who is compassionate toward the wretched, the helpless, and beggars, arrived at that house in due course.
Thinking, "This man is suffering," he held out his alms-bowl as he stood at the door.
It was filled with divine ambrosia by Śakra, the lord of the gods. Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "This is divine ambrosia, and this house is vast."
"Thinking it to be highly contradictory, doubt has arisen in my heart. (3) Thus [he spoke].

For this is the nature of things: the knowledge and vision of Arhats does not function without focused attention. He began to apply his attention, and as he did so, he saw Śakra, the lord of the gods.
He said, "Kauśika,

why do you create an obstacle for a person in distress, for whom the thorn of doubt and uncertainty that has followed him for a long time has been pulled out by the roots by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One?"
"Noble Mahākāśyapa, why do you create an obstacle for these suffering people?
These men, who have not yet seen the fruits of merit for themselves, give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Since I am one who has directly witnessed the fruits of merit, why should I not give gifts?"
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
"Meritorious deeds ought to be performed, for the lack of performed merit is indeed suffering;
those who have performed meritorious deeds rejoice in this world and in the next. (4)
From that time forth, the venerable Mahākāśyapa began to enter households for alms after having reflected upon them.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, standing in the sky, filled the bowl of the venerable Mahākāśyapa with divine ambrosia as he was walking for alms;
yet the venerable Mahākāśyapa turned his bowl upside down.
053.018. Food and drink were being stolen.
053.018. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
053.019. The Blessed One said: "Therefore, I authorize that a bowl-rest should be carried."

The news spread throughout the vicinity: "A certain female dependent of the city has provided the noble Mahākāśyapa with a rinsing of water (ācāma), and she has been reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
King Prasenajit of Kośala heard that a certain female dependent of the city had provided the noble Mahākāśyapa with a rinsing of water.
"She has been reborn among the Tuṣita devas. Having heard this, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As King Prasenajit of Kosala sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and [approached] where...
Having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One consent to accept a meal from me for seven days, intended for the noble Mahākāśyapa.
The Blessed One gave his consent to King Prasenajit by remaining silent.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that his request had been accepted, departed from the presence of the Blessed One. Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, having prepared exquisite hard and soft foods for that very night, rose early in the morning, arranged seats, set out water-jars, and [went] to the Blessed One.
By messenger he announced the time: "It is time, Venerable One; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems it the right time.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to where King Prasenajit of Kośala’s meal was being served.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
And a certain wrestler stood at the edge of the assembly, his mind filled with serene faith, thinking: "This king is one who has seen for himself the fruits of merit;
established in the very results of his own meritorious deeds, he remains insatiable in merit, bestowing gifts and performing virtuous acts."

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, in many ways, having personally satisfied and served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, and perceiving that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, took a lower seat and [sat] before the Blessed One.
Seated before him to hear the Dharma,
he was then addressed by the Blessed One: "Great King,
in whose name shall I dedicate the offering?"
"Is it you, or rather, who else has produced more abundant merit than from your presence?
The king reflected: "The Blessed One partakes of almsfood from me;
who else could produce more abundant merit than from my presence? Having understood this, he said: "Blessed One, [tell me] of him by whom more abundant merit than mine has been produced."
"May the Blessed One designate the name for the dedication of merit.
Then the Blessed One designated the name for the dedication of merit for Kroḍamallaka.
In this manner, it continued for six days.
Then, on another day, the king sat with his cheek resting on his hand, lost in thought: "The Blessed One partakes of my alms-food, yet he assigns the merit to the name of Kroḍamallaka.
He was seen by the ministers.
They asked, "For what reason do you stand there, lost in thought, with your cheek resting on your hand?
The king replied, "Sirs,
how could I not remain lost in thought?"
"Why is it that now the Blessed One, while consuming my alms-food, assigns the dedication of merit (*dakṣiṇā*) by name to Kroḍamallaka?
Then one elderly minister said: "Be of little concern."
"We shall act in such a way that tomorrow the Blessed One will assign the alms-offering under the very name of Your Majesty.

They gave orders to their servants, saying, "Therefore, tomorrow you must prepare excellent food and collect it in great abundance, so that half falls into the bowls of the monks and half falls upon the ground."
On the following day, the ministers prepared and set out an abundant and exquisite meal.
Then, they began to serve the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, as they sat comfortably.
Half of the food fell into the bowls of the monks.
Half fell upon the ground.
Then the beggars ran forward, thinking, "We shall seize what has fallen on the ground!
They were stopped by the servers.
Then Kroḍamallaka said, "If this king has abundant food and wealth, there are others like us who are suffering and who desire it."

"Why is it not given? Why should this be cast away so that it cannot be used? At these words, a distraction of mind arose in that beggar; he was no longer able to compose his heart with such clarity as he had before.

Then the king, having fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, realized that the Buddha had not dedicated the merit of the gift (dakṣiṇā) in his name; thus, having failed to hear the dedication of the merit, he entered [the city].
Thereupon, the Blessed One dedicated the merit of the gift in the name of King Prasenajit of Kośala:
"May he who rides upon elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry enjoy a city with its peaceful streets."
Do you see the fruit of a mere *rūṣkikā*—a lump of saltless boiled grain? //5//

Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, many times indeed have I eaten at the residence of King Prasenajit of Kośala; yet I do not recall ever before having been instructed by the Blessed One in such a manner regarding a gift.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do you wish to hear the unfolding of karma concerning the saltless ball of boiled beans belonging to King Prasenajit of Kośala?"
"O Blessed One, this is the time; O Sugata, this is the occasion.
May the Blessed One, beginning with the saltless lump of sour gruel belonging to King Prasenajit of Kośala, describe the web of karma."
"Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"In the past, monks, there lived a householder in a certain small town."
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status. He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her; while he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.
He was raised and nurtured until he became proficient.
Then the householder addressed his wife: "My dear, we have been born with one who will clear our debts and take charge of our wealth."
"I am going to another country taking my merchandise.
She said, "Noble son, do so."
Taking his merchandise, he went to another country;
there, through misconduct, he met with disaster.
That householder possessed very few attendants.
The wealth of that householder was completely exhausted,
and his son became distressed.
That householder had a friend.
He said to the boy’s mother, "Let this son of yours guard the field; I shall provide for his sustenance with pleasant food. She replied, "So be it."
He began to protect his field;
he began to provide him with the requisites for his livelihood by means of a share of the food.
Then, at another time, a festival arrived.
The mother of that boy thought to herself: "Today the householder’s wife will be preoccupied with providing a meal for the ascetics, brahmins, friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
I shall go at the appropriate time and bring food for this boy.
Having gone at the appropriate time, she informed the householder’s wife of this matter.
Enraged, she said: "I will not give to ascetics or brahmins, nor even to my kinsmen;
shall I give it to a servant?
Let this matter rest for today."
"I will give you double tomorrow.
Then the boy's mother thought, "Let it not be that my son remains hungry," and she prepared for her own sake a lump of saltless boiled beans.
She took her and departed. The boy saw her from afar and said, "Mother!"
"Is there anything delicious, anything delicious?
She replied, "Son,
even that which is our daily provision does not exist today."
"For my own sake, I prepared a lump of unsalted boiled beans.
Having taken it with me, I have come;
please eat this."
He said, "Leave it behind and go.
She left it behind and departed.

055.026. When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, content with remote lodgings and food, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
055.027. Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha arrived at that place. He was seen by him [the householder], majestic in body and radiant in appearance, moving with a peaceful and composed deportment.
He reflected: "Surely it is because I have not performed acts of service toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings that I am in such a state.
If he would accept from me this lump of saltless boiled beans..."
"I shall give to him.
Then that Pratyekabuddha, knowing the mind of that poor man with his own mind, extended his alms-bowl and said, "O gentle-faced one, if it has been relinquished by you,"
"Let this be given to this worthy recipient.
Then, with intense faith, she offered that lump of saltless boiled grain to that Pratyekabuddha.
"What do you think, monks? That poor man was none other than this King Prasenajit of Kośala at that time and on that occasion.
Because he offered a lump of saltless boiled beans to the pratyekabuddha,"
By that karma, he exercised sovereignty, lordship, and dominion six times among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
six times he was a consecrated Kṣatriya king in this very Śrāvastī;
and by the remainder of that same karma, he has now become a consecrated Kṣatriya king.

With reference to this, I say to him: "For one who travels with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and enjoys a city with its suburbs, do you see that as the fruit of a mere lump of coarse, saltless boiled grain? Thus I speak.
The news spread throughout the vicinity: "The Blessed One has explained the web of karma for King Prasenajit, beginning with the lump of saltless sour gruel.
King Prasenajit heard this as well, and he approached the place where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As King Prasenajit of Kośala sat there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, accept from me for the three-month period the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick."
The Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kośala by remaining silent.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit of Kośala provided the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with food of a hundred flavors for three months;
and each individual monk was clothed in a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Having collected ten million jars of oil, he was prepared to offer a garland of lamps.
A great clamor arose there during the meal and the worship. At that time, a certain female beggar from the city was in extreme distress.
056.019. As she was wandering for alms with a bowl in her lap, she heard a loud noise.
Having heard it, she asked again: "Sirs, what is this loud and great noise?"
Others reported: "King Prasenajit of Kosala has fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha for the three-month retreat;
he has clothed each individual monk in a garment worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and having procured ten million jars of oil, he is prepared to offer rows of lamps."
Then this thought occurred to that city-dwelling woman: "This King Prasenajit of Kośala is still not satiated with merit; even now he gives gifts and performs meritorious deeds.
What if I were also to gather something from somewhere and offer it as a lamp to the Blessed One?"
She requested a small amount of oil from a broken bowl, lit a lamp, and offered it at the Blessed One’s walking path.

Prostrating at his feet, she made this aspiration: "By this root of merit, just as this Blessed One Śākyamuni is a teacher named Śākyamuni when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, may I too become a teacher named Śākyamuni when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years."
And just as he had the pair of foremost disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, as his auspicious pair; Ānanda as his attendant monk;
Śuddhodana as his father; and Mahāmāyā as his mother; so too [was it for him].
Prince Rāhulabhadra was his son.
[He thought: "Just as this Blessed One will enter parinirvāṇa after dividing his relics, so too shall I enter parinirvāṇa after dividing my relics."
When all those lamps had been extinguished,
that lamp lit by her continued to burn. Indeed,
it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Blessed Buddhas that their attendants do not withdraw until the Blessed Buddhas themselves have withdrawn into seclusion.
Then the Venerable Ānanda reflected: "It is impossible, it is out of the question that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would make their bed in the light.
What if I were to extinguish the lamp?
He began to try to extinguish it with his hand, but he was unable to do so.
Then with the corner of his robe,
and then with a fan; even so, he was unable to extinguish it.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "What is this, Ānanda?
He replied: "Blessed One, the thought occurred to me: 'It is impossible, it is out of the question, that the Blessed Buddhas would prepare their bed in the light.'"
"What if I were to extinguish the lamp? Thinking thus, I began to try to extinguish it with my hand, but I could not; then I tried with the corner of my robe.
Then [he tried] with a fan,
but even so he could not [do it].
The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, you will fall into exhaustion."
057.006. Even if the Vairambhaka winds were to blow, they would not be able to extinguish it, let alone a corner of a robe or a fan held in the hand.
057.007. For indeed, this lamp was lit by that maiden with a great mental exertion.
Moreover, Ānanda, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, this girl shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Śākyamuni.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana will be his foremost pair, the auspicious pair; and Ānanda will be a monk and a lay devotee.
His father was Śuddhodana,
his mother was Mahāmāyā, and his city was Kapilavastu.
The prince Rāhulabhadra is his son;
he too, having performed the distribution of the relics, will enter final nirvāṇa.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the *Nagarāvalambikā-avadāna*, in the glorious *Divyāvadāna*.
Avadāna 8:
The Story of Supriya.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, being honored with respect.
Honored, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, brahmins,
