householders, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—

thus revered by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— the Buddha, the Blessed One, together with the community of his disciples, was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for use in sickness.
There, indeed, the Blessed One entered upon the rains retreat in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then, when the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) had arrived, a great number of merchants residing in Śrāvastī approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As the many merchants residing in Śrāvastī sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then the many [merchants]...
The merchants residing in Śrāvastī, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
They approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Ānanda instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened a great many merchants residing in Śrāvastī with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he became silent.
Then those merchants rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extended their joined palms toward the Venerable Ānanda.
Having prostrated before the Venerable Ānanda, they said this to him: "Venerable Ānanda, have you heard anything regarding where the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat,
will travel on his journey through which countries, so that we may prepare the necessary provisions for that trip?"

This is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for merchants residing in the six great cities: in whichever direction the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, desire to go, they gather the necessary provisions for that journey.
He said, "Why do you not ask the Buddha, the Blessed One?"
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indeed difficult to approach and hard to endure.
We are not able to question the Blessed One. It is the same for me, sirs; for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indeed difficult to approach and hard to endure.
"I too am unable to question the Blessed One. Venerable Ānanda, if even for you the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and hard to endure,
how does the venerable Ānanda know in which direction the Blessed One will go?"
Either by a sign or by verbal description, O venerable ones.
How by a sign?
The Blessed One sits facing the direction in which he intends to go.
Thus by means of a sign. How by means of indirect discourse?
He speaks in praise of those regions.
Thus he spoke by way of indirect discourse:
"Venerable Ānanda, in which direction is the Blessed One seated,
and of which regions does he speak the praises?"
"Gentlemen, the Blessed One is traveling toward Magadha and speaks in praise of the Magadhan districts.
Furthermore, gentlemen, there are eighteen advantages in the wandering of a Buddha."
What are the eighteen? They are:

no fear of fire, no fear of water, no fear of lions, no fear of tigers, no fear of leopards, no fear of wild beasts, no fear of enemy armies, no fear of thieves, no fear of military outposts, river crossings, or caravan travel, and no fear of humans or non-humans.
And from time to time, divine forms are seen.
Divine sounds are heard,
sublime radiances are perceived,
and proclamations concerning one's own destiny are heard.
The enjoyment of the Dharma and the enjoyment of material things;
and the moonlight of the Buddha is the remedy for affliction.
Then many merchants residing in Śrāvastī, having rejoiced and approved of what the venerable Ānanda had said, bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Ānanda,

rose from their seats, and departed. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while living, remaining, and maintaining themselves, being impelled by great compassion and intent on benefiting others, go out on forest walks from time to time.
They wander along the rivers, along the mountains, along the cemeteries, and through the countryside.
Now, on this occasion, the Buddha, the Blessed One, desiring to wander through the Magadha country, offered the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda."
"Announce to the monks: 'On the seventh day from now, the Tathāgata will set out on a journey through the Magadha country.
Whoever among you is able to travel through the countryside with the Tathāgata, let him prepare his robes.'"

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he announced to the monks: "Venerable friends, on the seventh day from now, the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour through the Magadha country.
Whoever among you is able to wander through the Magadha country together with the Blessed One, let him prepare."
"Let him perform the work of making robes.

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a multitude of monks and preceded by the community of monks, set out on a journey through the Magadha country together with many merchants, brahmins, and householders residing in Śrāvastī.
Then a great many merchants residing in Śrāvastī approached the Blessed One.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they said this to him: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consent to accept from us [offerings] of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick throughout the interval between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha."
The Blessed One consented to the many merchants residing in Śrāvastī by remaining silent.
Then, the many merchants residing in Śrāvastī, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, as the Buddha, the Blessed One, was setting out on the road between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha,
there lived in a great wilderness along that route a thousand bandits.
That thousand of bandits saw the Blessed One surrounded by a caravan and preceded by the community of monks.
Having seen one another, they said, "Let the Blessed One depart with his community of disciples;
we shall plunder the rest of the caravan.
Having reflected thus, they all rushed with speed toward where the caravan was.
The Blessed One asked, "Venerable sirs, what is this you have undertaken?
The thieves replied, "Venerable sir, we are forest-dwelling thieves.
For us there is no agriculture, nor trade, nor cattle-herding."
"By this means we shall provide for our livelihood.
Let the Blessed One go with his community of disciples;
we shall plunder the rest of the caravan."
The Blessed One said, "This caravan is dependent upon me.
Nevertheless, having calculated the gold for the entire caravan, you may take it.
"So be it," the thousand thieves promised.

059.026. Among the merchants in this caravan, those who were lay followers (upāsakas) calculated the total value of the entire caravan and informed the bandits, saying, "It is this many hundreds and thousands. 059.028. Thereupon, for the sake of ransoming the caravan from those bandits, the Blessed One revealed a hidden treasure.
059.029. Then, that thousand of bandits took gold equal in measure to the value of the caravan.
The remainder vanished right there.
Thus was the caravan liberated from the thousand thieves by the Blessed One.
059.031. In due course, the Blessed One arrived at Rājagṛha.
059.031. Again, the Blessed One, surrounded by a caravan and preceded by the community of monks, set out from Rājagṛha for Śrāvastī.
059.032. And in the same manner, the caravan was rescued from the presence of the thousand thieves.
In this manner, by coming and going six times from the presence of the thousand bandits, the caravan was protected and the price was paid.
But on the seventh occasion, the Blessed One, separated from the caravan and preceded by the community of monks, set out from Śrāvastī toward Rājagṛha.
The thousand bandits saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, who was without the caravan and surrounded by the community of monks.
And having seen one another, they spoke to each other: "Let the Blessed One go;
we shall rob the community of monks.
Why is that?
"For this Blessed One is the giver of gold!
Having said this, they ran with all their speed and began to plunder the monks.
And the Blessed One addressed them: "O children," he said.
"These are my disciples.
The thieves said, "The Blessed One surely knows us—we are thieves who roam the wilderness.
We have no agriculture, no trade, and no cattle-herding."
"By this we make our living. Then the Blessed One showed a great treasure to the thieves and spoke thus: "O children,"
"Take as much wealth as you require.
Then, from that great treasure, that thousandfold band of thieves took as much gold as they desired;
the remainder vanished right there.
Then the Blessed One, having satisfied that thousand of thieves with as much wealth as they desired, subsequently arrived at Rājagṛha.
Thereupon, a thought arose among those thieves: "Whatever prosperity, good fortune, or wealth we possess, it has all come about through our approaching the Buddha, the Blessed One."

"What if we were to feed the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, in this place? At that moment, there is nothing that the Blessed Buddhas— who are great in compassion, the sole protectors, the solitary heroes, teachers of non-duality, dwellers in tranquility and insight, skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, and whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— cannot accomplish.

[They are] those who have crossed over the four floods, who have long practiced the four means of attraction, who possess the power of the ten strengths, who are confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, who utter the noble, heroic, and perfect lion’s roar, who are free from the five hindrances, who liberate others from the five aggregates, who have transcended the five destinies, who have destroyed the six sense-bases, and who dwell in the community.
To those whose glory is perfected by the six pāramitās;

who are enriched with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening; who bestow the requisites for the seven meditative concentrations; who teach the noble eightfold path; who lead persons on the noble path; who are skilled in the nine successive attainments; who sever the nine fetters; and whose glory fills the ten directions.

Three times during the night and three times during the day—six times throughout the day and night—I survey the world with the eye of a Buddha, surpassing those who rule over a thousand worlds, to see:
"In whom shall I plant roots of merit that have not yet been planted? In whom shall I cause those already planted to increase?"
Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity?
Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and confinement? Whom shall I liberate from hardship, distress, and confinement?
Who is headed for the lower realms?
Who is inclined toward the states of woe?
Who is prone to the states of woe? Whom shall I raise up from the states of woe and establish in heaven and in the fruit of liberation?
Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I provide with a hand to pull him out?
Whose world, adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, shall I make fruitful? And whom, destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereign mastery of that noble wealth?
Who declines and who prospers?
Even the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might exceed its shore; but the Buddha would never exceed the proper time for those who are to be trained, like his own young calves. //1//
Just as a mother gazes upon her beloved only son and protects his life, even so does the Tathāgata gaze upon those people who are to be trained and protects their spiritual continuity. //2//

The cow of compassion, dwelling within the continuum of the Omniscient One, seeks out those to be trained who have been lost in the suffering of existence, never wearying, just as a mother cow laments for her strayed calves. (3)
Then the Blessed One, considering that the time had come to convert those thieves, departed from Rājagṛha in due course, surrounded by a host of monks and preceded by a host of monks—

tamed himself with a tamed retinue, peaceful himself with a peaceful retinue, like sandalwood with its retinue of sandalwood, liberated himself with a liberated retinue, comforted himself with a comforted retinue— and as described before, up until: endowed with great compassion.
He arrived at that Sāl forest.
From afar, he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, approaching together with the community of disciples.
Upon seeing him, their hearts were filled with serene faith, and they approached the Blessed One.

Having approached and prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, they addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal tomorrow in our home.
The Blessed One accepted the invitation of those thousand thieves by remaining silent.
Then, the thousand thieves, understanding that the Blessed One had accepted by his silence, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, during that very night, those thousand thieves prepared pure and excellent food and drink. Rising early in the morning, they arranged seats and set out water jars.
Then, by means of a messenger, they informed the Blessed One of the time: "It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready. Now, Blessed One, please do as you deem fit."

Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the place where the meal for those thousand bandits was being prepared.
Then that thousand of bandits washed the feet of the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with sandalwood water.
Then the Blessed One, having washed his hands and feet, sat down on the seat prepared before the community of monks.
Having perceived that the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, was seated, she personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent solid and soft foods.
When she knew that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl,
she took lower seats and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood their inclinations and latent tendencies and knowing their elements and natures, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that, upon hearing it, those thousand bandits—while remaining seated on those very seats—shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity rising with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, they said: "Venerable Sir, this was not done for us by mother, nor by father."

Neither by kings, nor by deities, nor by ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by those we sacrifice for, nor by our circle of kinsmen and relatives, has that which has been accomplished by us been done— namely, that having approached the Blessed One as a virtuous friend,
our foot has been lifted out from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
They have been established among gods and humans;
saṃsāra has been brought to its limit;
and the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up.
We have crossed the ocean of tears;
we have leaped over the mountains of bones.
Venerable Sir, may we receive the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
"May we practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One addressed them with a Brahma-voice: "Come, dear children; practice the holy life."

At the conclusion of the Blessed One’s speech, they became shaven-headed, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with minds like the open sky or the palm of a hand; they were like an axe and sandalwood (indifferent to injury or honor), having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights, and having turned their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
They became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how this thousand of thieves has been satisfied by the Blessed One with wealth seven times and established in the ultimate, unsurpassed security of Nirvana."
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I ransomed a caravan consisting of many thousands of goods from this very same thousand of thieves, yet I was not able to satisfy them."

Then, after accomplishing this journey to Badaradvīpa— which is difficult for gods and humans to attain and hard even for Śakra, Brahmā, and others to reach— through hundreds of thousands of various hardships over the course of a hundred years, I filled the entirety of Jambudvīpa, beginning with these very ten thousand thieves, with gold, silver, beryl, crystal, and other such excellent jewels, as well as with various implements desired by the heart.
Having satisfied him, he was established in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Listen to this: once upon a time, monks, in the past, in this very Jambudvīpa, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, secure, and well-supplied with food.
It was crowded with many people and inhabitants, and it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, riots, thieves, famine, and disease;
he ruled his kingdom as if it were dear to him, like an only son.
At that time, there lived in Vārāṇasī a caravan leader named Priyasena, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in wealth.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status. He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.
Then, a certain being of noble merit and great renown, having passed away from a certain sublime celestial realm, descended into the womb of that lady.
062.014. There are five unique qualities found here in certain women who are of a wise nature.
062.015. What are the five?
She knows when a man is impassioned.
She knows the time; she knows the season; she knows when the embryo has entered the womb;
and she knows from whom the embryo has entered her.
He knows whether it is a boy or a girl.
If it is a boy,
he remains resting against the right side of the womb.
If it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb.
Joyful, she informs her husband: "By good fortune, noble son, may you prosper!"
"I have become pregnant;
and since it remains resting against my right side,
it will certainly be a boy."
He too, filled with joy and great delight, uttered this inspired exclamation: "May I indeed behold the face of a son long desired;
may one be born to me who is not base-born;
may he perform my duties."
He should support those who have supported him;
he should receive his inheritance;
and thus my family lineage shall endure for a long time.

And for our sake, once we have passed away, after giving gifts and performing meritorious deeds, one should dedicate the merit by mentioning our names, saying: "May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever state of rebirth they have attained.

And knowing that she is pregnant, he keeps her in the upper story of the palace, untroubled, providing her with warm things when it is hot and cool things when it is cold, and with food prescribed by physicians that is neither too cold nor too hot.

She was provided with foods that were not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent, and not too astringent—foods free from the extremes of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.

Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, as she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat, never descending to the ground below until the fetus had fully matured. Furthermore, she heard nothing whatsoever unpleasant to her mind, until the completion of the pregnancy.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.

A boy was born, handsome, beautiful, pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-hued, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, joined eyebrows, a prominent nose, and a firm, sturdy body. His kinsmen, having gathered together, performed the birth ceremonies for him for three times seven nights—twenty-one days—and then established his name.
"What shall be the name of this boy?
Since this boy is the son of the caravan leader Priyasena,
let the boy's name be Supriya."
The boy Supriya was entrusted to eight nurses: two to provide milk, two to carry him on their hips, two to cleanse him of impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nurtured by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions, most refined of all.
He grew rapidly, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing;
and to arithmetic, calculation, finger-reckoning, subtraction, and depositing;

as well as to the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, the examination of jewels, the examination of timber, the examination of garments, the examination of men, and the examination of women.

He was thoroughly proficient in the examination of various commodities, a knower of all treatises, skilled in all arts, an expert in all crafts, a knower of the cries of all living beings, and one who understood the destinies of all states of existence. He was a debater, an expounder, a scholar, and possessed of swift activity;
his intellect had become supremely sharp and keen, like fire in its knowledge.

Whatever various crafts and occupations there are for Kṣatriya kings who have been consecrated on the head, who have attained sovereignty, power, and valor over their territories, and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—
namely, those concerning the neck of the elephant, the back of the horse, the chariot, the sword, the bow, the approach, the retreat, and the grasping of the goad— [he mastered them all].

In seizing with the hand, in cutting, in piercing, in binding with the fist, in binding the feet, in shooting at a distance, in shooting by sound, in shooting at a mark not previously seen, and in hitting vital points—
he became an expert in these five areas.
063.013. This is the natural law: a son’s name does not go forth as long as the father still lives.

063.014. Then, at another time, the caravan leader Priyasena became ill. Although he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, he continued only to decline.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation; and life ends in death. //4//
Thus, he was joined with the law of time [and passed away].
When the caravan leader Priyasena had died, Brahmadatta, the King of Kāśi, consecrated Supriya in the position of great caravan leader.
Having become a caravan leader, he made this kind of great vow: "I must satisfy all sentient beings with wealth."
063.020. "The gift is small and the beggars are many. Consequently, in a few days, that wealth reached exhaustion and depletion.
Then the great caravan leader Supriya reflected: "The gift is small and the beggars are many."
Then, within a few days, that wealth was exhausted and completely spent.
[Supriya thought: "What if I were to procure a sea-going vessel and descend upon the great ocean to fetch more wealth?
Thereupon, the great caravan leader Supriya procured a sea-going vessel and, together with about five hundred merchants, descended upon the great ocean.

Then, having proceeded by stages to the Island of Jewels and gathered a collection of gems, he safely and securely emerged from the great ocean. Having loaded his merchandise onto land-going vessels, he set out toward Vārāṇasī.
While passing through the midst of a wilderness forest, he was encountered by a thousand bandits.
Then those bandits, desiring to plunder him, rushed forward with all their speed.
And Supriya, the leader of all the merchants, having looked back at them, said: "Sirs, what is this that you have undertaken?
The thieves replied: "Caravan leader, you alone go in safety and security."
"We shall rob the remainder of the caravan.
The caravan leader said, "Gentlemen, this caravan is dependent upon me;
you ought not to rob it."
Thus addressed, the thieves said: "We are caravan-robbers who roam the wilderness.
We have no agriculture, no trade, and no cattle-herding;
by this we make our living."
Supriya, the caravan leader, said to them, "Gentlemen, let the value of the caravan be calculated;
I shall provide the payment for these [goods].
Then those merchants, having calculated the value among themselves, informed the bandits, "It amounts to this many hundreds and thousands."
Then Supriya, the caravan leader, provided his own wealth for the purpose of purchasing the goods;
thus the caravan was rescued from the presence of the bandits.
In this manner, two, three, four, five, or six times, Supriya, the caravan leader, rescued the caravan from that very same thousand-strong band of thieves and provided the price for the goods.
064.003. Thus, for as many as seven times, the caravan leader Supriya set out upon the great ocean. 064.004.
Then, having returned with his ship successfully completed its voyage, he entered the midst of a wilderness forest and was encountered by that very same thousand of thieves.
064.005. Thereupon, those thieves, desiring to plunder him, rushed forward with all their speed.
And Supriya the caravan leader, having looked at them, said: "Gentlemen, I am the caravan leader Supriya.
The bandits replied: "Great caravan leader, you surely know that we are bandits who roam the wilderness.
We have no agriculture, no trade, and no cattle-rearing."
"By this we shall provide ourselves with a livelihood.
Then the caravan leader Supriya, recollecting his former vow and being firm in his resolve, gave the goods to that thousand of thieves.
The great caravan leader Supriya reflected: "These thieves are amassing whatever wealth they have acquired."
"I have made a great vow that all sentient beings must be satisfied by me with wealth.
Yet, I am unable to satisfy even this thousand of thieves with wealth;
how then shall I satisfy all sentient beings with wealth?"—lost in such thoughts, he fell asleep.

Then, a certain deity of great renown approached that Great Being— who was endowed with noble merit and great majesty, possessed of a noble mind, the fulfiller of the desires of all sentient beings, and who had arisen for the sake of the welfare of the world— and comforted him, saying: "O caravan leader, do not fall into despair."
"Your prayer shall be fulfilled.
"Indeed, Great Caravan Leader, in this very Jambudvīpa there is a great city named Badaradvīpa, inaccessible to humans and presided over by men of great power.
In that Badaradvīpa there are preeminent jewels that fulfill the diverse desires of all sentient beings."
064.017. If the great caravan leader succeeds in his journey to Badara Island, he will thus fulfill this great vow.
064.018. For this great vow is difficult to accomplish even for Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods.
"How much more so, then, for one who has become human!
Having said this, the deity vanished right there.
And Supriya, the great caravan leader, was unable to ask that deity: "In which direction is Badaradvīpa, and how is one to go there?"

Then, as the merchant leader Supriya was waking from his sleep, this thought occurred to him: "Oh, would that the goddess might show herself to me once more, and point out the direction and the means for traveling to the great city of Badaradvīpa! Lost in such reflection, he fell back into sleep.

Then that goddess [perceived] the firmness, nobility, and resolve of that great-souled one—who was renowned for his sublime merit, and whose vigor, prowess, and energy were never despondent—[and she appeared].
Having understood this, he approached him and said: "O caravan leader, do not fall into despair.
Indeed, O great caravan leader, in the western direction, beyond five hundred intermediate islands and seven great mountains, there are seven lofty and towering great rivers."

Having leaped over those by the power of his vigor, [he crossed] the intermediate summary, the two in forward and reverse order, the whirlpool, the conch-nave, and the conch-nave-like [ocean], the Nīlodadhi, the Tārakākṣa mountain, and the Nīlagrīva mountain; then the Vairambhas, the Copper Forest, the Vemṇu thicket, the seven mountains with their thorns, the salt river Triśaṅku, and the eighteen-fold Iron-Clump (Ayaskila).
The river Ślakṣṇa and the water of the Dhūmanetra are there; the western river becomes the mountain of seven venomous serpents.
There is a great ocean named Anuloma-pratiloma.
In the great ocean Anuloma-pratiloma, which is not frequented by humans, winds blow that are both favorable and adverse.
In that regard, there is a man who is of great renown and is protected by deities of great renown;
by means of the power of great merit, the power of vigor, and the power of mind, he embarks upon a great raft and descends into the great ocean, both with the current and against the current.
He travels what another would take a month to reach.
Thus it is withdrawn in a single day;
likewise twice, thrice.
And while being carried away and withdrawn, if it encounters the middle stream of water, [it is not lost].
Thus, embraced by the power of loving-kindness, he sets out for the welfare of the world, crosses over, traverses, and goes forth.
065.003. Having crossed the Mahāsamudra both forward and backward, there is a mountain named Anulomapratiloma.

065.004. On that great mountain Anulomapratiloma, which is inaccessible to humans, winds named Anulomapratiloma blow, by which a person’s eyes become blinded with darkness and they remain with their consciousness lost.
Sustaining himself by the power of his vigor, he must search for and take the medicinal herb named Amoghā from that very same great mountain;
having applied it to his eyes, bound it upon his head, and rubbed it [into his body], he must set out for the great mountain named Anulomapratiloma.
If one performs this rite,
no delusion shall arise for them,
and they will cross the great mountain, both with its slopes facing downward and upward, in safety and well-being.
If he does not follow this procedure, or if he does not obtain the medicinal herb,
or having obtained it, does not take it,
he will become deluded for six months.
He may even fall into madness,
or he may die after having lived out his full lifespan.
Having crossed the great mountain range in both forward and reverse order, there is the great ocean named Āvarta.
There, the Vairambha winds blow, by which that water is stirred. Therein, a certain person— possessing the great renown resulting from the ripening of noble merit, and protected by the deities—
having embarked upon a great raft through the power of his vast merit, the power of his vigor, the power of his mind, and the power of his body, crosses over the whirlpools of the great ocean.
Having been whirled around seven times in one eddy, it is extinguished;
having traveled a yojana, it emerges in a second eddy. Having been whirled around seven times in that eddy as well, it is extinguished.
In this way, having been whirled around seven times in the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth revolutions, it ceases;
having gone a *yojana*, it emerges.
Thus, embraced by the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he who has arisen for the sake of the welfare of the world crosses over, traverses, and goes forth.
Having emerged from the whirlpool of the great ocean, there is a mountain named Āvarta, frequented by non-human beings.
There dwells a rākṣasa named Śaṅkha, who is fierce, a taker of others' lives, possessed of great strength and a massive body.
At a distance of one yojana above him is a medicinal herb named Śaṅkhanābhī, which smokes during the day and blazes at night.
She remained there, held in the grasp of a nāga.
That nāga indeed slept during the day and moved about at night.

Thereupon, while the nāga was sleeping comfortably by day, that man—protecting himself, not harming the body of the nāga, and through the power of medicinal herbs, the power of mantras, and the power of merit—[entered].
The Śaṅkhanābhi herb should be taken.
Having taken it, one should apply it to the eyes, bind it upon the head, and after anointing oneself, ascend Mount Āvarta.
If one performs this ritual procedure, [the goal will be attained].
He passes safely and securely across Mount Āvarta, unhindered by the rākṣasa Śaṅkhanābha, provided he follows this procedure or obtains the medicinal herb.
If he does not perform this rite or does not obtain the herb, [he will not succeed].
Or if he does not take what has been obtained,
the rākṣasa Śaṅkhanābha brings him to his death.
Having crossed the mountain Āvarta, there is the great ocean named Nīloda.
"This is deep and appears deep.
In the great ocean Nīloda dwells a rākṣasa named Tārākṣa, who has blood-red eyes, flaming hair, deformed feet, teeth, and eyes, and a belly as vast as a mountain.
If he sleeps..."
His eyes become wide open,
just like the sun when it has newly risen;
and his coarse inhalations and exhalations proceed with a heavy, labored sound, like the noise of a thundering cloud or a crashing bolt of lightning.
When he awakens, his eyes become closed.
Then, that man, having searched for the medicinal herb named Mahāmakarī right there on the seashore, [obtains it].

Having taken [the ointment], anointed the eyes, tied it upon the head, and rubbed [the body], one should mount the great boat *Mahānata*. Recognizing that the water-demon *Tārākṣa* is asleep, one should proceed near the water-demon while reciting the words of the mantra called *Eraṇḍā*, a great spell spoken by former Buddhas.
If he does not carry out this procedure,
or if he does not obtain the medicinal herb,
or having obtained it, does not take it;
Then that water-rākṣasa, Tārākṣa, either strikes at his vital strength,
deranges his mind, or deprives him entirely of life.
Having crossed the great ocean Nīloda, there is a great mountain named Nīloda.
There dwells a rākṣasa named Nīlagrīva with a retinue of five hundred; he is of fierce majesty, cruel, and a destroyer of the lives of others.
The great mountain Nīloda is entirely blue, unbroken, without cracks, without hollows, solid, and compact.
Even now, as he gazes with unblinking eyes, it causes his eyes pain and induces fainting.
At a distance of one yojana above him is a medicinal herb named Amoghā, which possesses various forms.
She remains there, protected by a nāga.
That nāga is indeed one whose gaze is poisonous, whose breath is poisonous, whose touch is poisonous, and whose fangs are poisonous.
When he sleeps, [she remains there].
Then it emits smoke; indeed,
whatever deer or bird is touched by that smoke meets its death.

There, that man—having bathed his head, observed a fast, and being filled with loving-kindness (*maitrāyata*), compassion (*karuṇāyata*), and a mind free from malice, protecting himself while not harming the body of the *nāga*—should apply medicinal ointment to his eyes, bind it upon his head, and anoint himself. Having performed this rite according to the prescribed method by one who knows it, he should ascend Mount Nīloda.
Darkness will no longer exist for him.
There will be no fainting,
nor will the guhyakas strike his body.
However, if he does not carry out this procedure, [the result will be otherwise].
If he does not find the medicinal herb,
or having found it, does not take it,
then the Rākṣasa Nīlagrīva will bring him to his death.
066.014. Having crossed beyond Mount Nīloda, there is a great ocean named Vairambha.
In the great ocean Vairambha, winds called Vairambhas blow, by which its waters are agitated;
therein, even makaras, tortoises, vallakas, śiśumāras, and the like cannot enter, nor can pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth—what need is there to mention human beings?
Leaving that behind, to the north of the great ocean Vairambha, there is a vast copper forest (*tāmrāṭavī*) many yojanas in length and breadth.
In the middle of that copper forest is a great *sāla* grove and a large water reservoir.
There dwells a python named Tāmrākṣa, fierce, a taker of others' lives, extremely foul-smelling, and five yojanas in length.
He sleeps for six months.
When he sleeps,
his saliva spreads throughout the surrounding area for a distance of one yojana.
When he stands or when he is awake,
his saliva is scanty;
above him is a great thicket of bamboo.
In that bamboo thicket there was a large stone slab. Having uprooted it by means of his heroic strength, he [found] a cave;
in that cave was a medicinal herb named Sammohanī.
It burns throughout that night and day.

Having taken it, one should apply it as collyrium to the eyes, bind it upon the head, and rub it on. Then, perceiving the copper-eyed python to be asleep, by means of the power of the herb or the power of the mantra, if one performs this ritual near the python's dwelling—
Having passed through with safety and well-being, unharmed by the copper-eyed python, you must then proceed while eating roots and fruits.
Having crossed the vast Copper Forest, there are seven mountains covered with thorny bamboo.
There, that man, having bound his feet with copper bands, must leap over those mountains by the power of his vigor, followed by seven rivers of caustic brine.
On their banks is a great forest of *śālmali* trees.
Thereupon, having bound together a raft from the planks of *śālmali* wood and having boarded it, one must cross over without touching the water.
If one should touch it, [the consequence would be as follows].
Then his limb falls away. Having crossed seven rivers of caustic liquid, there is a mountain named Triśaṅku.
On the Triśaṅku mountain, there are thorns named Triśaṅkus, which are sharp and exceedingly sharp.
Then, having bound his feet with copper plates and cane-nooses, that man must carry him across.
Having crossed beyond Mount Triśaṅku, there is a river named Triśaṅku. There are thorns called Triśaṅkus, sharp and eighteen finger-breadths long, which remain submerged within the water.
There, that man must cross by binding together a raft from *śālmalī* wood-boards, without touching the water.
If he falls [into the water],
he will meet with disaster right there through his own misconduct.
Just as there is the mountain Triśaṅku,
so too is there the river named Triśaṅkukā;
likewise, there is the mountain Ayaskila and the river named Ayaskilā.

Having crossed the river Ayaskilā, there is a mountain named Aṣṭādaśavakra. It is lofty and enclosed on all sides, being without a gate. There is no way to cross it except by climbing up a tree and proceeding from the treetop.
Having crossed the mountain Aṣṭādaśavakra, there is a river named Aṣṭādaśavakrikā, infested with crocodiles and sea-monsters, and obstructed.
There, one must cross by fastening a cane-noose;
if one falls, [one will be seized].
Through misconduct, one falls into calamity.
Having crossed the river Aṣṭādaśavakrikā, there is a mountain named Ślakṣṇa.
The mountain Ślakṣṇa is smooth, lofty, and without gates.
And there is no way for him to escape from it;
there, he must pass over millions of iron spikes.
Having crossed the smooth mountain, there is a river named Ślakṣṇā, teeming with crocodiles and makaras.
And that river is enclosed;
one must cross it by binding together willow-fences.
If one falls, [one is lost].
Through misconduct, one falls into calamity.
Having crossed the smooth river, there is a mountain named Dhūmanetra which smokes and billows with smoke.
Indeed, by that smoke, whatever deer or birds are touched, [they perish].
They meet their end.
There is a towering mountain named Dhūmanetra, with a great precipice and no gateway;
therein that man must search for a cave.
Having searched for the cave, the entrance to that cave must be opened by him through the power of medicinal herbs and the power of mantras.
That cave, moreover, remains filled with venomous serpents;
indeed, those venomous serpents possess poison in their very gaze.
There are also those whose poison is touch.
On top of Mount Dhūmanetra is a large pool of water;
in that pool of water is a great stone slab.
Having uprooted that cave by the power of his vigor,
[he finds] within that cave a medicinal herb named *saṃjīvanī* and a jewel called *jyotīrasa* which shines with the light of a lamp.
Having taken that herb and having anointed himself from head to foot, he should enter the cave while holding that herb.
067.016. By the power of medicinal herbs, by the power of mantras, and through the efficacy of medicinal herbs, venomous serpents shall not attack his body.
067.017. In this way, indeed, there will be a crossing from that mountain.
067.018. Having passed beyond the mountain Dhūmanetra, there are seven mountains of venomous serpents.

By the power of medicinal herbs and the power of mantras, one must cross seven mountains of venomous serpents. Having crossed the seven mountains of venomous serpents, there are seven rivers of venomous serpents.
There, the venomous serpents are named Tīkṣṇagandhā (Sharp-Smelling).
There, that man must search for pieces of flesh. On the banks of those rivers of venomous snakes is a forest of *śālmalī* trees.
Then, having constructed a raft from *śālmalī* wood and having covered himself with the pieces of flesh, he must board it.
Then those venomous snakes, distracted by the smell of the flesh, will go from one shore to the other.
Having crossed over seven venomous snakes, there is a great mountain, white as nectar, high and towering.
"You must ascend it; there you will see a vast region of golden ground, adorned with trees bearing flowers, fruits, and shade.
You will see the Rohitaka districts—prosperous, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people.
And you will see the great city of Rohitaka, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, surrounded by seven walls."
It was adorned with sixty-two gates, resplendent with hundreds of thousands of palaces, and featured well-laid-out streets, roads, squares, crossroads, and marketplaces.
There, the constant performance of music—accompanied by the lute, the *vallikā*, the *mahatī*, and the *sughoṣaka*, and filled with the delightful sounds of song—never ceased;

it abounded in various commodities, was crowded with throngs of people who were perpetually joyful, and was endowed with gardens, assembly halls, and lotus ponds comparable to those of Indra and Upendra, the lords of the thirty-three gods.
The lake Rohitaka was adorned with *kādamba*, swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and *cakravāka* birds; it was inhabited by great kings and frequented by eminent persons.

There dwelt the caravan leader Māgha, who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, learned, articulate, wise, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-reaching possessions, and endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa.
Rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, he knows the methods for traveling to other islands and is a voyager on great ocean-going vessels;
he will tell you the news of the great city of Badaradvīpa and its omens.
And he will show you [the way]; and you shall carry out the prescribed rite as it has been told,
and you shall not fall into weariness.

"Thus, O Great Caravan Leader, you who perform what is most difficult to do, you shall fulfill this firm vow which is like Mount Sumeru, Malaya, and Mandara. This great vow is difficult even for Śakra, Brahmā, and others to accomplish,
let alone for those who have become human beings."
Having spoken thus, that deity vanished right there.
Then Supriya, the caravan leader, having awakened from sleep and heard the words of the deity, was struck with great wonder and reflected:
"Surely this deity has [prepared] for the journey to Badaradvīpa through many hundreds of thousands of such extremely difficult tasks."
She must have been successful previously;
if she has indeed succeeded,
this deity is a performer of difficult deeds.

Then, as they were being accomplished, those men were seen performing what is supremely difficult to do— those by whom the journey to Badaradvīpa was achieved through many hundreds of thousands of difficult feats.
068.009. This which must be done by us is exceedingly difficult;
nevertheless, if I were to apply myself for the sake of the welfare of the world, my exertion would bear fruit.
"Just as I shall accomplish the journey to the great city of Badaradvīpa through hundreds of thousands of various hardships,
so too shall I bring supreme benefit to the world.
Those people as well— "
"By those many hundreds of thousands of difficult feats, the journey to Badaradvīpa was previously accomplished;
I too am a human being,
and by them it was accomplished."

Thinking, "Why should I not succeed? the great caravan leader Supriya—firm in his vow, possessed of firm vigor and prowess, undaunted in his enthusiasm, and endowed with the great majesty that is the ripening of noble merit—set out for the welfare of the world. Sustained by mindfulness of the instructions as they were taught, and recollecting his firm vow, he crossed over the five hundred intermediate islands as instructed, alone, without a second, and with resolute determination, through the power of great vigor.

Having bound himself upon a virtuous raft—subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits according to the prescribed method for crossing all narrow passages including the seven great mountains and the seven great rivers—he remained in the Rohitaka garden for twelve full years.
Then, he addressed a certain man: "Ho, man! Does a caravan leader named Magha reside in this great city of Rohitaka?"
He spoke thus: "O man, there is indeed such a thing.
However, he is seized by a great malady;
it is possible that he will pass away from that very affliction."
Then this thought occurred to Supriya, the great caravan leader: "May it not be that Magha, the great caravan leader, passes away before he can be seen;
who then will give me instructions for the journey to that great city of Badaradvīpa? Realizing this, he went with great haste to the residence of the caravan leader Magha.
He was stopped at the gate.
He did not obtain entry for the purpose of seeing the Great Caravan Leader.
Indeed, it is the nature of things that bodhisattvas are skilled in various arts and crafts;
therefore, having announced himself as a physician, he entered.

Supriya, the great caravan leader, who was well-versed in the chapters on omens, perceived that the caravan leader Magha would die within six months. Having understood this, Supriya, the great caravan leader,
having studied the medical treatises, himself prescribed appropriate medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
He did so for the sake of alleviating his illness;
moreover, he delighted him with various syllables, phonemes, words, and expressions,
composed in accordance with the treatises.
He delights [his father] with stories— various narratives, scriptures, and legends—
and in the performance of service, endowed with skill, courtesy, cleverness, and sweetness, he attends upon him with devotion and reverence like a virtuous son toward his father.
Then, for the caravan leader Magha, it became more secure and more comfortable to travel.
He regained consciousness.
Then the great caravan leader Magha, having regained his senses, said this to the great caravan leader Supriya:

— Whence have you come, you who are endowed with knowledge and discernment, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, learned, articulate, wise, of quick movement, a knower of all treatises, proficient in all treatises, skilled in all arts,
a knower of the cries of all beings, and a knower of gestures?
"What is your caste? What is your lineage? For what reason have you come to this region inhabited by non-human beings?"
Thus addressed, the caravan leader Supriya said: "Excellent, excellent, great caravan leader!
It is timely that you, great caravan leader, have asked me about my birth, family, lineage, arrival, and purpose.
Then the great caravan leader Supriya related in detail to the caravan leader Magha his birth, family, lineage, arrival, and purpose.
And he informed him further: "Through the power of your majesty, may I behold the great city of Badaradvīpa.
In this way, may my heart's desire be fulfilled, my firm vow accomplished, and may I become one who fulfills the desires of all sentient beings.
Then, the great caravan leader Magha [heard] from the great caravan leader Supriya that which he had never heard before—[this resolve] undertaken for the sake of the welfare of others.

Hearing her firm resolve, he was filled with supreme wonder; gazing at Supriya, the great caravan leader, with unblinking eyes for a very long time, he said this to him: "You are young and yet you desire the Dharma.
I behold your marvelous, superhuman prowess."
Since you, sir, have come here from Jambudvīpa after crossing mountains, oceans, and rivers that are beyond the reach of humans—
where even non-humans meet their destruction,
let alone humans— [you are truly remarkable].
"I see you as a god, or one of the gods wearing human guise.
Nothing is difficult for you, nor is anything unachievable. Nevertheless, I am seized by a great malady and am on the verge of death."
"And you have arrived.
Moreover, who would not even sacrifice their own life for your sake, when you are so intent on the welfare of others?
Therefore, my child, quickly prepare the auspicious ship."
"Enter into a partnership so that there shall be a means of travel for both of us.
Having thus agreed to Magha’s proposal, the great caravan leader Supriya prepared an auspicious ship, entered into the partnership, and went to where Magha was.
Having approached, he said this to the caravan leader Magha: "O Lord, the auspicious ship has been prepared and the protective rites have been performed;
now, Great Caravan Leader, do as you deem timely."

Then Magha, the great caravan leader, having resolved to go to the great city of Badaradvīpa, was restrained by his circle of kinsmen, relatives, sons, wives, friends, ministers, acquaintances, and blood relations,

as well as by his retinue of servants and King Rohitaka; yet, having fastened himself to a sturdy plank and accompanied by the caravan leader Supriya, he quickly boarded an auspicious ship and set out upon the great ocean.
Then Magha, the great caravan leader, said to Supriya, the great caravan leader: "I am very ill and am unable to walk.
Therefore, you ought to prepare a couch so that, leaning upon it, I may travel.
Moreover, whatever such signs there are in this great ocean, as well as the colors and shapes of the water, they must be reported to me."
069.023. After traveling many hundreds of yojanas, Supriya, the great caravan leader, saw a body of water that was entirely white.
Having seen it, he informed the caravan leader Magha: "O great caravan leader, you should know that I see a body of water that is entirely white."
When this was said, Magha the caravan leader replied: "Great caravan leader, this water is not white on one side alone.
Do you not see that great mountain of lime to the south? It is by its power that this water has been colored, wherein there are twenty-one types of mineral veins."
When gold, silver, and lapis lazuli are smelted and produced,
and when some humans of Jambudvīpa take up these jewels and return—
this is the first sign of the great city of Badaradvīpa.
069.029. As he proceeded further, Supriya, the great caravan leader, saw water with the color of weapons.

Having seen it, he informed the caravan leader Magha: "Great caravan leader, you should know that water with the color of weapons is visible. The caravan leader Magha said, "This is not water with the color of weapons."
"Do you see that great mountain of weapons to the south? It is by its power that the water has been colored.
Here, too, there are many varieties of mineral ores."
Having been smelted, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal are produced,
which some humans of Jambudvīpa take up and return with;
this is the second sign of the great city of Badaradvīpa.
In this way, there were mountains of iron, mountains of copper, mountains of silver, mountains of gold, mountains of crystal, and mountains of lapis lazuli.
Supriya, the great caravan leader, saw water that was blue, yellow, red, and white;
and within the water, he saw the flames of lamps burning brightly.

Having seen this, he then informed the caravan leader Magha: "Great caravan leader, you should know that blue, yellow, red, and white water is visible, and within the water, the flames of lamps are burning.
When this was said, the great caravan leader Magha replied: "Great caravan leader, this is not blue, yellow, red, or white water."
Nor do these shine like lamps.
Do you see that mountain composed of the four jewels to the south? It is by its power that the water is colored.
070.009. Those which shine like lamps—these are medicinal herbs shining from within.
070.010. Herein, too, there are many lineages of mineral elements (*dhātugotra*).
Having smelted this, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal are produced;
from there, some people of Jambudvīpa take jewels and return.
This is the tenth sign of the great city of Badaradvīpa.
"Furthermore, Great Caravan Leader, I know these ten signs regarding the journey to the great city of Badaradvīpa;
beyond this, I do not know.
When this was said, Supriya, the Great Caravan Leader, asked: "When will the end of the journey to the great city of Badaradvīpa come?"
When this had been said, the caravan leader Magha replied: "Supriya, I too have not seen the great city of Badaradvīpa in its entirety.
However, I have heard from ancient, aged, elderly, and venerable great caravan leaders that one must leave the water here and proceed by land toward the western direction. And he spoke thus:
The sensations of his final death appeared.
Then he said to the great caravan leader Supriya: "The sensations of my final death have appeared.
Therefore, having brought this auspicious ship to the shore and fastened it with a rope of reeds, perform the funeral rites for my body."
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, brought that auspicious ship to the shore and fastened it with a rope of cane.
In the meantime, the great caravan leader Magha passed away.

Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, having learned that the caravan leader Magha had passed away, raised him onto dry land, performed the funeral rites for his body, and reflected: "Having boarded the auspicious ship..."
And that ship, having cut its cane mooring, was carried away by the wind.
Then the great caravan leader Supriya set out across the land through the wilderness on the southern side of the mountain consisting of the four jewels, eating roots and fruits.
After traveling many yojanas, he saw a smooth mountain that sloped gradually and inclined gently.
"It is not possible to mount it.
Thereupon, Supriya, the great caravan leader, smeared his feet with honey, mounted,
and then descended.
Having traveled many yojanas, subsisting on roots and fruits, he arrived there.
There he saw a great mountain, both high and towering. While searching for a way out, he could find none.
And there was no one to instruct him in the means of escape.
Consequently, he lay down lost in thought.
On that mountain lived a yakṣa named Nīlāda.
He reflected: "This Bodhisattva, striving for the welfare of the world, is undergoing great hardship;
what if I were to provide him with assistance?

Having considered this, he said to the great caravan leader Supriya: "Great caravan leader, having gone one yojana from here to the east, there are three mountain peaks that are gradually sloping, gradually inclining, and gradually descending."
"There you must cross by binding yourself with a cane-bundle.
Then the great caravan leader Supriya, having awakened from sleep, bound himself with a cane-bundle and crossed over those mountain peaks.
071.001. Setting out once more, Supriya, the great caravan leader, saw a crystal mountain that was smooth, without support, and inaccessible to ordinary men.
071.002. Seeing no means by which he might ascend that mountain, and realizing this, he remained there for a day and night, lost in thought.
071.003. And on that mountain dwelt a yakṣa named Candraprabha.

Perceiving that the caravan leader was lost in thought—intent on the welfare of the world, set out upon the Mahāyāna, and possessed of a serene mind—he approached him and offered consolation, saying: "O Great Caravan Leader, you must certainly not give way to despondency.
Having gone about one *krośa* toward the east, he saw a vast sandalwood forest.
And in that sandalwood grove there is a great stone slab;
by lifting it up with the power of your vigor, you will see a cave.
In that cave is a medicinal herb named Prabhāsvarā, endowed with five qualities.
When this is held by her, no weapon shall penetrate his body, non-human beings shall find no opportunity to enter him,
and it generates strength and vigor.
And he creates light;
by that light you will see a staircase made of the four jewels. By means of that staircase, you must cross over the crystal mountain.
"Once you have passed beyond the crystal mountain, those luminous medicinal herbs will disappear.
There, you must not grieve, nor weep, nor lament.
Then the yakṣa Candraprabha, having thus instructed the great caravan leader Supriya, vanished right there.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, having been comforted by the great yakṣa Candraprabha and shown the way, passed beyond the crystal mountain according to the prescribed method.
As he was passing beyond it, the luminous medicinal herbs vanished.
Continuing further on his journey, Supriya, the great caravan leader, beheld a great golden city, complete with groves and lotus ponds.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, went to the city gate. Upon arriving, he saw that the city was besieged.
Having seen this, he went to the park and reflected: "Even though I have seen the city,"
That too was empty.
Having realized, "When will the road for traveling to the great city of Badaradvīpa be open? he lay down.
Then that former deity, perceiving that the great caravan leader Supriya was dejected, approached him at the break of dawn, comforted him, and encouraged him, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Great Caravan Leader!
You have successfully crossed the great oceans, mountains, rivers, and wildernesses that are inaccessible to both humans and non-humans.
You have now reached the great city-port of Badara Island, a place frequented by neither humans nor non-humans, yet inhabited by men of great renown.
What then? One must now practice heedfulness;
the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, must be guarded, and mindfulness directed toward the body must be cultivated.
When tomorrow comes, the city gate is to be triple-barred.

Then four kinnara maidens will emerge— beautiful, lovely to behold, inspiring confidence, endowed with cleverness and sweetness, possessed of every major and minor limb, of supreme beauty and noble birth, adorned with all ornaments, and skilled in the arts of laughing, conversing, attending upon, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
They will treat you with excessive affection and speak thus: "Let the Great Caravan Leader come!
Welcome, Great Caravan Leader!"

"Be the master of us who have no master; be the husband of us who have no husband; be the shelter for us who have no shelter; be the island for us who have no island; be the protection for us who have no protection; be the refuge for us who have no refuge; be the final resort for us who have no final resort.
And here are these houses of food, houses of drink, houses of clothing, and houses of bedding, as well as delightful parks and groves."
And there were abundant Jambudvīpa gems, namely: jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, emerald, musāragalva, ruby, and right-spiraling shells.
These were your gems.
"And you, sport, delight, and enjoy yourself together with us.
In that regard, you should maintain the perception of them as mothers, and maintain the perception of them as sisters or daughters."
The ten unwholesome paths of action are to be censured,
and the ten wholesome paths of action are to be praised. Even if you are greatly tempted, you must not give rise to the perception of passion.
If you should give rise [to such thoughts], you will meet with calamity through that very misconduct. For you who possess well-established mindfulness, your exertion will be fruitful,
even if they were to offer you a wish-fulfilling jewel for a well-spoken word.
Then you should skillfully ask them: "O sisters, what is the power of this jewel?
When you have thus reached the second city of the kinnaras, eight kinnara maidens will come forth, who are even more beautiful than those previously mentioned.
There too, you must follow this same sequence:
until you reach the fourth city of the kiṃnaras, thirty-two kiṃnara maidens will come out to meet you—
more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more graceful than those who preceded them, like celestial nymphs (apsaras).
They shall be rivalrous and adorned by hundreds of thousands. There too,
this same sequence must be followed by you.
Having spoken thus, that deity vanished right there.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, having awakened happily with a joyful mind, rose early in the morning and arrived at the golden city of the kinnaras.
Approaching the gateway, he knocked three times.
When the great caravan leader Supriya had knocked three times on the gate, four kinnara maidens emerged.
They were handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; endowed with cleverness and sweetness, they possessed all major and minor limbs and were of supreme beauty and noble birth.
They were experts in the arts of laughing, playing, conversing, joking, dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
They spoke thus: "Let the Great Caravan Leader come!"
Welcome, Great Caravan Leader! Be the master to us who have no master, the husband to us who have no husband,

the shelter for those without shelter, the island for those without an island, the refuge for those without refuge, the protection for those without protection, and the final resort for those without a resort.
And here are these houses for food, houses for drink, houses for clothing, and houses for bedding; delightful parks, delightful groves, and delightful lotus ponds;
and the jewels of Jambudvīpa, such as gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, emeralds, musāragalva, rubies, and right-spiraling shells—these too.

"And you, play, enjoy yourself, and amuse yourself with us. Then those kinnara maidens, having taken the great caravan leader Supriya— who possessed well-established mindfulness— by all his limbs, led him into the golden city of the kinnaras, brought him up to the palace, and seated him upon a prepared seat.

Seated there, Supriya the great caravan leader censured the ten unwholesome paths of action and praised the ten wholesome paths of action; even when tempted with very great things, he could not be made to falter.
And those kinnara maidens, being delighted, said: "It is wonderful that you, though so young, now desire the Dharma;
you neither cling to nor are bound by sensual pleasures.
And they invited him with abundant jewels.
And being won over by his teaching of the Dharma, they presented him with a single *saubhāṣinika* jewel.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, seeking to discover the power of that jewel, said: "Sisters, what is the efficacy of this jewel?
They replied: "Caravan leader, you should know that on the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha*,..."

Having bathed his head and observed the *upoṣadha* fast, he should mount this jewel-gem upon the top of a banner; then, for a thousand leagues all around, whoever may be in need— whether of silver or gold, food or clothing, drink or a particular ornament, or of bipeds or quadrupeds, vehicles or mounts, wealth or grain— [it shall be provided].
Let him generate the thought and utter the words;
with the generation of that thought and the utterance of those words, the various requisites he desires will descend from the sky.
"This is the power of this jewel.

Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those kinnara maidens with a discourse on the Dharma, and having greeted them affectionately as if they were his own mothers, sisters, or daughters, departed from the golden city of the kinnaras.

Supriya, the great caravan leader, saw a city of kinnaras made of silver, complete with groves, forests, and lotus ponds. When Supriya, the caravan leader, knocked at the gate there three times, eight kinnara maidens came out.
They spoke thus: "Let the great caravan leader enter."
"Welcome to the great caravan leader!
Be the master of us who are without a master.
Then, having been won over by his teaching of the Dharma, they also presented him with an even more excellent jewel, a mani-gem that rains down for two thousand yojanas.

There too, the great caravan leader Supriya, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those kinnara maidens with a discourse on the Dharma, and having greeted them affectionately like mothers, sisters, or daughters, departed from that silver city of the kinnaras until he reached the third city of the kinnaras, which was made of beryl.
There too, when the door was opened by the caravan leader Supriya, sixteen kinnara maidens emerged;
they were more beautiful and more pleasing than those previously mentioned.
They also, being won over by the teaching of the Dharma, presented him with an even more exquisite jewel of three thousand *yojanas* in size.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, seeking to discover the power of that jewel, asked: "Sisters, what is the majesty of this jewel?
The kinnara maidens replied as before.
Supriya, the great caravan leader, having instructed, exhorted, and inspired those kinnara maidens with a discourse on the Dharma, [proceeded].
Having encouraged them, gladdened them, and greeted them with affection like a mother, a sister, or a daughter, he departed from the third city of the Kinnaras.

Supriya, the great caravan leader, beheld the fourth city of the Kinnaras, composed of the four precious gems. It was adorned with groves, gardens, palaces, temples, lotus ponds, and lakes; its streets, lanes, crossroads, squares, and marketplaces were well-laid out;

it was radiant with exquisite perfumes and beautifully fashioned with various songs, instrumental music, and the sweet voices of young women. Its walls, archways, and gateways were embellished with diamonds, lapis lazuli, and gold.
He knocked three times at the door.
Then, when the door had been knocked upon three times by the caravan leader Supriya, thirty-two kinnara maidens emerged;
they were more beautiful and more lovely to behold than those previously mentioned, rivalling the apsarases and graced by hundreds of thousands of beauties.
They also spoke thus: "Let the Great Caravan Leader come!
Welcome to the Great Caravan Leader!
Be the master of those who are without equal and without a master."

He is the lord of those without a lord, the shelter for those without shelter, the island for those without an island, the refuge for those without refuge, the protection for those without protection, and the final resort for those without a resort.
And here are for you houses of food, houses of drink, houses of clothing, and houses of bedding; delightful parks, delightful groves, and delightful lotus ponds;
and abundant jewels from Jambudvīpa.
Namely: gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, emerald, musāragalva, ruby, and right-spiraling shells.
These belong to you and we belong to you;
sport, enjoy yourself, and amuse yourself with us.
There, too, the great caravan leader Supriya, with mindfulness well-established, delighted those kinnara maidens with various Dharma words and phrases.

Delighted, those kinnara maidens embraced the great caravan leader Supriya with all their limbs, led him into the city of the kinnaras made of the four jewels, and having seated him upon a palace, they had him sit on a prepared seat.
Seated there, Supriya, the great caravan leader, censured the ten unwholesome paths of action and praised the ten wholesome paths of action;
even when tempted with many alluring things, he could not be made to falter.
And those kinnara maidens, being delighted, said: "It is wonderful that you, though so young, now desire the Dharma;
you neither cling to nor are bound by sensual pleasures.
And they invited him with abundant jewels.

They too, won over by his teaching of the Dharma, gave him the most excellent jewel of Jambudvīpa, known as Saubhāsinika—a gem of priceless value and infinite power and majesty—which was the very lifeblood of the great city of Badaradvīpa.
And they spoke thus: "O Great Caravan Leader, this precious jewel was bestowed upon us by our brother Badara, the king of the kinnaras;
it serves as a sign, a landmark, and an ornament for this great city of Badaradvīpa."

Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, asked, "What is the power of this jewel? They replied, "Great caravan leader, you should know this: having fasted on the *poṣadha* day, one should fasten this precious gem upon the tip of a banner and hoist it up, and then a proclamation by bell should be made throughout all of Jambudvīpa: 'Listen!'"
"O noble men, you inhabitants of Jambudvīpa! Whosoever among you requires any particular requisite— whether gold, or fine gold, or jewels, or food, or drink,
or clothing, or delicacies, or ornaments, or bipeds, or quadrupeds— "
Whether it be by means of a mount, a vehicle, wealth, or grain, let him generate that thought and utter those words;
and simultaneously with the arising of that thought and the utterance of those words, whatever specific requisites he desires shall descend from the sky through the power of this jewel.

But this is the specific distinction: whatever great fears there may be for this world, such as those arising from kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, or from yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, or calamities and misfortunes;
Whether it be calamities, droughts,
or the terrors of famine, when this sublime jewel is raised aloft, these afflictions shall not occur.
Having spoken thus, those kinnara maidens gratified Supriya, the great caravan leader: "Excellent, excellent, great caravan leader!
You have crossed over the great oceans, mountains, rivers, and wildernesses.
Your firm and noble vow has been fulfilled."
Your faith has been made fruitful;
your faculties have been guarded;
the voyage to the great city of Badaradvīpa has been successfully accomplished.
074.015. You have obtained that preeminent jewel of Jambudvīpa, which fulfills the desires of all people.
However, as for the path by which you have come, there are non-human beings there; therefore—
Human beings would have perished long ago;
we shall instead point out another true path for a swift journey to Vārāṇasī.
Listen to that, and take it to heart.
"We shall speak: seven *pratāna*s beyond this western direction, there is a high great mountain.
On that mountain dwells a fierce *rākṣasa* named Lohitākṣa, who takes the lives of others.
That mountain is frequented by non-humans and releases a black darkness along with wind and sparks."

There, you should proceed by hoisting this very jewel upon the tip of a banner. By the power of the jewel, your calamities will come to an end. Having crossed over the great mountain, there is another mountain.
On that mountain dwells a nāga named Agnimukha.
Upon smelling your scent, he will hurl thunderbolts for seven days and nights.
You must search for a jeweled cave there and enter it.
After the passing of seven nights, the wicked nāga will sleep. When the wicked nāga is asleep, you must ascend the mountain.

There you will see a level stretch of ground, unplowed and unsown, yet covered with rice-śāli that bears grain without broken kernels or husks—pure, free from unpleasant odors, and growing to a height of four finger-breadths.

On the eighth or the fifteenth day, having fed upon Bālāha, the king of horses, one becomes happy, free from disease, strong, with the sense-faculties delighted, and raising the forepart of the body, utters this exclamation:
"Who is going to the further shore? Who is going to the further shore?"
"To whom shall I lead across? To whom shall I bring safely and securely to Jambudvīpa?
Having approached him, you should speak these words: "I am one who seeks to go to the further shore."
"Lead me to the further shore;
bring me safely and securely to Vārāṇasī.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, instructed those kinnara maidens with a discourse on the Dharma.

Having exhorted, inspired, gladdened, and consoled them like a mother or a daughter, he reached that spot of ground by the path as indicated and according to the method as described, proceeding in due order.
And as the horse-king Bālāha was moving along, he spoke thus: "Who is going to the further shore?"
Who is one who goes to the further shore?
Whom shall I lead to the further shore?
Whom shall I cause to reach Jambudvīpa in safety and security?
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, approached Bālāha, the king of horses.

Having approached him, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward Bālāha, the king of horses, he said this to him: "I am one who desires to go to the further shore."
"I am one who goes to the further shore; lead me! Bring me safely and securely to Vārāṇasī.
When this was said, Bālāha, the king of horses, spoke thus to the great caravan leader Supriya: "Great caravan leader, you must not look toward the directions while mounted upon my back."
"You must remain with your eyes closed," he said;
having spoken thus, Bālāha, the king of horses, offered his back.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, mounted the back of Bālāha, the king of horses, and following the instructions, reached Vārāṇasī in a matter of a few moments, instants, and hours.
He descended at his own monastery.
Having descended, Supriya, the great caravan leader, circumambulated the king of horses, Bālāha, three times to the right and prostrated at his feet.
Then the king of horses, Bālāha, expressed his approval to Supriya, the great caravan leader: "Excellent, excellent, great caravan leader!"
075.009. You have crossed over the great oceans, mountains, rivers, and wildernesses. 075.009. Your firm vow has been fulfilled. 075.010. Your journey has been made fruitful.
Your senses have been guarded;
your voyage to the great city of Badaradvīpa has been successfully accomplished;
and you have obtained that preeminent jewel of Jambudvīpa which fulfills the desires of all people.
"Thus do those distinguished beings exert themselves for the sake of the welfare of others.
Having said this, Bālāha, the king of horses, departed.
Not long after Bālāha, the king of horses, had left, Supriya, the great caravan leader, entered his own home.

The citizens residing in Vārāṇasī and Brahmadatta, the King of Kāśi, heard that Supriya, the great caravan leader, had successfully completed his journey after a full hundred years and, with his desires fulfilled,
had arrived at his own home. Upon hearing this, Brahmadatta, the King of Kāśi, was filled with joy.
The group of citizens propitiated Supriya, the caravan leader.

That previous band of a thousand thieves and other people seeking wealth heard that the great caravan leader Supriya had returned with his journey successfully accomplished and his desires fulfilled. Having heard this, they approached the great caravan leader Supriya and said to him, "Our wealth has been exhausted."
When this had been said, the Great Caravan Leader looked upon them all with a benevolent eye and addressed them: "Go, sirs, to your respective realms.
Whosoever requires any particular necessity, let him generate the thought for its sake."
And let him utter these words.
Having heard this, he departed once more.
Then Supriya, the great caravan leader, on that very fifteenth day of the *poṣadha*, having bathed his head and observed the fast, placed the jewel-gem he had first obtained upon the top of a banner.
And he utters a voice,

by which desired requisites for sentient beings arise throughout a surrounding area of a thousand yojanas; and simultaneously with its utterance, whatever anyone desires, that very thing rains down for them.
Then those beings had their desires completely fulfilled.
And that thousand of thieves was established by the great caravan leader Supriya in the ten paths of wholesome action.
In the meantime, when Brahmadatta, the King of Kāśi, had passed away, the citizens and ministers consecrated Supriya, the great caravan leader, with the royal inauguration.

Having been consecrated as Great King, Supriya mounted the second jewel-treasure upon the tip of his banner and, according to the previous ritual, made this aspiration: "May all the requisites desired by sentient beings within a radius of two thousand *yojanas* arise."
And by the mere mention of it, whatever anyone desired, that it rained down for him.

By means of the third jewel, the wish-fulfilling gem (*maṇiratna*), according to the prescribed method and raised upon the top of a banner, the rains of various desired requisites were successfully brought about.
In this way, within a radius of three thousand *yojanas*, women and men were fully satisfied with all necessary provisions.

Then, in due course, King Supriya, having become the sovereign of Jambudvīpa, on the fifteenth day of the poṣadha, having bathed his head and observed the fast, caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout all of Jambudvīpa for the sake of the women and men dwelling in Jambudvīpa who desired various requisites: "That jewel-gem which is the very essence of the great port-city of Badaradvīpa— "
He hoisted upon the tip of his banner that foremost jewel of Jambudvīpa, which rained down all manner of requisites according to one's desires.

Immediately upon its being placed at the top of the banner, the entire great multitude of inhabitants of Jambudvīpa was satisfied with various requisites as they desired; and the population of Jambudvīpa was established by King Supriya in the ten paths of wholesome action.
