Then, having established his eldest son in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom, he practiced the celibate life of a royal seer (*rājarṣi*), cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and by abandoning desire for sensual pleasures and dwelling frequently therein,
he was reborn in the company of the Brahma-world and became a Great Brahmā (*mahābrahmā*).

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, monks? He who was the great caravan leader named Supriya at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself, while I was engaged in the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
And as for those thousand thieves..."
This very group of one thousand monks was that former deity;
at that time and on that occasion, he was Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened Buddha while he was still a bodhisattva.
And he who was that great caravan leader, Magha, was none other than this monk Śāriputra at that time and on that occasion.
And he who was that great yakṣa named Nīlāda was, at that time and on that occasion, the monk Ānanda.
And he who was that yakṣa Candraprabha—
This very monk Aniruddha was that one at that time, on that occasion;
and he who was the great yakṣa named Lohitākṣa was none other than Devadatta at that time, on that occasion.
And he who was the nāga named Agnimukha was none other than Māra, the Evil One, at that time and on that occasion. And he who was Bālāha, the king of horses, was [the Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva Maitreya was, at that time and on that occasion, [the caravan leader] Dṛḍhapratijña.

At that time, monks, for the sake of fulfilling my vow, I, being firm in my promise, rescued the caravan from a band of seven thousand thieves seven times. And perceiving that the thieves were not yet satisfied, I made a further firm vow.
Having performed hundreds of thousands of various difficult feats and accomplished the journey to the great city of Badaradvīpa,

I satisfied the entire land of Jambudvīpa, headed by the thousand thieves, with wealth and established them in the ten paths of wholesome action. Even now, having attained unsurpassed knowledge through hundreds of thousands of various difficult feats, I have, out of loving-kindness and compassion, protected this caravan from the presence of the thousand thieves seven times.
Perceiving that the thousand thieves were dissatisfied, he satisfied them with as much wealth as they desired and established them in the ultimate, unsurpassed security of Nirvana.

Furthermore, many hundreds of thousands of gods and humans, and hundreds of thousands of millions of yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas, were established in the taking of refuge and the precepts of training.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Supriyāvadāna, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 9 ********** Chapter on the Prosperity of Mendhaka’s House / 077.002. The setting was Śrāvastī.

At that time, six persons of great merit resided in the city of Bhadraṅkara: the householder Meṇḍhaka, Meṇḍhaka’s wife, Meṇḍhaka’s son, Meṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law, Meṇḍhaka’s male slave, and Meṇḍhaka’s female slave.
How was the householder Meṇḍhaka known to be of great merit?
If he sees that his treasuries and storehouses are empty, they become full at the very moment of his seeing them.
Thus was the householder Meṇḍhaka renowned as one of great merit.
How was it with Meṇḍhakapatnī?
She would prepare a single cooking pot for one person's sake,
yet hundreds and thousands would eat from it.
Such was the case with Meṇḍhakapatnī.
How about Meṇḍhakaputra?
A pouch containing five hundred [coins] remained tied around his waist.
If he gives away a hundred or a thousand,
it remains full and is not exhausted.
Such was the case with Meṇḍhaka’s son;
how then was it with Meṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law?
She prepared perfumes for the sake of a single person.
There is sufficient for a hundred thousand.
Thus it was with Meṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law.
How was it with Meṇḍhaka’s slave?
Whenever he plows with a single plow, seven furrows are thereby plowed;
such was the case with the slave Meṇḍhaka.
How is it that the servant-girl Meṇḍhakadāsī possesses great merit?
Whenever she guards a single article, it becomes sevenfold.
When she awakens for one measure, seven measures are completed.
Thus was the maidservant Maṇḍhakā possessed of great merit.

It is the natural law (dharmatā) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— those of great compassion who have crossed over the four floods, whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power, who have long practiced the four means of attraction, who are devoid of the five hindrances, who have transcended the five destinies,
who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections, who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, and who are teachers of the eightfold path.

For those who are skilled in the nine successive attainments, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods,

there proceeds three times during the night and three times during the day— six times in a single day and night— the vision of knowledge as they survey the world with the Buddha-eye: "Who is declining?"
Who is prospering?
Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress?
Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into hardship, calamity, and confinement?
Who is headed for the lower realms?
Who is inclined toward the states of woe?
Who is leaning toward the states of woe? Whom shall I cause to emerge from the path to the states of woe and establish in the fruit of heaven and in liberation?
To whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I grant the hand of uplift?
Whom, deprived of the noble wealth, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the noble wealth? For whom shall I plant roots of merit that have not yet been planted?
Whose planted [roots of merit] should I bring to maturity? Whose matured [roots] should I liberate?
For whom—whose eyes are shrouded by the film of the cataract of ignorance—should I purify the vision with the medicinal salve-stick of knowledge?
Even the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might exceed its shore; but the Buddha would never exceed the proper time for those who are to be trained, as if they were his own children. //1//
For the cow of compassion, dwelling within the continuum of the Omniscient One, seeks out without weariness those to be trained— her calves— who have strayed into the wilderness of existence.
Like a loving cow for her lost calves. //2//
The Blessed One reflected: "This householder Meṇḍhaka, together with his retinue, resides in the city of Bhadramkara.
The time for his conversion has arrived, like a boil ready to burst awaiting the stroke of a blade.
Suppose I were to travel on a wandering tour through the districts of Bhadramkara."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata will travel on a journey through the country of the Bhadraṅkaras.
Whoever among you is able to travel with the Tathāgata through the country of the Bhadraṅkaras [should prepare himself].'"

"Let him accept these robes. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he announced to the monks: "Venerable sirs, the Tathāgata will go on a wandering tour through the country of the Bhadraṃkaras.
Whoever among you is willing to go on a wandering tour through the country of the Bhadraṃkaras together with the Tathāgata..."
"Let him accept the robes.
"Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda and followed closely behind him as they went.
Then the Blessed One was tamed, with a tamed retinue; peaceful, with a peaceful retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue;
comforted, with a comforted retinue; disciplined, with a disciplined retinue; an arhat, with a retinue of arhats; free from passion, with a retinue free from passion;
and inspiring, with an inspiring retinue.
Like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle,
like a lion surrounded by a pack of tusked beasts,
like a king of swans surrounded by a flock of swans.
Like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of birds,
like a brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples,
like a skilled physician surrounded by a multitude of patients.
Like a hero surrounded by a host of warriors, like a guide surrounded by a caravan of travelers, like a merchant-leader surrounded by a company of traders.
Like a guild-president surrounded by the citizens, like a provincial king surrounded by a host of ministers,
like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons.
Like the moon surrounded by a host of stars,
like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays,
like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas.
Like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas, like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas,
like Dhanada surrounded by a host of yakṣas, and like Vemacitrin surrounded by a host of asuras.
Like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of the thirty-three gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika deities,
like the ocean when it is calm;
Like an ocean free of its waters,
like a lordly elephant divested of his rut,
with his senses perfectly subdued, his movements and conduct undisturbed, and his body resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics;

Endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion— thus possessed of a multitude of manifold qualities— the Buddha, the Blessed One, set out on a journey through the countryside toward the city of Bhadraṅkara. This was after the Blessed One had displayed the Great Miracle at Śrāvastī.
Gods and humans were reproved and gladdened,
and the hearts of the virtuous were satisfied;
then the heretics, their power broken, retreated to the borderlands.
Then some went to the city of Bhadramkara and stayed there. They heard that the ascetic Gautama was coming.
Having heard this, they were distressed and said to one another, "Previously, we were driven out from the Middle Country by the ascetic Gautama."
"If he should come here,
he will certainly banish him from this place as well;
therefore, a strategic plan must be devised."
They approached those storehouses for household goods and said, "Dharma-gain! Dharma-gain!
They asked, "What is this?
[The others replied,] "We shall go after having looked around."
"For what purpose?
We have seen your prosperity;
we shall not see your misfortune."
"Noble sirs, disaster will befall us!
Gentlemen, the ascetic Gautama is coming, raining down a thunderbolt of razors and leaving many women without sons and without husbands.
Noble ladies, if this is so—"
"At the very time when we ought to remain, our abandonment is being carried out.
Stay! You must not go.
They replied, "Why should we not stay?"
"You will not hear us.
"Noble sirs, speak; we shall listen.
They said, "Expel the entire population from the vicinity of Bhadraṅkara and banish them from the city of Bhadraṅkara."
Plow the meadows;
demolish the altars;
cut down the trees bearing flowers and fruit.
"Defile the drinks with poison.
They replied, "Noble ones, wait!"
"We shall carry out everything," they said,
and so they remained there.
Then, having caused the entire population in the vicinity of the city of Bhadraṅkara to vacate, they drove them out of the city of Bhadraṅkara.
The grassy meadows were plowed, the sacrificial altars were overturned, and the trees bearing flowers and fruit were cut down.
The drinking water was poisoned.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, reflected: "It is not fitting for me to overlook this act of disrespect toward the Blessed One.
For by the Blessed One, over three incalculable eons and through hundreds of thousands of manifold hardships, the six perfections were fulfilled and unsurpassed knowledge was attained."
"That Blessed One, indeed, who is distinguished above all the world and victorious over all disputants, will wander on a journey through an empty countryside.
What if I were to exert myself for the sake of providing comfort to the Blessed One and his community of disciples?
He then gave an order to the sons of the gods known as the Vātabalāhakas: "Go to the vicinity of the city of Bhadramkara."
"Absorb the poisonous waters!
he commanded. He gave orders to the sons of the gods who are the rain-clouds: "Fill [the land] with water endowed with the eight qualities.
He addressed the gods of the Four Great Kings: "You must cause the people of the Bhaḍraṃkara districts to dwell [there]."
Then, by the sons of the gods who are the wind-clouds, the waters tainted by poison were dried up;
and by the rain-clouds, those very wells, water-cisterns, ponds, lakes, and reservoirs were filled with water endowed with the eight qualities.
By the gods of the Four Great Kings, the entire vicinity of the city of Bhadraṃkara was occupied.
The countryside became prosperous and flourishing.
The non-Buddhist teachers, together with the body of city-dwellers, dispatched scouts, saying, "Go and see what the countryside is like.
They went and saw that the countryside was exceedingly prosperous and flourishing.
Then, having arrived, they said:
"Sirs, never before have we seen such districts so prosperous and flourishing.
The non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) said: "Sirs,"
If that which even turns insentient things toward you will not turn you [toward it], how can this be?
Why is that?
"You have been looked after by us in every way; this is our final sight of you.
We are going."
They said, "Noble ones, stay!
What can the ascetic Gautama do for you?"
"He too has gone forth,
and you also have gone forth as mendicants;
will he then wander for alms among you?"
The heretics said, "We will abide by an agreement if you make a formal covenant: no one shall approach the śramaṇa Gautama for the purpose of seeing him.
Whoever approaches him shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas."
They agreed and made a formal covenant.

Then the Blessed One, wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at the city of Bhadraṅkara. He stayed in the southern sanctuary in the city of Bhadraṅkara. At that time, a brahmin girl from Kapilavastu had been married into the city of Bhadraṅkara.
Standing upon the wall, she saw the Blessed One in the darkness.
She reflected: "This Blessed One, the joy of the Śākya clan, has gone forth into homelessness after renouncing his kingdom from the Śākya family;
he is now standing here in the darkness."
"If there were a staircase here, I would descend taking a lamp.
Then the Blessed One, knowing her thought with his own mind, manifested a staircase.
Then, joyful, satisfied, and delighted, she took a lamp and descended by the stairs to where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and placed the lamp before the Blessed One, she bowed her head at his feet and sat down to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, knowing her disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, taught a discourse such as that which leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, as previously described, until she had gone for refuge and become full of faith.
Then the Blessed One said this to that girl: "Come, girl, go to where the householder Meṇḍhaka is; having approached him, inquire after his health in my name and say this: 'Householder,..."
"I have come here with you in mind,
yet you stand there having bolted the door. Is it proper for a guest to be treated in the manner that you have treated me?"
If he says, "A formal agreement has been made by the guild," he should be told: "Five hundred *nakulakas* worth of your son's goods remain tied at his waist;
whether he spends a hundred or a thousand, [it will come from there]."
"It is indeed being filled and does not diminish.
Are you unable to come after giving sixty kārṣāpaṇas?"
"So be it, Venerable Sir," that girl replied to the Blessed One and set out. As soon as she had departed, she went to the presence of the householder Meṇḍaka as if she already knew him.
Having arrived, she said, "Householder, the Blessed One sends his greetings to you."
He said, "I pay homage to the Blessed Buddha.
Householder, the Blessed One himself has said this: 'I have come specifically for you, yet you remain with the door closed.'"
"Is it right for you to receive a guest in this manner, just as you have received him?
He replied, "Maiden, a formal agreement has been made by the community: 'No one shall approach the ascetic Gautama to see him.'"
"Whoever approaches [him] shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas by the assembly.
"Householder, the Blessed One says: 'A five-hundred-pieces nakulaka cloth is tied around your son's waist.'"
If he spends a hundred or a thousand, it is always replenished and never exhausted.
"Are you not able to come after paying sixty kārṣāpaṇas?
He reflected: "No one knows this;
surely that Blessed One is omniscient."
"I am going," he said.
Having placed sixty kārṣāpaṇas at the gate, he descended by the staircase pointed out by the brahmin girl and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, underlying tendencies, elements, and nature of the householder Meṇḍhaka, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, the householder Meṇḍhaka realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he said: "Blessed One,..."
"Is this entire body of people residing in the city of Bhadraṃkara also recipients of such qualities?
The Blessed One said, "Householder,
it is because of you that almost the entire body of people has become a recipient."
Then the householder Meṇḍhaka, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone to his own home, he set out a heap of kārṣāpaṇas in the middle of the city and spoke this verse:
"Whoever wishes to see the Jina, who has conquered passion and hatred, who is free from obstruction, peerless, and pure with compassion—"
080.023. With an unwavering and well-ascertained heart, let him depart quickly; I shall bestow his wealth upon him. (3) Thus.
The multitude of people said, "Householder,
is it better to see the ascetic Gautama?
He replied, "It is better."
They said:
"If that is so, let the community itself open [the seal], for such a formal agreement was made by the community;
what contradiction is there in this?"
Having broken their agreement, they began to depart;
however, because they were unable to exit due to crowding against one another, the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, out of compassion for those beings to be converted, hurled his vajra.
A section of the wall fell down.
Many hundreds of thousands of living beings went forth—
some out of curiosity,
and some impelled by their previous roots of merit.
080.030. Having gone there, they paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him.
080.031. Eventually, an assembly gathered around the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having entered into that assembly and sat upon the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks, delivered a teaching of the Dharma that establishes roots of merit within the mental continuums of many beings.
Having heard it, some realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*),
while others took up the precepts for going for refuge.
As the Blessed One continued teaching the Dharma for a long time, the time for his meal passed by.
The householder Meṇḍhaka said, "Blessed One, please partake of the meal.
The Blessed One replied, "Householder, the time for the meal has passed."
He said, "Blessed One,
what is permissible out of season?
The Blessed One replied, "Clarified butter, molasses, sugar, and drinks."
Then the householder Meṇḍhaka summoned the artisans and said to them, "Prepare out-of-season delicacies quickly for the Blessed One. They prepared the out-of-season delicacies.
Then the householder Meṇḍhaka satisfied the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with those out-of-season delicacies and out-of-season drinks.

Then the Blessed One, having established the householder Meṇḍhaka along with his retinue in the truths, and having disciplined the people living in the market town according to their spiritual capacities, departed.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Section on the Prosperity of the Householder Meṇḍhaka, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 10 ********** 082.001. Divyāvadāna 10: The Legend of Meṇḍhaka.
082.002. The monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "What..."

Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Meṇḍhaka, by Meṇḍhaka’s wife, by Meṇḍhaka’s son, by Meṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law, and by Meṇḍhaka’s servant and maid, by which they became endowed with great merit and the six superknowledges,
and perceived the Truths in the presence of the Blessed One?
"Has the Blessed One been pleased by these [monks], and not displeased?
The Blessed One said: "Monks, these very deeds were performed and accumulated by them; their conditions have reached full maturity, they have come together like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These deeds were performed and accumulated by them."
082.007. Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element,
but rather only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases do the performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. //1//

082.012. Monks, once upon a time in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people.

It was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest; it was devoid of thieves, diseases, and calamities; and it was abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, being entirely without blemish or thorns.
He protected the kingdom as if it were his only son.
At that time, the fortune-tellers in Vārāṇasī predicted a twelve-year drought.
There would be a threefold famine: the "beak" famine, the "white bones" famine, and the "living by tally-sticks" famine.

In this context, "cañcu" refers to a small box: people place seeds inside it and set it aside with the intention of using them for future beings, thinking, "When they have died, we shall use these to provide a body of seeds for them.
Having tied up this box, it is called *cañcu*.
082.018. There is a famine called *śvetāsthi* (white-bone): at that time, people collect bones and boil them until those bones have become white; then they drink that broth.
082.019. Then they drink that broth.
This is called the "White Bone" famine (*śvetāsthi-durbhikṣa*).

As for that which is called "subsistence by tally-sticks" (*śalākāvṛtti*): at that time, people indeed extract grains of rice from pits with a tally-stick, boil them in a large pot of water, and drink the broth.
Because it is connected with tally-sticks, this is called "subsistence by tally-sticks."
Then King Brahmadatta had a proclamation made by the sounding of a bell in Vārāṇasī: "Listen, O citizens dwelling in Vārāṇasī!
The astrologers have predicted a twelve-year drought, along with a famine characterized by 'living by the stick,' 'the beak,' and 'white bones.
Those among you who possess provisions for twelve years—"
They should remain there;
those who have nothing should go wherever they please.
Free from the fear of famine, they will once again return to a time of plenty.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, and had an extensive retinue.
He summoned his steward and said, "O man,..."
"Will there be food for me and my attendants for twelve years?
He replied, "Noble sir, there will be.
He remained right there.
This famine followed immediately upon that [previous one]; his treasuries and granaries were completely exhausted,
and his entire retinue had passed away.
He himself stood as the sixth.
Then, that householder, having cleared out his treasuries and granaries, gathered a *prastha* measure of grain.
His wife placed it in a cooking pot and prepared it.

082.031. When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the destitute, frequent remote lodgings, and are the sole objects of offerings for the world.
082.032. At one time, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
083.001. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Vārāṇasī for alms.
That householder was seated as the sixth person, about to eat.
That Pratyekabuddha, wandering for alms in due order, arrived at the householder’s residence.
He was seen by that householder, inspiring confidence both in his mind and in his physical appearance.
Having seen this, he reflected again: "Even by giving up this, I shall certainly be parted from my life.
What if I were to give my own portion to this renunciant?
He then said to his wife: "My dear lady,"
"Whatever is my own portion, that I shall bestow upon this renunciant.
He reflected: "My master does not consume it;
how then shall I consume it?"
She said, "Noble son,
I too shall give my own share to him.
Thus, after the son, the daughter-in-law, the male servant, and the female servant had deliberated, each relinquished their respective shares.
Then, having gathered together, they all provided alms-food to that Pratyekabuddha.
The teaching of the Dharma by those great beings was physical, not verbal.
Like a king of swans with outspread wings, he rose up into the sky above and began to perform the miraculous displays of blazing, radiating heat, raining down, and flashing lightning.
083.010. His supernormal power (ṛddhi) quickly won over the ordinary people.
083.011. Like trees cut at their roots, they fell at his feet and began to make a formal vow (praṇidhāna).
083.012. The householder also began to make a vow: "Since I have performed such service for one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings (sadbhūtadakṣiṇīya)..."
"By this root of merit, may my empty treasuries and storehouses become full upon the mere sight of me; may I become a recipient of such qualities as these;
and may I please, and never displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one.
Then his wife began to make a vow: "Since I have performed such service for one who is a true and worthy recipient of offerings..."
By this root of merit, if I were to cook a single vessel of food for the sake of one person,
it would be consumed by a hundred,
even by a thousand.
May it not come to exhaustion as long as my application remains uninterrupted;
and may I be a recipient of such qualities as these.
"May I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and may I never displease him.

Then the son began to make a formal vow: "By this root of merit from having performed such service for one who is a worthy recipient of offerings, may a five-hundred-fold *nakulaka* pouch remain fastened around my waist."
And if one were to spend a hundred or a thousand from it,
it would remain full and not go to depletion— may I be a recipient of such qualities as these.
"May I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and may I never displease him.

Then the daughter-in-law began to make a formal vow: "By this root of merit from having performed such service for one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings, if I were to prepare a single scent for anyone,"
Or she may smell a hundredfold fragrance,
and it shall not be exhausted as long as I have not ceased [this practice]— may I be a recipient of such qualities,
and may I please, and never displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this.

The slave began to make a formal vow: "By this root of merit from the service I have rendered to such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may it be that if I plow with a single ploughshare, seven furrows are produced; and may I likewise become a possessor of such qualities as these."
"May I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and may I never displease him.

Then the maidservant began to make a formal vow: "Since such service has been rendered to one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings, by this root of merit, if I should ever undertake even a single [unwholesome] act..."

"May these seven aspirations be fulfilled: may I be one who attains such qualities as these, and may I please, and never displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one. Thus did they make their vow.
And that Great Being, the Pratyekabuddha, out of compassion for them, set out through the air above by means of his supernatural power, passing over the royal palace.
At that time, King Brahmadatta was staying on the upper terrace of his palace. As he was traveling through the air by means of his supernatural power, his shadow fell upon the king.
He began to look upward.
He saw that Pratyekabuddha.
This thought occurred to him: "By this Great Being, with the great ploughs of his supernatural powers, the very roots of poverty have been uprooted for someone.
How powerful is hope!"

Then that householder began to inspect his treasuries and storehouses, and he saw that they were full. He addressed his wife: "My vow has been fulfilled; let us now see whether yours has been fulfilled as well."
Then the maidservant began to process a single measure of grain,
and seven measures were produced.
Many neighbors and hundreds of thousands of living beings partook of it.
It remained exactly as it was.
In that very same way, the aspirations of the son, the daughter-in-law, and the slave were fulfilled.
Then the householder had a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell throughout Vārāṇasī: "Sirs, whoever is in need of food..."
"Let him come!
A loud noise, a great clamor, arose in Vārāṇasī.
The king heard it.
He asked, "Sirs, why is there this loud noise, this great clamor? The ministers replied, "Your Majesty,
the treasury and storehouses have been opened by such-and-such a householder."
The king summoned him and said, "At the very moment the world passed away, you opened the treasuries and storehouses.
He replied, "Your Majesty, whose treasuries and storehouses were opened?"
"Moreover, the seed was sown by me this very day, and it yields fruit this very day.
The king asked, "How so?
He then related this matter in detail.
The king said, "Householder,
was that Great Being provided with almsfood by you?
"Your Majesty, it was indeed provided by me."
Filled with faith, he spoke this verse:
"Oh, what a field consisting of virtues, entirely free from all defects!
Wherein a seed sown this very day yields fruit this very day! (2)

"What do you think, monks? That householder, the householder’s wife, the householder’s son, the householder’s daughter-in-law, the householder’s male slave, and the householder’s female slave were none other than this householder Meṇḍhaka, Meṇḍhaka’s wife, Meṇḍhaka’s son, Meṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law, Meṇḍhaka’s male slave, and Meṇḍhaka’s female slave.
Because they performed services for the Pratyekabuddha and made a formal aspiration," [the result was as follows].
As the ripening of that karma, six individuals of great merit were born,
who perceived the truths in my presence.
And by them, I— the Teacher, who am more distinguished than hundreds of thousands of millions of Pratyekabuddhas— was pleased and not displeased.

"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for actions that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed."
Therefore, one should train oneself in this way:
having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself solely to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the tenth [tale] in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Meṇḍhaka-avadāna.
The Legend of Aśokavarṇa.
085.002. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas,

gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; the Buddha, the Blessed One, was renowned, possessed of great merit, and a recipient of gains.

Together with the community of his disciples, he was dwelling at Vaiśālī on the bank of the Markaṭahrada, in the Gabled Hall, provided with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī made this formal agreement: "On the fifteenth day..."
"Sirs, on the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, living beings must be killed for this reason: that people may come seeking meat.
Now at that time, a certain butcher was leading out a large bull from the city in order to slaughter it.
A great crowd of people followed closely behind him, seeking meat, and said, "Kill this bull quickly;
we are in need of its flesh!
He replied, "I shall do so."
"But wait for a moment.

Then, having heard such ignoble and ill-spoken words, the bull became afraid, terrified, and agitated; his hair stood on end, and bewildered, he looked here and there and thought: "Who might shield me—with my beloved life—from this peril, distress, and confinement, where I am now without protection and without refuge?"
And he stood there with a distressed countenance, searching for protection.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Vaiśālī for alms, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks.
Thereupon, he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics.
Adorned with a fathom-wide aura and possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns, he was like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides.
Upon merely seeing him, his mind became serene in the presence of the Blessed One. With a serene mind, he reflected: "This is a distinguished being, truly gracious."
"He will be able to save my life;
what if I were to approach him?
Then that bull, looking toward the Blessed One with a mind bound by devotion, thinking "He is my refuge," suddenly snapped those firm leather straps and bonds and rushed forward.
He approached the place where the Blessed One was;
having approached, he prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet with both knees and began to lick his feet with his tongue.
And that butcher of cows, a man of fierce deeds, followed closely behind him with a weapon held ready in his hand.
Then the Blessed One said this to that cow-slaughterer of fierce deeds: "O man, make yourself friendly with this bull;
save his life.
He replied: "Venerable Sir, I am not capable of saving him by giving up my own life."
For what reason?
Because I purchased him at a high price,
and I have many children and a wife to support.
The Blessed One said, "If a price is given,
will you release it?
He replied, "I shall release it, Blessed One."
Then the Blessed One gave rise to a worldly thought: "O, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, were to come bringing three thousand kārṣāpaṇas!
Simultaneously with the arising of this thought in the Blessed One, Śakra, the lord of the gods, took three thousand kārṣāpaṇas and stood before the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Give, Kauśika, a triple price to this cow-slaughterer."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave three thousand kārṣāpaṇas to that cow-slaughterer as the price for the bull.

Then the cow-slaughterer, having received one thousand kārṣāpaṇas as the price for the bull, was thrilled, satisfied, and delighted; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, released the bull from its bonds, and Śakra, the lord of the gods, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished right there.

Then the bull, his life-breath having returned, became even more deeply devoted to the Blessed One; he circumambulated the Blessed One three times and stood behind him, following closely, gazing at the face of the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One smiled. It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile,

at that moment rays of light— blue, yellow, red, and white, with the colors of flower-pollen, ruby, diamond, beryl, emerald, coral, red pearl, right-spiraling conch, stone, agate, gold, and silver— emanate forth.
Emitting rays from his mouth, some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward—

Having gone to those hells— Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma— they descend into the hot hells having become cool.
In those cold hells, they fall down having become warm;
thereby, the particular causes of suffering for those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them: "Have we, sirs, passed away from here?"
"Or have we been reborn elsewhere?
In order to inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them: "Indeed, sirs, we have not passed away from here."
"Nor have they been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being never seen before,
and by his power our various afflictions have been stilled."
Having developed faith in their minds toward that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans, where they become vessels for the truths.
Those who go upward [pass through] the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins.

Having gone to the gods of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā realms; to the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara realms; to the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna realms; and to the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and up to the Akaniṣṭha realms, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless."
They spoke these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket! (1)
"For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,

having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end to suffering. Then those rays of light, having circled the trichiliocosm— the world-system of three thousandfold great thousands— followed closely behind the Blessed One.
086.023. If the Blessed One intends to declare past karma, they disappear behind the Blessed One. 086.024. If he intends to declare future karma, [they disappear in front of him].
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell,
they disappear into the soles of his feet.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among animals,
they disappear into his heel.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), they disappear into his big toe.
If he intends to prophesy rebirth among humans,
the light disappears into his knees.
If he intends to prophesy a kingdom as a powerful wheel-turning monarch,
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.
If he intends to prophesy a universal wheel-turning monarch's kingdom, [they disappear into the palm of his right hand].
If he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel.

If he wishes to prophesy the awakening of a disciple (śrāvakabodhi), they disappear into his mouth. If he wishes to prophesy the awakening of a solitary buddha (pratyekabodhi), [they disappear into his ūrṇā-kośa].

If he intends to prophesy supreme, perfect enlightenment, they vanish into the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows). If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they vanish into the *uṣṇīṣa* (the crown of the head).
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the ūrṇā between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.

Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One: "A multitude of rays, variegated with thousands of different colors, has issued forth from within your mouth, illuminating all directions just as when the sun rises. (3)
And he spoke this verse:
"Free from rebirth, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world.
These Conquerors, who have vanquished all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause. (4)

O steadfast one, O Śramaṇa, Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at this very moment through your own wisdom, dispel the arisen doubt of the listeners who long for it, with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words, O Bull among Sages. (5)
"It is not without cause that the Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, manifest a smile.
Those multitudes of people desire to hear the purpose for which the Wise Ones manifest a smile. (6) Thus it was said.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda; it is so.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition.
Have you seen this bull, Ānanda?"
"I have seen him, Venerable Sir.
"Ānanda, this bull, with a mind full of faith toward the Tathāgata, will pass away on the seventh day and be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
He will become the son of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa."
Falling from there, he will be reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
he will become a son of Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Falling from there, he will be reborn among the Yāma gods.
He will become the son of the god Yāma. Having passed away from there, he will be reborn among the Tuṣita gods;
he will become the son of the god Tuṣita.
Passing away from there, he will be reborn among the gods who delight in emanations (nirmāṇarati).
He will become the son of the divine son Sunirmita. Passing away from there, he will be reborn among the gods who wield power over the emanations of others (paranirmitavaśavartin).
He will become the son of the divine son Vaśavartin.
Through this continuity, for ninety-nine thousand kalpas he shall not go to a state of ruin.
Then, having experienced divine pleasure among the gods of the desire realm, in his final existence, his final abode—

In his final existence, having attained a human body, he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin) named Aśokavarṇa, a conqueror of the regions bounded by the four oceans, a righteous king of dharma endowed with the seven treasures.
These are the seven treasures he will possess, which are as follows:
They are as follows: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Furthermore, he will have a full thousand sons—brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Having completely conquered this entire great earth, bounded by the ocean, making it free from thorns and free from oppression, he will dwell there, having subdued it through righteousness and a just covenant, without punishment and without weapons.
At a later time, having given gifts and renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), he will shave off his hair and beard,
don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless life; he will realize solitary enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*) and become a solitary buddha named Aśokavarṇa.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by this bull so that he was reborn in the animal realm?
And what karma was performed so that, having experienced divine and human happiness, he will attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, these very karmas were performed and accumulated by this bull; their causal conditions have been gathered, they have reached maturity, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable."
088.002. Govṛṣa performed and accumulated these actions.
088.003. Who else shall experience them? For indeed, Ānanda, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Furthermore, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that the performed actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

088.008. "In the past, Ānanda, in a time long gone, ninety-one aeons ago, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī,
in a certain forest grove. Not far from him lived sixty monks who were forest-dwellers and alms-collectors.
And all of them were free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion. Meanwhile, about five hundred rogues, wandering here and there, arrived at that place.
They thought to themselves: "These great-souled renunciants take delight in such places.
If we do not put an end to their lives, [they will remain here]."
"From now on, it will no longer be safe for those who are well-disposed to dwell in this region.
Even if these great-souled ones, being engaged in promoting the welfare of all beings, do not inform others,
nevertheless their principal followers will approach [this place]."
"They will hand us over to our king;
there we shall have to die, imprisoned in a prison.
How should we proceed in this matter?"
There was one among them there whose heart was merciless and who had abandoned the world beyond;
he said, "How can there be safety without having these people executed?
and they were deprived of life by him.
Having committed this sinful and unwholesome deed, they were reborn in the states of woe for ninety-one eons.
For the most part, having been reborn in the hells and in the animal realm, they were constantly slaughtered with weapons.
Among them, he who was the thief was the one who incited them to it.
This very bull is that same one.
As the ripening of that karma, he was not born in a happy rebirth for all this time.
However, because his mind has now been cleared of impurity in my presence, [he will attain liberation].
Through the ripening of that karma, having experienced divine and human happiness, he will attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Thus, Ānanda, even a mere clarity of mind toward the Tathāgatas has inconceivable ripening; how much more so a formal vow?

Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall recollect the Tathāgata by way of his physical form, even for a moment, even for a brief instant, at the very least for the duration of a finger-snap.
It is in this manner, Ānanda, that you should train yourself.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, spoke these verses before the monks:
"Oh, how great is the compassion of the Protector, the All-Knowing One who seeks our welfare! How truly wonderful is his affection, manifested through such a virtuous deed! (8)
"For he who has liberated the bull from extreme distress has been prophesied for a divine existence; indeed, he shall become a Pratyekabuddha. (9) Thus it was said.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what was said.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the glorious *Divyāvadāna*, the *Aśokavarṇāvadāna*.
********** Avadāna 12 ********** 089.001. The Sūtra on the Miracles (Prātihāryasūtra). 089.002.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, being honored and revered.

Honored and revered by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan-chiefs— and worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— the Blessed Buddha was thus venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned, possessed of great merit, and a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Together with the community of disciples, the Blessed One dwells untainted by divine or human things, like a lotus leaf by water.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there lived six teachers, including Pūraṇa and others, who were not omniscient yet imagined themselves to be omniscient. They were as follows:
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, and so forth.
Saṃjayī Vairaṭṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambala, and Kakuda Kātyāyana.
The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.

Then, while the six heretics, Pūrṇa and the others, were seated and assembled together in the Hall of Wonders, this kind of conversation arose among them: "Sirs, you should know that when the ascetic..."
When Gautama had not yet appeared in the world,

we were then honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, merchants, countryfolk, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders. We also obtained the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
But when the ascetic Gautama appeared in the world,

then the ascetic Gautama was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, country folk, wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders. And the ascetic Gautama, together with the community of his disciples, obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for use in sickness.

Our gains and honors have been completely cut off in every respect. We were those possessed of supernatural powers and proclaimers of knowledge; yet the ascetic Gautama also claims for himself that he is one possessed of supernatural powers and a proclaimer of knowledge.
"A proponent of knowledge ought to display a miracle of supernatural power regarding the unsurpassed human state alongside another proponent of knowledge.
If the ascetic Gautama displays one miracle of supernatural power regarding the unsurpassed human state, we shall display two. If the ascetic Gautama displays two, [we shall display four]."
We are four;
the ascetic Gautama is one, making us eight.
"The ascetic Gautama has eight [disciples], while we have sixteen. The ascetic Gautama has sixteen [disciples], while we have thirty-two."
"We, thirty-two of us," they said, "will display twice or thrice as many miracles of supernatural power regarding the superhuman state as the ascetic Gautama displays;
let the ascetic Gautama come halfway along the road."
"We too shall travel half the way;
there, let there be a contest of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state between us and the ascetic Gautama.
Then, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "Time and again I have challenged the ascetic Gautama [to such a contest]."
"And yet, I have never found an opportunity [to strike].
Suppose I were to strike at these heretics.
Having thought this, he transformed himself into the likeness of Pūraṇa, rose high into the sky, and performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
Having done so, he addressed Maskarin Gośālīputra: "Maskarin, you should know this: I am one possessed of supernatural power (*ṛddhimat*) and a proclaimer of knowledge;
and the ascetic Gautama likewise considers himself to be one possessed of supernatural power and a proclaimer of knowledge.
It is fitting for a proclaimer of knowledge to display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) together with another proclaimer of knowledge."
"If the ascetic Gautama displays one miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state, I shall display two. If the ascetic Gautama displays two, I shall display four."
The ascetic Gautama has four [disciples], while I have eight.
The ascetic Gautama has eight, while I have sixteen.

"Śramaṇa Gautama has sixteen [disciples], while I have thirty-two. ... "As long as Śramaṇa Gautama displays a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*), we shall display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state that is twice as great as his."
"Let the ascetic Gautama come for half the way,
and I too shall go for half the way. There,
let there be a display of supernatural power regarding the superhuman state in competition with the ascetic Gautama."
Then it occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "Again and again I have exerted my power against the ascetic Gautama, yet I have never found an opportunity.
What if I were now to strike at the heretics?"

Having understood this, he transformed himself into the likeness of Maskarin and, rising high into the air, performed the miracles of blazing, heating, flashing light, and raining down water; then he addressed Sañjayin Vairaṭṭīputra: "Indeed, Sañjayin, you should know that I am one possessed of supernatural power and a proclaimer of knowledge.
The ascetic Gautama likewise claims for himself that he is one possessed of supernatural power and a proclaimer of knowledge."
"One who professes knowledge ought to display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state in competition with one who professes knowledge.
If the ascetic Gautama displays one miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state, I shall display two; if the ascetic Gautama displays two, [I shall display four]."
"I have four; the ascetic Gautama has four. I have eight;
the ascetic Gautama has eight."
"I am sixteen;

Śramaṇa Gautama is sixteen, and I am thirty-two. [He continued] until Śramaṇa Gautama would display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*).
"I shall display a miraculous feat of human power twice as great as that.
Let the ascetic Gautama come half the way;
I too shall go half the way."
"In that regard, let there be a contest of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) with the ascetic Gautama concerning a superhuman state.
Thus, they all challenged one another, and each one said: 'I am not a possessor of supernatural power.'"

The six teachers, Pūraṇa and the others, who claimed to possess the knowledge of an omniscient one, approached King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha. Having approached him, they said this to King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha: "Your Majesty, you should know that we are possessed of supernatural powers and proclaimers of wisdom.
The ascetic Gautama also claims for himself that he is possessed of supernatural powers and a proclaimer of wisdom."

"One who claims to possess knowledge ought to display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttaro manuṣyadharma*) alongside another who claims to possess knowledge.
If the ascetic Gautama displays one miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state, we shall display two. If the ascetic Gautama displays two, [we shall display four]."
"We are four; O Śramaṇa Gautama, we are eight."
"The ascetic Gautama has eight [disciples], while we have sixteen. The ascetic Gautama has sixteen [disciples], while we have thirty-two."

"We, thirty-two of us, will display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*) twice or even thrice as great as that which the ascetic Gautama displays;
let the ascetic Gautama come halfway along the road."
"We too shall travel half the way. There, let there be a display of miracles of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) with the ascetic Gautama regarding the higher human states.
When this was said, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha, said this to the heterodox teachers: "Are you also, having become corpses, beginning a contest of supernatural power with the Blessed One?"

Then the six teachers, Pūraṇa and the others—who were not omniscient and did not possess the knowledge of an omniscient one—petitioned King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha while on the way: "Your Majesty, we are possessed of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). The ascetic Gautama also claims for himself that he is possessed of supernatural powers and a teacher of knowledge. A teacher of knowledge ought to display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) in competition with another teacher of knowledge."
"Let there be a contest with the ascetic Gautama here to display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state.
When this was said, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha spoke to those wandering mendicants of other sects: "If you request this matter even a third time, I shall banish you from my realm."
Then this thought occurred to the non-Buddhist teachers: "This King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha is a disciple of the ascetic Gautama.
Let Bimbisāra be;
King Prasenajit of Kośala is impartial."
"When the ascetic Gautama goes to Śrāvastī,
we shall go there and challenge the ascetic Gautama to a demonstration of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state.
Having said this, they departed.

Then King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed a certain man: "Go, my good man, quickly prepare an excellent vehicle, so that having mounted it, I may approach the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing him and paying him homage."

"So be it, Your Majesty," that man replied to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha. Having quickly harnessed an excellent vehicle, he approached King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha and said to him: "The excellent vehicle for Your Majesty is ready; now, Your Majesty, please do as you deem fit."
Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having mounted an excellent vehicle, set out from Rājagṛha to go into the presence of the Blessed One, in order to see and attend upon the Blessed One.
Having traveled by vehicle as far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, he alighted from the vehicle and entered the monastery on foot.
On the way, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha saw the Blessed One.

In the meantime, having set aside the five insignia— namely, the turban, the parasol, the sword, the jewel, and the yak-tail fan, as well as his variegated sandals— he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Knowing that King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having expressed his approval and delight, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Where did the previous perfectly awakened ones display the great miracle for the benefit of living beings?
The deities informed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it has been heard before that the previous perfectly awakened ones displayed the great miracle for the benefit of living beings.
The Blessed One’s knowledge and vision then proceeded: "In Śrāvastī, the previous perfectly awakened ones displayed the great miracle for the benefit of living beings."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and announce to the monks:
'The Tathāgata will set out on a journey through the Kośala country.'"
"Whoever among you is able to go on a walking tour through the Kośala country together with the Tathāgata, let him wash, sew, and dye his robes.

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he announced to the monks: "Venerable sirs, the Blessed One will go on a walking tour through the Kośala country."
"Whoever among you is able to go on a journey through the Kośala country together with the Tathāgata,
let him wash, sew, and dye his robes.
Those monks gave their assent to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Blessed One—tamed, with a tamed retinue; peaceful, with a peaceful retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue;
comforted, with a comforted retinue; disciplined, with a disciplined retinue; an Arhat, with a retinue of Arhats; free from passion, with a retinue free from passion;
gracious, with a gracious retinue—was like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle, or like an elephant surrounded by a troop of young elephants.
Like a lion surrounded by a pack of tigers; like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans; like Garuḍa surrounded by a host of birds;

like a brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples; like a skilled physician surrounded by a multitude of patients; like a hero surrounded by a troop of warriors; like a guide surrounded by a company of travelers; like a caravan leader surrounded by a group of merchants; like a guild-master surrounded by a body of citizens.

He was like a provincial king surrounded by a host of ministers; like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons; like the moon surrounded by a host of stars; like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays; like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas;
like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas; like Dhanada surrounded by a host of yakṣas; and like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas.

Surrounded by a host of asuras like Vemacitra, surrounded by a host of the thirty-three gods like Śakra, and surrounded by a host of Brahmakāyika gods like Brahmā; like a calm ocean, like a rain-cloud filled with water, and like a lordly elephant free from rut; with his sense-faculties well-subdued and his deportment and movements undisturbed, he was endowed with great majesty through many unique qualities of a Buddha.
Honored by the community of monks, he set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī.
Followed by many hundreds of thousands of deities, traveling by stages along the road, he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
The non-Buddhist ascetics heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had gone to Śrāvastī.
Having heard this, they set out for Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving at Śrāvastī, they said this to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Your Majesty, please know this: we are possessors of supernatural power and proclaimers of knowledge."
"The ascetic Gautama claims for himself that he possesses supernatural power and is a speaker of knowledge.
A speaker of knowledge ought to display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state alongside another speaker of knowledge.
If the ascetic Gautama displays one miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state, we shall display two."
"The ascetic Gautama has two [disciples], while we have four.
The ascetic Gautama has four..."
"We are eight; the ascetic Gautama is one,
so we are sixteen."

"Śramaṇa Gautama has sixteen followers, while we have thirty-two. Therefore, when Śramaṇa Gautama displays a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*), we shall display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state that is double or triple his."
"Let the ascetic Gautama come for half the way,
and we too shall go for half the way.
There, let there be a display of supernatural power regarding the superhuman state (uttara-manuṣya-dharma) between us and the ascetic Gautama."
When this had been said, King Prasenajit of Kośala spoke thus to the heretics: "Wait for a moment, sirs, until I have beheld the Blessed One.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala addressed a certain man: "Go, my good man, and quickly prepare an excellent vehicle."

"Having mounted [the chariot], I shall go this very day to see the Blessed One and to attend upon him. "So be it, Your Majesty," that man replied to King Prasenajit of Kośala. Having quickly prepared an excellent vehicle, he went to where King Prasenajit of Kośala was.
Upon arriving, he said to King Prasenajit of Kośala: "The excellent vehicle for Your Majesty is ready; may Your Majesty now consider it time to depart."
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, having mounted a magnificent vehicle, set out from Śrāvastī toward the Blessed One in order to visit and attend upon him.
Having traveled by vehicle as far as the ground would allow, he alighted from the vehicle and entered the monastery on foot.
Approaching the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, these heretics are challenging the Blessed One to a contest of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state.
May the Blessed One display a supernatural power regarding a superhuman state for the benefit of living beings;
may the Blessed One rebuke the heretics."
"May it gladden gods and humans;
may it satisfy the hearts and minds of virtuous people.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "I do not, Great King..."

"In this way, monks, I teach the Dharma to my disciples: 'In this manner, you should display miracles of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) beyond the human condition to the brahmins and householders who come to you.
However, I also teach the Dharma to my disciples in this way: 'Monks, dwell with your virtues concealed and your faults revealed.'"

A second and even a third time, King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a state superior to the human condition for the benefit of living beings.
May he rebuke the heretics.
May the Blessed One gladden gods and humans."
May it gladden the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
It is indeed the nature of things that for the Blessed Buddhas who live, stay, endure, and maintain themselves, there are ten necessary duties to be performed.
The Blessed Buddhas do not pass into final nirvana as long as a Buddha has not been prophesied by another Buddha.

As long as no second being has been inspired to generate the mind set on unexcelled perfect enlightenment, as long as all those to be disciplined by the Buddhas have not been disciplined, and as long as one-third of his lifespan has not been relinquished, [he does not pass away].
The boundary has been established;
the pair of foremost disciples has been designated;
and the descent of the deities at the city of Sāṃkāśya has been displayed.
At the great lake Anavatapta, the past web of karma was explained together with the disciples;
his mother and father were established in the truths;
and the great miracle was displayed at Śrāvastī.
093.012. Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "This is something that must necessarily be done by a Tathāgata. Having understood this, he addressed King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Go, Great King!

On the seventh day from now, the Tathāgata will manifest a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*) before the eyes of the great multitude, for the benefit of living beings.
093.013. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One would grant permission," [he continued].
"I shall have a pavilion for the Blessed One’s miracles constructed.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "In which location was the Great Miracle displayed by previous perfectly awakened Buddhas for the benefit of living beings?

The deities informed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove, in that interval, the Great Miracle was displayed by previous perfectly awakened Buddhas for the benefit [of beings]."

The Blessed One’s vision of knowledge also proceeded: "Between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove, in this interval, the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones displayed the Great Miracle for the benefit of living beings.
The Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kosala by remaining silent.

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that his request had been granted, said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, in which location shall the pavilion for the miracles be set up?
“Between Śrāvastī and Jetavana, O Great King.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the non-Buddhist teachers: "Venerable sirs, you should know that on the seventh day from now, the Blessed One will display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state.
Then this thought occurred to the non-Buddhist teachers: "What then? Will the ascetic Gautama achieve in seven days what he has not yet achieved, or will he flee?"
Alternatively, desiring to investigate their position,
they thought: "The ascetic Gautama will certainly not flee,
nor will he attain what has not yet been attained."
"Surely the ascetic Gautama wishes to seek out allies; we too shall seek out allies.
Having understood this, he summoned a wandering mendicant named Raktākṣa, who was skilled in the art of sorcery.

They reported this matter in detail to the wanderer Raktākṣa and spoke thus: "Raktākṣa, you should know that we have challenged the śramaṇa Gautama by means of supernatural power (ṛddhi). He has said: 'On the seventh day from now, I shall display a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state.'"
"Surely the ascetic Gautama wishes to seek out a faction.
You, too, should first seek out a faction among your fellow celibates.
He agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa went to where the various heterodox śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, and parivrājakas were.
Having approached them, he reported this matter in detail to those various heterodox śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, and parivrājakas, and spoke thus:
"Sirs, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has been challenged by us to a contest of supernatural power."
He said, "On the seventh day from now, I shall display a miraculous feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) that transcends the human condition. [The king thought:
"Surely the ascetic Gautama wishes to seek out supporters.
You too must provide assistance to these celibate practitioners (*brahmacārin*)."
"On the seventh day, you must go outside of Śrāvastī. They agreed, saying, "So be it.
Now, on a certain mountain, there lived about five hundred sages.
Then the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa approached those sages.
Having approached them, he reported this matter to them in detail and spoke thus: "Sirs, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has been summoned by means of his supernatural power."
He said, "On the seventh day from now, I shall display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) that transcends the human condition.
[The others thought,] "Surely the ascetic Gautama wishes to seek out a partisan.
You too must provide assistance to your fellow religious practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*)."
"On the seventh day, you must come to Śrāvastī. They promised, "So be it.
Now at that time, there was a wandering mendicant named Subhadra who possessed the five superknowledges.
094.015. His residence was in Kuśinagarī, and his daytime retreat was at the great lake Anavatapta.
094.016. Then the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa approached the wandering mendicant Subhadra.
094.017. Having approached him, he related this matter in detail.
And he spoke thus: "Subhadra, you should know this: the ascetic Gautama has been challenged by us through his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
He said, 'On the seventh day from now, I shall display a miracle of supernormal power regarding the superhuman states (*uttare manuṣyadharme*).
Surely the ascetic Gautama wishes to seek out partisans."
"You must provide assistance to your fellow religious practitioners.
On the seventh day, you must come to Śrāvastī.
Subhadra said, "It was not well done by you, that the ascetic Gautama was challenged by you through supernatural power."
For what reason?
My residence is in Kuśinagarī, and my daytime dwelling is at the great lake Anavatapta.
The disciple of the ascetic Gautama is named Śāriputra; his novice monk is named Cunda, and his daytime dwelling is likewise at that very same great lake Anavatapta.
094.024. Even the deities belonging to the Anavatapta body do not consider their services to be as worthy of being performed as his [the Buddha’s] are.
094.025. This is one occasion:
here, having wandered for alms in Kuśinagarī and taken up my alms-food, I am going to the great lake Anavatapta.
094.026. A deity belonging to the body of Lake Anavatapta would draw water from the great lake Anavatapta and not give it to me.
094.027. The novice monk Cunda, taking some rag-robes, went to the great lake Anavatapta.
094.027. A deity belonging to the body of Lake Anavatapta washed those rag-robes and sprinkled herself with that water.

"He with whom we are not even equal as disciples and grand-disciples has been challenged by you to a display of supernatural power (ṛddhiprātihārya) regarding a superhuman state. You have acted improperly in challenging the ascetic Gautama to a display of supernatural power."
"In this way, I know that the ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty.
Rakta-kṣa said, "You are speaking in favor of the ascetic Gautama;
you must certainly not go."
Subhadra said, "I certainly will not go."

095.001. Now, King Prasenajit of Kośala had a younger brother named Kāla, who was handsome, pleasing to behold, and gracious; he was faithful, noble, and possessed of virtuous intentions. 095.002. He used to go out through the gate of King Prasenajit of Kośala’s palace. 095.003. One day, a certain concubine, having gone up to the roof of the palace, saw the prince and threw down a garland of flowers.
It fell upon him.
The world consists of friends, enemies, and neutrals.
They informed the king: "Your Majesty, you should know that in due course, the harem has been sought after by the god."
King Prasenajit of Kośala was fierce, impetuous, and harsh.
Without investigation, he gave an order to his attendants: "Go, sirs;
quickly cut off Kāla's hands and feet!"
"Very well, Your Majesty," the king's attendants replied to King Prasenajit of Kosala, and they cut off Kāla's hands and feet in the middle of the street.
He cried out with a piteous voice,
experiencing a sensation that was painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.
Upon seeing Prince Kāla, a great multitude of people began to cry out in lamentation.
At that moment, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the Nirgranthas arrived at that place.
Kāla’s kinsmen said to them, "Noble sirs, please restore this Prince Kāla to his former state through a formal declaration of truth."
Pūraṇa declared, "This is a disciple of the ascetic Gautama;
by means of the ascetic’s dharma, Gautama will restore him to his former state.
Then, this thought occurred to Prince Kāla: "The Blessed One does not take heed of me, who have fallen into such hardship, distress, and peril. Realizing this, he spoke this verse:
"Why does the Lord of the World not know this condition of mine, fallen as I am into such distress? Homage be to him who is free from fever and compassionate toward all beings! //1//
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of non-forgetfulness.

On that occasion, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, taking the *saṃghāṭī* robe and with a certain monk as your attendant, go to where Kāla, the king’s brother, is. Having approached Prince Kāla, place his hands and feet back in their proper positions, and then [speak] thus:"

Speak—whatever beings there may be, whether footless, two-footed, or many-footed; whether formless or possessing form; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, is declared to be the foremost among those beings.
"Whatever phenomena there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them.
By this truth, by these words of truth, may your body become as it was before."

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Taking his outer robe (saṃghāṭī) and accompanied by another monk as his attendant, he went to where Kāla, the king’s brother, was staying.

Upon arriving, he restored Kāla the prince’s hands and feet to their proper places and spoke thus: "Whatever beings there may be—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed, up to those who are neither percipient nor non-percipient—"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, is declared to be the foremost among those beings.
Whatever phenomena there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, detachment (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them.
"Whatever assemblies, groups, guilds, or congregations there may be,
the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them.
By this truth, by this word of truth, may your body become as it was before!"
095.032. As soon as he was addressed, Prince Kāla’s body became restored to its former state—just as it had happened there through the power of the Buddha and the power of the deities.
096.001. Through that very same sense of spiritual urgency, Prince Kāla realized the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) and also manifested supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
The Blessed One was presented with a monastery by him.
He began to attend upon the Blessed One;
because his body was covered in boils, he became known as Gaṇḍaka the monastery attendant.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala invited him with all necessary provisions. After some time, he said: "I have no need for you;
I shall attend solely upon the Blessed One."

King Prasenajit of Kośala had a pavilion for the Blessed One’s miracles constructed between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove; it was one hundred thousand cubits in extent, and four such pavilions were spread out. A lion throne was prepared for the Blessed One.
The disciples of other sects also had individual pavilions constructed for each of the Nirgranthas, such as Pūrṇa and the others.
On the seventh day, King Prasenajit of Kośala cleared the entire area from Jetavana to the Blessed One’s pavilion of miracles, removing all stones, gravel, and pebbles,
and covered it with a cloud of incense powder.
It was delightful, sprinkled with perfumed water and adorned with parasols, banners, flags, and various scattered flowers; and here and there, flower pavilions had been prepared.
