Then, on the seventh day, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.

Having walked for alms in Śrāvastī and finished his meal, he returned from his alms round after the meal; having set aside his bowl and robe and washed his feet outside the monastery, he entered the monastery for seclusion.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands, approached the pavilion of the Blessed One’s miraculous display. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared for him.
The heretics also, surrounded by a great multitude of people, approached the pavilion.
Having approached, they each sat down on individual seats.
Once seated, they said this to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Your Majesty, please know that we have come here.
Where, at present, is the ascetic Gautama?"
"Therefore, sirs, wait for a moment;
the Blessed One will now arrive.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala addressed the young man Uttara: "Come here, Uttara."
Go to where the Blessed One is; having approached, bow your head at the feet of the Blessed One in our name, and inquire after his freedom from illness,
freedom from affliction, ease of movement, vigor, strength, well-being, blamelessness, and his dwelling in comfort.
"And say this: 'Venerable sir, King Prasenajit of Kośala says: "Venerable sir, these heretics have arrived; please do as you deem it the right time for now.
"Very well, Your Majesty," the young man Uttara replied to King Prasenajit of Kośala and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the young brahmin Uttara said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, King Prasenajit of Kosala bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One;
he inquires after your freedom from illness, your freedom from affliction, your lightness of body, your vigor, your strength, your well-being, your blamelessness, and your state of comfort.
"May King Prasenajit of Kosala and you yourself be happy, young man."
"Venerable sir, King Prasenajit of Kośala says this: 'Venerable sir, these heretics have arrived; it is now time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the young brahmin Uttara: "Young brahmin, here I come today.
The Blessed One empowered him in such a way that the young brahmin Uttara departed from that very spot, traveling through the air above.
He approached where King Prasenajit of Kośala was.
King Prasenajit of Kośala saw the young man Uttara coming through the air above.
Having seen him, he said this to the non-Buddhist teachers: "The Blessed One has displayed a miracle of supernatural power within the human domain for Uttara."
"You too should display [your powers]!
The heretics said, "Great King, a great multitude of people has gathered here.
How will you know whether this was displayed by us or by the ascetic Gautama?"

Then the Blessed One entered such a state of meditative concentration that, as his mind was thus composed, rays of light issued forth through the keyhole and fell upon the Blessed One’s pavilion of miracles;
the entire pavilion of miracles blazed up.
The non-Buddhist teachers saw the Blessed One’s pavilion of miracles ablaze.
Having seen this, they then said to Prasenajit of Kosala: "Great King, this pavilion for the miracles of the ascetic Gautama is now ablaze!
Go now and extinguish it!
Then that fire, without even touching the water, was extinguished of its own accord before it could burn the entire pavilion of miracles—just as happens through the power of a Buddha and the deities.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas): "The Blessed One has displayed a miracle of supernatural power (ṛddhiprātihārya) regarding a superhuman state. You too should display one.
The non-Buddhist teachers replied: "Great King, a great multitude of people has gathered here."
"What will you know? By whom was this shown—by us, or by the ascetic Gautama?
Then the Blessed One emitted rays like the luster of golden mirages, by which the entire world was suffused with a sublime radiance.
King Prasenajit of Kośala saw the entire world suffused with a sublime radiance.

Having seen this, he addressed the non-Buddhist teachers: "The Blessed One has displayed a miraculous feat of supernatural power regarding a state superior to the human condition. You too should display one."
The non-Buddhist teachers said, "Great King, a great multitude of people has gathered here. How will you know whether this was displayed by us or by the ascetic Gautama?
The Blessed One has emitted rays like the shimmering of golden light, by which the entire world has been suffused with a sublime radiance."
King Prasenajit of Kośala saw the entire world suffused with a sublime radiance.
Having seen this, he addressed the non-Buddhist teachers: "The Blessed One has displayed a miracle of supernatural power regarding a state superior to the human condition;
you too should display one."

The heretics said, "Great King, a great multitude has gathered here. How will you know whether this was displayed by us or by the ascetic Gautama? Gaṇḍaka, the monastery attendant, having taken a *karṇikāra* tree from the continent of Uttarakuru, placed it before the Blessed One’s pavilion of miracles.
The park-keeper Ratnaka also brought an aśoka tree from Mount Gandhamādana and placed it behind the Blessed One’s pavilion for the miracle.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the heretics: "The Blessed One has displayed a superhuman miracle of supernatural power;
you too should display one."
The heretics said, "A great multitude has gathered here. What will you know? By whom was this displayed—by us, or by the ascetic Gautama?
Then the Blessed One placed his feet upon the ground with deliberate effort.
A great earthquake occurred.
This trichiliocosm, this great earth, shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways;
it moved, trembled, and quaked violently.
It trembles, it trembles violently, it trembles intensely; it sinks down in the east and rises up in the west. (It rises up in the east and sinks down in the west.)
The south rises and the north sinks; the north rises and the south sinks;
the center rises and the edges sink.
The center sinks and the edges rise;
these two, the sun and the moon, shine, glow, and radiate;
and various wonderful, marvelous, and extraordinary phenomena have appeared.
Deities stationed in the expanse of the sky scattered divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses over the Blessed One; they scattered powders of agallochum,
sandalwood, and tagara, as well as divine māndārava flowers,
and they played divine musical instruments.
And they waved their garments.

Then this thought occurred to those seers: "For what reason has this great earthquake occurred? It occurred to them: "Surely the ascetic Gautama must have been challenged by our fellow-celibates through supernatural power. Having understood this, five hundred seers set out for Śrāvastī.
As they were coming along, the Blessed One empowered a single path for them.

From afar, those sages beheld the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man— like the Dharma incarnate, like a sacrificial fire fed with oblations, like a lamp set within a golden vessel, like a moving mountain of gold, like a form of gold variegated with various jewels, and possessed of a mind that was manifest, vast, great, stainless, and pure.

Having seen the Buddha, the Blessed One, the mental fitness of those who have planted roots of merit under previous Buddhas for the very first time is not produced by twelve years of practiced *śamatha* by a practitioner of yoga, nor by a son’s birth to one without a son, nor by the discovery of a treasure by a poor man, nor by the consecration to kingship for one who longs for a kingdom.
First of all, there was the sight of the Buddha.
Then those sages approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.

Standing to one side, those seers said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may we receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya?
May we practice the holy life under the Blessed One after having gone forth.
They were addressed by the Blessed One with a Brahma-like voice: "Come, monks; practice the holy life."

Simultaneously with that utterance, they became shaven-headed, clad in saṃghāṭī robes, with bowls and water-strainers held in their hands; though their hair and beards had been grown for seven days, they stood possessed of the deportment of a monk ordained for a hundred years.
"Come," said the Tathāgata, and they were shaven-headed, their bodies enveloped in saṃghāṭī robes.
With their faculties immediately calmed, they remained thus established through the power of the Buddha’s resolve. (Verse 2)
Then the Blessed One—honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped with divine and human offerings and hospitality;
an Arhat accompanied by a retinue of Arhats; surrounded by the seven assemblies and a great multitude of people—approached the pavilion of miracles.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
098.025. Rays of light issued forth from the body of the Blessed One and rendered the entire pavilion of miracles radiant with a golden hue. 098.026.

Then the householder Lūhasudatta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One be free from anxiety."

"I shall display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding the superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*) together with the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthya*). I shall humiliate the non-Buddhist teachers and,
in accordance with the Dharma, bring joy to gods and humans."
"I shall satisfy the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
Householder, you were not challenged by these through supernatural power; rather, I was challenged by the heretics through supernatural power."
"I shall display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a state superior to the human condition.
It is possible that the heretics might say: 'The ascetic Gautama has no miracle of supernatural power regarding a state superior to the human condition;
this is merely the supernatural power of a disciple who is a householder wearing white garments.'"
"Sit down, householder, on your own seat.
Lūhasudatta the householder sat down on his own seat.
Just as Lūhasudatta the householder [did], so too did Kāla, the king’s brother.
The gardener Rambhaka,
the female lay follower Ṛddhilatā who was a novice nun,
and the novice monk Cunda.
The nun Utpalavarṇā.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One be free from anxiety."

"I shall display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) regarding the superhuman state (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) together with the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthya*). I will subdue the non-Buddhist teachers and, in accordance with the Dharma, bring joy to gods and humans."
"I shall satisfy the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
You, Maudgalyāyana, are capable of refuting the heretics through the Dharma. However, you have not been challenged by the heretics on account of supernatural power."
099.008. "I shall display a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state for the benefit of living beings.
099.009. I shall rebuke the heretics and gladden gods and humans."
"I shall gladden the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
Sit down, Maudgalyāyana, upon your own seat.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat down upon his own seat.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed King Prasenajit of Kośala: "Great King, who requests the Tathāgata for a demonstration of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state for the benefit [of others]?

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "I..."
"Venerable One, I entreat the Blessed One to display a miraculous feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) that transcends the human condition.
May the Blessed One display a miraculous feat of supernatural power that transcends the human condition for the benefit of living beings,
and may he put the heretics to shame."
May he gladden gods and humans;
may he satisfy the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
Then the Blessed One entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he remained upon his own seat.
Having vanished, he rose up into the air in the eastern direction and performed the four modes of conduct, namely: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
he also attained mastery over the fire element.

099.020. From the body of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who had entered the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), various rays of light issued forth—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and crystal-colored.
099.021. He also displayed many other miracles.
099.022. He set his lower body ablaze.
From his upper body, streams of cool water flowed forth.

Just as in the eastern direction, so too in the southern direction— in this way, having displayed the fourfold miraculous power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) in the four directions, he withdrew those supernatural transformations and sat down upon the seat that had been prepared.
Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Great King, this is the supernatural power (ṛddhi) of the Tathāgata that is common to all his disciples.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed King Prasenajit of Kosala a second time: "Great King, who requests the Tathāgata to display the miracle of supernatural power regarding the superhuman state (uttare manuṣyadharme)—an uncommon power—for the benefit of living beings?"

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Venerable Sir, I entreat the Blessed One to display a miracle of supernatural power— an extraordinary human feat— for the benefit of living beings."
May he rebuke the heretics;
may he gladden gods and humans;
may he satisfy the hearts and minds of the virtuous.
The Blessed One generated a mundane thought.
It is indeed the nature of things (dharmatā) regarding the Blessed Buddhas that when they generate a mundane thought,
even a creature as small as an ant or an insect perceives that thought in the mind of the Blessed One.
100.001. <100> Now, when they give rise to the supramundane mind,
even Pratyekabuddhas find no way to reach it,
let alone Śrāvakas.
Then it occurred to the gods, headed by Śakra and Brahmā: "For what purpose has the Blessed One generated a worldly thought?
It occurred to them: "He desires to display the Great Miracle at Śrāvastī for the benefit of living beings.

Then Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods, along with many hundreds of thousands of deities, having known the Blessed One’s thought with their own minds—just as a strong man might bend his drawn-in arm—[proceeded].
Or as one might extend what was contracted;
even so, Śakra, Brahmā, and other gods, along with many hundreds of thousands of deities, vanished from the world of the gods and stood before the Blessed One.
100.006. Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down leaning against his right side.
100.008. The gods, headed by Śakra, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down leaning against his left side.
100.009. The two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, offered to the Blessed One a magically created thousand-petaled lotus, the size of a chariot wheel, made entirely of gold with a jeweled stem.
And the Blessed One sat upon the pericarp of the lotus, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Above that lotus, another lotus was manifested;
there too, the Blessed One sat cross-legged.

100.012. Likewise in front, behind, and at the sides. 100.012. Thus the Blessed One manifested a mass of Buddhas extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, and the Blessed Buddhas manifested assemblies [of disciples]. 100.013. Some of these Buddha-emanations were walking back and forth.
Some stand,
some sit,
and some create shade.
They also enter the fire element and perform miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning;
others ask questions.
Others dismissed [the question] and spoke these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut. //3//
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. (4)
The Blessed One exercised such an empowerment that the entire world, down to even young children, saw the Buddha-ornamentation as unobstructed, extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
this was indeed through the power of the Buddha and the power of the deities.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, take note of the signs of this Buddha-meal as it stands in its proper sequence;
it will vanish in a single instant.
And so it vanished in a single instant.
100.025. Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn that miraculous manifestation, sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
100.026. Having sat down, at that time the Blessed One spoke this verse:
100.028. A glowworm shines only so long as the sun has not arisen.
But when Virocana has risen, one becomes afflicted by enmity and does not shine. //5//
The logicians shone only so long as the Tathāgata had not arisen. But once the world was illuminated by the Perfectly Awakened One, neither the logician nor his disciple shines.

100.032. Then King Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the non-Buddhist teachers: "The Blessed One has displayed a miracle of supernatural power regarding a superhuman state. You too should display one.
When this was said, the non-Buddhist teachers remained silent, standing there intent on departing.

101.001. A second time, Prasenajit of Kośala said this to the heretics: "The Blessed One has displayed a miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) regarding a superhuman state (*uttare manuṣyadharme*). You too should display one.
When this was said, the heretics, jostling one another, said: "You stand up! You stand up!"
Not a single person rose up.

Now at that time, Pāñcika the great general was also present, having assembled in that very assembly. Then this thought occurred to Pāñcika, the yakṣa general: "For a long time these deluded men will harass the Blessed One and the community of monks. Realizing this, he produced a tumultuous wind and rain and unleashed a great storm.
101.006. By means of a tumultuous wind and rain, the pavilions of the non-Buddhist teachers were cast out of sight.

101.007. Oppressed by that rain of thunderbolts, the non-Buddhist teachers fled in every direction from all quarters. 101.008. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings, oppressed by the excessive rain, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
The Blessed One exercised such supernatural power that not even a single drop of water fell upon that assembly.
As those many hundreds of thousands of living beings sat to one side, they uttered this inspired exclamation: "O, the Buddha!"
Oh, the Dharma! Oh, the Saṅgha!
Oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dharma!
101.012. Pāñcika, the general of the yakṣas, addressed the heretics: "O deluded men, go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of monks!
101.013. As they were fleeing, they said: "We shall go for refuge to the mountains;
we shall go for refuge to trees, walls, and groves."
101.015. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
101.016. Many people, driven by fear, go for refuge to mountains and forests, 101.017. to groves and sacred trees, being terrified by danger. (6)
101.018. For this refuge is not the best; this refuge is not the supreme. 101.019.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering. (7)
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
when he perceives the four noble truths with wisdom— (8)
Suffering, the origin of suffering, its cessation, and the transcendence [of suffering],
as well as the noble eightfold path, which leads to security and Nirvana.
101.024. This indeed is the best refuge; this is the supreme refuge. 101.025. Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering. //10//
Then this thought occurred to Pūraṇa: "The ascetic Gautama will cause my disciples to turn away from me.
Having realized this, he fled and said: "I shall tell you the entire essence of my teaching.
Thereupon, he began to instill in them various speculative views.
Namely: the world is finite,
it is infinite,
or it is both finite and infinite.
"Neither finite nor infinite;
that soul is the body, or the soul is one thing and the body another.
Thus they dwell having given rise to quarrels, having become contentious, hostile, and fallen into dispute.
101.030. Pūraṇa, too, being afraid, began to flee.
As he was fleeing, he was seen by the paṇḍaka on the path.
Having seen him, the paṇḍaka spoke this verse:
102.001. "From where do you come, Muktapāṇi, like a carpenter whose horns have been cut off?
Having understood the Dharma praised by the Jina, you wander about like a donkey from Kolī. (11)
Pūraṇa said:
"The time for my departure has arrived; there is no strength or vigor remaining in my body.
All states of pleasure and pain have been touched by me; here, the knowledge of the Arhats is unobstructed. (12)
"I have gone far away... and I fall into thirst, dispelling the darkness of others.
O Dūṣika, tell me this matter: where is that lotus pond of cool water?"
The eunuch said:
"Indeed, this cool lotus pond shines with its stream of water.
O lowest of ascetics, you base and wicked man, do you not see this pond?"
"You are neither a man nor are you a woman; you have no beard and no breasts. Your voice is different from that of a cakravāka bird; thus you are called one who is driven by the wind. (15)
Then Pūraṇa Nirgrantha, having tied a jar of sand around his neck, threw himself into the cool lotus pond;
he died right there.

102.026. Then those Nirgranthas, searching for Pūraṇa, saw a courtesan on a side road and asked her: "Lady, have you seen anyone passing here—Pūraṇa, covered in a Dharma-robe and subsisting on food from a ladle?
The courtesan replied:
102.028. Bound for the states of woe and destined for hell, this Pūraṇa wanders about with hands and feet as white as those of a corpse.
102.029. With his white hands and feet, this Pūraṇa perishes.
102.030. "O noble lady, do not speak thus; this is not well-spoken by you. 102.031.
Cloaked in the garment of Dharma, the Sage practices (or resorts to) the Dharma. (17)
The courtesan said:
"How can that man be considered wise and endowed with discernment, who wanders naked through the village while the world looks on? (18)
103.001. "If such a person as this has a hem of his garment hanging down in front, 103.002.
let the king cut off his ears with a razor-edged arrow. (19)
103.003. Then those Nirgranthas approached the Śītikā lotus pond.
103.003. Those Nirgranthas saw Pūraṇa Kāśyapa dead in the lotus pond.
103.004. Having seen that he had passed away, they lifted him out of the lotus pond, cast him aside in a secluded spot, and departed.
103.006. The Blessed One created an emanation of a Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, shaven-headed and clad in a monastic robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
103.007. It is indeed the nature of things that the Blessed Buddhas deliberate together with an emanation.
Now, whatever emanation a disciple (*śrāvaka*) might conjure forth—
If the disciple speaks,
the emanation also speaks;
when the disciple becomes silent, the emanation also becomes silent.
103.010. When one speaks, all the emanations speak;
103.011. when one becomes silent, they all become silent. (20)
The Blessed One asks the question through his emanation,
and the Blessed One provides the answer;
for this is the natural law of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly awakened Buddhas.

103.014. Having understood the disposition (*āśaya*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the element (*dhātu*), and the nature (*prakṛti*) of that great multitude who were thus inspired with faith, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths,
such that many hundreds of thousands of living beings took refuge and received the precepts, while some attained the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*).
The stages of the aids to penetration—namely, the summits (*mūrdhānaḥ*), the patiences (*kṣāntayaḥ*), and the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikā agradharmāḥ*)—were traversed and attained.
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Others, having gone forth into homelessness, realized arhatship (*arhattva*) through the abandonment of all afflictions (*sarvakleśaprahāṇa*).

103.018. Some śrāvakas planted seeds for great enlightenment (mahābodhi); some planted seeds for individual enlightenment (pratyekabodhi). For the most part, that assembly was established as inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha.
103.020. Then the Blessed One, having established that assembly as inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha, rose from his seat and departed.
103.022. Blessed are those people in the world who have gone for refuge to the Buddha; 103.023. those persons who have performed the work of a Buddha will attain final nirvana. //21//
103.024. Those who shall perform even small acts of service toward the Jina, the Leader, 103.025. having attained various celestial realms, shall obtain the state of immortality. //22//
103.026. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
103.027. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
103.028. Thus ends the twelfth sūtra, the Prātihāryasūtra, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 13 ********** 104.001. Divyāvadāna 13: The Story of Svāgata.
104.002. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

Now at that time, on Śiśumāragiri there lived a householder named Bodha, who was wealthy, possessed of great property and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-reaching holdings; he was as affluent as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal standing.
104.005. He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.

While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, after some time his wife became pregnant. She remained on the upper terrace of the palace, supported by attendants who provided her with unrestrained care.

She was attended with seasonal requisites and with foods prescribed by physicians—foods that were neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent; indeed, they were free from the qualities of bitterness, acidity, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
With her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, she did not descend from couch to couch or from seat to seat to the ground below.
And she did not hear any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the fetus was fully matured.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A daughter was born, beautiful, lovely to behold, excellent, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.

104.012. After performing an extensive birth celebration for her for three times seven days—twenty-one days—in accordance with her particular complexion and physical form, a name was established for her.
104.013. Placed in the care of nurses, she was raised and nourished with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various highly refined and excellent provisions.
104.014. She grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.

104.015. When she had grown up, Rūpiṇī—illuminating that house like a celestial maiden with her youthful conduct, deportment, and gestures—inspired joy in her father-in-law, her kinsmen, her relatives, and the household staff.

104.016. Having heard of her such splendor, princes, sons of ministers, sons of householders, wealthy men, sons of guild-leaders, and sons of caravan leaders from various countries came seeking her as a wife.
They sent forth beggars;
and the more that man was entreated, the more joy did the householder Bodha produce within himself.
He reflected: "I must not give her away on account of anyone's beauty,
nor because of their craft,
nor even because of their authority."
"But rather, I must give it to one who is my equal in family, character, or wealth"—
thus he reflects.

104.021. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that on Śiśumāragiri there was a householder named Bodha, whose daughter was endowed with such beauty and youth that she was being sought after for the sake of the sons of kings, ministers, householders, wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan-merchants residing in various countries.
104.023. Having heard this, it occurred to him: "I, too, shall now seek her for the sake of my son."
104.024. Thinking that the householder Bodha might perhaps give [his daughter], he sent suitors for her.
After the householder Bodha had considered the conduct and wealth of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, he gave her to him.
Then, with great magnificence, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada married his son to her.
104.026. Furthermore, while the householder Bodha was again sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with his wife, his wife became pregnant.
104.027. On the very day she became pregnant, many hundreds of misfortunes appeared for the householder Bodha.
104.028. He summoned the fortune-tellers and asked them, "Sirs, consider this: by whose power have these hundreds of misfortunes arisen for me?
104.029. After deliberating, the fortune-tellers spoke with one accord: "Householder, [it is by the power of such-and-such]."
"This one who has entered the womb of your wife—
this is his power.
Therefore, let him be abandoned."
104.031. Having heard this, the householder Bodha fell into great despair and said: "Sirs, I will not abandon Svāgata."
104.032. Having said, "May it be well," the soothsayers departed.
104.032. Then the householder Bodha, although distressed by the thought of separation, remained indifferent out of fear of public scandal.
105.001. As that fetus grew, so did [his distress].
In that manner, as the householder Bodha’s status increased further and further, hundreds of misfortunes arose.
He reflected: "Who will hear of these?
Having resolved, "I shall go and stay in the pleasure grove," he spoke to his servants: "If some great misfortune should befall me..."
Having said, "He alone is to be informed, and no one else," he went to the park and remained there until that wife of his gave birth.
A son was born.
Then, a certain man went very quickly to the presence of the householder Bodha.
He saw him from afar.
He reflected: "Since he is coming with such great haste, surely some great calamity has arisen."
105.007. Having understood this, he asked with agitation: "O man, why do you come in such great haste?
He replied: "Householder,..."
"Congratulations on your prosperity!
A son has been born to you.
He replied, "O man,"
"Although my son was born after producing hundreds of unworthy [sons], nevertheless, welcome to him!
Immediately thereafter, a second man, likewise with eyes overwhelmed by tears, went in great haste to the presence of the householder Bodha.
He too, questioned with agitation because of that misfortune, asked: "O man, why do you come in such great haste?
With a throat choked by tears, he spoke in words faltering with compassion and drawn out by distress: "Householder,..."
"A fire has broken out in the house; all my property has been consumed! His mental continuum was thus reinforced by hearing this misfortune again and again, and he said, "O man!"
"This must be attained.
Enough with despondency; remain silent."
105.014. Then his kinsmen, following worldly custom, began to determine his name with an air of disdain, asking, "What shall the boy's name be?
105.015. Some there said, "Let it be something that accords with his family.
Others said, "Since he brought the house of the householder Bodha—which was filled with manifold wealth—to its destruction even while still in his mother's womb," [let his name be accordingly].
What kind of name, befitting his family, is established for him?
Rather, as soon as he was born, he was greeted by his father with the words of welcome;
therefore, let his name be "Svāgata" (Welcome).
The name "Svāgata" was established for him.
As Svāgata grew, so too did the wealth, grain, gold, bullion, female slaves, male slaves, laborers, and servants of the householder Bodha undergo diminution, exhaustion, and total depletion.
105.020. Then, at another time, the householder Bodha passed away.
105.021. His wife also passed away.
105.021. That house, having been renovated, was again consumed by fire.
Furthermore, those among his employees who took merchandise and went to other lands, even as far as crossing the great ocean—
some had their ships wrecked, while for others the merchandise became unsaleable.
Some there met with disaster through their own misconduct;

for some who were in the midst of a wilderness, their goods were plundered by bandits; and for others who had reached the vicinity of a city, their valuable cargo was seized by customs officials while they were inspecting their goods.
When some had reached the city, their entire property was confiscated by officials appointed by the king after he had instigated charges against them.
Others, having heard of the death of the householder Bodha, remained right there.
Some among his kinsmen also passed away.
Some fled, while others remained right there and did not even offer a word of welcome;
even among the female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, some had passed away.
Some had fled,
while others remained right there under the protection of another, refusing even to utter the name of Svāgata.
However, Bodha’s old maidservant remained, out of gratitude, continuing her service to Svāgata.

She was entrusted by her to learn the letters from a master of writing. She reflected: "The house of the householder Bodha is filled with manifold wealth, possesses an extensive circle of kinsmen and relatives, and has many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; it is inexhaustible, yet I have remained here."
106.001. "I shall first investigate whose lack of merit has caused this calamity:
is it Svāgata's or mine?
106.002. She placed rice into a pot under the name of Svāgata for the purpose of cooking a meal, but it was ruined.
106.003. Then, having added his own name in the same manner, excellent food was prepared.
106.004. She reflected: "This man is unfortunate."

"Having come upon this, the house of the householder Bodha—which was abundant with much wealth, possessed a vast circle of kinsmen and relatives, and had many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants—has reached exhaustion and depletion.
Yet I shall not go; rather, I shall remain here. Why do you say, "I shall remain"?
"In this matter, the time has come; we must flee by all means before our lives are severed.
Having realized this, they took whatever valuables were there and fled.

In that empty house, some dogs entered and began to quarrel. Just then, a certain rogue man was passing by that place. Hearing the quarreling of the dogs, he reflected: "The dogs in the house of the householder Bodha are quarreling."
"Could it be something else?
Let me look," he thought. He entered there and saw that it was empty.
He too, taking whatever small remainder was left from that, departed.
Then Svāgata, having learned that it was mealtime, left the writing school and returned to his own home to eat; however, when he looked, he saw it was empty.
With his mental continuum set on eating and his mind distressed by hunger, he began to call out, "Mother! Mother!"
No one gave him any reply.
Having looked here and there in that house and becoming hopeless, he departed.
Not far from that house was another house.

106.015. Svāgata’s kinsmen were staying there. He went into their presence, and just as he arrived, a quarrel broke out. After they had finished quarreling and calmed down, they said to one another: "Sirs,..."
"Previously, when we saw one another, affection arose; but now there is hatred.
Look! Could it be that some other person has arrived?"
106.018. They began to search for him and eventually saw Svāgata.
Thereupon, some said, "Sirs, Svāgata has entered!"
Others said, "This is not a welcome guest, but rather an ill-omened one; it was because of his arrival that strife has appeared among us."
They seized him by the neck and expelled him; he went elsewhere.
Expelled from there as well, he eventually entered among the wrestlers.
Wherever they entered seeking alms, [he followed].
There they were rebuked and driven out.
Having fallen into despair, with empty hands and empty bowls, they returned to deserted temples, pavilions, and the roots of trees.
They asked one another: "Sirs," they said, "what shall we do?"
"In the past, wherever we went, we returned with full hands and full bowls.
Now, what is the cause by which we have come here with empty hands, empty bowls, and having fallen into despair?
Thereupon, some said, "Surely some unfortunate person has entered among us, because of whom we have come here with empty hands and empty bowls."
Others said, "That plan has failed;
let us enter by dividing into two groups.
On the following day, they entered in two groups.
106.028. Among them, those in whose midst Svāgata was found were likewise rebuked and expelled; having fallen into despair, they returned to their dwellings with empty hands and empty bowls.
106.029. But the others arrived with full hands and full bowls. 106.030. Those who had come with empty hands and empty vessels split into two groups and entered once more.
106.030. Among them, those who were the Svāgatas likewise arrived with empty hands and empty bowls.

106.031. They split into two groups once more, and so on until the Svāgatas and Kroḍamallakas entered [the city] with empty hands and empty bowls. 106.032. But the others arrived with full hands and full bowls.

107.001. Then all those beggars gathered together and began to make a resolution: "Sirs, this unfortunate man has entered among us, because of whom we have come away empty-handed and with empty bowls. Let us expel him!
107.002. "Let us drive him out," they said.
107.003. Having dealt him many blows and broken his bowl over his head, they drove him out.
In the meantime, a merchant from Śrāvastī who was a friend of the householder Bodha arrived at Śiśumāragiri taking his merchandise.
He recognized him by the friendly greeting, the water-pot in his hand, and the familiar features of his face, and said: "Son, are you the son of the householder Bodha?
He replied: "Father, yes."
"I am his son, Durāgata.
Having remained silent for a moment, with eyes clouded by tears, he said: "Son, have those two, your mother and father, passed away?"
"Are they his kinsmen?
He replied, "Of them, some have passed away; others, remaining right here, do not even offer a word.
Are they his female and male slaves, laborers, and servants?"
Among them, some have passed away,
some have fled,
and some, having taken refuge with others right here, do not even offer a word.
Whatever wealth remained was also partially consumed by fire.
As for those merchant employees who, seeking profit, had taken merchandise and set out for other lands or across the great ocean, even among them, the merchandise of some became unsaleable.
Some there met with disaster through their own misconduct;
for some who had entered the middle of a wilderness, their goods were plundered by bandits;
and for some who had reached the vicinity of a city, their valuable cargo was seized by customs officials while they were examining the merchandise.
When some of them reached the city, those appointed by the king instigated trouble against them and seized all their property.
Others, having heard of his death, remained right there.
He, sighing long and hot, said: "Son, why do you not go to Śrāvastī?"
"Father, what will happen to one who goes there?
"Son, Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder, lives there; his son has married your sister."
"She will provide for your livelihood.
He said, "Father,
if that is so, then I shall go."
He gave him two kārṣāpaṇas and said, "Son,
sustain yourself for now with these two."
"Wait until I have disposed of my merchandise;
you shall go with me.
He then tied those two kārṣāpaṇas together and placed them inside the hem of his garment.

Due to the ripening of karma, they had forgotten [everything]. In that same state, he encountered something from somewhere and did not encounter something else; he remained there, oppressed by hunger.
107.021. When that merchant had disposed of his merchandise and taken up goods for trade, he set out, having forgotten Svāgata.
Svāgata also set out together with him. 107.022–107.023.
Eventually, those caravan traders began to quarrel.
The oxen began to fight.
The caravan leaders said, "Sirs,
look after the caravan!"
"Lest this ill-omened person have come here," they thought.
As they looked about, they saw him.
Having struck him with kicks, slaps, and other blows, and having seized him by the neck with a half-moon grip, they began to expel him.
107.025. He was expelled.
107.026. As he was being led out, he began to cry out.
107.026. Hearing that tumultuous noise, the caravan leader began to look around.
When he saw him being led out,
he said, "Sirs,
do not lead him out!"
"This is my friend's son," he said.
They replied, "O caravan leader,
it is because of him that the house of the householder Bodha— abounding in manifold wealth, along with his friends, associates, and kinsmen— has been ruined."
"How shall we go together with him?
In every respect, you are the master of the caravan. If he goes, [we shall go]."
"We will not go," they said.
The caravan leader said to him, "Son,
there will be opposition from the great multitude here."
"The caravan leaders have become agitated. You go first with your upper robe tucked up;
I shall set aside food for your sake."
107.031. His mind tormented by the suffering and dejection resulting from the power of his past misdeeds—a grief rivalling the loss of his parents—he remained silent with a tearful throat.
108.001. The caravan set out;
he too began to travel, gathering up his bedding.

108.001. That caravan leader, having bound her food in a leaf-cup, would place some of it on the ground, covering it with dust, and some he would cover with leaves from the branches of trees. 108.002. Of these, that which he placed on the ground—
He is devoured by jackals and other quadrupeds;
that which is on the branches of trees is devoured by birds and monkeys.
Then he mastered some [of the teachings] and did not master others.
It is impossible and out of the question that a being in his final existence should die prematurely before attaining a superior realization. With great difficulty, he reached Śrāvastī.
108.005. He rested outside Śrāvastī, near a well.
108.006. Just then, a maidservant belonging to his sister went there carrying a water-jar, seeking water.
108.007. She recognized him by the likeness of his face.
Having gazed at him for a long time, with a face dejected and distressed, she said, "Child,
are you the son of the householder Bodha of Śuśumāragiri?
He replied, "That is how my sisters know me."
108.009. With eyes clouded by tears and her throat choked with sobs, she struck her breast and began to ask in a piteous, distressed, and faltering voice:
"108.010. Have those two, your mother and father, passed away? They have passed away. 108.011. And what of those kinsmen?"
He said: "Of them as well, some have passed away,
some have fled,
and some remain right there and do not even give a word."
As for those female and male slaves, laborers, and servants,
some of them have died and some have run away.
Some remained right there, not relying on others and not uttering even a word.
As for the wealth that was there, some of it was consumed by fire, while some was taken away by other men; those seeking wealth set out for foreign lands and descended into the great ocean.
There too, the ship of some was wrecked; for some, their merchandise became unsaleable;
and some met with disaster right there through misconduct.
Some, while in the midst of a wilderness, had their goods plundered by bandits;

some, having reached the vicinity of a city, had their valuable property seized by customs officials while they were inspecting the goods; and some, having arrived at a town, had all their possessions taken away after officials appointed by the king had fabricated charges against them.
Some, having heard of his loss of life, remained right there.
She, sighing long and hot, said: "Stay right here until I inform your sister.
Having gone, she delivered her message to her.
"What kind of merchandise does he have? She replied, "How could he have merchandise?
He has a staff in his hand and an alms-bowl."
She gave him costly garments for his sake,
and having given him kārṣāpaṇas, she said: "He should be told that if either your nephew or your niece approaches you,
you should give those very kārṣāpaṇas to him alone."
"Lest he become an object of suspicion among his kinsmen," she thought.
Taking some garments and kārṣāpaṇa coins, she went to him and said, "These garments and kārṣāpaṇa coins have been sent to you by your sister.
She further said, "If your nephew or your niece should come here..."
"You should give him these kārṣāpaṇa coins.
Do not become an object of reproach among your kinsmen.
He replied, "That is indeed excellent."
Having said this, he remained silent.
The young woman departed.
He reflected: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has an extensive circle of kinsmen and attendants."
"Our father also has an extensive retinue.
He examines the news of each of them one by one.
There will be a long conversation with his sister."
"And because he was exhausted from the fatigue of the journey and afflicted by hunger, he was unable to do it.
'I will first eat my fill,' he thought.
Once satiated, he went to the garden and lay down for pleasant conversation."
108.031. It was the custom in Śrāvastī for men who plundered the parks to roam about every day.
108.032. Whenever they saw a sleeping man, they would kick him with their foot.
If he awakens,
they say this to him: "O man,
have you not heard that in Śrāvastī, men who plunder the parks are patrolling every day?"
If they see a sleeping man, they say, "Arise, go!
If he does not wake up, [they continue].
They depart after having stolen [the goods].
Though he was kicked by their feet, he did not wake up.
Having stolen [the goods], they departed.
109.003. Having awakened from his intoxication, once he looked, he saw that those very same Anantakas were standing there dressed as before.
109.004. Then his sister thought to herself, "He is taking far too long."
"Surely there must be a reason for this.
He sent that girl back again, saying, "Girl, go;
he is taking a long time."
"See why he has not come. She went and saw that he was standing there in that very same dress, looking like a thief.
She went back in great haste and said to her, "Noble lady,"
"He remains there, having been robbed while still wearing that very same dress.

She reflected: "If I allow him—who, by coming here, caused the destruction of Householder Bodha’s home, which was filled with manifold wealth along with his friends, relatives, and kinsmen—to enter here,"
"It is possible that I too shall meet with misfortune by going to my father-in-law's house through such misconduct;
he must not be allowed to enter here.
Having realized this, she also neglected him.
109.011. This too was forgotten due to the transgression of his past karma. He entered among the *kroḍamallakas*.
Wherever they entered seeking alms, [he followed].
In various places they were scolded and driven out.
Having fallen into despair, with empty hands and empty begging bowls, they returned to empty temples, pavilions, and the roots of trees.
There they asked one another, "Sirs,"
"Previously, wherever we went, we returned with full hands and full bowls.
Now, what is the reason that we have come here with empty hands and empty bowls, having fallen into despair?
Thereupon, some said, "Surely some unfortunate person has entered among us, because of whom we have come here with empty hands and empty bowls."
109.016. Others said, "Let us enter by dividing into two groups.
109.017. On the following day, they entered after having divided into two groups.
Among them, Svāgata was in one group.
Having been rebuked and driven out in that very manner, they returned having fallen into despair, with empty hands and empty bowls.
But those others returned with full hands and full bowls.
As for those who had returned with empty hands and empty bowls—
They split again into two groups and entered.
Of those, the group in whose midst Svāgata was likewise arrived with empty hands and empty bowls.
109.020. They split further into two groups in this manner until Svāgata and another Kroḍamallaka entered.
Those two arrived with empty hands and empty bowls, while the others arrived with full hands and full bowls.

109.022. All those bowl-beggars gathered together and began to consult one another: "Sirs, this unfortunate creature has entered among us, because of whom we have returned with empty hands and empty bowls. Let us expel him!
109.024. "Let us drive him out," they said.
109.024. Having dealt him many blows and broken the bowl upon his head, they drove him out.

In the meantime, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a meal at his home. He gave an order to his gatekeepers: "No one, not even a street-sweeper, is to be allowed entry until the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished eating.
Afterwards, I shall feed them."
109.027. Those who were his personal attendants and had taken refuge in his house all assembled together and began to enter. 109.028. They were stopped by the gatekeeper. 109.029. They said: "O man!"
"This householder is known by our very name as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada;
why then do you treat us with such disregard, asking, 'What is this?
He replied, 'The householder has given this command: "No one among the *kroḍamallakas* is to be admitted until the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished their meal.'"
109.032. "Later, I shall feed them.
109.032. They replied, "Sirs, we have never been detained before."
"Look at him, lest some ill-omened person have arrived here!
They began to search and, after a while, saw him standing hidden in a certain spot.
Then they raised a great clamor, saying, "Sirs, there is that ill-omened person; he is standing hidden!"
110.003. Having been struck by them with many blows, he was driven out; and in a state of intense agitation, they dealt him a blow on the head with a water-jar.
110.004. His head was shattered.
He turned back and began to lament.
110.005. Then, seizing him by his hands and feet, they threw him onto a heap of refuse, saying, "You ill-fated one, stay here!
He remained on that heap of refuse while blood flowed profusely from him.

110.006. Meanwhile, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went toward the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Blessed One saw Svāgata fallen upon a heap of refuse, afflicted by flies; his fingers were harsh and rough, his hair was long, his body was covered with dust, he was emaciated and weak, clad in soiled and tattered garments, with a broken head from which blood was flowing and covered with other wounds.
Having seen this, he then addressed the monks: "Monks, be satisfied with all rebirths into existence!
Be satisfied with all the requisites for rebirth into existence, for such is the state even of a being in their final existence!"
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Svāgata: "My son, do you desire the remains of the alms-bowl? "Blessed One, I do.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, the remains of Svāgata's alms-bowl must be set aside.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
110.015. Then the Blessed One went to where the meal was being prepared for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared before the community of monks. 110.016.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, [approached them].

Having satisfied and served [the Blessed One] with his own hands with excellent hard and soft foods, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
The Venerable Ānanda forgot to give the remains of that bowl to Svāgata.
110.019. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of non-forgetfulness.
110.020. [The food] was offered by the Blessed One. The Venerable Ānanda began to take the Blessed One’s bowl, when he saw that what remained in the bowl had not been set aside.
110.021. Upon seeing him, mindfulness arose;
then, realizing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), he began to weep.
The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, why are you weeping?
He replied, "Venerable Sir, never before have I ever disobeyed the command of the Blessed One.
[The Blessed One asked,] "What have you done? [He answered,] "I did not set aside the remains of the alms-food from Svāgata's bowl."
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, it was not that you failed to remember my command;
rather, those karmas of Svāgata alone—whose accumulations had been gathered and whose conditions had ripened—arose like a flood and were inevitable, such that you forgot them.
Enough with this despondency."
"Go, summon him.
He went and began to summon him;
many people gave their responses.

110.027. Svāgata had also forgotten that which the Blessed One had promised: "I shall set aside for you the remainder of my alms-bowl. He reflected: "Surely this person of meritorious deeds has been taken into the mind of the Blessed One, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, by his very name. The Venerable Ānanda went and informed the Blessed One.
110.029. "Welcome, Blessed One," they said, and many offered their greetings.
110.030. [Ānanda thought,] "I do not know whom I should summon.
The Blessed One said, "Go, Ānanda."
"Go and say: 'Let Svāgata, the son of the householder Bodha of Śuśumāragiri, come.
The venerable Ānanda went and called out in a loud voice: "Svāgata, the son of the householder Bodha of Śuśumāragiri, let him come!"
"Let him come.
Upon hearing his father's name, he remembered his own name.
Slowly rising by leaning upon his staff, he spoke this verse:
111.001. This cry of "Welcome! has vanished; from where, then, has it come here?
111.002. Surely there must be both the destruction of prosperity and the emergence of prosperity. //1//
111.003. O Omniscient One, you are the Protector of those who have gone to you for refuge.
111.004. Welcome to those noble ones who delight in your teaching!
"But I am devoid of fortune, abandoned by all my kinsmen;
pitiable, having reached a miserable state, pierced by the thorn of grief. Thus he spoke.
Then the Venerable Ānanda took him and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, welcome!
He, whose distress was born of hunger, was comforted by the Blessed One, who said to him: "Son,"
"Partake of this remnant in the bowl.

Seeing it, he reflected: "Even though I have been taken into account by the Blessed One, the teacher of the three worlds, through his divine power, nevertheless, only a small remnant in the bowl has been set aside for me."
"What shall I eat here? [he asked].
The Blessed One, knowing his thought with his own mind, said: "Child, even if you were to eat from a bowl as vast as the ocean, using morsels as large as Mount Sumeru,"
"Nevertheless, that inexhaustible [food] will not be consumed; eat as much as you please until you are satisfied.
He then ate until he was satisfied.
111.013. With his senses fully satisfied, he began to gaze upon the face of the Blessed One.
111.014. The Blessed One said, "Child, welcome; are you satisfied?
"I am satisfied, Blessed One."
"Child, if it is so, take this final mouthful; this bowl will disappear. He took that final mouthful.
He vanished.
Having delivered his instruction on the gift, the Blessed One departed.
That being, who was in his final existence, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
111.017. When the Blessed One had gone to the monastery, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
He too, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
The Blessed One reflected: "I shall send these flowers to him."
"His removal from this [state] must be performed.
Having understood this, he addressed Svāgata: "Dear Svāgata, do you have any kārṣāpaṇas?"
"There are none, Blessed One. Child, welcome;
look at the edge of my garment."
111.020. He began to look at the edge of his garment and saw two kārṣāpaṇas.
111.021. He said, "Blessed One, there are two kārṣāpaṇas."
"Child, go,
take blue lotuses from the presence of Gaṇḍaka the gardener, and then return. He went to his presence.
111.022. Seeing him from afar, he became agitated.
111.023. He reflected: "This man has arrived from a great distance;
surely some misfortune will befall me."
111.023. Having understood this, he spoke harshly: "You ill-begotten one, for what purpose have you come here?
111.024. He then recited a verse:
111.025. I have need of blue lotuses, nor indeed of other lotuses; 111.026.
for I am the messenger of the Lord of Sages, the renowned Omniscient One. (4)
Having said this, he began to turn back.
He too spoke this verse:
"Come, come, if you are a messenger of that Sage of peaceful soul."
He is worthy of worship by kings and gods; he is worthy of worship even by those most worthy of worship. //5//
Having said this, he asked: "Are you a messenger of the Buddha?
"I am a messenger of the Buddha.
"For what purpose have you come?"
"For the sake of flowers:
if you are a messenger of the Buddha,
take as much as you desire."
111.031. Having taken a bundle of blue lotuses, he came into the presence of the Blessed One and began to distribute them among the monks.
112.001. He proceeded to distribute them to the monks.
112.001. The monks did not accept it.
112.002. The Blessed One said: "Monks, you must accept the *sarvasaugandha* [perfume].
You must perform the removal of karma from his eyes."
The monks took them;
having taken them, they were in bloom.
By that means, he produced for the first time the previously unarisen "all-blue" (nīlakṛtsna) attainment.
112.003. Standing at the edge of the assembly, he saw those flowers and began to gaze at them even more intently.
112.004. For him, that "totality of the blue" (*nīlakṛtsna*) became manifest before his eyes.
112.005. Then the Blessed One said to him: "Child,..."
"Why do you not go forth? He replied, "I shall go forth, Blessed One.
The Blessed One granted him the going-forth, conferred full ordination, and gave him instructions for mental attention.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and moving; having struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction,
he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, for whom a clod of earth and gold were equal, whose mind was like space or the palm of a hand, who was the same toward an axe or sandalwood paste, who had split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, who had attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings, and who turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became one worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by Indra and Upendra.

112.011. Having attained arhatship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, at that moment he spoke this verse: 112.012–112.013. "Bound by the snares of skillful means by the Hero who perceives reality, I have been drawn out from suffering through his compassion, like an aged elephant from the mud. (6)
112.014. Previously I was "Welcome," but thereafter I became "Ill-come.
112.015. O Lord, having heard your supreme words, I have now come as one who has truly arrived. (7)
112.016. Now Svāgata has clearly become [one who is] well-arrived, not ill-arrived. 112.017. Now I maintain a golden body, free from outflows (*anāsrava*). (8)
112.018. Indeed, for those who desire heaven and liberation, they obtain the jewels;

112.019. the service of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who always seek one's welfare is the most excellent. (9) Thus it was said. 112.020. When the Venerable Svāgata had gone forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya,

Then a report spread throughout the surrounding area: "The ascetic Gautama has ordained that ill-behaved wrestler Durāgata. When the heretics heard this, they reviled, censured, and disputed it, saying: "Sirs, the ascetic Gautama says, 'My teaching is pleasing to all.'"
112.023. In this regard, what is meant by "the splendor of the neighborhood"? It refers to the fact that even those such as the Durāgatas and the Kroḍamallakas now go forth into homelessness.
In the meantime, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
The Blessed One reflected: "A great multitude of people is manifesting faith toward Mahāśrāvaka, who is like Mount Sumeru."
112.025. His virtues must be proclaimed; where should they be proclaimed?
Precisely where he has fallen.
112.026. Having understood this, he addressed Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata will travel on a journey through the Bharga country.
Whoever among you is able to travel on a journey with the Tathāgata through the Bhargas, let him take up his robes.'"

"Very well, venerable sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having done so, he announced to the monks: "Venerable sirs, the Blessed One will travel on tour through the Bharga country.
Whoever among you is able to travel on tour with the Blessed One through the Bharga country, let him take his robes."

112.031. Then the Blessed One—tamed, with a tamed retinue; peaceful, with a peaceful retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue; comforted, with a comforted retinue; disciplined, with a disciplined retinue; an Arhat, with a retinue of Arhats; free from passion, with a retinue free from passion;
gracious, with a gracious retinue—was like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle, or like an elephant surrounded by its young.

Like a lion surrounded by a pack of tigers; like a king of swans surrounded by a flock of swans; like Garuḍa surrounded by a host of birds; like a brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples; like a skilled physician surrounded by a multitude of patients;

like a hero surrounded by a troop of warriors; like a guide surrounded by a company of travelers; like a caravan leader surrounded by a host of merchants; like a guild-president surrounded by a body of citizens.

Like a provincial king surrounded by a host of ministers; like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons; like the moon surrounded by a host of stars; like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays; like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas; like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas;
like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas; like Dhanada surrounded by a host of yakṣas.

Surrounded by a host of asuras like Vemacitrī, like Śakra surrounded by the host of the Thirty-three Gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the host of the Brahmakāyika gods; like a calm ocean, like a rain-cloud filled with water, like an elephant in rut who has lost his passion;
with senses well-subdued and the movement of his deportment undisturbed, he was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

Adorned with the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), his body radiant, his form graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, he was like a moving mountain of jewels. Auspicious in every respect, he was endowed with the ten powers (*bala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the three unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). He was accompanied by great disciples such as Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Aniruddha, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Raivata.
Surrounded by another great community of monks, he approached Śuśumāragiri.
Traveling by stages on his journey,
he arrived at Śuśumāragiri and stayed there in the Bhīṣaṇikā Forest, in the Deer Park.

113.014. The brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Bharga country, had arrived at Śuśumāragiri and was staying there in the Mṛgadāva (Deer Park) in the Bhīṣaṇikā forest. 113.016. Having heard this, they gathered from group to group and assembly to assembly, departed from Śuśumāragiri, and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
The Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he became silent.

113.020. Then the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, they said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal at our home tomorrow."
113.022. The Blessed One consented to the request of the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri by remaining silent.

113.023. Then the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by his silence, rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and [departed] from the Blessed One.
...departed from his presence.

Then, that very night, the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri prepared pure and excellent hard and soft foods; rising early in the morning, they arranged seats and set out water-jars for the Blessed One.
They announced the time by means of a messenger: "It is time, Venerable One; the meal is prepared; may the Blessed One now do as he deems fit.

Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to where the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri were.
Having approached, he sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.

When the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri perceived that the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, was comfortably seated, they themselves, with their own hands, satisfied and served them with pure and excellent solid and soft foods.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served the Blessed One with pure and exquisite foods, both solid and soft, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, she took a very low seat and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
114.002. Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri with a discourse on the Dharma.
114.004. Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.

114.005. Then the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, by the Blessed One in various regions and in various settlements, those various wicked nāgas and wicked yakṣas have been subdued. But this nāga Aśvatīrthika, venerable sir, is an enemy to us who are without enmity, an adversary to us who are without rivals, and a malicious one to us who are without malice. He constantly destroys our crops as they grow."

"Women, men, boys, girls, cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep— oh, would that the Blessed One, out of compassion, might discipline them! The Blessed One consented to the request of the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri.
114.010. He consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One, having consented to the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri by his silence, rose from his seat and departed.
114.011. Then the Blessed One, having gone to the monastery, sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
114.012. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, and announce this to the monks:
'Distribute the voting sticks (śalākā) to those among you who are able to subdue the nāga Aśvatīrthika.'"
"Let him take a voting stick.

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having informed the community of monks, he began to distribute the voting sticks among the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Blessed One did not take a voting stick.
The elder monks began to reflect: "For what reason did the Blessed One not take a voting stick?
They saw that he intended to proclaim the virtues of the venerable Svāgata. They, too, did not take one.
The venerable Svāgata began to reflect: "For what reason has the Blessed One not taken a voting stick (*śalākā*), nor have the elder monks?
He saw that [the Blessed One] desired to proclaim his virtues. "Therefore, I shall fulfill the Teacher's intention."
"I shall take the voting stick," he said.
Then, leaving half of his seat and extending out his arm like the trunk of an elephant, he took the stick.
The Blessed Buddhas are those who know and those who inquire.
114.021. The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, by which monk was the voting stick taken?
He replied: "By Svāgata, Venerable Sir.
The Blessed One said: "Go, Ānanda."
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! Speak thus: 'That is a wicked nāga; you must guard your faculty of the body.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the venerable Svāgata.
Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Svāgata: "Venerable Svāgata, the Blessed One has spoken thus: 'That is a wicked nāga;
you must guard your faculty of the body.'"
He said, "Venerable Ānanda, the Teacher’s command is not to be transgressed.
However, if Jambudvīpa were filled with such nāgas as the nāga Aśvatīrthika, like a thicket of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds,"
"Nevertheless, they would not even be able to move a single hair of mine,
let alone cause an obstruction to my faculty of the body, such as the Naga Aśvatīrthika.
Having said, "May you be well," the Venerable Ānanda departed.
114.029. Then, at the end of that very night, in the forenoon, the venerable Svāgata dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śuśumāragiri for alms.
114.030. Having walked for alms in Śuśumāragiri, he approached the abode of the nāga Aśvatīrthika.
114.031. The nāga Aśvatīrthika saw the venerable Svāgata from afar.
Having seen him, he reflected again: "What does this wretched ascetic have to do with my death that he comes to my house?
Then he reflected once more: "He is a guest;
let him come for now."

115.001. Then the Venerable Svāgata, having gone to that lake, set aside his bowl and robe in a secluded spot, washed his feet, rinsed his hands, strained the water, gathered some withered leaves, and sat down; he then began to perform his meal.
115.003. The nāga Aśvatīrthika, considering him a guest, overlooked him.

The Venerable Svāgata reflected: "Evil nāgas do not come to subjection unless they have been provoked. Thinking, "I shall provoke him," he washed his alms-bowl and poured the water from that bowl into the lake.
115.005. He became agitated.
115.005. He reflected: "This ascetic was overlooked by me as he was coming; he was also overlooked while eating."
"He has poured out leftover water in my house!
I shall reduce him to nothing but a name!"—thus he was possessed by intense fury.
Rising into the air above, he began to hurl weapons such as discuses, arrows, axes, and javelins at the Venerable Svāgata.
The venerable Svāgata entered into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Divine flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and *mandārava* blossoms—began to fall upon his body.
Then the nāga Aśvatīrthika began to rain down a shower of glowing coals.
115.010. Even those [dust particles] began to fall upon his body, having turned into divine *māndāraka* flowers.
115.011. The nāga Aśvatīrthika began to rain down dust.
115.012. Even that began to fall, having turned into divine powders of agallochum and powders of *tamāla* leaves.
115.013. The nāga Aśvatīrthika, through the power of his obsession with anger, began to emit smoke.
The venerable Svāgata, too, through the power of his supernatural might, began to emit smoke.
115.014. The nāga Aśvatīrthika, through the power of his obsession with anger, burst into flames.
The Venerable Svāgata also entered the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu*).

Thus, through the power of the anger of the Nāga Aśvatīrthika and the power of the Venerable Svāgata’s supernatural might (*ṛddhi*), a great radiance appeared; seeing which, the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri were thrown into a state of agitation.
They began to look here and there, saying: "Sirs, this Blessed One is subduing the nāga Aśvatīrthika;
come, let us go see him!"
115.018. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings emerged.
115.019. Even while remaining right there, the monks began to gaze at that sublime radiance.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples, who frequently enter the fire-element (tejodhātu), namely—"
115.021. When the Naga Aśvatīrthika had become free from intoxication and pride and his weapons were exhausted, he began to flee. 115.022. The Venerable Svāgata then conjured up a fire on all sides.
115.022. In whichever direction the nāga Aśvatīrthaka goes, he sees that very direction as burning, blazing, set ablaze, and become a single mass of flame.

115.023. Confounded on all sides by the fire of his own emanation, he is without protection and sees everything as unpeaceful, except for the vicinity of the venerable Svāgata, which is peaceful and cooled.
He approached the Venerable Svāgata;
having approached, he said this to the Venerable Svāgata: "Venerable Svāgata, why do you harass me?"
He said, "I am subject to old age; I do not harm you, but rather you yourself harm me.
Had I not attained such a multitude of virtues as these,"
"Today you would have made me nothing but a name.
He replied, "Venerable Svāgata, welcome;
please give your command."
"What should I do?
"Noble sir, go into the presence of the Blessed One and receive the precepts for taking refuge."
He said, "Venerable Svāgata, welcome; it is well.
I shall do so."
115.030. Then the venerable Svāgata, having taken the nāga Aśvatīrthika with him, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
115.031. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
115.032. Seated to one side, the venerable Svāgata said this to the Blessed One: "This is that nāga Aśvatīrthika."
There, the Blessed One addressed the nāga Aśvatīrthika: "My good sir, you were born in this inferior animal womb because of your past misconduct.
Now, moreover, you are intent on killing and striking others; you make your living by taking the lives of other beings and by obstructing their lives."
"When you have passed away from here, what will be your destination, what will be your rebirth, and what will be your future state?"
He said, "Blessed One,
give the command; what should be done by me?"
The Blessed One said, "Receive from me the precepts of taking refuge, and grant fearlessness to the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri.
He replied, "I go for refuge to the Blessed One."
"I take up the precepts,
and from this day forward, I grant safety to the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri.
Then the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri, taking with them a great abundance of provisions, approached the Blessed One.
116.009. Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, has the nāga Aśvatīrthika been converted by the Blessed One?
The Blessed One replied: "Brahmins and householders, the nāga Aśvatīrthika has not been converted by me."
"Rather, it was by the monk Svāgata.
"By which one, venerable sir?
"By the son of the householder Bodha, a resident of this very place."
The world desires prosperity and is averse to misfortune.
Regarding this, some say, "He is the son of our brother," while others say, "He is our nephew."
Others said, "He is the son of our friend.

Then the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, they said this to the Blessed One: "May you consent to [our invitation]."
"The Blessed One, having accepted the invitation of the venerable Svāgata, will partake of a meal together with the community of monks for seven days.
The Blessed One consented to the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri by remaining silent.
Then, the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by his silence, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
116.020. On Mount Śuśumāra, there was a certain brahmin snake-charmer who was a friend of the householder Bodha. Fleeing out of fear of the nāga Aśvatīrthika, he went to Śrāvastī.
