There, King Prasenajit of Kośala appointed him as a trusted official over the elephant corps.
116.022. On some business or other, he arrived at Mount Śuśumāragiri.
He heard that the nāga Aśvatīrthika had been tamed by the monk Svāgata, the son of the householder Bodha.
Having heard this, he approached the venerable Svāgata.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Svāgata and sat down to one side.
That brahmin said this to the venerable Svāgata: "Venerable Svāgata, may you please accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow. The venerable Svāgata replied: "Brahmin," [he said].
"Having approached me, the brahmins and householders of Śuśumāragiri invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal for seven days.
I did not accept.
The brahmin said: 'Noble sir,..."
"If you do not consent now,
then when you have gone to Śrāvastī, you must first accept almsfood at my house."
He replied, "So be it.
Having paid homage at his feet, the brahmin departed.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Śuśumāragiri for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Śrāvastī.
116.031. Wandering on his journey in due course, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
He stayed in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
116.032. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One, while wandering through the country of Bharga, had arrived at Śrāvastī.
"He dwells right here; this is our very own grove.
Having heard this, he departed from Śrāvastī and approached the Blessed One.
Upon arrival, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
117.003. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
117.004. Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
117.005. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One.
Having bowed down to the Blessed One, he said this: "May the Blessed One consent to take his meal tomorrow at my home, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
He departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
That brahmin heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the Bharga country, had arrived there and was staying right there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having heard this, he approached the Venerable Svāgata.
Having approached, he said this to the venerable Svāgata: "May the noble one consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow.
The venerable Svāgata consented to that brahmin by remaining silent.
Then, perceiving through his silence that the venerable Svāgata had consented, the brahmin rose from his seat and departed.
117.014. Then, on that very night, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
Rising early in the morning, he arranged seats, set out water-jars, and informed the Blessed One of the time through a messenger:
"It is time, venerable sir."
"The meal is prepared; may the Blessed One now consider it the right time.

Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the residence of Anāthapiṇḍada.
That brahmin had also prepared a sumptuous meal for the venerable Svāgata.
117.019. The venerable Svāgata, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of that brahmin.
117.020. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared for him.
117.021. Once seated to one side, the venerable Svāgata was regaled with excellent food by that brahmin.
That brahmin reflected: "The noble Svāgata has consumed the excellent food;
he will not digest it. I shall give him a drink."
117.023. Having understood this, he said to the Venerable Svāgata: "Noble one, have you finished eating that excellent food? Drink some beverage.
117.024. "Drink the beverage."
"It will digest the drink," [he said].
He replied, "Excellent;
I shall do so."
117.024. Having prepared a beverage, he threw an elephant's ichor-finger into it.
117.025. The knowledge and vision of Arhats does not function without focused attention. The Venerable Svāgata drank that beverage.
117.026. Then, having performed the formal assignment of the gift, he set out for the streets of Śrāvastī, which were covered with mats of reeds.
117.027. Having passed through them, he was struck by the heat of the sun; overcome by intoxication, he fell to the ground.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of non-forgetfulness.
117.028. The Blessed One created a hut made of *suparṇika* grass, thinking, "Lest someone, seeing this, should manifest a lack of faith in the Teaching.

117.029. Anāthapiṇḍada, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent solid foods. 117.030. Having in many ways personally satisfied and served them, he [waited upon] the Blessed One when he had finished eating.
Knowing that the Blessed One had washed his hands and set aside his bowl, he took a very low seat and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
He proceeded by stages until he reached that region.
118.002. Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn those miraculous feats, addressed the monks: "Monks, this is that monk Svāgata, by whom the nāga Aśvatirthika—who was so fierce—was subdued.
118.003. Is he now able to remove even the poison of one who has eaten unwholesome food?
"No, Venerable Sir."
"Monks, these and other such dangers exist in the drinking of intoxicants.
Therefore, a monk must neither drink intoxicants nor give them to others.
Then the Blessed One, having awakened the venerable Svāgata who was asleep under the influence of intoxicants, said this to him: "Svāgata, what is this?"
"It was not through my attention, Blessed One; it was not through my attention, Sugata.
Then the Blessed One, taking the venerable Svāgata with him, went to the monastery and sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

118.007. Having sat down, he addressed the monks: "O monks, designating me as your teacher, you must not drink intoxicants, nor give them away, even to the extent of a drop on the tip of a blade of kusha grass."

118.009. The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Svāgata, by which he was born into a wealthy family of great riches and great enjoyments?
What karma was performed by which he became a wrestler?"
How did the designation "Durāgata" come about? What karma was performed by which he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions,
and was declared foremost among those who enter the fire-element concentration?

The Blessed One said: "Monks, by Svāgata himself were these actions performed and accumulated; their conditions have been gathered, they have reached maturity, they stand before him like a surging flood, and they are inevitable.
By Svāgata were these actions performed and accumulated.
Who else shall experience them?"
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.

Actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the element of wind, but rather they ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit. //10//

118.020. Once upon a time, monks, there lived in a certain mountain village a householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
118.021. On another occasion, surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, and relatives, and accompanied by his household, he went out to a park.

118.022. When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, frequent remote lodgings, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
118.023. Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small town.
118.024. Exhausted from the fatigue of the road and suffering from an imbalance of the bodily elements, he entered that park seeking alms.
118.025. Upon seeing him, the householder became agitated with resentment.
118.025. He gave an order to his attendants: "Sirs, expel this renunciant!
118.026. Not one among them dared to expel him.

118.027. Overcome by intense resentment, that householder seized the Great Being by the neck himself and expelled him, saying, "You shall dwell among the wrestlers! 118.028. With his strength exhausted, he fell to the ground.
He reflected: "This poor householder has been ruined and brought to ruin.
I must effect his rescue.
Having understood this, he rose into the air above and began to perform the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
118.030. The supernatural power of an ordinary person acts quickly to win over others.

118.031. Like a tree cut at its root, he fell at his feet and said: "Descend, descend, O one most worthy of offerings! Grant me, who am submerged in the mire of my own evil conduct, the hand that shall pull me out."
He descended for the sake of favoring him.

Having performed worship and honor for him, he made this aspiration: "Since I have committed an injury toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may I not be a partaker of the fruit of this action."

119.002. "As for the assistance that has been rendered, by this root of merit may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, and may I become a recipient of such qualities as these."
And may I, rather than being superior to this [teacher], please the Teacher who is even more distinguished than him, and may I not displease him.
The Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, what do you think? That householder was none other than the bhikṣu Svāgata at that time and on that occasion.
Because he performed acts of service for the pratyekabuddha,"
Because of that, he was born into a family that was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
however, because of the harm he committed, for five hundred births he was born as a pig-herder.
Even now, in his final existence, he was born as that very same Kroḍamallaka.
Because of the vow he made, he has gone forth in my teaching and, through the abandonment of all afflictions, has realized arhatship.

119.009. "I have pleased, and never displeased, a Teacher who is far more distinguished than hundreds of thousands of millions of Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, I went forth as a monk. It was under a certain monk that I went forth."
He was declared by the Blessed One, Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, to be the foremost among those who frequently enter the fire-element.
There, he practiced the holy life for as long as he lived,
yet he did not attain any collection of spiritual qualities.

119.013. At the time of his death, he began to make this aspiration: "By whatever root of merit I have cultivated the holy life under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed object of offerings, yet no quality or virtue was attained by me—by this root of merit, may I become that very young brahmin Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One: 'You shall become...'"
"Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will be a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Śākyamuni.
Having gone forth in his teaching, I shall realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Just as my preceptor was designated by the Blessed One, the Samyaksambuddha Kāśyapa, as the foremost among those who frequently enter the fire-element concentration,"

"In this way, may that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Sovereign of the Śākyas, also designate me as the foremost among those who frequently enter the fire-element. By the power of that vow, the Tathāgata has now designated me as the foremost among those who frequently enter the fire-element. Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [you should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure.
Thus, O monks, should you train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
119.025. Thus ends the thirteenth [tale] in the glorious Divyāvadāna, titled "The Story of Svāgata."
********** Avadāna 14 ********** 120.001. The Story of the Sow (Sūkarikāvadāna).

120.002. It is indeed the nature of things that for a son of the gods subject to falling from his celestial state, five portents appear: his unstained garments become soiled; [the remaining portents follow].
His unfading garlands wither,
a foul odor emanates from his body,
and sweat breaks out from both armpits.
A son of the gods subject to the law of decay finds no stability on his own seat.
Then, a certain son of the gods subject to the law of decay rolls upon the ground;
having rolled about, he speaks thus: "Alas, Mandākinī!"
Alas, Puṣkariṇī! Alas, Vāpī! Alas, Caitraratha!
Alas, Pāruṣyaka! Alas, Nandana Grove! Alas, Miśrakāvana!
Alas, Pāriyātraka! Alas, Puṇḍrakambala-śilā!
Alas, Devasabhā!
"Alas, Sudarśana!
he lamented most piteously.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, saw that son of the gods rolling and tossing about excessively upon the ground.
Having seen him, he approached where that son of the gods was.
Having approached, he said this to that son of the gods: "Alas, my friend, why are you rolling and tossing about so excessively upon the ground?"
You lament most piteously: "Alas, Mandākinī! Alas, Puṣkiriṇī!
Alas, Vāpī!"
Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, Pāruṣyaka! Alas, Nandana Grove!
Alas, Miśrakāvana! Alas, Pāriyātraka! Alas, Pāṇḍukambalaśilā!
"Alas, the assembly of the gods!
Alas, Sudarśana! you lament most piteously.

When this was said, the son of the gods spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "O Kauśika, having experienced divine happiness here, on the seventh day from now, I shall [be reborn] in the city of Rājagṛha in the womb of a sow."
"In that place, I must consume excrement and urine for many years.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, out of compassion, said this to that son of the gods: "Come, friend, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds."
"Go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of all things free from passion;
go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of all assemblies.
Then that son of the gods, terrified by the fear of rebirth in the animal realm and terrified by the fear of death, said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "O Kauśika, I take refuge in the Buddha."
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost among things free from passion; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost among assemblies; I go for refuge to the Best of Bipeds.
120.019. Then that son of the gods, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, passed away and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
120.021. It is indeed the nature of things that the knowledge and vision of the gods extends downward but not upward.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, looked toward that son of the gods, wondering, "Has this son of the gods been reborn in the womb of the sow, or not?
When he saw that he had not been reborn among animals or hungry ghosts, [he was relieved].
He sees that [the being] has been reborn in the hells; he sees that it has not been reborn there;
he sees that it has been reborn in the commonality of human beings.
He was not reborn there.
He began to look toward the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
yet even there he did not see him.
120.025. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, filled with curiosity, approached the Blessed One.
120.026. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
120.026. Seated to one side, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "In this regard, venerable sir..."
I saw a certain son of the gods, subject to the law of falling, rolling upon the ground and lamenting most piteously: "Alas, Mandākinī!
Alas, Puṣkiriṇī!"
Alas, Lake Mānasa!
Alas, Caitraratha Grove!
Alas, Pāruṣyaka Grove!
Alas, Nandana Grove! Alas, Miśraka Grove! Alas, Pāriyātraka!
"Alas, the Pāṇḍukambala stone! Alas, the assembly hall of the gods! Alas, Sudarśana!"
120.029. I said this to him: "Friend, why do you grieve so excessively, lament, weep, beat your breast, and fall into a state of confusion?
He replied: "O Kauśika, having abandoned divine happiness, on the seventh day from now I shall be reborn in the city of Rājagṛha in the womb of a sow.
There, for many years, I shall have to consume excrement and urine."
I say this to him: "Come, friend, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds;
go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion; go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies."

He spoke thus: "O Kauśika, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds; I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies."
121.004. Having spoken thus, that son of the gods passed away.
121.005. "Venerable sir, where has this son of the gods been reborn?
The Blessed One said, "Kauśika, there are gods called Tuṣita, for whom all desires are fulfilled."

121.006. There that god rejoices, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels here. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, with a joyful mind, at that time spoke this verse: 121.008. Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to a state of misery.
Having abandoned human bodies, they resort to divine bodies. //1//
121.010. Those who go for refuge to the Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth; 121.011. having abandoned human bodies, they abide in divine bodies. (2)
121.012. Those who go for refuge to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil rebirth; 121.013. having abandoned human bodies, they dwell in celestial bodies. (3)
121.014. Then the Blessed One, commending the speech of Śakra, lord of the gods, said this: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil destiny;
having cast off human bodies, they abide in divine bodies. (4)
121.018. Those who go for refuge to the Dharma do not go to a state of misery;
121.019. having abandoned human bodies, they dwell in celestial bodies. (5)
121.020. Those who go for refuge to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil rebirth; 121.021. having abandoned human bodies, they attend upon divine bodies. (6)

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and with palms joined in reverent salutation, paid homage to the Blessed One and vanished right there.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced and praised his words.
121.025. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Sūkarikāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 15 ********** 122.001. The Avadāna of the Prophecy Concerning the Wheel-Turning King.
122.002. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
122.002. It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while they are living, remaining, and maintaining themselves, that there are stūpas for their hair and nails.
When the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are in seclusion, the monks, having performed worship at the stūpas of hair and nails, some enter for alms.
Some experience the bliss of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, gladdened his mind by recollecting the Tathāgata according to his characteristics:
"That Blessed One is indeed the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One."
“The Teacher, the charioteer of men to be tamed, the Buddha, the Blessed One, [is the teacher] of gods and humans.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
The Blessed One saw that monk prostrating with his entire body at the stūpa of the hair and nails, his mind full of serene faith.
Having seen him, he addressed the monks: "Monks, do you see this monk prostrating with his entire body at the hair-and-nail stūpa, his mind full of serene faith?
"Yes, Venerable Sir.
"By this monk, as much ground as has been traversed—downward eighty thousand *yojanas* as far as the golden wheel (*kāñcanacakra*)—within this interval,"
"As many as there are grains of sand, so many thousands of universal monarchies (cakravarti-rājya) must this monk enjoy.
Then, it occurred to those monks: "It is impossible to count the grains of sand even in a pit the size of a man;
how much more so for those reaching eighty thousand yojanas down to the golden wheel?"
"Who is able to wander in saṃsāra for such a long time?
Then those monks no longer began to perform services at the Hair-and-Nail Stūpa.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of those monks with his own mind, addressed the monks: "Without beginning or end..."
"Monks, for beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, and bound by the bolt of craving, as they run and wander through the long course of saṃsāra,
no prior limit of this suffering is discerned."

The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Blessed One, regarding what was said by the Blessed One—that this monk has such a mass of merit—where, O Venerable One, will such a mass of merit reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total depletion?
"Upāli, I do not perceive anywhere outside of this [community] any harm or injury such as that which a fellow practitioner inflicts upon another fellow practitioner."
"In that regard, Upāli, these great roots of merit undergo diminution, exhaustion, and total depletion.
Therefore, Upāli, you should train yourself in this way: 'We shall not allow our minds to become corrupted even toward a burnt pillar.'"
How much more so, then, when the body is endowed with consciousness?
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in his words.
122.027. Thus ends the fifteenth [tale] in the glorious Divyāvadāna, concerning a certain monk who was prophesied to become a universal monarch.
********** Avadāna 16 ********** 123.001. Divyāvadāna 16: The Story of the Young Parrot (Śukapotakāvadāna). 123.002. The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada obtained two young parrots.
He took them home, spoke to them, nourished them, raised them, and taught them human speech.
The Venerable Ānanda frequently came to them and delivered a Dharma teaching for the realization of the Four Noble Truths—namely, "This is suffering," and so forth.
"This is the origin of suffering,
this is the cessation of suffering,
and this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
123.005. Even the most senior monks—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Raivata, and others—would go to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
123.007. As they went there from time to time, those two young parrots came to know their names.
123.008. Then, on another occasion, the Venerable Śāriputra arrived at the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
123.011. Those two young parrots saw the Venerable Śāriputra.
123.009. Having seen him, they addressed their own people: "The venerable elder Śāriputra is coming;
prepare a seat for him."
123.010. Having seen the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Raivata, and the venerable Ānanda, they said, "Here comes our teacher Ānanda;
prepare a seat for him. 123.012.
Then, at another time, the Blessed One arrived at the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

123.012. Those two young parrots saw the Blessed One approaching from afar—gracious, inspiring, with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind, endowed with supreme mental serenity, blazing with splendor like a golden sacrificial pillar.
123.014. Having seen him, they quickly addressed their own people: "The venerable Blessed One is coming!"
"Prepare a seat for him," they cried out with joyful and sweet voices.

Then the Blessed One, having entered for their sake, sat down upon the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One established the two young parrots in the precepts of taking refuge through a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.
123.018. Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the two young parrots and the household folk with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
123.019. While those two were living among the household folk, they became negligent in their conduct and were seized by a cat.
123.020. With their faces distraught as their vital organs were being torn apart and their joints were being severed, they cried out, "Homage to the Buddha!"
Having said, "Homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha," they passed away and were reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
123.022. Then, in a certain place, the Blessed One smiled.
123.022. The venerable Ānanda saw the Blessed One manifesting a smile.
Having seen him, he spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition."
"Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting a smile?
"It is so, Ānanda; it is so.
Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause and a condition."
"Ānanda, did you see those two young parrots?
I saw them, Venerable Sir. Ānanda, as soon as I had departed, those two young parrots were deprived of life by a living creature, a cat."
123.027. Having passed away with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, they were reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
123.029. Then, a great many monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken their bowls and robes, entered Śrāvastī for alms.

123.030. While wandering for alms in Śrāvastī, a great many monks heard that in the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada there were two young parrots saying: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma!"
"Salutation to the Saṃgha; [these two] were killed by a cat.

Having heard this, and having again entered Śrāvastī for alms, they finished their meal, returned from their alms-round after the meal, put away their bowls and robes, washed their feet, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the many monks said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, here we, many monks—as before—[saw] two young parrots in the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, [who were saying]: 'Homage to the Buddha!'"
"Having uttered, 'Homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha,' they were deprived of life by a living cat.
Venerable Sir, what is their destination?"
"What will be their rebirth? What is their future destiny?
The Blessed One said: "Monks, as the result of that taking of refuge, those two young parrots will be reborn thirty-six times among the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm."
Thirty-six times among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, and the Tuṣita gods;
They are reborn among the gods who delight in emanations (*nirmāṇarati*) and those who wield power over the emanations of others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*).
Then, after those beings have passed away from the six classes of gods belonging to the realm of desire, they [attain] their final existence in their last birth.
In their final existence, having obtained a human birth, they will fully awaken to the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha;
Dharma and Sudharma will become Pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, monks, hearing the Dharma has great fruit and brings great benefits.
How much more so, then, the teaching of the Dharma or the realization of the Dharma?
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall take delight in hearing the Dharma.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
124.015. Thus ends the sixteenth story in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Story of the Young Parrot.
********** Avadāna 17 ********** 125.001. The Legend of Māndhātṛ/ 125.002.
Thus have I heard:
125.002. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī on the bank of the Markaṭahrada, in the Gabled Hall.
125.003. Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Vaiśālī for alms.
125.004. Having walked for alms in Vaiśālī and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after the meal, put away his bowl and robe, and approached the Cāpāla Shrine.
Having approached, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.

There, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, Vaiśālī is delightful, as are the land of the Vrjis, the Cāpāla shrine, the Saptāmra grove, the Bahupatra grove, the Gautama banyan tree, the Śālavana grove, the Dhurānikṣepana site, and the Makuṭabandhana shrine of the Mallas."
125.008. Variegated is Jambudvīpa; sweet is the life of human beings.
Ānanda, for anyone by whom the four bases of psychic power have been cultivated, developed, and practiced extensively, [there is no difficulty in attaining mastery].
If he so desired, Ānanda, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
For the Tathāgata, Ānanda, the four bases of psychic power have been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed.
If the Tathāgata so desired, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda remained silent.

A second and even a third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, Vaiśālī is delightful, as are the Vṛji lands, the Cāpāla shrine, the Saptāmra grove, the Bahupatra grove, the Gautama banyan tree, the Śālavana grove, and Dhuranikṣepana."
The Makuṭabandhana Caitya of the Mallas; Jambudvīpa is variegated,
and the life of humans is sweet.
"Ānanda, whoever has cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the four bases of psychic power can,
if they so desire, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata has cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the four bases of psychic power."
"If the Tathāgata so desires, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
For a second and even a third time, the Venerable Ānanda remained silent. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "The monk Ānanda has been overcome by Māra, the Evil One."
Since even now, when the coarse sign of light has been manifested as many as three times, he is unable to discern that sign—
just as he was previously made obscure by Māra, the Evil One—
the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda."
"Reside depending on the root of one tree or another;
let us not both be dwellers in a crowded place.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having so agreed, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for his midday rest.
125.022. That Māra, the Evil One, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
125.023. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One pass into final nirvāṇa; it is now the time for the Sugata’s final nirvāṇa."
125.024. "Why do you speak thus, O wicked one: 'May the Blessed One pass into parinirvāṇa; it is the time for the Sugata’s parinirvāṇa'?
Venerable sir, there was this one occasion: the Blessed One was staying at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having recently attained perfect enlightenment."
125.026. So I approached the Blessed One; having approached him, I said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One pass into final nirvāṇa; the time for the Sugata’s final nirvāṇa has arrived."

The Blessed One spoke thus: "O Evil One, I shall not enter final nirvana as long as my disciples have not become disciplined, proficient, and confident; as long as they are not capable of refuting, through the Dharma, various opposing disputants as they arise."
"Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās shall be those who bring your own doctrine to full purification.
They will practice the holy life extensively, making it widespread and well-established among many people, correctly proclaimed as far as the realms of gods and humans.

At present, O Venerable One, the Blessed One’s disciples are wise, discerning, disciplined, and confident; they are capable of refuting, by means of the Dharma, whatever opposing doctrines may arise."
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen are those who will bring your own doctrine to its complete purification.
Your holy life has been widely propagated, made popular among many people, and correctly proclaimed as far as the realms of gods and humans.
Therefore, I say this: "May the Blessed One pass into parinirvāṇa."
"It is the time for the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata.
O Evil One, be of little concern;
for now, after the passing of three months from this day, the Tathāgata will attain Parinirvāṇa in the realm of Nirvāṇa without remainder."
Then this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "Alas, the ascetic Gautama is about to attain final nirvāṇa!"
Having understood this, he—elated, satisfied, joyful, exultant, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness—vanished right there.
126.007. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Who is the one to be converted in the presence of the Tathāgata?
It is Supriya, the king of the gandharvas, and Subhadra, the wandering mendicant.
After the passing of three months of the rainy season, their faculties will have reached maturity, or they will be established in happiness."
126.009. It is possible for a Tathāgata to discipline one who is to be disciplined by a Śrāvaka, but it is not possible for a Śrāvaka to discipline one who is to be disciplined by a Tathāgata.

126.010. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were now to enter such a state of meditative concentration that, with my mind thus composed, I might sustain the formative forces of vitality (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) and relinquish the formative forces of life (*āyus-saṃskāra*)?

126.011. Thereupon, the Blessed One entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he began to sustain the formative forces of vitality and relinquish the formative forces of life.
126.012. Immediately upon the sustaining of the formative forces of vitality, there was a great earthquake, the falling of meteors, and the blazing of the quarters of the sky.

In the sky, the drums of the gods resounded. Immediately after the life-formations had been relinquished, six omens appeared among the gods of the desire realm: the flowering trees withered, and the jewel-trees withered.
The trees laden with ornaments were shattered, thousands of palaces trembled,
and the peaks of Mount Sumeru crumbled.
The divine musical instruments were struck.
Then the Blessed One, having arisen from that meditative absorption, at that moment spoke this verse:
"The Sage, casting off both the equal and the unequal, as well as the arising and the formative forces (saṃskāra)."
Delighting in the internal, composed in meditation, he is like a chick within its eggshell. //1//

126.020. Immediately after the life-force formations had been relinquished, the gods of the six classes of the desire realm made a formal agreement and approached the Blessed One to see him and pay him homage.
126.021. The Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma that many hundreds of thousands of deities perceived the truths; having perceived the truths, they returned to their own abodes.
126.022. Immediately after the life-forces had been relinquished, many hundreds of thousands of seers arrived from mountain clefts and mountain caves.

126.023. They were ordained by the Blessed One with the words, "Come, monks; lead the holy life," and they became renunciants. 126.024. By applying themselves with diligence and striving, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
126.024. Immediately after the life-formations had been relinquished, many nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas approached the Blessed One in order to behold him.
126.026. The Blessed One gave them such a teaching of the Dharma that many nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas took up the training precepts of going for refuge, and so forth.
126.028. Then, in the evening, the venerable Ānanda rose from his meditative seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for this great earthquake?
"Ānanda, there are these eight causes and eight reasons for a great earthquake."
126.031. What are the eight?
Ānanda, this great earth is established upon the waters;
the waters are established upon the wind.
The wind is established in space.
Ānanda, there comes a time when uneven winds blow in space and agitate the waters.
The waters, being agitated, cause the earth to tremble.
Ānanda, this is the first cause, the first condition for a great earthquake. Furthermore, Ānanda, there is a monk who possesses great supernormal power and great majesty.
127.003. Desiring it, he causes the earth to tremble.
127.004. A deity becomes possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty;
she too sustains a limited perception of earth and an immeasurable perception of water.
She too, desiring it, causes the earth to quake.
This is the second cause, the second condition for a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda:
At the time when the Bodhisattva descends from the Tuṣita host of gods into his mother’s womb, at that moment a great earthquake occurs,
and this entire world becomes suffused with a sublime radiance.

127.008. Those intermediate spaces between worlds—blind, dark, shrouded in gloom, and enveloped in thick darkness, where even these sun and moon, despite such great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not experience their light—those too, at that time, become suffused with a sublime radiance.
And those beings who have been reborn there, [perceive it].
Seeing one another through that light, those beings perceive: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here;
other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here.
Ānanda, this is the third cause, the third condition for a great earthquake of the earth.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at the time when the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother’s womb,
at that very moment a great earthquake occurs, and this entire world becomes suffused with a sublime radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— which are blind, shrouded in darkness, and enveloped in thick gloom, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite their such great majesty, do not experience their light— [become illuminated].
At that time, they too become suffused with a sublime radiance.
There, those beings who have been reborn, by means of that light, see one another as beings and recognize: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here."
"Other beings, venerable sirs, have also been reborn here.
Ānanda, this is the fourth cause and the fourth condition for a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at the time when the Bodhisattva attains unsurpassed knowledge...
Then, at that time, a great earthquake occurs,
and this entire world becomes suffused with a sublime radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— which are blind, shrouded in darkness, and enveloped in thick gloom, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite being so powerful and so majestic, cannot reach with their light— [become illuminated].
They do not experience it [as such],
yet at that time even they become suffused with a sublime radiance.
As for those beings who have been reborn there, [they too perceive it].
Seeing one another through that light, those beings perceive each other, thinking: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here;
other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here.
Ānanda, this is the fifth cause, the fifth condition for a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at the time when the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects,
at that very moment a great earthquake occurs,
and this entire world becomes suffused with a sublime radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— blind, dark, shrouded in gloom, and enveloped in thick darkness, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite such great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not experience their light with their own radiance—
even those spaces, at that time, become suffused with a sublime splendor.
127.029. Those beings who were reborn there, through that light, perceived one another as soon as they saw a being, thinking: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here;
other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here."

"Ānanda, this is the sixth cause, the sixth condition for a great earthquake. Furthermore, Ānanda, on that occasion when the Tathāgata, having sustained the formative forces of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*), relinquishes the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*),
at that time there occurs an exceedingly great earthquake, with the falling of meteors and the blazing of the quarters."
In the sky, the drums of the gods resounded,
and this entire world became suffused with a sublime radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— blind, dark, shrouded in gloom, and thick with darkness, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite being so powerful and so majestic, cannot with their light...
They do not experience [it],
yet at that time even those [realms] become suffused with a sublime radiance;
and whatever beings are born there, [they too perceive it].
Seeing one another through that light, those beings perceive: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here;
other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here.
Ānanda, this is the seventh cause, the seventh condition for a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it will not be long now until the Tathāgata’s final passing away (parinirvāṇa) into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
At that time, there will be a great earthquake, falling meteors, and the blazing of the quarters;
and in the sky, the drums of the gods will resound in celebration.
And this entire world was pervaded by a sublime radiance such that even the sun and moon—possessing such great miraculous power and such great majesty—could not outshine its light with their own;
at that time, even they were suffused by that sublime radiance.
And those beings there...
Having been reborn there, they perceive one another by means of that radiance and recognize: "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here;
other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here."
Ānanda, this is the eighth cause, the eighth condition for a great earthquake of the earth.

Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, as I understand the meaning of what has been spoken by the Blessed One, it appears that the Blessed One has here, having sustained the formative forces of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*), relinquished the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda; it is so."
"Ānanda, at this time the Tathāgata, having no longer sustained the formative forces of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*), has relinquished the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).

Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One and have received it directly from his presence: 'If anyone has cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the Tathāgata, if he so desires, can remain for an eon.'"
"Or for the remainder of a kalpa.
Venerable sir, the four bases of psychic power have been practiced, cultivated, and frequently exercised by the Blessed One.
If the Tathāgata so desired, he could remain for a kalpa or for the remainder of a kalpa."
"May the Blessed One remain for an eon;
may the Sugata remain for the remainder of an eon.

Ānanda, this is your own fault, this is your own misdeed, in that even though such a sublime sign of illumination was manifested by the Tathāgata up to three times, you were unable to perceive its cause."
"Was it not then, Ānanda, that he was clearly deceived by Māra, the Evil One? What other word could the Tathāgata speak that would be subject to duality?
"No, Venerable Sir."
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question that the Tathāgata would utter a word that should prove to be otherwise. Go now, Ānanda."
"Summon all the bhikṣus who dwell in dependence upon the Cāpāla shrine to the assembly hall.
"So be it, Venerable Sir."

128.027. Having assented to the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda gathered all the monks who were dwelling in dependence upon the Cāpāla shrine and assembled them in the assembly hall; he then approached the Blessed One.
128.029. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.

128.030. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, as many monks as there are who dwell depending on the Cāpāla shrine, they have all sat down and assembled in the assembly hall;
it is now time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit."
128.032. Then the Blessed One went to the hall of attendance.
129.001. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, subject to change, and—monks, they are simply not enough."
I am capable of fashioning all conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, monks, desist from that!
Whether now or after my passing, those teachings which conduce to welfare in the present life and to happiness in the present life—
For the benefit of future lives and for the happiness of future lives,
those [teachings] should be taken up by the monks, mastered, and maintained, recited,
and taught in such a way that the holy life (brahmacarya) therein may endure, become widespread among many people, and extend as far as gods and humans.
It has been perfectly revealed. Monks, these teachings now conduce to welfare in this present life and to happiness in this present life;
they conduce to welfare in future lives and to happiness in future lives.

Those monks who have taken it up and mastered it should preserve, cause others to grasp, and recite it in such a way that this holy life may endure for a long time, become widespread and extensive, and be correctly proclaimed as far as gods and humans.
Namely: the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts,
and the four bases of psychic power.
the five faculties, the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment;
The noble eightfold path.
Monks, these dharmas conduce to welfare in the present life and to happiness in the present life;
they conduce to welfare in future lives and to happiness in future lives.

"Having taken up this [teaching], monks, you should master it, retain it in such a way, cause others to grasp it, and recite it, so that this holy life may endure for a long time, become widespread among many people, and be correctly proclaimed as far as gods and humans.
Wait, Ānanda, until we reach the village of Kuśigrāma."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
As the Blessed One was proceeding toward the grove of Vaiśālī, he gazed back with his entire body in the manner of a Naga's look.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not look back with the Naga’s gaze without a cause or a reason."
"Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the 'elephant-look'? It is so, Ānanda; it is so."

129.018. It is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas look back with their entire bodies in the manner of an elephant’s gaze. 129.019. Ānanda, this is the Tathāgata’s final sight of Vaiśālī. 129.019. Ānanda, the Tathāgata will never again come to Vaiśālī.
129.020. He will go to the twin śāla grove at Upavartana of the Mallas for his final nirvāṇa.
129.021. Then, at that time, a certain monk spoke this verse:
129.022. "O Protector, this is the very last sight of you from Vaiśālī."
The Sugata, the Buddha, will not come to Vaiśālī again.
129.024. "He will go to the Yamaka-śāla grove in the vicinity of the Mallas for the sake of parinirvāṇa.
When these words were spoken by the Blessed One—"This is indeed the final sight of Vaiśālī"—then many deities dwelling in the groves of Vaiśālī shed tears.
The Elder Ānanda said, "Lord, has it not rained from a cloud during the rainy season?
The Blessed One replied, "The deities dwelling in the Vaiśālī grove have shed tears because of my departure.
Those deities as well—
In Vaiśālī, a cry went forth: "The Blessed One is departing for final nirvāṇa;
the Blessed One will not come to Vaiśālī again. Having heard the cry of the deities, many hundreds of thousands of living beings from Vaiśālī approached the presence of the Blessed One.

129.030. The Blessed One, having understood their intentions, underlying tendencies, elements, and natures, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that many hundreds of thousands of living beings took up the precepts of going for refuge.
129.031. Some attained the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, and some the fruit of non-returning.

129.032. Some, having gone forth, attained arhatship. 129.032. Some generated the mind directed toward the enlightenment of a śrāvaka. 130.001. Some generated the mind directed toward pratyekabuddha enlightenment.

130.001. Some generated the mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; some took up the precepts for going for refuge. For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha.

130.003. The Elder Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, said this to the Blessed One: "Behold, Venerable Sir, how great [is your achievement]. 130.004. As the Blessed One set out for his final nirvana, hundreds of thousands of deities were established in the truths. 130.005. From many mountain clefts and mountain caves, hundreds of thousands of sages have come forth."
130.006. These monks were ordained by the Blessed One. By applying themselves, striving, and exerting effort, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
130.007. Many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas took refuge and received the precepts of training.
130.008. Indeed, many hundreds of thousands of living beings from Vaiśālī were established in the fruit of stream-entry;
some in the fruit of once-returning, and some in the fruit of non-returning.
Some were ordained;
having gone forth, they attained arhatship. Some were established in the taking of refuge and the precepts of training.

130.010. In this regard, Ānanda, what is so wonderful that I— now omniscient, possessing knowledge of all modes, having attained mastery over the knowable through unsurpassed wisdom, free from thirst, without grasping, and having abandoned such things as all notions of "I," "mine," the conceit "I am," and the underlying tendencies of dogmatic attachment— should perform such a task for those to be trained?

130.012. Whatever discourse on purification I have delivered—even in the past—while still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, unliberated from the nature of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, and while being touched by the sensations of the time of death;
by that [merit], may these many hundreds of thousands of living beings abandon the life of a householder.

The four seers, having gone forth and cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), abandoned a multitude of eons; dwelling frequently therein, they were reborn in the company of the Brahma-world.
Listen to this:
Once upon a time, Ānanda, there was a king named Upoṣadha.
On the crown of King Upoṣadha’s head a tumor grew— soft, very soft, like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
It caused him no affliction whatsoever.
It ripened and burst open;
a prince was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
King Uposadha had sixty thousand women.
The breasts of all [the women] flowed with milk.
Each one said, "Suck me! Suck me!
Because he was born from the head (*mūrdhan*), the name Mūrdhāta came into being.
"Drink me! Drink me!"—from this [exclamation], the name Māndhātṛ came to be.
Others say that some knew him as Mādhāta.
While Prince Māndhātṛ was playing at the games of childhood, six wheels fell away.
130.023. When he was established in the position of crown prince, six wheels fell away. 130.023. Māndhātṛ went to the provinces.
130.023. While he was in the provinces, his father fell ill.
Although he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, leaves, stalks, and flowers, he continued to decline.
Thereupon, those ministers sent a message: "Your father has fallen ill;
please come."
"Accept the sovereignty of the gods.
While he was not returning, his father passed away.
Those ministers sent another message: "Your father has been joined with the law of time."
"Come, accept the sovereignty of the gods.
Then he reflected: "If my father has passed away, why should I go back?"
Then, once again, a message arrived:
"Come and accept the sovereignty of the gods.
He replied, "If my kingship shall be obtained through righteousness (dharma), [then let it be so]."
"Let the royal consecration come right here!
Then they said to the ministers, "Your Majesty, there is need for a precious stone.
And for that, there is a yakṣa named Divaukas who goes before us."
130.030. He brought a precious stone slab.
130.031. When the precious stone slab had been brought, those ministers spoke again: "Your Majesty, there is a need here for the Śrīparyaṅka."

130.032. Then that very deity brought the glorious couch. 130.032. Thereupon those ministers spoke again: "The consecration shall be performed in the center of the royal capital. He replied: "If my kingship is to be obtained through righteousness (dharma), [let it be so]."

"Let the Adhiṣṭhāna come right here! Thereupon, the Adhiṣṭhāna went to that place of its own accord. Because it had come of its own accord, "Svayamāgata" became its name; and because it was from Sāketa, "Sāketaka" became its designation.
131.003. Afterwards, those ministers, the army officers, the merchants, and the people of the countryside arrived having taken the consecration water.
They said, "O Lord, please accept the consecration.
He replied, "Will men bind a turban upon me?"
"If he shall obtain the kingdom through righteousness,
let non-human beings bind the turban. Thereupon, the non-human beings bound the turban.

131.005. Seven precious jewels appeared for him, namely: the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the counselor-jewel, the woman-jewel, and the householder-jewel as the seventh.
131.007. And he had a full thousand sons, who were brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
In the vicinity of Vaiśālī, there was a delightful forest grove. There, five hundred sages possessing the five supernormal powers were practicing meditation.
In that forest grove, many birds and deer lived.
131.009. And meditations have sounds as their thorns.
131.010. Those birds, as they were descending, one after another, made a noise.
There was a seer named Durmukha.
131.010. He became angry. 131.011. He said, "May the wings of the cranes wither away! When their wings had withered through the wrath of the ṛṣi, [he was struck by remorse].
Then they set out by way of the foot-bridge.
The king, having traveled through the countryside, saw them going by way of the foot-bridge.
Thereupon, he asked those ministers: "Why are you going by way of the foot-bridge?"
Afterwards, those ministers said, "Your Majesty, it is said that meditations have sound as their thorn; by the wrath of these sages, their wings have been shattered.
Then the king remarked, "There are even such sages as these."
"Towards which beings do they have no compassion?
Then the king commanded his ministers: "Go, sirs, and say this to the seers: 'Go to that place where I do not dwell.'"
131.017. Then those ministers said to the seers:
"The king commands: 'You must not dwell in my kingdom.
Go, sirs, to where I do not reside.'"
Then they reflected: "This is the lord of the four continents.
Let us go to the region surrounding Mount Sumeru.
Having gone there, they remained.
131.020. King Mūrdhāta’s ministers were thinkers, weighers, and investigators.

Having thought, weighed, and investigated, they were each individually eager to measure out the sites for crafts and works. Because they were thinkers, weighers, and investigators, they were known as "those born of counsel" (*mantraja*). 131.021. They were known as "those born of counsel."
131.022. They began to engage in the work of agriculture.
Then, as that king was traveling through the countryside, he saw the people performing agricultural labor.
Thereupon, the king asked: "What are these men doing?"
Then those ministers said to the king: "Your Majesty, these men will plow with seeds and the like, and from that, medicinal herbs will arise.
Thereupon, the king asked: "Will men plow in my kingdom?"
Then he said, "May the god rain down twenty-seven kinds of seeds.
Immediately upon the arising of that thought, the god rained down twenty-seven kinds of seeds for King Mūrdhāta.
King Mūrdhāta asked the people of the countryside, "To whom do these merits belong?"
They replied, "Both for Your Majesty and for ourselves.
Since those men had begun to measure the cotton-bales,
King Mūrdhāta again traveled through the provinces and questioned them.
131.029. Then the king asked, "What are these men doing?
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, the men are measuring the cotton bales."
131.030. Afterwards, the king asked, "For whose sake? Those ministers replied, "Your Majesty, for the sake of garments."
Then the king said, "In my kingdom, people shall measure cotton-wool; therefore, may the god send rain only as cotton-wool.
As soon as that thought arose in King Mūrdhāta, the god sent down rain consisting only of cotton-wool.
And the king questioned the people of the countryside.
132.001. "To whom do these merits belong?
They replied, "To both Your Majesty and ourselves.
132.002. Afterwards, that group of people began to spin that cotton.
The king asked, "What are these men doing? The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, they need thread. Then the king said, "Will men spin thread in my kingdom?"
"May the rain fall as a drizzle!
132.004. As soon as King Māndhātṛ gave rise to this thought, the rain fell as a drizzle.
132.005. And that king said: "To whom do these merits belong?"
Because they said, "For the King and for ourselves.
Then, they gradually began to have garments woven.
The king asked, "What are these men doing?"
Those ministers said: "Your Majesty, they are having garments woven;
there is need for garments."
132.008. Then the king reflected: "In my kingdom, will humans have to weave clothes?
Let the god rain down only clothes!
132.009. As soon as King Māndhātṛ gave rise to this thought, the god rained down only clothes.
The king asked, "To whom do these merits belong?
They replied, "To Your Majesty and to us.
Thereupon, the king reflected, "People do not understand the power of my merits."
132.011. Then this thought occurred to King Māndhātṛ:
"I possess Jambudvīpa, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
I possess the seven jewels."
Namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the householder-treasure, the woman-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Furthermore, may I have a full thousand sons—heroic, brave, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Oh, would that a rain of gold might fall upon my inner apartments for seven days!
Not even a single kārṣāpaṇa fell outside.
As soon as that thought arose, a rain of gold fell for seven days within King Māndhātṛ’s inner palace;

not even a single kārṣāpaṇa fell outside, just as is the case when a being of great psychic power, great majesty, who has performed meritorious deeds and cultivated wholesome roots, experiences the fruit of his own merit.
132.018. When the king asked, "To whom do these merits belong?
they replied, "To Your Majesty and to ourselves.
132.019. Then the king said, "You have been at fault, sirs, had you not spoken previously that 'these are the merits of Your Majesty'."
I would have rained down jewels upon the entire Jambudvīpa;
however, whoever among you has need of jewels,
let him take as many jewels as he desires.
132.022. While King Mūrdhāta was exercising his great sovereignty there, six wheels fell away.
King Mūrdhāta had a yakṣa named Divaukāsa as his vanguard.
He was addressed by King Mūrdhāta: "Is there any other island that has not yet been commanded, which we might now command?"

Thereupon, a divinity spoke to him: "Your Majesty, there is a continent named Pūrvavideha, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people and inhabitants.
May Your Majesty go there in person and issue your commands."
Then, this thought occurred to King Mūrdhāta: "I possess Jambudvīpa, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
I possess the seven jewels, namely: the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh.
And I have a full thousand sons, who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies."
"For seven days, a rain of gold fell within my inner apartments.
Now it is heard that there is indeed a continent named Pūrvavideha;
what if I were to go there as well and instruct them?"

132.030. At the very moment that thought arose, King Māndhātṛ ascended into the air above, accompanied by eighteen hundred million elite troops, surrounded by his thousand sons, and preceded by the seven precious jewels.
132.031. King Māndhātṛ went to the continent of Pūrvavideha.
132.032. King Māndhātṛ established himself upon the continent of Pūrvavideha.
132.032. King Mūrdhāta governed the continent of Pūrvavideha. 133.001. While he was ruling there, six wheels fell away from him.
Again, that king addressed the yakṣa Divaukasa: "Divaukasa, is there any other continent that has not yet been commanded by me?"
The celestial being said: "O Lord, there is a continent named Aparagodānīya, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
What if Your Majesty were to go there as well and rule over it?
Then, this thought occurred to King Mūrdhāta: "I already possess Jambudvīpa, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants."
"I possess seven precious jewels.
I have a full thousand sons, who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

For seven days, a rain of gold fell within my inner apartments—just as it happens for a being of great psychic power and majesty who has performed wholesome deeds and is experiencing the fruit of his own merit."
"It is heard that there is a continent named Aparagodānīya, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
What if I were to go there as well and instruct them?

At the very moment this thought arose, King Māndhātṛ ascended into the sky above together with eighteen koṭis of the elite of his army, surrounded by his thousand sons, and preceded by the seven precious jewels.
133.011. King Māndhātā went to the continent of Aparagodānīya. 133.011. King Māndhātā ruled over Aparagodānīya. 133.012. While he was ruling, six wheels fell away from him.

133.012. Thereupon King Māndhātṛ asked the celestial yakṣa: "Is there any other continent that has not been commanded by me? I have come from the east. 133.013. "There is, O Lord, a continent named Uttarakuru."
"Moreover, although those men are without 'mine-ness' and without possessions, what if Your Majesty were to go and instruct your own army?
Then it occurred to King Māndhātṛ: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.'"
133.016. I possess seven precious jewels.
133.016. I have a full thousand sons, brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
133.017. For seven days, a rain of gold fell within my inner apartments.
"It is heard that there is a continent named Uttarakuru.
Although those humans there are without the sense of 'mine' and possess nothing they own,
what if I were to go there as well and instruct my own elite vanguard of soldiers?"

133.019. As soon as that thought arose, King Māndhātṛ, accompanied by eighteen koṭis of the elite of his army and surrounded by his thousand sons, rose into the air, preceded by the seven precious jewels.
133.020. As King Māndhātṛ was traveling along the side of Mount Sumeru, he saw trees of various and variegated colors, covered with clusters of blossoms.
133.021. Having seen them, he addressed a celestial yakṣa: "What are these, O celestial being, these trees of various and variegated colors, covered with clusters of blossoms?"
"Your Majesty, these are the *kalpadūṣya* trees of the humans of Uttarakuru,
from which the humans of Uttarakuru clothe themselves in *kalpadūṣya* garments. Your Majesty should also go to this very place and clothe yourself in *kalpadūṣya* garments."

133.024. Having heard this, King Māndhātā addressed his ministers: "Do you see, O village chiefs, these variegated and beautiful trees that have produced clusters of blossoms? "We do, Your Majesty. 133.026.
"O village chiefs, these are the *kalpadūṣya* (wish-fulfilling) garment-trees of the humans of Uttarakuru, from which the humans of Uttarakuru clothe themselves in *kalpadūṣya* garments.
You too, having gone there, should clothe yourselves in pairs of *kalpadūṣya* garments."
133.027. As King Māndhātā was traveling along the side of Mount Sumeru, he saw a region of the earth that was white as snow.

"Your Majesty, this is the rice with grains of *taṇḍula* that grows without being ploughed or sown among the people of Uttarakuru, from which the people of Uttarakuru enjoy rice with grains of *taṇḍula* that grows without being ploughed or sown.
May Your Majesty also go there and enjoy rice with grains of *taṇḍula* that grows without being ploughed or sown."
133.031. King Māndhātā went to the continent of Uttarakuru.
133.032. King Māndhātā settled in the continent of Uttarakuru.
133.032. King Māndhātā governed his own army and forces in the continent of Uttarakuru.
134.001. While he was governing his own army there, six wheels fell away.

Then King Māndhātṛ addressed the yakṣa Divaukasa: "Is there any other continent that has not yet been commanded? "There is none, O Lord. "It is heard that the Trāyastriṃśa gods are long-lived, beautiful, possessed of much happiness, and dwell for a long time in lofty celestial palaces."
"What if the King were to go to see the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven?
Then this thought occurred to King Mūrdhāta: "I possess Jambudvīpa—prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people."
134.005. I possess the seven precious jewels. 134.006. I have a full thousand sons, who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
134.006. For seven days, a rain of gold fell within my inner apartments.
134.007. I have instructed Aparagodānīya Island.
134.008. I have instructed my own army on Uttarakuru Island.
It is heard that the Trāyastriṃśa gods are long-lived, beautiful, full of happiness, and remain for a long time in lofty celestial palaces.
"What if I were now to approach the Trāyastriṃśa gods in order to see them?
At the very moment this thought arose, King Māndhātṛ ascended into the air above together with eighteen koṭis of the finest troops, preceded by the seven jewels and surrounded by his thousand sons.
Sumeru, the king of mountains, was likewise surrounded by seven golden mountain ranges.
134.012. Then King [Mahāsudarśana] established himself on Mount Nimiṃdhara, which is made of gold.
While he was governing his own elite army there, six wheels fell away.
From Mount Nimiṃdhara, he established himself on Mount Vinataka, which is also made of gold.
134.013. While he was governing his own army there, six wheels fell away.
134.014. From Mount Vinataka, he established himself on Mount Aśvakarṇa, which is made of gold.
134.015. While he was governing his own army there, six wheels fell away.
134.015. From Mount Aśvakarṇa as well, he established himself on Mount Sudarśana, which is made of gold.
134.016. While he was there governing his own elite army, six wheels fell away.
134.017. From Mount Sudarśana, he established himself on Mount Khadiraka, which is made of gold.
While he was governing his own army there, six wheels fell away.
From Mount Khadiraka, he established himself on Mount Īṣādhāra, which is made of gold.
While he was governing his own army there, six wheels fell away.
134.019. From Mount Īṣādhāra, he established himself on Mount Yugandhara, which is made of gold.
134.020. While he was governing his own elite army there, six wheels fell away.
134.021. He then rose up into the air above Mount Yugandhara.
134.021. There, on the terraces of Mount Sumeru, five hundred sages were practicing meditation. They saw the king approaching and said, "Sirs, here comes that King Kali."
134.022. There was a seer named Durmukha.
134.023. He took a handful of water and threw it;
the army division was brought to a standstill.
And the jewel of the counselor followed before him.
He said to the sages:
"Go! This is a mere Brahmin; this will not succeed everywhere."
This is indeed King Mūrdhāta; these are not the cranes of Vaiśālī. //3//
134.027. Then the king arrived at that teaching and asked, "By whom has this army been repelled?
He replied, "O King, that army was repelled by the sages.
134.028. Afterwards, the king said, "What is it that is dear to all these sages?"
The Jewel of the Counsellor said, "Matted locks are desired by all sages.
Thereupon the king declared, "Let the matted locks of the sages fall away,
and let my vanguard of troops travel through the air!"
The matted locks of those seers fell away,
and King Mūrdhāta’s vanguard of troops set out through the air.
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is established eighty thousand yojanas below upon the ground made of gold.

It rises eighty thousand yojanas above the water; and including sixty hundred thousand yojanas above and below, each side is eighty thousand yojanas. Thus, its total circumference is three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas.
135.002. It was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and composed of the four jewels.
135.003. Upon its summit is the city of the Trāyastriṃśa gods named Sudarśana.
Five guardians have been established for the Trāyastriṃśa gods: the water-dwelling nāgas, [the earth-dwelling nāgas, the mountain-dwelling nāgas, the sky-dwelling nāgas, and the wind-dwelling nāgas].
the Karoṭapāṇi gods,
the Mālādhāra gods, and the Sadāmatta gods;
And the four Great Kings [were present].
King Mūrdhāta’s army was held back by the water-dwelling nāgas,
and King Mūrdhāta arrived at that place.
He asked, "By whom has this vanguard of troops been checked?
They replied, "Your Majesty, by the nāgas who dwell in the water."
The king said, "Are even animals fighting for me?
"Therefore," he continued, "let my nāgas who dwell in the water be my vanguard.
Thereupon, those nāgas became followers, marching in front of King Mūrdhāta.
135.009. As those *nāgas* were marching along, the Karoṭapāṇi gods arrived.
Thereupon, having come into contact with those Karoṭapāṇi gods, the *nāgas* again paralyzed that vanguard of the army.
King Mūrdhāta asked, "By whom has this vanguard of the soldiers been paralyzed?"
They replied, "Your Majesty, these are the Karoṭapāṇi gods;
by them the vanguard of the army has been paralyzed."
King Mūrdhāta said, "Let these Karoṭapāṇi gods also be my precursors.
Since they ran ahead of him,
the Mālādhāra gods arrived behind them as they were running together with the Nāgas.
135.013. The Mālādhāra gods asked them, "Why are you running?
They replied, "This king of men is coming. 135.014.
Thereupon, those nāgas and gods together paralyzed that vanguard of the army once more.
135.015. And King Māndhātṛ arrived at that place. He asked, "What is this, sirs?
They replied, "Your Majesty,"
By the Mālādhāra gods.
King [Mūrdhāta] said: "May the Mālādhāra gods be my precursors.
Thereupon, the Mālādhāra gods, together with those *nāgas* and gods, ran ahead of Mūrdhāta.
135.018. As they were running, the Sadāmatta gods arrived. The Sadāmatta gods asked them, "Why are you running?
They were told by those nāgas and the Karoṭapāṇi and other gods, "This king of men is coming."

135.019. Furthermore, when the Sadāmatta gods and other gods, such as the Karoṭapāṇis, together with the nāgas, had joined forces and checked the vanguard of the army, King Mūrdhāta arrived at that place. He asked: "Why has this vanguard of the army been checked?"
They replied, "Your Majesty, these are the Sadāmatta gods.
The king said, "Let the Sadāmatta gods alone be my precursors.
Thereupon, the Sadāmatta gods, together with those other gods and nāgas, ran ahead.
135.023. As they were running, the gods of the Four Great Kings arrived there. They asked, "Sirs, why are you running?
Thereupon, the gods, such as the Nāgas and others, who were following behind them, replied, "This king of men is coming!"
135.025. The four Great Kings reflected: "This being is of great power through his merit; it is not possible to oppose him. 135.026. Thus they thought.
135.026. Then those four great kings announced to the Trāyastriṃśa gods: "Sirs, this human king Mūrdhāta is coming.
135.027. The Trāyastriṃśa gods reflected: "This being is one of great renown due to the ripening of his merit. One must not oppose him."
"We shall go out to meet him with an offering of honor (*argha*).
Thereupon, those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven went out to meet him with an offering of honor.
As King Mūrdhāta was ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru, he saw a row of dark-blue forests rising up like a mass of clouds.

135.029. Having seen it, he addressed the celestial yakṣa: "What is this, O celestial one, that appears so dark-blue, like a row of forests or a mass of clouds rising up? "O Lord, this is the *pārijātaka* tree, a *kovidāra* belonging to the gods, where the gods of the Thirty-three, provided and endowed with the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure, sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves during the four months of the rainy season."

135.032. "Let the god also go there and, provided and endowed with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, sport, enjoy himself, and amuse himself. 136.001. Having heard this, King Mūrdhāta addressed his ministers: "Do you see that deep-blue line of forest, rising up like a row of clouds? 136.003. "Yes, Your Majesty. "This, Your Majesty, is the Pārijātaka *kovidāra* tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, where the Trāyastriṃśa gods [spend] the four..."
"For the months of the rainy season, they sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves, provided and endowed with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure.
You too, village chiefs, having gone there, sport, enjoy yourselves, and amuse yourselves, provided and endowed with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure."
136.006. King Mūrdhāta, while ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru, saw something exceedingly white, rising up like a peak of clouds.
Having seen it, he addressed a celestial yakṣa: "What is this, O celestial one, that is so exceedingly white, rising up like a peak of clouds?
"O Lord, this is the assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, named Sudharmā."
"Where the gods of the Thirty-three and the four Great Kings are seated together, they deliberate, weigh, and examine the welfare and the Dharma of both gods and humans.
May Your Majesty also go there.
Having heard this, he addressed his ministers: "Do you see, O village leaders, that which is as white as a mass of clouds and so lofty? "Yes, Your Majesty."

136.011. This is the assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa gods named Sudharmā, where the Trāyastriṃśa gods and the four Great Kings sit together and assemble to reflect upon, weigh, and examine the welfare and the Dharma of both gods and humans.
136.013. "You too, village chiefs, shall go there.

136.014. The city of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is named Sudarśana; it is two thousand five hundred yojanas in length and two thousand five hundred yojanas in width, making ten thousand yojanas in circumference all around."
It is encircled by seven walls made of gold.
Those walls are two and a half yojanas in height.
On those walls, there are four kinds of [turrets].
Stairways were constructed made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
A single flight was built leading upward for the purpose of crossing over.

Within the city of Sudarśana, the ground was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, variegated, and exquisitely adorned with hundreds of various patterns; it was soft and very supple, like a tuft of cotton wool.
136.020. Or it is like a tuft of cotton-wool:
when the foot is placed upon it, it sinks; when the foot is lifted, it rises. It is strewn knee-deep with a flood of divine mandārava flowers.
And through the contact of the wind, the old flowers are scattered away.
