Fresh flowers are being strewn about. In the city of Sudarśana, there are nine thousand gates.

At each gate, five hundred yakṣas dressed in blue garments have been stationed, fully armored and equipped with colorful quivers, for the sole purpose of providing exceptional protection for the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

The streets of the city of Sudarśana were two thousand five hundred yojanas in length and twelve yojanas in width; they were beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing, strewn with golden sand, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and covered with nets of gold.
All around them, various lotus ponds had been constructed.
Those lotus ponds were built with four kinds of bricks: made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. The railings had crystal posts as their supports and foundations;
the crystal railings had posts made of lapis lazuli as their supports and foundations.

Those lotus ponds were filled with cool water, water as sweet as honey, covered with blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, and resounded with the warbling of various water-birds that possessed charming and delightful voices and could assume forms at will.
In their vicinity stood various flowering trees and fruit trees, well-grown, well-established, and laden with blossoms like floral garlands.
It was, for example, like garlands or crest-ornaments beautifully fashioned by a skilled garland-maker or his apprentice;
they were filled with the warbling of various land-dwelling birds that possessed sweet, charming voices and could assume any form at will.
In the city of Sudarśana, there were four kinds of *kalpadūṣya* trees—blue, yellow, red, and white.
137.002. From the *kalpadūṣya* trees come four kinds of *tuṇḍicela* garments. With those *tuṇḍicela* garments, there are four kinds of *kalpadūṣya* fabrics: blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whatever kind [of garment] a god or a goddess desires, [it appears].
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, [ornaments] appear in their hands.
There are four kinds of ornament-trees: those that come to the hand, those that come to the foot, those that are secret, and those that are manifest.
Whatever kind [of ornament] a god or a celestial maiden desires, [that appears].
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, musical instruments appear in their hands:
four kinds of musical instrument trees— flutes, lutes, and sweet-sounding drums—
whatever kind a god or a goddess desires.
As soon as that thought arises, [the vessels] appear in his hand;
and there are four kinds of ambrosia: blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whatever a god or a celestial maiden desires,
it appears in their hand as soon as the thought arises—
honey, *mādhava* wine, *kādambarī*, and *pāripāna*.
There are houses, gabled chambers, mansions, palaces, excellent seats, viewing galleries, and walkways.
Adorned by throngs of women and frequented by hosts of thousands of apsarases, it resounds with the music of instruments and is provided with food and drink.
Therein the Trāyastriṃśa gods play, delight, and enjoy themselves.
They experience the fruit of their own merit.

The Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is three hundred yojanas in length, three hundred yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference; it is beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and made of crystal.
It rose four and a half yojanas above that city;
there, seats were prepared for the Trāyastriṃśa gods, whereon were the individual seats for the thirty-two Upendras.
The thirty-third [throne] was for Śakra, the lord of the gods;
at the very end of those [seats] was the throne prepared for King Mūrdhāta. Thereafter, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven came forth to meet King Mūrdhāta, taking up the guest-offering (*argha*).
137.017. Therein, those beings who were of great merit and power entered one after another, while the remainder remained outside.
Then King Mūrdhāta reflected: "Of these seats that have been prepared, which is the very last seat?"
"This shall be mine.
Then, this thought occurred to King Mūrdhāta: "Oh, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, invite me to share half his throne!
At the very moment this thought arose, Śakra, the lord of the gods, offered half of his throne to King Māndhātṛ.
King Mūrdhāta entered and sat upon half the throne of Śakra, the lord of the gods. Indeed,
when King Mūrdhāta and Śakra, the lord of the gods, were seated on the same seat, there was no distinction, nor any difference in intention, nor any disparity between them.

That is to say, his height and girth, the excellence of his complexion, and the protection of his voice— through the protection of his voice— were such that none other than Śakra, the lord of the gods, could equal him by even a single blink of an eye.
While King Mūrdhāta was dwelling among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, thirty-six *cakravartins* fell from their celestial abodes.
And there, a battle between those gods and the asuras takes place.
If the asuras are defeated therein, they subsequently close the gates of the city of the asuras.
137.025. Even among the gods, there are five who suffer defeat.
137.026. They too close the gates of the city of the gods. Thus, a state of mutual agitation arose between those gods and asuras.
137.027. Thereupon, King Mūrdhāta asked the Trāyastriṃśa gods, "O gods, why have you become so greatly agitated?
The Trāyastriṃśa gods replied, "These asuras have broken our five defenses, which is why we have closed the gates."
137.029. Then King Mūrdhāta said, "My men, bring the bow! Thereupon, the bow was brought to him.
137.030. Thereupon, he took up his bow and drew the string; as he drew the string of that bow, a sound was produced. 137.031. The asuras heard it.
137.031. Having heard that, the asuras asked, "Whose sound of virtue is this?
They heard: "This is the sound of the virtues of King Mūrdhāta.
137.032. Upon hearing that sound, they were filled with wonder.

137.032. Afterwards, King Mūrdhāta emerged from that very city of the gods and, having armored his own body, [set out] against those gods who had been defeated by the asuras. Furthermore, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of these fighting gods and asuras that their chariots remain suspended in the air.
Among them, no one was either superior or inferior to another.
King Mūrdhāta rose into the air and stood above all the asuras.
Thereupon, those asuras asked, "Who is this who has risen into the sky above us?
Then they heard: "This is a king of men named Mūrdhāta."
138.004. Afterwards, they reflected: "This being possesses great power through the ripening of merit, for his chariot travels through the air above us.
138.005. [The asuras] were conquered, broken, defeated, turned back, and entered the city of the asuras.
138.006. Afterwards, King Mūrdhāta asked: "Whose victory was it?"

When the ministers said, "Victory to Your Majesty," King Mūrdhāta reflected: "I alone am superior even to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. Then this thought occurred to King Mūrdhāta: "This Jambudvīpa belongs to me."
I possess the seven precious jewels;
I have a thousand sons;
and for seven days a rain of gold fell within my inner apartments.
I have instructed Pūrvavideha; I have instructed the continent of Aparagodānīya;
and I have instructed my own army among the Uttarakurus.
I have been granted dominion over the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
I have entered the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods;
and a half-seat has been offered to me by Śakra, the lord of the gods.

"O, would that I could displace Śakra, the lord of the gods, from this station, and myself exercise the sovereignty, power, and dominion over both gods and men! As soon as this thought arose, King Mūrdhāta fell from that state of supernatural power and landed in Jambudvīpa. He was afflicted with a severe illness.
138.014. It was a severe trial for the gods, reaching unto death.
Then the group of ministers, the chief ministers, the administrators of the kingdom, and the counselors who lived with him, approached King Mūrdhāta.
Having approached, they said this to King Mūrdhāta: "After the passing away of Your Majesty, will the western provinces indeed remain?"
They asked: "What was prophesied by King Mūrdhāta at the time of his death?

If, after my passing, O villagers, someone should approach you and ask: 'What was prophesied by King Mūrdhāta at the time of his death?', you should say this to them: 'Sirs, King Mūrdhāta was endowed with jewels.'"
Having exercised sovereign power and lordship over the four continents through the four human supernatural powers, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Yet, still unsated with the five strands of sensual pleasure, he passed away.
There is no satisfaction in sensual desires, even by a rain of kārṣāpaṇa coins.
Having understood, in their totality, that sensual pleasures offer little enjoyment and involve much suffering. //4//
Even toward divine sensual pleasures, he finds no delight;
the disciple of the Perfectly Awakened One finds joy in the destruction of craving. //5//
Even a mountain of gold equal to the Himalayas would not suffice for one person alone; knowing this, a wise person should practice accordingly.

138.028. How could one who perceives suffering as originating from this source ever find delight in sensual pleasures? 138.030. Having understood that worldly acquisitions are like a thorn, the wise person should train for their very removal. (7)

139.001. Furthermore, when that multitude of people heard that King Mūrdhāta was ill and at the point of death, those ministers and the inhabitants of the countryside, along with many hundreds of thousands of living beings, approached King Mūrdhāta in order to see him.
139.002. Thereupon, the king gave such a teaching of the Dharma to those people: he spoke of the peril inherent in sensual pleasures and described the peril of the household life.
Sensual desire is so loathsome that many hundreds of thousands of living beings, having gone forth in the presence of the seers and abandoned their household lives, took refuge in the forest;

and having gone forth under those seers and cultivated the four divine abodes, they abandoned sensual longing for desires and, dwelling frequently therein, were reborn in the company of the Brahma-world.
This extended as far as Jambudvīpa, as far as Pūrvavideha Island, as far as Aparagodānīya Island, as far as Uttarakuru, and as far as the seven mountains made of gold.
In the meantime, one hundred and fourteen Śakras passed away.
Monks, the measure of the lifespan of Śakra, the lord of the gods, is as follows: that which is one year for humans is a single day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
By that reckoning—thirty such days making a month, and twelve such months making a year—the measure of the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is one thousand divine years.
By human calculation, that amounts to three hundred and sixty thousand years.

139.014. Ānanda, at the time when King Mūrdhāta had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa gods and such a thought arose in him— "O, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, would invite me to share his half-seat"—
at that very time and on that occasion, Kāśyapa the monk was Śakra, the lord of the gods.

139.016. Ānanda, at the time when such a thought arose in King Mūrdhāta— “What if I were to displace Śakra, the lord of the gods, from this position, and myself exercise the sovereignty, power, and dominion over both gods and men”—
at that very time and on that occasion, Kāśyapa the Perfectly Enlightened One was Śakra, the lord of the gods.
139.019. His mind became corrupted toward a being of great majesty; consequently, he fell from his supernatural power and descended into Jambudvīpa, where he was afflicted by a severe illness.
"Ānanda,
at that time and on that occasion, King Mūrdhāta was none other than myself, who experienced intense, death-bed pain."

139.021. In that regard, Ānanda, while I was still possessed of passion, possessed of hatred, possessed of delusion, and not yet liberated from the nature of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, at the very time of my death, I gave such a discourse that many hundreds of thousands of living beings abandoned the life of a householder,
went forth under the sages, cast off sensual desire for pleasures, dwelt frequently in that state, and were reborn in the Brahma-world.

139.024. Now, by the Omniscient One—who has attained mastery over the knowable through unsurpassed knowledge and has set out for Nirvāṇa—such a teaching of the Dharma has been performed that many hundreds of thousands of deities have been established in the Truths.
139.026. Many hundreds of thousands of sages have gone forth into homelessness, saying, "We are monks."
139.027. By striving, exerting themselves, and applying effort, they attained arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
139.027. Many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas were established in the refuges and the precepts.
139.028. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings from Vaiśālī were established, some in the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth.
Some attained the fruit of once-returning,
some the fruit of non-returning, and some, having gone forth, attained arhatship.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Some took up the precepts for going for refuge.

140.001. The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by King Mūrdhāta, as the result of which, immediately upon the arising of that thought, a rain of gold fell within his inner apartments for seven days?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there arose in the world a Tathāgata named Sarvābhibhū— worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
At that time, there was a certain son of a merchant who had recently been established in life.
In that region, it was the custom that when a girl newly married was given away to her husband by means of a carriage,
she was presented to her lord after being strewn with flowers made of the four jewels and bound [with ornaments].
She, taking her husband with her, was going to her own home.
And that merchant’s son, having taken flowers made of the four jewels and mounting his vehicle, set out for his father-in-law’s house.
As he was traveling, the Samyaksambuddha Sarvābhibhū, wandering on his tour through the countryside, arrived there in due course.
140.010. Upon seeing him, adorned with the thirty-two marks and of such a lovely appearance that one could never tire of beholding him, an exceeding faith arose within him.
140.011. With his mind thus filled with faith, he descended from his vehicle and scattered those flowers made of the four jewels over the Blessed One.
140.012. Those flowers were empowered by the Perfectly Awakened One Sarvābhibhū in such a way that they manifested as being the size of chariot wheels.
140.013. Having been tied as a canopy, they followed him as he walked and remained stationary when he stood still.
140.013. Filled with serene faith, he spoke this verse:
140.015. By this vast gift, may I become a Buddha, a Sugata, a Self-Existent One;
140.017. having crossed over myself, may I ferry across the great floods of people who have not been ferried across by previous Lords of Jinas. //8//
140.019. The Blessed One, the Great Seer Sarvābhibhū, was strewn with most delightful flowers. 140.021. And there I made a noble aspiration, desiring this supreme enlightenment. (9)
140.023. It was through the ripening of that very same karma that I attained auspicious, unsurpassed enlightenment.
140.025. And for seven days, a rain of gold fell upon King Mūrdhāta of great power. //10//
Through the ripening of that very same karma, even my city became made of gold and refined gold; for Mahāsudarśana, there was a delightful city named Kuśāvatī.

140.029. The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what kind of karma was performed by King Mūrdhāta, as a result of which he exercised sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over the four continents and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa gods?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world.
Then that Samyaksambuddha Vipaśyin, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, eventually arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī."
141.003. Then, in the forenoon, the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Bandhumatī for alms.

141.004. There, a certain merchant named Autkarika saw the Blessed One Vipaśyin, whose form was of such a beautiful appearance that one could never tire of beholding it, and an exceeding faith arose within him.
141.005. Having conceived faith, he took a handful of mung beans and placed them in the bowl.
141.006. Then four mung beans fell into the bowl;
one struck a thorn and fell to the ground.
141.006. "The remainder was not even reached; before reaching [the mouth], they fell to the ground. 141.007. Then the merchant, filled with faith, made this aspiration:
"By this great gift, may I become a Buddha, a Sugata, a Self-Existent One;
having crossed over myself, may I ferry across the great floods of people who have not been ferried across by previous Lords of Jinas.
The Blessed One said: "That merchant Otkarika..."
I myself was that person at that time and on that occasion.
When, having conceived faith in Vipaśyin, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, I placed a handful of mung beans into his alms bowl,
four of those beans fell into the bowl while the remainder fell upon the ground.
Through the ripening of that karma, he exercised sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over the four continents. Furthermore,
because that mung bean struck the rim of his bowl and fell to the ground,
through the ripening of that karma, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
141.017. "Monks, had that mung bean fallen into the bowl instead of on the ground, it is possible that he would have exercised sovereignty, lordship, and dominion among both gods and humans.
At that time and at that occasion, he who was the merchant Otkarika..."
This very King Mūrdhāta is he;
I myself was that King Mūrdhāta at that time, on that occasion.

141.020. Since, in this way, services rendered to the Blessed Buddha, who possesses great compassion, result in exceedingly great fruit, great benefits, great splendor, and great expansion, therefore one should awaken to existence.
141.021. What is to be done?
Service should be rendered to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and right aspirations should be made.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
141.024. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the glorious Divyāvadāna, the Māndhātāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 18 ********** 142.001. Divyāvadāna 18: The Legend of Dharmaruci/ 142.003.
Thus have I heard:
142.003. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

142.004. Now at that time, about five hundred merchants, having gathered their wares, were traveling by stages through villages, market towns, hamlets, cities, and royal capitals, until they reached the shore of the great ocean.
142.005. They carefully prepared a sea-going vessel.

142.006. When the merchants saw that great ocean, their minds were shattered and they did not dare to embark upon it. 142.007. Thereafter, those merchants said to the pilot: "Proclaim to us the true nature of the great ocean. 142.008. Thereupon, the pilot began to proclaim: "Listen, O men of Jambudvīpa!"
In this great ocean there are such jewels as these:
namely, gems, pearls, beryl, conch-shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, emerald, musāragalva, ruby, and right-spiraling shells.

Whoever wishes to properly gladden himself with such jewels, or his mother and father, wife and children, female and male slaves, laborers and servants, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations;
"And from time to time, he should bestow offerings upon worthy recipients—monks and brahmins—that lead upward, bring good fortune, result in happiness, and conduce to heaven in the future.
Therefore, let him embark upon this great ocean for the sake of wealth.
When this was said, all those beings, desiring prosperity and averse to misfortune, heard it and resolved to embark upon that great ocean.
142.015. Since that ship was overwhelmed by an excessive number of men and an excessive weight, it began to sink right there.
Then the helmsman said, "The ship is beyond saving.
Thereupon the merchants said, "To whom shall we now say, 'Come down from the ship'?"
Those merchants said to the helmsman, "Proclaim the true nature of the great ocean.
Thereupon, he began to proclaim: "Listen, you people of Jambudvīpa!
In this great ocean there exist such great and terrible dangers as these."

Namely: the fear of the *timi* fish, the fear of the *timiṃgila*, the fear of waves, the fear of sea turtles, the fear of being stranded on dry land, the fear of sinking in the water, and the fear of colliding with mountains submerged within the waters.
Furthermore, thieves arrive—clad in blue garments and plunderers of wealth.

Because of this, one may even resolve to abandon one's own life, as well as one's mother and father, children and wife, male and female slaves, laborers and servants, friends, ministers, kinsmen, blood relations, and the wondrous Jambudvīpa.
"Let him embark upon the great ocean!
There are few who are brave and many who are cowardly.
Having heard that and having it thus proclaimed, many descended from that ship.
Some remained.
Then those merchants cut one thong of the ship;
afterwards two, three, and so on, until all the thongs were cut in succession.

When those [ropes] were cut, that ship, impelled by the great helmsman, set out swiftly like a cloud driven by a great wind or a cloud impelled by a powerful gale, having been launched into the sky. Eventually, it reached the Jewel Island (*ratnadvīpa*).
Upon reaching that region, the helmsman said to them: "On this Jewel Island there are glass trinkets that resemble jewels."
You must examine them again and again before accepting them;
otherwise, you will later feel regret when you have returned to Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, there are women there known as the *Kroñca-kumārikās*.
Having found a man, they strike him with stones in such a way that he meets with calamity right there through their misconduct.
And it is in this very place that intoxicating fruits grow.
Whoever eats them remains asleep for seven days and nights.
Furthermore, after seven days on this very Jewel Island, non-human beings cannot tolerate [the presence of others].
They produce winds of such a kind, or even contrary ones, by which the ship is carried away, just as happens to those who have not yet accomplished their task.
"These things you have obtained must not be eaten.
Having heard this, the merchants remained attentive in mind and established themselves in heedfulness.

143.001. Having reached that island of jewels, they applied themselves with effort and searched for gems; examining them one by one in due order, they filled that ship with jewels, just as one might fill it with barley, wheat, mung beans, or lentils.
143.003. Having filled the ship, they set out under a favorable wind directed toward Jambudvīpa.
And in the great ocean, living beings are mixed together in three groups:
those with bodies one hundred *yojanas* in height, and those with bodies two or three hundred *yojanas* in height.
In the second tier, the bodies range from eight hundred *yojanas* up to nine, ten, and as far as fourteen hundred *yojanas*.
In the third tier, the bodies range from fifteen hundred *yojanas* up to sixteen, seventeen, and as far as twenty-one hundred *yojanas*.
And there in that great ocean, those species of fish are intent upon devouring one another;
those situated on the first level are devoured by those situated on the second level.
143.008. Those who abide on the second stage are devoured by those who abide on the third stage.
143.009. There, a fish named Timiṅgila, having emerged from the third mass of water and taking hold of the upper mass of water, moves about.
At whatever moment he covers his mouth, at that very moment the water from the great ocean is driven with great force toward the opening of his mouth;
by that very mass of water, the various species of fish— such as fish, tortoises, *vallabhakas*, *śuśumāras*, and *makaras*— are cast through the mouth-opening and fall into his belly.
As he was practicing in this way, his head alone could be discerned from afar as if it were a mountain reaching the height of the sky;
and his eyes could be seen from afar like two suns in the heavens.
143.014. When those merchants perceived it from afar, having discerned that it was the form of the great ocean, they began to reflect: "Sirs, could this be the rising of two suns?
While they were thus reflecting, that ship began to be carried away with great speed toward its entrance.

143.016. Seeing their ship being carried away by the force of the current and perceiving the arising of the two suns, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him: "Sirs, is it not so that it is heard that seven suns will appear at the dissolution of the eon?
Could it be that they have now risen?"
143.018. Then the helmsman said to them, who were filled with apprehension: "Sirs, that which you hear called the *timitimiṅgila*—this is the fear of the *timitimiṅgila*.
Let your honors behold it! 143.019. "Therefore, let your honors look."
143.020. This head of his appears like a mountain rising out of water.
143.020. And behold this row of teeth of his!
143.022. Behold these two pupils of his; even from afar they appear like two suns.
143.022. Again, that helmsman said to the merchants: "Listen, sirs!
There is now no means of survival for us by which we might be freed from this danger.
Death has arrived for every one of us."
143.024. Therefore, what should be done by you now?
Whichever deity you have devotion for, let him entreat her. 143.025.
Perhaps, through that very entreaty, some deity might deliver us from this great danger.
143.026. And there was no other means for their survival.
Therefore, those merchants, terrified by the fear of death, began to supplicate the gods—Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Mahendra, Upendra, and the rest—for the sake of protecting their lives.
Yet, despite their supplications, there was no particular protection of life for them from that fear of death.
In that very same way, the ship was cast by the force of the water toward the mouth of a *timiṅgila* fish from which it was being carried away.
And there, a lay follower (*upāsaka*) had boarded it. He said: "Sirs!"
"There is no liberation for us whatsoever from this fear of death; we must all die. However, let us all together with one voice say, 'Homage to the Buddha!'"
"Even if death occurs, we shall pass away with mindfulness focused upon the Buddha;
thus, there will be a journey to a happy rebirth.
Then, all those merchants together with one voice made this prostration, saying, "Homage to the Buddha!"
144.001. And the Blessed One, staying in the Jeta Grove, heard that conversation with his pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans.
144.002. Having heard it, the Blessed One then empowered that sound in such a way that it was heard by the *timiṅgila*.
144.003. Upon hearing that cry of "Homage to the Buddha! from him, indignation arose in his mind and he became distraught: "A Buddha, alas, has appeared in the world!"
"It would not be fitting for me that, having heard the proclamation of the name of the Buddha, the Blessed One, I should take food.
He began to reflect: "If I were to close my mouth suddenly now, the ship, struck by the force of the water, will be destroyed."
"And the destruction of the lives of these many beings [is at hand].
What if I were to gently, very gradually, close my mouth?
Then that *timiṅgila* fish gently, very gradually, closed its own mouth.
144.008. Afterwards, that vessel, having escaped from the mouth of that great sea-monster and encountered a favorable wind, reached the shore.

144.009. Then those merchants, having reached the shore, filled their goods onto carts, camels, oxen, donkeys, and so forth; traveling by stages through villages, market towns, hamlets, cities, and other settlements, they eventually arrived at Śrāvastī.
144.010. Having gone there, they reflected: "It is a natural law that the one whose name the vessel bears shall arrive with the ship successfully completed."
"These jewels belong only to him; they are accessible to him alone.
"What if we were to give these jewels to the Blessed Buddha?
Having thus gathered those jewels, they approached the presence of the Blessed One.

144.013. Having approached in due order and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when we had embarked upon the ocean in a ship and were being seized by a *timiṃgila* fish, while that ship was being carried away and our lives were at stake, we took refuge solely in the recollection of the Blessed One; by uttering his name, we were released from the mouth of that great fish."
Then, O Blessed One, having successfully completed our voyage, we arrived here in safety and well-being.
This is the natural law: whatever ship arrives with its cargo successfully delivered belongs to the one whose name it bears.
"144.017. Thus, by the mere mention of the Blessed One's name, we have been delivered from the fear of death.
144.018. Therefore, may the Blessed One accept these jewels of ours.
The Blessed One said: "By whom was I [appointed] for Indra?"
The jewels of the factors of enlightenment have been attained;
what further use has the Tathāgata for ordinary jewels? If you, my children, desire to go forth in our teaching, [then do so].
"Come!
Then those merchants reflected: "Whatever life we possess, all of it is due to the majesty of the Blessed Buddha."
144.021. "Since we have these jewels, let us renounce them and go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One.

144.022. Thereupon, they distributed those jewels among their parents, children, wives, female and male slaves, laborers, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations according to what was appropriate, and then went forth.
144.023. Having gone forth, by applying themselves, striving, and exerting themselves, they eventually realized arhatship.

144.024. Thereupon, the monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Blessed One, what kind of actions were performed and accumulated by these merchants, the ripening of which caused them to please the Blessed One and not displease him?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, in the past, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa appeared in the world.
And it was under his teaching that these very individuals went forth as renunciants."
144.028. Having gone forth there, they did not attain any collection of qualities whatsoever, other than what was taught, studied, and recited for their fellow celibates.

144.029. At the time of death, they made this aspiration: "Since we have approached the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and have taught, studied, and recited [the scriptures], yet no collection of qualities has been attained by us—"
By the ripening of this karma, may we please and not displease that Samyaksambuddha Śākyamuni, who was prophesied by the Samyaksambuddha Kāśyapa in the future time.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, monks? Those five hundred monks who in the past were ordained in the teaching of Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One—these very five hundred monks are they.
At that time, their faculties were brought to maturity."
Now, arhatship has been realized.
And as for that fish named Timiṃgilas in the great ocean who, upon hearing the word "Buddha," remained without food—
he, by his very nature, possessed such a sharp digestive fire that, unable to endure the suffering of hunger, he passed away and died.
145.005. He took rebirth in Śrāvastī in a brahmin family devoted to the six duties.
145.006. That corpse of his floated out upon the great ocean.
And because the nāgas could not bear its odor when it was near their own abode, they cast it away elsewhere.
And wherever it was thrown, even there, near that very spot, was the abode of a nāga. Unable to endure the odor, he too threw it elsewhere.
In this manner, through successive throwing, that corpse was eventually brought to the shore of the great ocean.
Immediately thereafter, it was washed away by the tide of the ocean and cast onto dry land.

There, being devoured by many birds such as crows, vultures, dogs, jackals, and wild beasts, and by swarms of insects that had gathered there, its bones became a skeleton with the flesh decayed until it remained entirely white.
And at that time, in Śrāvastī, the wife of that brahmin became pregnant.
Because she was being tormented by the extreme suffering of hunger due to the development of the fetus, she said to her husband: "Noble Lord, I am being greatly oppressed by the pain of hunger.
As she was speaking thus, the husband said to her: "My dear lady,"
"Whatever food and drink there is in our house, consume it all.
She began to consume it;
and having consumed all that food and drink, she still did not reach satiety.
145.015. Again the master of the house informed him: "Noble son, I do not reach satiety at all.
For he has sought out food and drink from his neighbors, friends, kinsmen, and others nearby, and bestowed it upon her."
Having devoured even that, she did not reach satiety.
Again she said to the master of the house: "Noble son, I do not reach satiety at all."
145.017. Thereupon, that brahmin, with an agitated mind, fell into distress:
"Sirs, what could this be—is there a being born in her womb, because of whose birth she finds no satisfaction?

145.018. Then that brahmin, having shown [the matter] to the soothsayers, showed it to physicians and those who know the science of spirits (*bhūtatantra*) in order to resolve his doubt: "Sirs, please look!"
"Could this Brahmin woman be overcome by a great disease, or perhaps possessed by a spirit or a graha, or could it be that some other sign of death has manifested through this approach?
Having heard this, they employed such a course of action.
They observed a change in the faculties of that Brahmin woman.

145.022. When they did not perceive any alteration in her sense faculties, those physicians—experts in medicine, omens, and the science of elemental spirits—questioned that Brahmin woman: "From what time onwards has such a state of intense digestive fire arisen in you?
She replied: "At the very moment of conception, this same kind of regimen was undertaken."

145.025. Thereupon, the soothsayers, physicians, and healers declared: "No other disease of this kind has arisen in her, nor has any affliction caused by the possession of spirits or demons occurred; rather, it is solely through the power of this very fetus that she possesses such intense heat. 145.027. Consequently, having learned the facts of the matter, the brahmin was restored to health.
That brahmin woman, too, was never satiated with food and drink. In due course, at that very same time, a son was born.
As soon as that boy was born, the brahmin woman became free from the suffering of hunger.
145.029. As soon as that boy was born, he was afflicted by extreme hunger.
145.030. While he was being tormented by hunger, his mother began to give him her breast.
145.031. And although that boy drank from the breast, he did not reach satisfaction at all.

145.031. Afterwards, that brahmin and his wife, having entreated their neighbors and the young women of their own kin who had been slighted by them, proceeded to have them give breast milk to that boy.
146.001. And although that boy drank from the breasts of all of them, he did not reach satiety at all.
146.001. Thereafter, for his sake, that brahmin had a she-goat slaughtered.
146.002. That boy, having drunk the milk of that she-goat as well, was not at all satiated by his mother’s breast.
146.003. There, from time to time, monks and nuns would enter for almsfood and deliver religious discourses.
146.004. Upon hearing those discourses, the boy would not cry at that time.
With attentive ears, he became silent and listened to that discourse on hearing the Dharma.
When the monks and nuns had departed, he began to wander about again, experiencing the suffering of thirst.
They observed this and concluded: "The calf has a taste for the Dharma."
The name Dharmaruci was established for him.
And as that boy gradually passed through the course of months and half-months while eating, he was never at all satiated with food and drink.
And when he had reached a distinguished stage of life, he remained there.
Then his parents gave him an alms-bowl, saying,
"Go, my child;
here is your bowl for alms."
"Take this and wander for alms in Śrāvastī; perform your meal there.
Thereupon, that boy took the alms-bowl and wandered for alms in Śrāvastī.
Even as he wandered, eating again and again, he returned home still not satiated.
146.011. Then he reflected: "What deed have I committed, the ripening of which causes me never to find satisfaction when obtaining food?
With a dejected mind, he began to think: "Should I enter the fire, or enter the water, or perhaps throw myself down from a precipice?"
As he remained thus absorbed in thought, he was noticed by a lay follower (upāsaka). The lay follower said to him, "Why do you remain here so preoccupied with anxiety?"
Go!
Enter the great teaching of the Buddha, which possesses great supernatural power and great majesty;
there, go forth as a renunciant.
And there, having gone forth, you will accumulate a store of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*).
Furthermore, those unwholesome qualities (*akuśala-dharma*) which have been accumulated even in this life will be attenuated.
"If you should indeed attain the multitude of virtues,
your cycle of existence will be brought to an end.
Then that Great Being, urged by the lay follower, went to the Jeta Grove.
Having gone to the Jeta Grove and seeing there the monks intent upon recitation, study, and mental application, he was filled with extreme faith.
Approaching a monk, he spoke thus: "Noble sir, I wish to go forth."
146.020. When he was asked by the monks, "Have you been permitted by your mother and father?
he replied, "I have not been permitted by my mother and father.
They said to him, "Go, dear boy."
"Seek permission from your mother and father.
Thereupon, he set out to seek permission from his mother and father.
He was addressed by his parents: "Go, my son."
"Do as you intend.
Having received permission, he went into the presence of the monk;
subsequently, he was ordained by the monk.
And there, at times the monks receive almsfood, and at other times they receive invitations.
On whichever day the almsfood is received, [it is as follows].
Thereupon the preceptor said, "Child,
are you satisfied or not?
He replied to the preceptor, "There is no satisfaction."
146.026. Thereupon, the preceptor observed: "Having gone forth at a young age, he does not reach satiety because of his intense appetite.
146.027. He began to share even from his own alms-food with him.
146.028. And again he asked: "Child,..."
"Are you now satisfied?
Then he said to his preceptor, "I am not yet satisfied.
When the preceptor heard this, he began to speak with affection to the monks and other fellow-residents.
146.030. Thereupon, his fellow monks—those with the same preceptors and teachers, as well as others who were affectionate toward him—began to provide for him.
146.031. Even while receiving from them, he did not reach satiety.
And whenever there was an invitation, [he would go].
Even then, they continue to provide him with those very same things.
The donor, having understood this, gives him whatever is in excess and then departs.
If there is a beverage, that too is given to him in the same manner, whatever is in excess.
147.001. Since he had gone forth as a renunciant, his belly was never filled with food and drink.
147.002. At that time, a certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha.
147.003. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered the house together with the community of monks.
147.004. Dharmaruci was appointed as the superintendent of the monastery's material goods.
147.005. Now, a certain householder lived there in Śrāvastī.
He had learned that whoever provides a meal for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, without even being aware of it, immediately prospers in wealth.
Consequently, he prepared food for about five hundred monks.

Having filled a cart with that food— most excellent, refined, and pure— he went out from the monastery, accompanied by all his friends and kinsmen, thinking, "I shall feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
However, he saw that there were no monks at all in that Jetavana.
147.009. While wandering there, he saw Dharmaruci, the steward of the community.
147.010. The householder said to him, "Noble sir, where have the monks gone?"
He replied, "They have been invited into the inner apartments and have entered.
Upon hearing this, the householder became dejected and thought, "Alas!
Thus our labor has become fruitless."
Having reflected, he said to Dharmaruci, "Noble sir, please eat some as well.
He replied, "If it has been relinquished by you, O Great-souled One."

147.013. Then, having reflected on this, the householder took a cart filled with as much food and drink as would suffice for a single monk and set about serving Dharmaruci. 147.014. As Dharmaruci began to eat, it was all consumed without remainder.
He was not at all satisfied.
The householder reflected, "This man is not satisfied," and said to him, "Noble sir,..."
"Will you eat again? He replied, "Noble sir, if it has been relinquished by you."
147.016. Thereupon, the householder took as much food and drink as would suffice for the meal of two monks from that very cart and set about feeding them.
147.018. But even after Dharmaruci had eaten that as well, he was still not satisfied.
The householder observed again, "He is not yet satisfied. He said, "Noble sir, will you eat more?"
He said, "O Great-souled One,
if it has been relinquished by you,
then take food and drink from that cart so that there may be enough for three monks," and he proceeded to feed them again.
Having eaten even that, Dharmaruci was still not satisfied.
He was asked, "Noble sir,
will you eat again?"
He said, "If it has been relinquished by you.
Thereupon, that householder took food and drink sufficient for four monks and set about feeding him again.
Dharmaruci, having eaten even that, was still not satiated.
He was asked, "Noble sir,
will you eat again? He replied once more, "If it has been relinquished by you."
147.024. Then, taking as much from that cart as would satisfy the five monks with food and drink, he set about feeding them again.
147.025. And they consumed it as well.
He was not at all satisfied.
In detail, even after eating as much food and drink as would suffice for ten monks, he was still not satisfied.
147.026. Then he reflected: "This is no human being; he is a transformation of a human.

For it is heard that the Jeta Grove is never empty of five hundred yakṣas dressed in blue robes; surely one of them must be this. 147.027–028. Having thought thus, he began to usher the children into the house, saying: "Go, all of you, quickly back to the house!"
"If I alone am to live or die," [he thought].
Having dismissed his household, and being terrified by the fear of death, he took food and drink from that cart and began to serve it;
and he ate at his own leisure.
The householder said, "Noble sir,
receive it very quickly! Thereupon, Dharmaruci accepted it promptly and began to eat.
147.032. That householder, having served [the food] with great haste and having given that food and drink to the cart without leaving any remainder,
departed for the city in great haste without looking back, saying "I pay homage to the Noble One," while seized by fear even before hearing the instruction for the dedication of merit.
From that city, a monk who was carrying almsfood departed, taking that very almsfood for him. He ate that as well.
For Dharmaruci, from the time of his birth, his stomach had never once been full.
On that day, he became satiated with that food.
As the householder was entering the city, the Blessed One arrived before him, surrounded by the community of monks.
The householder said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One,..."
Having filled a cart with food and drink for the sake of the community of five hundred monks headed by the Buddha, I went to Jetavana;
however, I did not find any monks there,
and I saw only a single monk.

He informed me that the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, had entered the house for an invitation. Then this thought arose in me: "Let him eat alone for now. Thereupon, I gave him the entire cartload of food and drink in succession.
He consumed it all with great relish.
"Blessed One, was this a human or a non-human?
The Blessed One replied, "Householder,"
That monk is named Dharmaruci.
Rejoice!
Today, satiated by your food and drink, he will realize arhatship.
148.012. Then the Blessed One arrived at the Jeta Grove.
The Blessed One reflected: "Who will be that patron who shall provide such a quantity of food every day to Dharmaruci for his sustenance?
Thereupon the Blessed One said to him: "Dharmaruci, have you seen the great ocean?"
He replied, "No, Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One said, "Take hold of the corner of my robe; afterwards, I will show you the great ocean."

148.015. When Dharmaruci let go of the corner of the Blessed One’s robe, the Blessed One—like a king of swans with outspread wings—by the mere arising of a thought, took hold of Dharmaruci through his supernatural power and reached the shore of the ocean. 148.017. And at that spot where the fragments of the bones of him who had become a *timi-timiṅgila* fish lay, [he placed him].
Having led him there, he was established [in that place]. And it was said to him: "Go, my child; contemplate mental attention."
148.018. Thereupon, Dharmaruci began to examine it:
"What is this? Is it wood, or a fragment of bone, or perhaps a wooden plank?"
Not finding that person there, he set out to search for the limit [of the forest]. Having found the person,
he followed along its side here and there, searching for it, until he fell into exhaustion.
And he could not find its limit. This thought occurred to him: "I shall not know the nature of this—what it is—and I shall not reach its end."
"I shall go; I will ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. Thereupon, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One, he asked the Blessed One: "What is that, Blessed One?
I do not perceive its manifestation."
148.024. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Child, this is merely a fragment of bone.
148.025. He replied, "Blessed One," and so on.
"Is such a being as this, whose skeletal fragments are like these?
The Blessed One said: "Be satisfied, Dharmaruci, with regard to existences; be satisfied with regard to the requisites of existence."
"This is a fragment of your bone.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Dharmaruci, his mind agitated, said, "Is such a fragment of bone mine?
He was told, "Dharmaruci, this is a fragment of your bone."
Having heard such a thing, he was extremely agitated;
for the Blessed One had given him this instruction: "Dharmaruci, attend to this and that."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, like a royal swan with outspread wings, arrived at the Jeta Grove by means of his supernatural power.

Then, as Dharmaruci reflected and applied his attention, he produced the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), the summits (*mūrdhan*), the patient acceptances (*kṣānti*), and the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); he realized the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
He attained the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship.
He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, having abandoned attraction and aversion.

Having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, he attained the clear knowledges, the superknowledges, and the analytical insights. He turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor, and was like one to whom an axe and sandalwood are the same.
149.002. He became one to be honored, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
149.003. He began to reflect upon his own previous birth, wondering: "From where have I passed away, and where have I been reborn?"

149.014. Since he saw many hundreds of births—having passed away from and been reborn among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts—the following thought occurred to him: "If I had not been taken into the Blessed One’s care, I would have continued to wander even through future births."
149.005. Then he reflected: "Even my own future succession of births will consist of an uninterrupted and continuous stream of rebirths in the hells and as hungry ghosts.
149.006. Having reflected thus, he thought: "Alas, the Blessed One has performed a most difficult task for me alone!
149.007. If the Blessed One had attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the sake of me alone,"
That would indeed be a great benefit; it would even more so remove the descent into the states of woe for many thousands of beings.
Then, through his supernatural power, Dharmaruci arrived at the Jeta Grove in order to see the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks,
teaching the Dharma.
Then Dharmaruci approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him, "It has been a long time, Dharmaruci?
Dharmaruci replied, "It has been a long time, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said, "It has been a very long time, Dharmaruci?
Dharmaruci replied, "It has been a very long time, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It has been a very, very long time, Dharmaruci?"
He has a delight in the Dharma, Blessed One.

149.015. Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Blessed One, Dharmaruci was born right here in Śrāvastī and went forth in this very Jeta Grove; he has not come from anywhere, nor has he gone anywhere.
While staying right here, he was addressed by the Blessed One thus: 'After a long time, Dharmaruci!'"
After so long, Dharmaruci;
after such a very long time, Dharmaruci! With what intention does the Blessed One speak thus?
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I do not speak with reference to the present;
I speak with reference to the past. It was with reference to the past that I spoke thus."
"Monks, do you wish to hear a discourse on the Dharma concerning the previous course of karma of this Dharmaruci?
O Blessed One, this is the time; O Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to deliver a discourse on the Dharma to the monks concerning Dharmaruci."
Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it.
149.023. Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during the first incalculable eon, a Tathāgata named Kṣemaṃkara appeared in the world—
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

149.025. He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Kṣemāvatī. And in that Kṣemāvatī, a king named Kṣema reigned. In that royal capital of Kṣemāvatī, there lived a certain merchant guild-president.
For sixty three-month periods, that merchant provided all the necessary requisites for the Samyaksambuddha Kṣemaṃkara together with the community of monks.
Then the merchant reflected: "I shall go to the great ocean;
having procured goods and brought back jewels from there, I will perform a quinquennial festival for the Saṃgha."
149.029. Having reflected thus, he gathered his merchandise and, traveling by stages through villages, market towns, hamlets, cities, and royal capitals, he eventually reached the ocean.
149.030. After having the bell sounded for a public proclamation, he embarked upon the great ocean in a sea-going vessel.
149.031. While he was thus embarked upon that great ocean, the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṅkara, having completed all the work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder.
149.032. After he had passed into final nirvāṇa, the monks who were his disciples also passed into final nirvāṇa.
150.001. Seven days after his final nirvāṇa, the teaching vanished.
And that merchant, having crossed over from that great ocean with a successful ship protected by gods and humans, reached the shore.
150.002. Having crossed that [river], he loaded the merchandise onto carts, camels, oxen, and donkeys, and set out by stages.
150.003. As he was traveling along the road, he asked those he met on the way: "Do you know what is happening in the capital city of Kṣemavatī?
They replied, "We know."
He asked, "Is there anyone in the capital city of Kṣemāvatī named Kṣemaṅkara who is a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksambuddha)?
They replied, "That Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha Kṣemaṅkara, has entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, he fell into great distress.
150.006. He fainted and fell to the ground.
150.007. Then, having regained his breath through the sprinkling of water and returned to life, he rose and asked again: "Do you know whether even the disciples of that Blessed One still remain?
They replied: "Those self-controlled monks have also entered final nirvana."
150.009. Seven days after the parinirvāṇa of the Blessed Buddha Kṣemaṃkara, the Perfectly Awakened One, King Kṣema established a caitya known as Alpeśākhya.
150.010. Having gone there, that merchant asked the people of the countryside:
"Sirs, has any stūpa been established for that Blessed Buddha?"
They said, "Yes;
King Kṣema has established a caitya named Alpeśākhya.
Then this thought occurred to him: "I have brought this gold for the sake of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kṣemaṃkara."
And he has passed into final nirvāṇa.
What if I were to have a more magnificent stūpa built for that very Blessed One using this very gold?
Having reflected thus, he informed King Kṣema: "Great King," he said.
"This gold has been brought by me for the sake of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kṣemaṃkara.
And that Blessed One has passed into final nirvāṇa.
Now, O Great King, if you would grant permission,"
"By means of this very gold, I shall have a monument for that Blessed One constructed that is even more magnificent.
The king said to him, "Do as you intend.
Then all the brahmins residing in the city gathered together, went to that great merchant, and said, "O great merchant!"
When the Buddha Kṣemaṃkara had not yet appeared in the world, we were the ones worthy of offerings for the world;
but when he had appeared, [we were no longer so].
At that time, he became one worthy of offerings;
but now that he has passed into final nirvana, we alone are the ones worthy of offerings.
This gold belongs to us.
He said to them, "I will not give this gold to you.
They replied, "If you will not give it to us,
we will not grant you your wish."
150.022. Those brahmins were many, while the merchant had a small retinue.
As they were thus competing, he was unable to have that caitya constructed with the gold as he desired.
150.023. Then that merchant went into the presence of the king and said: "Your Majesty, I am unable to have that caitya constructed according to my wishes from the brahmins.
For this reason, the king has assigned me a man of his own who is a warrior of a thousand."
150.025. And the king thus commanded his own man: "If anyone causes any obstruction to this great merchant while he is constructing the stūpa, you must punish him with a severe penalty.
150.026. "As the king commands," replied the thousand-man warrior, and having given his word to the king, he departed.

Having gone out, he spoke thus to those brahmins: "Listen, sirs! I have been appointed as this king’s personal agent for this great merchant-chief with these instructions: 'If anyone should cause an obstruction while he is restoring this stūpa, you must punish him with a severe penalty.'"
150.029. "If you cause any obstacle here, I shall punish you with a severe penalty.
150.030. Having heard these words from the man, those Brahmins, who were warriors capable of fighting a thousand men, became terrified.

150.030. Then, that great merchant, having reflected that he must act in such a way that this gold would remain right there within the womb [of the stupa], began to have four staircases constructed for that stupa on all four sides, one after another.
150.032. Thus, in due order, [the structure was built] from the first pillar, then the second, then the third pillar, and so on until the dome (*aṇḍa*).
151.001. The dome of the stūpa was constructed in such a way that the sacrificial post (*yūpayaṣṭi*) was set within it. 151.002. Afterwards, a harmikā was constructed atop that very new dome.
151.003. Gradually, the raising of the sacrificial pole was completed.
151.003. Those great precious jewels were placed upon the rain-trough.
151.004. While that was being done, this thought occurred to a man who was a thousand-fold warrior: "No one will strike now."
151.005. With a mind full of confidence, he went to the countryside on a certain business.
By that great merchant, four door-chambers were constructed for the four sides of that stūpa, and four great caityas were caused to be built for its four sides.
Namely: his birth, his perfect enlightenment, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and his final nirvana.
That courtyard of the stupa was paved with precious stones, and four subsidiary shrines were constructed in the four directions.
151.008. Lotus ponds were constructed along the sides on all four directions.

There, various water-born flowers were planted, namely: the blue lotus (*utpala*), the red lotus (*padma*), the night-blooming lily (*kumuda*), the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), the sweet-scented lotus (*sugandhika*), and the soft-scented lotus (*mṛdugandhika*).
And various land-born flowers were planted upon the banks of the ponds.
Namely: the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *avārṣika*, *mallikā*, *sumanā*, *yūthikā*, and *dhātuṣkārī*.
These flowers and fruits, available in all seasons, were designated as a permanent endowment for the purpose of worshiping the stūpa.
151.012. Stūpa-shelters were given. 151.013. Conch shells, drums, and musical instruments were given. And those who perform services at that caitya with perfumes, incense, garlands, and powders—
151.014. And having come from that foundation and from the surrounding regions, people perform worship at that shrine with perfumes, garlands, incense, and powders.
And when the southern wind blows, by that southern wind, the shrine and its courtyard become filled and permeated with the fragrance of all kinds of flowers.
151.016. Thus, by the western wind and also by the gradual breeze,
as it blew and blew, that courtyard of the shrine became filled and permeated with various fragrant garlands.
When that stūpa had been completely finished according to the *Sarvajātaka*, a thousand-man warrior arrived.
Seeing that the stūpa was fully completed, he said, "What is gained by performing service at this shrine?
For that merchant was intent on providing an illustration of the Buddha, [showing] how unsurpassed enlightenment is attained through such exertion and vigor over three incalculable eons.

151.020. Having heard that, he fell into despair and, with his enthusiasm diminished, said: "I shall not be able to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. 151.021. Thereupon, that merchant proceeded to cite the example of the *pratyekabuddha*; having heard even that description of the one who fights a thousand, the man, dejected in heart, said: "Even this *pratyekabuddha*-enlightenment, I—"
He was unable to gather [the necessary provisions].
Then that great merchant, having offered a description of the qualities of a disciple, said: "In this matter as well, you should first fix your mind.
Thereupon, Sahasrayodhin asked: "But you, great merchant, in which enlightenment have you made your vow?"
The great merchant said, "I have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed awakening.
The Thousand-Fighter said, "If you have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed awakening,
then I shall be your very disciple."
"You must keep me in mind.
Then the guild-leader said to him, "Alas, you have committed many sins!
However, when you hear the sound of the appearance of a Buddha in the world, you shall regain your memory."
151.029. And that merchant, having built that *caitya* and gazed upon it, prostrated at its feet and made this aspiration:
151.030. "By means of this gift of great scope, may I become a Buddha, a Sugata, a Self-Existent One (*svayambhū*).
Having crossed over myself, may I ferry across the multitudes of people who have not been ferried across by the former Lords of Jinas. (1)
The Blessed One said: "He who was that merchant in the past was none other than myself; at that time, I was engaged in the conduct of a bodhisattva.
He who was that warrior of a thousand [men]..."
This very Dharmaruci was he at that time, on that occasion.
This was my first meeting with this Dharmaruci during the first incalculable aeon.
It is with reference to this that I say: "After a long time, Dharmaruci!"
152.004. Then Dharmaruci, having recognized him, said: "It has been a long time, Blessed One!"

152.005. In the second [eon], the Perfectly Awakened One named Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world—a Perfectly Awakened One endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. 152.006. Then, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara arrived at the royal capital of Dvīpāvatī.
152.007. In the royal capital of Dvīpāvatī, a king named Dīpa reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people.
152.009. There, King Dīpa invited the Perfectly Awakened One, Dīpaṃkara, to enter the city with great honor.
152.010. And that King Dīpa had a neighboring king named Vāsava.
He sent a messenger to him, saying: "Come!
I have invited the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara with great ceremony for his entry into the city.
We shall perform worship for him."

152.012. And at that time, King Vāsava, having performed a sacrifice for twelve years, established five great gifts at the conclusion of the sacrifice, namely: a golden staff and water-pot, and a golden bowl with its lid.
A bed made of the four jewels,
five hundred kārṣāpaṇas,
and a maiden adorned with every ornament.
At that time, two young brahmins were living in other regions. They had completed their study of the Vedas under a teacher.
Knowing that it is the custom for the teacher’s property to be given to the teacher and the preceptor’s property to the preceptor, they reflected upon this.

152.017. And they heard that King Vāsava had prepared five great gifts at the conclusion of his sacrifice, declaring, "Whichever brahmin shall be perfected in the study of the Vedas, he shall receive them. 152.018. This thought occurred to the two of them: "Let us go there."
"Accept that gift.
Having reflected, "Who among us will be the most learned or the most proficient in recitation there? they set out for the great city of King Vāsava.
And a deity informed the king of their arrival.
"152.020. These two young brahmins who are coming, Sumati and Mati—of these two, give this gift to Sumati.
152.021. Since these two young brahmins are coming, Sumati and Mati..."
