152.023. The king reflected: "Surely these two are great-souled ones, for even the deities announce their arrival.
152.024. Then the king saw the two young brahmins approaching from afar, seated upon excellent vehicles.
152.025. Thereupon, the king asked Sumati, the son of Vāsava: "Are you Sumati?"
He said, "I am he.
For King Vāsava, having fed the young Brahmin Sumati at the seat of honor, bestows five gifts;
the young Brahmin Sumati accepts four great gifts, such as a staff, a water-pot, and so forth.
He did not accept the offering of the maiden.
He said, "I am a celibate student.
Thereupon, when that maiden saw the young man Sumati, who was gracious and handsome, she became enamored of him, and affection arose within her.
He spoke thus to the young brahmin Sumati: "O Brahmin, accept me!
He replied, "It is not possible to accept you;
for that maiden was abandoned by the king with the intention of giving her away, and has not been taken back again."
Not being accepted even by the young brahmin Sumati, she went to King Dīpa’s city of Dīpāvatī.

Having arrived there, she took her own ornaments off her body and gave them to a female garland-maker, saying, "In exchange for the value of these ornaments, give me blue lotuses every day for the sake of the King.
By that means, having given away that gold from the ornaments, she became an attendant to the King.
Then that young brahmin Sumati, having taken those four great gifts, went into the presence of his preceptor.
Having arrived, he presented those four great gifts to his preceptor.
And from them, the preceptor accepted three.
He gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to that very Sumati. And on that same night, Sumati saw ten dreams: "I am drinking the great ocean;
I am traveling through the air..."
These two, the moon and the sun, so possessed of great supernatural power and such great majesty, he wipes and strokes with his hand;
he yokes them to the king’s chariot, as well as white elephants and sages.
Swans, lions,
and great rocky mountains.
153.009. Upon seeing them, he awoke.
153.010. Having awakened, this thought occurred to him: "Who will provide me with an interpretation of these dreams?
Now, a seer possessing the five superknowledges lived not far from there.
153.011. Then the young brahmin Sumati went into the presence of the seer in order to have his doubts resolved.
153.012. After Sumati had exchanged greetings with the seer and related his dreams, he said: "Please provide an interpretation for these dreams of mine.
153.013. The seer replied: "I shall not provide an explanation of these dreams."
"Go to the capital city of Dīpāvatī.
There, King Dīpa has invited the Perfectly Awakened One named Dīpaṃkara to enter the city with great ceremony;
he will provide the interpretation of these dreams."
153.015. Then King Vāsava, having given his word to that king of Dīpa, arrived at the royal capital of Dīpavatī surrounded by eighty thousand ministers.

153.016. And from the seventh day onward, King Dīpa, with great effort, began to prepare for the entry of the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara into the city, and commenced collecting all kinds of flowers from throughout the entire realm.
And on that very day when King Dīpa began to make preparations for the entry of the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara into the city, Sumati also arrived at that same place.
Thereupon, the king had all the flowers collected.
153.020. That young woman, the attendant of the goddess, went to the florist and said, "Give me blue lotuses; I shall perform worship of the goddess.
153.022. The florist replied, "Today all the flowers have been taken by the king for the purpose of the entry of Dīpaṃkara into the city."
She said, "Go once more to that lotus pond; if, by my merit, a blue lotus can be found there without being pulled up.
By the power of Sumati’s merit, seven blue lotuses appeared in that lotus pond.
When the florist had gone,
he saw them.
Having seen them, the girl said to the florist, "Pick these lotuses."
The gardener said, "I will not dig it up;
otherwise, I shall be reprimanded by the royal court.
To this, she replied, "No."
153.027. "You have already taken all the flowers and given them to the king first.
The florist replied, "They were given;
for that girl said, 'These have appeared through my own merits.'"
"Give me these that have been extracted.
The garland-maker said, "How will these enter unnoticed by the royal household?
The girl said, "You may extract them."
"I shall place what has been thrown into the water-jar inside it.
When the gardener heard this, he took those [flowers] from the girl and gave them to her.
She took them, placed them in the water-jar, filled that jar with water, and set out for the capital.
And Sumati arrived at that place.
This thought occurred to him: "How is it that, having seen the Buddha, the Blessed One, I do not pay him honor?
He wandered through the houses of the florists, intent on searching for all kinds of flowers.
Yet he did not obtain even a single flower.
Afterwards, having gone out from the outer precincts, he wandered from garden to garden searching for flowers, but he still did not obtain even a single flower.
154.003. Then, while wandering about, he arrived at that park.
And that maiden came out from the park to meet the young brahmin Sumati.
Thereupon, by the power of his merit, those blue lotuses emerged from that water-jar.
154.005. When Sumati saw them, he said to that girl: "Give these lotuses to me.
Take five hundred kārṣāpaṇas from me as their price.
154.006. That girl said to Sumati: "At that time, you did not wish to accept me."
154.007. "Now you ask me for lotuses; I will not give them.
Having said this, he spoke to the young brahmin Sumati: "What will you do with these?"
Sumati said, "I shall worship the Blessed Buddha.
Afterwards, the girl said, "What need have I for kārṣāpaṇas?
In this way, I myself will give them to the Buddha."

"If you desire that, by the fruit of giving these lotuses, I too shall have a wife in birth after birth, then at the time of making this gift, you must make this vow: 'May she be my wife in birth after birth. Sumati said, "We are devoted to giving; we perform the sacrifice of our own offspring and the sacrifice of our own flesh."
154.012. Then that girl said to Sumati, "Make this vow: hereafter, when you are requested by someone, you must give me to him."
When she had spoken thus, she gave five lotuses to Sumati and took two for herself. Then she spoke this verse:
"Wherever you may make a vow after having encountered the Buddha, the Leader,
there may I be your wife, your constant companion in the practice of the Dharma."

The king had the entire area cleared of stones, pebbles, and potsherds; he caused banners, flags, and arches to be erected, silk streamers and garlands to be hung, and it to be sprinkled with scented water and fragrant powder.

From the city gate to the monastery, and from the monastery back to the city, he had this intervening space cleared of stones, pebbles, and potsherds, and had banners, flags, and arches erected, with silk streamers and garlands hung thereon.
And that king, taking up a parasol with a hundred ribs, went out to meet Dīpaṃkara, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
In the same way, the ministers [did so].
In the same way, King Vāsava, together with his ministers, went out to meet him.
King Dīpa prostrated at the feet of the Blessed Buddha and made this request: "Blessed One,..."
"Enter the capital.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, preceded by the community of monks, set out toward the entrance of the capital.
And King Dīpa held a hundred-ribbed parasol over the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara.

154.024. Likewise, the ministers and King Vāsava together with his ministers were empowered by the Blessed One through his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) such that each one perceived: "I am holding the parasol for the Blessed One."
154.025. Then the Blessed One, with such splendor, arrived in the midst of the people.
154.026. There, the Blessed One intentionally placed his foot upon the threshold pillar (indrakīla). 154.027. At the very moment the Blessed One placed his foot upon the threshold pillar,
At that very moment, immediately thereafter, the earth shook in six ways—it quaked, it trembled, it quaked violently; it quivered, it trembled, it quaked violently.
And it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Blessed Buddhas that when they place their feet upon the threshold of Indra’s pillar with deliberate effort, [the earth shakes].
Various wonderful and marvelous phenomena appeared: the insane regained their minds,
the blind regained their sight, and the deaf became capable of hearing with their ears.
The mute become capable of speech,
the lame become capable of walking,
and the fetuses of pregnant women who are deluded become healthy and well-formed.
The bonds of those beings bound by fetters and shackles become loosened; those who have been bound by enmity through successive births immediately thereafter attain a mind of loving-kindness;
and calves, having broken their tethers, reunite with their mothers.
The people cry out,
the horses neigh,
and the bulls bellow.
Parrots, mainas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvakas warbled sweetly,
and musical instruments, though unplayed, emitted melodious sounds.
Ornaments fashioned from precious gems emitted sweet sounds;
elevated regions of the earth sank down, and depressed regions rose up.
The ground was cleared of stones, pebbles, and potsherds,
and deities from the sky scattered divine blue lotuses.
They scatter lotuses, water lilies, white lotuses, powdered agallochum, powdered sandalwood, powdered tagara, tamāla leaves, and divine mandārava flowers;
the eastern quarter rises while the western sinks,
and the western rises while the eastern sinks.
The south rises and the north sinks;
the north rises and the south sinks; the center rises and the periphery sinks.
The edges rose up while the center sank down.
There, in the capital city of Dīpāvatī, many hundreds of thousands of living beings paid homage with flowers, incense, and perfumes.
Sumati and the maiden also followed after the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara, carrying lotuses in their hands.
And because they were surrounded by a great multitude of people there for the sake of making offerings, they could not get near the Blessed One.
The Blessed One perceived: "The young brahmin Sumati will generate much greater merit than this great multitude of people. Having thought this, he manifested a great, tumultuous wind and rainstorm.

155.014. Since that body of people granted him the opportunity, and having obtained the opportunity, the young brahmin Sumati, upon seeing the Blessed One whose appearance was beyond compare, was filled with exceeding faith.
And being filled with faith, he threw those five lotuses toward the Blessed One.
And those [lotuses] were empowered by the Blessed One, Dīpaṃkara, the Perfectly Awakened One, in such a way that they remained suspended as a canopy, the size of a wagon wheel;
as he walked, they followed after him.
They followed him as he stood there. Having seen this, the girl, filled with faith, threw two lotuses toward the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then performed such a miracle that the two lotuses remained suspended like a canopy near his ears, each as large as a wagon wheel.
And in that place, a mire was formed by a tumultuous wind and rain.
Later, the young brahmin Sumati approached that muddy spot of ground where the Buddha, the Blessed One, stood.
Having waded across that muddy patch of earth, he spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
155.022. "If I shall become a Buddha for the sake of awakening, may you, O Awakener of Buddhas, tread with your feet upon my matted locks, which bring an end to birth and old age. (3)
155.024. Then, Dīpaṃkara, the perfectly awakened Buddha, placed his feet upon the matted locks of that young brahmin Sumati. 155.025.
Standing directly behind Sumati was the young brahmin Mati, who was already enlightened;
being provoked to anger, he said to the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara: "Look here, sir!"
By this Samyaksambuddha Dīpaṃkara, the matted locks of this young brahmin Sumati were pressed down by his feet, as if they were those of an animal.
Afterwards, the Samyaksambuddha Dīpaṃkara prophesied for the young brahmin Sumati: "When you have escaped from human existence, you shall become a liberated teacher for the welfare of the world;
known by the name Śākyamuni, the son of the Śākyas, you will be the essence of the three worlds and the lamp of the universe. (Verse 4)
And as soon as the young brahmin Sumati was prophesied by the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara,
at that very moment he rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees,
and his matted locks fell away.
Other, even more distinguished matted locks appeared.
Standing in the air, he was seen by a great multitude of people.
Having seen him, they made this aspiration: "When he has attained unsurpassed knowledge, may we become his disciples."
And that girl also made a vow:
"O Leader, whatever vow you may make upon having encountered a Buddha, may I always be your wife there, your companion in the practice of the Dharma. (5)
When you have become a perfectly awakened one, the foremost leader in the world,
I shall be your female disciple when that time has arrived.
156.009. Seeing the young man seated in the sky, hundreds and thousands [of beings] there will all, in the future, aspire to the state of a disciple (śrāvaka). 156.010. //7//
When you become a perfectly awakened one, the supreme leader in the world,
we shall indeed be your disciples when that time has arrived.
And when the young brahmin Sumati was prophesied by the perfectly enlightened Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
King Dīpa seized his matted locks.
King Vāsava said, "Give these matted locks to me."
156.014. Thereupon, they were bestowed upon him by King Dīpa.
156.015. Having taken them, he counted them; there were eighty thousand horses.
The king’s ministers said to him: "Your Majesty,..."
"Give us each one hair.
"We shall build caityas for them.
Then the king gave one hair to each of those servants.
Those ministers went to their own territories and established shrines there.
When the young brahmin Sumati was prophesied for unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
King Dīpa and King Vāsava, along with many merchants and country folk, provided him with all necessary provisions out of regard for his future virtues.
Then that young man Mati was addressed: "I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; where did you first produce the thought [of awakening]?
He replied, "I am wounded, young man Sumati.
He asked, "In what way are you wounded?"

Then he said: "When your matted locks were stepped upon with the feet by the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara, you uttered these words in anger: 'The matted locks of this Vedic scholar have been stepped upon with the feet by the Perfectly Awakened One Dīpaṃkara, just as those of animals!
Thereupon Sumati said to him: 'Come here.'"
"We shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Then Sumati and Mati went forth into homelessness in the teaching of Dīpaṃkara, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. And having gone forth, Sumati studied the three Piṭakas.
The assembly was gathered together through the Dharma.
That young brahmin Sumati, having passed away and died, was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods; the young brahmin Mati, having passed away and died, was reborn in the hells.
The Blessed One said: "He who was King Vāsava at that time and on that occasion was King Bimbisāra.
Those eighty thousand ministers at that time and on that occasion..."
Those are now eighty thousand deities;
as for that populace of Dīpāvatī and that young girl, [they have all become these deities].
She who was Yaśodharā is this very person;
he who was Sumati was myself at that time, engaged in the conduct of a bodhisattva.
156.031. He who was Mati is this very Dharmaruci.
157.001. <157> This was the second incalculable aeon during which there was a meeting between this Dharmaruci and me, referring to which I say: "After a long time, Dharmaruci!"
After a very long time, O Dharmaruci!

157.003. Even prior to that, in the third incalculable eon, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Krakucchanda appeared in the world—one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
And in that royal capital, there lived a certain great merchant.
157.005. And he brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
157.006. Together with his wife, he played, took pleasure, and amused himself. While he was playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, a son was born to him.
That householder was faithful;
he had an arhat monk who served as his family preceptor.
That householder said this to his wife: "A debtor and a consumer of our wealth has been born to us."
"O noble lady, I am now going abroad to another country to take up merchandise according to the customs of merchants.
That merchant, having taken his goods, has gone a great distance surrounded by a crowd of people,
so that he does not return for a long time."
157.010. In the course of time, that boy grew up to be large, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
157.011. Then he asked his mother, "Mother, what is the traditional family occupation of ours?"
She said, "Child,
your father used to manage the shop.
Thereupon, that boy began to manage the shop."
And his mother, oppressed by her afflictions, began to reflect: "What means might there be by which I could dispel these afflictions so that no one would know of it?
Having reflected thus, she resolved: "I shall attend to him in this very way for the sake of my son's desire."
"In such a way that my illness will be dispelled together with him, and no suspicion will arise among my own kinsmen.
Then, having summoned an old woman and fed her twice or thrice, she subsequently covered her with a new cloth.
The old woman said to her, "For what purpose do you attend upon me with such acts as showing favor and so forth?
Having gained the confidence of that old woman, she spoke thus: "Mother, listen to my request."
"I am exceedingly oppressed by the afflictions; therefore,
conceiving affection for me, search among humans for one who is truly an insider and not suspicious of the people."
The old woman said, "There is no such person in this house, nor does anyone enter with such intimacy that he would be beyond suspicion to the people."
"157.021. 'Who will that man be whom I shall tell?
Then the merchant's wife said to the old woman: 'If there is no other man endowed with such capability, then this very son of mine shall be it.'"
"He will not be an object of suspicion for the world.
To her, that old woman said: "How indeed will you engage in amorous play with your son?
It would be more appropriate to experience amorous play with another man."
157.024. Then that merchant’s wife said, "If no other man of the household exists, let this very man be my son.
157.025. The old woman replied, "Do as you wish."
Then that elderly woman approached the merchant’s son and asked, "My child,
you are young and handsome. Have you established yourself financially?"
He asked her, "What is this?
Then the old woman said, "Since you are so handsome and young, at such an age you would shine while playing, sporting, and enjoying yourself with a young maiden;
why do you remain here deprived of the enjoyments of desire?"
Hearing this, the merchant’s son, his mind shrinking with shame and a sense of moral dread, did not accept the words of that old woman.
Then that old woman said this to the young man a second and even a third time: "A young maiden is being tormented by sufferings for your sake.
Being addressed thus a second and a third time, the merchant’s son said to that old woman: "Mother,"
"Was anything said to that young woman regarding the matter?
Then the old woman replied, "I spoke to her about that matter;
she did not give me her promise."
And that girl, being possessed of a lack of shame and modesty, will say nothing;
nor will she cover her body.
You should not make any effort to search for her.
158.003. Then that merchant’s son said to the old woman, "Where will our meeting take place? She replied, "In my house.
He asked, "In what part of the city is your house?"
Then that old woman pointed out his house to him.
That old woman went to the merchant’s wife and said, "This boy has been sent to you.
She asked, "In what place will they meet?"
"In my house.
And that boy, having finished his business, departed.
Having eaten in due course, he said to his mother, "I am going."
"I shall sleep in my friend's house. Then his mother also gave him permission, saying, "Go.
Having received permission, the boy went to the house of that old woman.
158.009. While that boy remained in that house, waiting for the time of pleasure and play, the night passed unnoticed by him.
158.010. At that very time, his mother went to that same house for the purpose of enjoying pleasure and play with that merchant’s son.
158.011. Having gone there, when it was late evening and the forms and features were indistinct, she began to enjoy pleasure and play with her son through secret means.
When the night had passed and she had experienced their amorous play, she would go to her own home during the pitch-black darkness of the night, when forms and shapes were indiscernible.
And that merchant’s son, having likewise experienced the amorous play, would go to the warehouse at daybreak and attend to his household affairs.
This occurred a second and even a third time.

158.015. While he was thus enjoying amorous play in the house of the old woman for a long time, as they continued in that manner of sexual dalliance, the boy’s mother began to reflect: "For how much longer shall I continue to experience such amorous play in this man's house while my own form remains unperceived?"
"What if I were to make him experience that very same sequence of amorous play in such a way that the amorous play occurs right here in this house?
Having reflected thus, he went to that very house of the old woman and experienced amorous play together with his son.
At the end of the night, during the time of blinding darkness, she put on the boy’s upper garment and,
having removed her own head-band, went to her own home. At dawn, the boy saw that band upon his head, resting on the couch.

158.022. Not finding his own upper cloak (*upariprāvaraṇa*) or shawl (*potrī*), he noticed that very strip of cloth there; leaving the marketplace (*bhāṇḍāvārī*), he put on another pair of garments and went to his own home.
158.023. Having arrived there, he saw that very same upper garment of his being worn upon the head of his mother.
158.024. Seeing this, he asked his mother: "Mother,..."
"Whence has this covering come upon your head?
To which she replied: "Am I still your mother even now?
After you have enjoyed sensual pleasures with me for such a long time, am I still that same mother of yours even now?"

When that merchant’s son heard such words from his mother, he fell to the ground, bewildered and with a distracted mind. Then she sprinkled him with water from a jar. Sprinkled with that water, the boy regained his senses after a long time, and his mother comforted him, saying, "Why have you fallen into such distress?"
"Having heard our words, be of steady mind;
you must not give way to despondency.
That boy said to her, "How could I not feel distress or confusion?"
"Why was such an evil deed committed by me? Then she said to him, "You should not give rise to remorse in your mind regarding this matter;
women are like a path."
158.031. For in whatever way the father goes, the son also goes by that very same way.
158.032. And that path does not become a source of harm to the son as he follows along.
In the same way,
the female sex is like an animal;
for even where an animal's father bathes, the female sex [is present].
The son also bathes in it,
and the animal does not cause any harm to the son as he bathes;
even so is it with women.
159.002. Moreover, in border regions, it is the very nature of things that whichever woman the father approaches through unrighteous means, that same woman the son also approaches.

159.004. Thus, although that merchant’s son had his grief dispelled by his mother with many kinds of conciliatory words, he developed an even stronger passion for that sinful, unrighteous act again and again.
And that merchant sent a letter by messenger, saying:
"My dear lady, be firm, resolute, and full of great courage;
I too shall come immediately upon the receipt of this letter."

159.006. Having heard the contents of such a letter, that merchant’s wife became despondent and began to reflect: "For a long time I have been waiting for his arrival. 159.007. Yet he did not come then.
159.008. Now, by means of this very stratagem, after I have attended to my son, he will surely come."
"What means might there be by which I could deprive him of life even before he has arrived here?
Having reflected thus, he summoned his son and said: "A letter from your father has been sent; it will arrive. Now, what should we do? The son replied: "What is to be done now?"
"Go, kill my father before he has even arrived. He replied, "How can I cause my father's death?
Since he was unable to carry out the killing of his father, [the king said: "Go..."

Then his mother addressed him again with words of persuasion; as he was being spoken to with those persuasive words, a resolve toward the killing of his father arose in him who was already stained by sensual desires.
"Indeed," I say, "for one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is no evil deed that is not to be committed.
Then he asked: "By what means shall I have him killed?"
She replied, "I myself shall devise a remedy.
Having said this, she took poison, mixed it with the flour, cooked the cakes (*maṇḍilaka*), and also cooked other cakes that were free of poison.
Then, having summoned the boy, she said to him, "Go!"
159.017. "These cakes are both poisonous and non-poisonous.
Take them, go into the presence of your father, and when he is trusting and eating with you in one place, give him these poisonous cakes, while you yourself eat the non-poisonous ones."
159.018. Then that boy, taking those small bags along with the messenger who had brought the letter, went into the presence of his father.

159.019. Upon his arrival, the father, seeing his son—who was exceedingly handsome, pleasing, and of noble appearance—was filled with great joy. 159.020. Having asked after his health and well-being, he announced him to those various merchants: "Gentlemen, this is our son."
159.021. When that boy perceived that his father was aware of everything, he said to his father, "Father,
Mother has sent some small cakes as a gift."
159.023. "Therefore, father, please eat. Later, while he was eating from the same single vessel with his father, he gave his father poisoned cakes and ate the poisonless ones himself.

159.024. Because his father had died after eating those poisoned cakes, 159.025. and while that father had passed away, the boy had not been suspected or accused by anyone of committing any evil deed. 159.026. Afterwards, after those beloved, affectionate friends—the merchants—had performed the funeral rites, whatever goods or gold and silver that merchant possessed, [were taken].
It was given to that boy.
Having taken that ancestral collection of goods consisting of silver and gold, the boy reached his own home.
After he had gone to his own home, his mother, while serving her son through secret and unrighteous conduct, found no pleasure.
Feeling dissatisfied, she said to her son: "For how much longer shall we continue to experience amorous play in this manner, in secret?
What if we were to go from this country to another land, live openly and without fear, and dwell happily with our duties well-known as husband and wife?

Then, abandoning their home, leaving behind their circle of friends, kinsmen, and relatives, and casting off their former male and female slaves and servants, they took whatever wealth of gold and bullion they possessed.
Taking [the child], they went to another region. Having gone there, they remained in the countryside, proclaiming themselves to be husband and wife while enjoying amorous play.
After some time, an Arhat monk, wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at that settlement.
160.004. While wandering there for alms, he sat down on the street and saw that boy engaged in trade according to the merchant's custom.
Having seen him, he greeted him with inquiries after his health and spoke: "Is your mother well?
Hearing the Arhat addressing him in that way, the boy’s mind became agitated; his heart filled with apprehension due to his own past misconduct, he began to reflect.
Having reflected thus, he went to his mother and informed her: "An ascetic has arrived;
he who approaches our house is that very person who will experience [the consequences] here in this place—he is the mother of this boy."
"We are known here as a husband and wife.
How can he be killed?
Therefore, having deliberated together, we shall invite him to our house and have him killed while he is eating."

160.010. Then, having reflected thus, that Arhat monk invited them into his home and began to feed them. 160.011. That boy, having hidden a weapon, went with his mother to a secluded part of the house to feed the Arhat. After the Arhat monk had eaten, he moved about the house with confidence. 160.013. Thereupon, the boy deprived him of life.
160.014. And sensual pleasures are like salt water:
the more they are indulged in, the more craving increases.
160.015. His mother, following that son with unrighteous conduct, was secretly lustful for the guild-president’s son in that very place, her mind attached to unrighteous acts.
160.016. That boy became aware of such an approach.
160.017. That boy became aware of such an approach.
160.017. Then he said to his mother, "Mother, turn back from such a transgression.
160.018. But she, her heart deeply attached to that merchant’s son, did not turn back even though she was told a second and a third time.
Thereupon, drawing his sword from its scabbard, he deprived his mother of life.
160.019. When his three immediate transgressions were complete, the deities announced it throughout the countryside: "This wicked man is a patricide, a slayer of an Arhat, and a matricide.
He has committed and accumulated three immediate transgressions—deeds that lead to rebirth in hell."
160.021. Then, having heard that, the people of that town banished him from that town.
160.022. When he was banished from that town, he began to reflect: "Is there some degree of devotion toward the Buddha's teaching?
Having thought thus, he resolved: "I shall go."
"I shall now go forth into the religious life.
Having gone to the monastery and approached a monk, he spoke thus: "Noble sir, may I go forth?"
160.025. Then that monk said, "Are you not, first of all, a patricide? The other monk replied, "My father has been killed by me.
160.026. Then he was asked again, "Are you not, first of all, a matricide?"
He said, "Noble sir, I have killed my mother.
He was asked again, "Have you not committed the murder of an Arhat?"
Then he said, "Even an Arhat has been killed.
Thereupon, that monk said to him, "By the performance of even one of these deeds, you are not worthy of the going-forth, let alone all of them together."
"Go, my son;
I will not let you go forth.
Thereupon, that man approached another monk and said, "Noble one, I would go forth."
160.031. Then that monk also, having been questioned in turn, refused him. Thereafter, he went to another monk and likewise requested ordination from him as well.
He, too, having been questioned in that same gradual manner, was refused.
When he had requested ordination a second and even a third time, yet was not ordained by the monks, he became filled with resentment and began to think: "Even though ordination is common to all,"...
I also entreated him for it, but I did not obtain it.
Thereupon, he set fire to the monks who were sleeping in that monastery.
Having set fire to that monastery, he went to another monastery.
Having gone there as well, he approached the monks and requested ordination.
They too questioned him in the same gradual manner and refused him.
There, with his mind likewise frustrated, he set fire to that place as well.
In that monastery as well, many monks, both those in training and those beyond training, were burned.

As he thus set fire to numerous monasteries, the news spread everywhere: "Such and such a man, a doer of evil deeds, having obtained the going forth among the monks, is now burning monasteries and monks."
That man set out for another monastery.
In that monastery lived a monk of the Bodhisattva lineage who was contented.
He heard that this very man, a performer of such difficult deeds, was coming here.

161.009. Then, before that man had even reached the monastery, the monk went out to meet him. 161.010. Having approached him, he said, "Noble sir, what is this? To which the man replied, "Venerable sir,"
"I do not obtain the going forth.
Then he said to the monks, "Come, child;
I shall ordain you."
161.012. Afterwards, that monk had the man’s head shaved and gave him the saffron robes.
161.013. Thereupon, the man said: "Noble sir, please grant me the precepts."
Then that monk said to him: "What need have you for the precepts? Always say this: 'Homage to the Buddha!
Homage to the Dharma!'"
"Homage to the Saṅgha!
Thereafter, that monk began to give a teaching of the Dharma to that man: "If you, a being who has committed such and such evil deeds, should ever regain mindfulness of the word 'Buddha'..."
161.016. Then that monk Tripiṭa, having passed away and died, was reborn among the gods.
161.017. And that man, too, having passed away and died, was reborn in the hells.
161.018. Therefore the Blessed One said: "What do you think, monks? He who was that monk, a master of the Tripitaka, in the past—at that time and on that occasion, it was I myself."
That being who committed evil deeds, the murderer of his mother, father,
and an Arhat, was none other than Dharmaruci.
This was my third encounter with this Dharmaruci during the first incalculable aeon.
161.020. Therefore, with this in mind, I say: "After a long time, Dharmaruci; after a very long time, Dharmaruci;
after an exceedingly long time, Dharmaruci!"

"Monks, for as long as it took me— through three incalculable eons, by means of the six perfections and hundreds of thousands of other difficult deeds— to fully realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, for that same length of time,
this Dharmaruci was for the most part cast into the realms of hell-beings and animals."
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
161.025. The eighteenth legend: Dharmaruci.
********** Avadāna 19 ********** 162.001. Divyāvadāna 19: The Story of Jyotiṣka/ 162.002.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

In the city of Rājagṛha there lived a householder named Subhadra, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and of vast enjoyments. He was exceedingly devoted to the Nirgranthas. He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.
While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, after some time his wife became pregnant.
In the forenoon, the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
162.006. While wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, he approached the residence of the householder Subhadra.
162.007. The householder Subhadra saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he took his wife and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this wife of mine has become pregnant.
What will she give birth to?"
The Blessed One said: "Householder, he will father a son;
he will illuminate his family."
"He will experience divine and human splendor;
having gone forth in my teaching, he will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Then, he offered a bowlful of pure and exquisite solid and soft food to the Blessed One.
Having said, "The Blessed One is healthy," he took his alms-food and departed.
Not far from there stood Bhūrika.
He reflected: "Even though we have but a single family that gives alms to the monks..."
"The ascetic Gautama is even converting that [person] to his own side.
I shall go and see what has been predicted by the ascetic Gautama.
Having gone there, he said, "Householder,"
"Did the ascetic Gautama come here? "He did. "What did he prophesy?
"Noble sir, I showed him his wife and asked, 'What will she give birth to?'"
He said: "She will give birth to a son;
she will illumine the family;
she will experience divine and human splendor."
"Having gone forth in my teaching, he will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Bhūrika, being skilled in calculation, took up white-colored counters and began to count; he saw that everything exactly as it had been prophesied by the Blessed One was indeed so.
He reflected: "If I were to describe this in detail..."
"The householder will praise the ascetic Gautama even more highly.
Realizing that "in this matter, some things must be extolled and some things must be disparaged," he wrings his hands and distorts his face.
162.021. The householder Subhadra said, "Noble sir, why do you wring your hands and distort your face?
He replied, "Householder,..."
"In this matter, some is true and some is false.
"Noble one, what is true and what is false?
"Householder, that which he said, 'She will give birth to a son,' is true."
"This speaks the truth;
that 'he will illuminate the family'—this too is true. 'The Supreme Light' is his name."
"That being is ill-fated; as soon as he is born, he will consume his family with fire.
As for what you say—that he will experience divine and human splendor—that is false.
Householder, have you ever seen any human being experiencing divine and human splendor?"
That which he says— "He will go forth into my teaching"—
is true. When he has neither food nor clothing, [he will do so].
"It is certain that he will go forth in the presence of the ascetic Gautama and,
through the abandonment of all defilements, realize arhatship— this is false.
For even the ascetic Gautama himself does not yet possess arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements."
"It will happen to him even sooner.
Subhadra fell into despair and said, "Noble sir,
how should I conduct myself in this matter?"
Bhūrika said: "Householder, we are renunciants who train in tranquility;
you yourself know this."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Subhadra reflected, "In every way, this man must be abandoned," and having realized this, he began to administer medicine.
This being was in his final existence.
"Thinking, 'This may serve as medicine for him,' he began to massage her left flank;
the fetus then moved to her right flank."
163.002. Subhadra began to rub his right flank;
it moved to his left flank.
It is impossible and out of the question that a being in his final existence should die prematurely before reaching the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
163.004. As her womb was being oppressed, that householder’s wife began to cry out.
Her neighbors heard her; they went in great haste and asked, "Sirs, what is this?"
"Why is this householder’s wife crying out?
Subhadra replied, "She is pregnant;
surely it is now the time for her delivery."
163.006. They departed.
Subhadra reflected: "It is not possible for me to approach her here; I shall lead her to the forest. 163.007. Thus he thought.
163.007. Having led her to the forest, he treated her in such a way that she died.
He then brought her secretly into his house and said to his friends, kinsmen, relatives, and neighbors: "Sirs, my wife has passed away."
163.009. They began to cry out.
163.009. While they were crying out, [the body] was adorned with a palanquin decorated with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths and carried out to the Śītavana cemetery.

163.010. The Nirgranthas heard this; delighted, satisfied, and overjoyed, they raised up parasols and banners and wandered through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions of the city of Rājagṛha.
They announced: "Listen, sirs!
The ascetic Gautama has prophesied regarding the wife of the householder Subhadra: 'She will give birth to a son who will illuminate his family.'"
She will experience divine and human splendor,
and having gone forth in my teaching, she will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
When she passed away, she was carried out to the Śītavana cemetery.

I said this, and he replied: "I do not request anything;
rather, I simply wish to see the householder. He said: "O man, if that is so, let him enter."
178.006. He was ushered in by him.
178.007. The brahmin asked, "Householder, why do you stand with your cheek resting on your hand, lost in thought?
That householder spoke this verse:
"One should not speak of one's grief to him who cannot release one from that grief;
rather, one should speak of one's grief to him who can fully release one from that grief.
Śakra said: "Householder,"
"What is your sorrow? Speak, and I shall release you from it. He then related it in detail.

178.012. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, vanished the form of the brahmin Kauśika and, standing in his own form, said: "Householder, the divine son Viśvakarman will provide you with assistance. Having said this, he departed. 178.013.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, went to the Trāyastriṃśa gods and addressed the divine son Viśvakarman: "Go!"
"Viśvakarman, provide assistance to the householder Anaṅgaṇa.
"May it be well with you, Kauśika," replied the divine son Viśvakarman to Śakra, the lord of the gods, and having given his promise, he departed.
An even more distinguished splendor was manifested for the city;
a divine circular pavilion was fashioned, divine seats were prepared, and divine food was provided.
Airāvaṇa, the king of elephants, held a hundred-ribbed parasol over the head of the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin.
The remaining nāgas [attended] the remaining monks.
Śacī, the daughter of the gods, fanned the Samyaksambuddha Vipaśyin with a golden fly-whisk adorned with jewels,
while the remaining apsarases fanned the monks.

178.019. King Bandhumat sent out a secret agent with these instructions: "Go, my good man, and find out what kind of food the householder Anaṅgaṇa is providing to satisfy the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
That man went there, and having seen that splendor, he remained right where he was.
178.021. Therefore, a minister was dispatched.
178.022. He too remained right there.
178.022. The prince was dispatched.
He too remained right there.
Then King Bandhumat went to that gate himself and stood waiting.
Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Enlightened One, said: "Householder,..."
King Bandhumān has seen the truth. You uttered harsh words toward him;
he himself is standing at the gate.
"Go and ask for his forgiveness.
Having gone out, he asked for forgiveness and said to him, "Great King,
please enter and serve the food with your own hand."
178.026. He entered.
178.026. He beheld a divine splendor.
178.026. Having seen it, he was struck with great wonder and said: "Householder,..."
"You alone are worthy to feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha day after day; we are not.

Then the householder Anaṅgaṇa, having satisfied the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin with such splendor and excellent food for three months, prostrated at his feet and began to make this aspiration: "By me, in such a [situation]..."

"Having performed a service for a truly worthy recipient of offerings, by this root of merit may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, and may I experience divine and human splendor."
"May I be a recipient of such qualities as these;
may I please a Teacher such as this, and never displease him."
179.001. "What do you think, monks? That householder named Anaṅgaṇa was none other than this noble son Jyotiṣka at that time and on that occasion.
Because he uttered harsh words toward King Bandhumat, who had seen the truths," [the result followed].
As the ripening of that karma, he was placed upon a funeral pyre along with his mother and cremated;
even now, he has been placed upon a funeral pyre and cremated.
This is because, having performed service for the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, he made a formal aspiration.
As the ripening of that karma, he was born into a family that was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
celestial and human splendor appeared for him.
Having gone forth in my teaching, through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship.

179.006. "I have pleased, and not displeased, this Teacher Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, being equal in speed, equal in strength, equal in burden, and having attained an equal commonality with him.
179.007. "Thus indeed, monks, for actions that are exclusively black, there is an exclusively black ripening; for those that are exclusively white, there is an exclusively white ripening."
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
179.012. Thus ends the nineteenth story, the Jyotiṣka-avadāna, in the Divyāvadāna.
********** Avadāna 20 ********** 180.001. The Story of Kanakavarṇa (Divyāvadāna 20).
Thus have I heard:
180.001. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
180.002. The Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen;
by kings, royal ministers, and various heretics, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, and parivrājakas; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas.

The Blessed One was a recipient of abundant and excellent requisites— robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick— both divine and human, [offered] by the *kiṃnaras* and *mahoragas*.
And yet, the Blessed One remained unsullied by them, like a lotus by water.
180.007. And this kind of noble, auspicious fame, renown, and verse concerning the Blessed One has arisen in all directions and intermediate directions:

"That Blessed One is indeed the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."

180.009. Having himself realized, witnessed, and attained it through direct higher knowledge in this very life, he [teaches] this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.
180.011. He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.
180.012. He proclaims the holy life (*brahmacarya*) which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and purified.

180.013. Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, if beings knew the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts, then even that which is the very last morsel, the final mouthful, would not [be withheld]."
Even after that, they would not consume [the food] without having given or shared it,
provided that they might find a worthy recipient;
nor would a mind of stinginess arise in them and persist to the point of overwhelming them.

180.017. Therefore, monks, because beings do not know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the sharing of gifts as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the sharing of gifts,
for that reason they consume [resources] without having given or shared them, grasping at them with their minds.
180.019. And the thought of stinginess arose in them and remained, completely taking possession of their minds.
180.020. For what reason?
180.021. Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there was a king named Kanakavarṇa, who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of golden complexion.
180.022. Monks, King Kanakavarṇa was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments.

180.023. He had abundant personal property and wealth, an abundance of assets and implements, and an abundance of money, grain, bullion, gold, gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and refined gold;
he possessed many elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and his treasuries and granaries were completely full.
180.024. Monks, King Kanakavarṇa had a royal capital named Kanakāvatī; it was twelve yojanas in length from east to west, and seven yojanas in width from south to north.
180.026. It was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, and delightful.
King Kanakavarṇa had eighty thousand cities.
There were eighteen *koṭis* of clans that were prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
There were fifty-seven *koṭis* of villages that were prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with great numbers of people and inhabitants.
180.030. There were sixty thousand market towns that were prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
180.031. King Kanakavarṇa had eighteen thousand ministers.
His harem consisted of twenty thousand women.
180.032. Monks, King Kanakavarṇa was righteous;
he ruled his kingdom according to the Dharma.

181.001. Then, at another time, while King Kanakavarṇa was alone, in seclusion, and retired in meditation, there arose in his mind this reflection: "What if I were to release all the merchants from customs duties and from the guard-posts? What if I were to release all the people of Jambudvīpa from taxes and from the guard-posts? 181.002. [He thought: "I shall release all the merchants from customs duties and from the guard-posts; I shall release all the people of Jambudvīpa from taxes and from the guard-posts."

181.003. Then King Kanakavarṇa addressed his astrologers, high officials, ministers, gatekeepers, and courtiers: "From this day forward, O village chiefs, I release all merchants from customs duties; I release all the people of Jambudvīpa from taxes and duties.
181.005. While he was thus exercising his sovereignty for many years by this means, at another time, the constellations became disordered.
For twelve years the god did not send rain.

Then the brahmins, who were experts in signs and omens, skilled in the mantras of the earth and the atmosphere, and proficient in the movements of the lunar mansions, Venus, and the planets— having observed those [omens]— approached King Kanakavarṇa.
181.008. Having approached King Kanakavarṇa, they said this to him: "Your Majesty, you should know that the constellations have become disordered;
for twelve years, Your Majesty will not send rain. 181.009. Then, having heard such a cry as this, King Kanakavarṇa shed tears, saying: "Alas for my people of Jambudvīpa!"
"Alas! My Jambudvīpa—prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with many people—is soon to become empty and devoid of humans.
Then, after King Kanakavarṇa had grieved for a moment, this thought occurred to him: "Those who are wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, will be able to sustain themselves."
181.013. "How will these who are poor, possessing little wealth and having meager food, drink, and enjoyments, sustain themselves?
This thought occurred to him: "What if I were to collect provisions of food from Jambudvīpa?"
I would count all the beings in Jambudvīpa;
having counted them, I would measure them out, and having measured them out, I would have a single granary constructed in every village, city, town, market-town, and royal capital.
181.016. "Having constructed a single storehouse, I shall distribute food equally to all the people of Jambudvīpa.

181.017. Then King Kanakavarṇa addressed his calculators, high officials, ministers, gatekeepers, and courtiers: "Go, leaders; having gathered all the food and provisions from throughout Jambudvīpa, count them."
"Having counted it, measure it;

having measured it, establish a single granary in every village, city, town, market-town, and capital. "As you command, Your Majesty," replied the accountants, high officials, ministers, doorkeepers, and courtiers to King Kanakavarṇa, and they began to count all the food and provisions throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa.
Having counted them, they measured them;
having measured them, they stored them all in a single granary within every village, city, town, market-town, and capital.
Having stored them in that single granary, [they went] to where King Kanakavarṇa was.

They approached him. Having approached, they said this to King Kanakavarṇa: "Your Majesty, you should know that food and provisions have been collected from all the villages, towns, market-towns, hamlets, and royal capitals; having been collected, they have been counted."

Having counted it and measured it, and having had it measured, it has been stored in a single granary within all the villages, towns, market towns, and royal capitals; now, O King, do as you deem timely.
Then King Kanakavarṇa, having summoned his enumerators, accountants, scribes, and officials, said this to them: "Go, you village headmen!"
"Count all the people of Jambudvīpa;

having counted them, O village chiefs, distribute food equally among all the people of Jambudvīpa. "So be it, Your Majesty," replied the enumerators, calculators, scribes, and officials, and having assented to King Kanakavarṇa, they proceeded to count all the people of Jambudvīpa.
Having assembled all the people of Jambudvīpa, beginning with King Kanakavarṇa, they provide an equal portion of food for them all.
They sustain themselves for eleven years,
but they do not sustain themselves for a twelfth year.
181.030. When one month of the twelfth year had passed, many men, women, boys, and girls, overcome by hunger and thirst, were dying.
181.031. At that time, indeed, all food and drink in the whole of Jambudvīpa was exhausted, except for a single *māṇikā* of cooked rice remaining for King Kanakavarṇa.
182.001. At that time, a certain bodhisattva who had set out for forty kalpas arrived in this Sahā world-system.
182.002. In a certain forest grove, the bodhisattva saw a son behaving improperly toward his mother.
182.003. Upon seeing this, it occurred to him: "Alas, these beings are suffering!"
Alas, these beings are afflicted,
in that having dwelt for nine months in the very womb of this [mother] and having drunk from her very breasts, [they are still thus].
"He will pass away right here.

"Enough for me with such beings—unrighteous, stained by unrighteous passion, possessed of false views, overcome by perverse greed, lacking reverence for their mothers, lacking the qualities of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, and failing to honor their elders in the family!
Who would venture to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of such beings?"
"What if I were now to attend to my own task?
Then the Bodhisattva approached the foot of a certain tree;
having approached, he sat down at the foot of that tree.

182.008. Having sat cross-legged, with body held erect and mindfulness established before him, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging, namely: "This is form;
this is the origin of form;
this is the cessation of form."
This is feeling, this is perception, these are mental formations.
"This is consciousness,
this is the arising of consciousness,
this is the passing away of consciousness."

182.011. Thus dwelling in the observation of the arising and passing away of these five aggregates of clinging, before long he understood that whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation;
having realized this, he attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha right there. 182.013. Then the Blessed One, the pratyekabuddha, surveying what he had attained, spoke this verse at that time:
"For one who associates closely with others, affections arise; from the sequence of affection, suffering comes into being here.
Having understood the peril inherent in affection, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Then, this thought occurred to that Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha: "For the sake of many sentient beings, I have performed difficult austerities."
"And no benefit has been done for any living being. Whom should I compassionately favor today?
Whose alms-food should I collect and consume today?"

Then the Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha, surveying this entire Jambudvīpa all around with his purified divine eye, which transcends that of humans, saw that throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa all food and provisions were exhausted, except for a single *mānikā* of cooked rice remaining from King Kanakavarṇa.
The thought occurred to him: "What if I were to have compassion for King Kanakavarṇa?
What if I were to take alms from King Kanakavarṇa’s residence and eat them?

Then the Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha, by means of that very supernatural power, rose up into the air and, with his body visible like a bird, proceeded by supernatural power toward the royal capital of Kanakāvatī.
At that time, King Kanakavarṇa was on the upper terrace of his palace, surrounded by about five thousand ministers.
One of the high officials saw the Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha, approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he addressed the high officials: "Look, look, O leaders!"
"From afar, a red-winged bird is coming here!
A second high official said, "This, village headman, is not a red-winged bird;
it is a *rākṣasa* who comes here to steal away vitality."
"He will devour us!
Then King Kanakavarṇa, having wiped his face with both hands, addressed the high ministers: "O village chiefs, this red-winged bird is not a rākṣasa who steals away vitality."
"This seer is coming here out of compassion for us.
Then that Blessed Pratyekabuddha alighted upon King Kanakavarṇa’s palace.
183.001. Then King Kanakavarṇa, having risen from his seat and gone forth to meet that Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha, bowed his head at his feet and requested him to sit upon the prepared seat.
183.002. Then King Kanakavarṇa said this to that Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha: "For what purpose, O Sage, have you come here?
"For the sake of food, Great King."
When this had been said, King Kanakavarṇa wept;
shedding tears, he spoke thus: "Alas for my poverty!
Alas for my poverty!"
For indeed, having exercised sovereign lordship over Jambudvīpa, he was unable to provide even a single alms-meal for one seer.
Then the deity who resided in the capital city of Kanakāvatī spoke this verse before King Kanakavarṇa:
183.007. What is suffering? Poverty. What is even more suffering than that? That very poverty. 183.008. Poverty is equal to death. //2//
183.009. Then King Kanakavarṇa addressed the steward: "My good man, is there any food in my residence that I might give to this seer?"
He spoke thus: "Your Majesty, you should know that the food and provisions throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa have been exhausted; only a single measure of cooked rice remains for Your Majesty.
Then, this thought occurred to King Kanakavarṇa: "If I consume it, I shall live."
183.012. "If I do not consume it, I shall die.
Then this thought occurred to him: "Whether I consume it or whether I do not consume it,"
"I must certainly bring about my own end;
enough of this life of mine!
How indeed could such a virtuous seer, possessed of noble qualities, depart today from my house with his alms-bowl as unwashed as it was when he brought it in?"
Then King Kanakavarṇa, having assembled his accountants, high officials, ministers, doorkeepers, and courtiers, spoke to them thus: "O leaders, rejoice!
This is the final distribution of rice from King Kanakavarṇa.
By this root of merit, may the poverty of all the people of Jambudvīpa be utterly destroyed."

Then King Kanakavarṇa, taking that bowl from the great seer and placing a single māṇikā of cooked rice into the bowl, held the bowl with both hands, knelt down, and placed the bowl into the right hand of that Blessed One, the Pratyekabuddha.
183.019. Furthermore, it is the nature of things that for the Blessed Pratyekabuddhas, the teaching of the Dharma is through the body, not through speech.
183.020. Then the Blessed Pratyekabuddha, having received his alms-bowl from King Kanakavarṇa, departed right then through the air above by means of his supernatural power.
183.022. Then King Kanakavarṇa, with palms joined in reverence, stood gazing at him without blinking.
"As long as he has not yet passed beyond the range of vision.
Then King Kanakavarṇa addressed his astrologers, high officials, ministers, gatekeepers, and courtiers: "Go, village chiefs, each to your own dwellings.
Do not all of you perish right here in this palace from hunger and thirst."

They spoke thus: "When Your Majesty possessed such abundance of glory and good fortune, we played and took delight together with you; how then shall we now abandon Your Majesty at this final hour, at this last moment?
Then King Kanakavarṇa wept.
He shed tears.
Wiping away his tears, he addressed the accountants, high officials, ministers, doorkeepers, and members of the assembly, saying: "Go, gentlemen, to your respective homes.
Do not all of you perish right here in this palace from hunger and thirst."

183.029. Having been addressed thus, the astrologers, high officials, ministers, doorkeepers, and courtiers wept, shedding tears and wiping their faces; they then approached King Kanakavarṇa. 183.030. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of King Kanakavarṇa, joined their palms in reverence, and said this to King Kanakavarṇa: "Whatever offense we may have committed against you, it must be forgiven. Today is our final sight of Your Majesty. 183.032. "Today is our last vision of the Lord."
184.001. Just as that Pratyekabuddha had finished consuming that alms-food,
at that very moment, four masses of clouds arose from all four directions,
and cool breezes began to blow.
Those who remove the impurities of Jambudvīpa,
and like clouds, they rain down and settle the dust.
Then, on that very same day, during the second half-watch, a rain of various kinds of solid and soft foods falls.
184.004. Such food as this—rice, barley-meal, sour gruel, fish, and meat;
such solid food as this—roots for eating, stalks for eating, leaves for eating, flowers for eating, fruits for eating, sesame for eating, and pieces of sugar, candied sugar, and molasses for eating.

184.006. Then King Kanakavarṇa, thrilled, satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer, addressed his accountants, high officials, ministers, doorkeepers, and courtiers: "Behold!"
"O village leaders,
this very day the sprout of that gift of a single alms-offering has appeared;
another fruit will yet come."
Then, on the second day, for seven days they rain down a shower of grain, namely: sesame, rice, mung beans, black gram, barley, wheat, lentils, and śāli rice.
For seven days they rain down a shower of clarified butter.
For seven days they rain down a shower of cotton;
for seven days they rain down a shower of various kinds of fine cloth;
for seven days they rain down a shower of the seven precious gems.
Of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald, and musāragalva;
through the majesty of King Kanakavarṇa, the poverty of all the people of Jambudvīpa was utterly eradicated.
"Monks, it may be that you have some doubt or uncertainty [thinking] that the King Kanakavarṇa at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time and on that occasion, I myself was the King Kanakavarṇa."
"Therefore, monks, by this method it should be understood: if, monks,

sentient beings were to know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts, then even now they would not consume even that which is their very last mouthful, their final morsel, without having given it away and shared it."
They would receive a worthy recipient as their object of offering,
and no thought of stinginess would arise within them to take possession of their minds.

For it is because, monks, beings do not know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of sharing gifts— as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of sharing gifts— [that they do not practice it].
And [they disregard] the ripening of the fruit;
therefore, they consume [their wealth] without having given it away or shared it, with minds characterized by grasping,
and the state of mind consisting of stinginess that has arisen remains as something that has completely overwhelmed them.
What was done previously, whether good or evil, does not perish; nor does service to those who live in community perish.
What is spoken among noble people does not perish, and what is done for the grateful never perishes at all. (3)
184.028. Well-performed action is beautiful, while ill-performed action is unwholesome.
184.029. There is indeed its ripening; the fruit will inevitably be bestowed. //4//
Thus spoke the Blessed One.

With joyful minds, those monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, and the entire assembly—along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
184.032. Thus ends the twentieth [tale] in the glorious *Divyāvadāna*, the *Kanakavarṇāvadāna*.
********** Avadāna 21 ********** 185.001. The *Sahasodgatāvadāna*.
185.002. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

185.002. It was the habit of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana to go on periodic visits to the hells, to visit the animal realm, to visit the realm of hungry ghosts, to visit the gods, and to visit the human world.
185.004. He [beheld] those sufferings of the beings in hell, such as being torn apart, split open, cut, and broken;
The mutual devouring and so forth of animals; the hunger, thirst, and so forth of hungry ghosts; and the falling away, falling down, scattering, and destruction, and so forth, of the gods.
Having seen the sufferings of human beings, such as the toil of seeking and the like, he comes to Jambudvīpa and announces it to the fourfold assembly:
"If any co-resident or disciple is practicing the holy life without joy..."
Taking him with him, he approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
thinking, "The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana will correctly instruct and admonish him."
185.009. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana exhorted him correctly and instructed him correctly.
185.010. Thus, being repeatedly exhorted and instructed correctly by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, they took delight in practicing the holy life and attained further distinction.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was dwelling surrounded by the four assemblies: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who inquire;
thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned the Venerable Ānanda.

He said, "Venerable sir, it is the habit of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana to go on periodic journeys to the hells, to the animal realm, to the realm of hungry ghosts, to the world of the gods, and to the world of humans.
He [sees] those sufferings of the beings in hell, such as being torn apart, split open, cut, and broken."
For animals, there are mutual devouring and so forth; for hungry ghosts, hunger, thirst, and so forth; and for gods, falling, descending, scattering, and destruction, and so forth.
Having seen the sufferings of human beings, such as the calamities of seeking after worldly things, he comes to Jambudvīpa and announces it to the fourfold assembly:
"If any co-resident or pupil is practicing the holy life without joy,"
Taking him with him, he approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
thinking, "The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana will instruct him correctly and will exhort him correctly.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana instructed him correctly and exhorted him correctly.
185.021. Thus, being correctly instructed and correctly exhorted by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana one after another, they took delight in practicing the holy life and attained further distinction.
185.023. "Venerable sir, this is the cause, this is the reason why the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana dwells surrounded by the fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen."
185.024. "Ānanda, there will not be a monk everywhere who is equal to Maudgalyāyana, nor one like Maudgalyāyana.
185.025. Therefore, a five-spoked wheel should be made at the gateway.
185.026. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "A five-spoked wheel should be made at the gateway."
185.026. The monks did not know how it should be made.
185.027. The Blessed One said: "The five destinies must be made: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
Among these, the hells must be made at the bottom."
Animals and hungry ghosts [are below], and above them are the gods and humans.
185.029. Four continents are to be made: Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, Uttarakuru, and Jambudvīpa.
185.029. In the center, passion, hatred, and delusion are to be depicted:
passion in the form of a pigeon, and hatred in the form of a serpent.
Delusion [is to be represented] in the form of a boar.
185.030. And images of the Buddha should be made, demonstrating this maṇḍala of nirvāṇa.
185.031. Beings who are not born by transformation should be depicted as passing away and being reborn through the mechanism of a waterwheel.

186.011. A certain householder lived in Rājagṛha. He took a wife from a family of equal status. He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
186.012. While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him.
186.013. Having performed the birth ceremonies for the newborn in full detail for three weeks—twenty-one days—he established a name for him that was appropriate to his family.
186.014. He addressed his wife: "My dear lady,"
"A son has been born to us who will pay off our debts and take away our wealth.
Therefore, I shall go;
taking my merchandise, I will embark upon the great ocean."
She said, "Noble son, do exactly as you say.

Having summoned his friends, relatives, and kinsmen, and having comforted his household, he took merchandise suitable for a voyage across the great ocean and set out upon the great sea on a specific day, lunar date, and auspicious moment.
And right there he met his end.
His wife, through the strength of her kin and the strength of her own hands, protected, nourished, and raised that boy; she introduced him to writing, and he became proficient in the art of letters.
When he had reached maturity, he went with a companion to the Bamboo Grove and entered a monastery, where he saw a wheel with five spokes painted on the gateway.
186.019. He asked, "Noble sir, what is this that has been depicted?
The monk replied, "O gentle-faced one,"
"These are the five destinies: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
"Noble one, what karma did these beings perform by which they experience such sufferings?

He replied, "These were those who took life, those who took what was not given, those who engaged in sexual misconduct, those who spoke falsehoods, those who were slanderous, those who were harsh in speech, those who indulged in idle chatter, those who were covetous, and those whose minds were full of malice."

186.024. Thus, these ten unwholesome paths of action were excessively practiced, cultivated, and multiplied by them, whereby they now experience such sufferings as being torn out, split open, cut, and broken.
186.025. Noble one, that is settled.
"186.026. What karma was performed by these and others, such that they experience such sufferings as devouring one another? 186.028.
Noble One, this matter has also been resolved."
"186.028. What karma did these others perform, by which they experience such sufferings?
"O gentle-faced one, these too were formerly miserly, stingy, and grasping at their possessions."
186.030. By that stinginess which was practiced, cultivated, and increased, they experience such sufferings as hunger, thirst, and other miseries.
186.031. Noble one, this matter is also understood. What other karma did these people perform, by which they experience such pleasures?

"O gentle-faced one, these have desisted from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, and from frivolous chatter; they are free from covetousness and possess right view.
Thus, these ten wholesome paths of action have been practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed by them to an extraordinary degree."
"By what [karma] do they experience such delights as these divine women, graceful celestial palaces, and gardens?
Noble sir, that too has passed away.
What other karma was performed by these beings, such that they now experience these pleasures?"
"O gentle-faced one, these too have practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the ten wholesome paths of action to a lesser and more mild degree,
by which they experience such pleasures as elephants, horses, chariots, food and drink, couches and seats, the delights of women, and pleasure gardens."
"Noble one, among these five destinies, those three destinies consisting of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts do not please me.
However, these two— gods and humans— are pleasing."
187.008. How, then, should these ten paths of wholesome action be undertaken and practiced?
O gentle-faced one, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, if you should attain full realization in this very life, [you will succeed].
"This indeed is the end of your suffering. Furthermore, if you should pass away while still having some fetters remaining,
you will be reborn among the gods."
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Perceiving five benefits, one who observes them should indeed be fully intent upon the life of renunciation.
What are the five?
Perceiving that 'I shall attain these unique personal goals,' one should indeed be fully intent upon the life of renunciation."

"Considering that I shall be worthy of honor and praise by those for whom I am a servant, a messenger, one to be commanded, a dependent, and one who goes wherever they wish according to their will, it is sufficient for me to be intent upon the mendicant’s life through my renunciation.
Considering that I shall attain the unsurpassed security of Nirvana, it is sufficient for me to be intent upon the mendicant’s life through my renunciation."

"187.015. For one who attains the unsurpassed security of Nirvana and remains free from transgression, it is clearly seen that rebirth among the gods will occur; therefore, enough with this mere mass [of worldly life]—one should be intent upon the going forth.
187.016. In many ways, the going forth has been praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
187.017. Noble sir, it is excellent!"
"What is performed there in the going forth?
"O gentle-faced one, the holy life (brahmacarya) is practiced for as long as life lasts."
"Noble one, this is not possible.

"Feed the community of monks with the Buddha at its head.
"Noble sir, for how many kārṣāpaṇas is the community of monks with the Buddha at its head fed? "Good sir," [he replied].

He went toward his own residence. Having arrived, he said this to his mother:

187.024. There, I saw a wheel with five spokes drawn upon the gateway.

187.028. Humans experience elephants, horses, chariots, food, drink, beds, seats, the delights of women, and gardens. Of these, three destinies are not desired by me; two are desired.
187.029. "Therefore, do you wish for me to be reborn among the gods?

"Mother, if that is so,"
"Give me five hundred kārṣāpaṇas;
I shall feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
"Son, you have been nourished, sustained, and raised by me through the strength of my kin and the strength of my own hands."
"Whence shall I have the means for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas?
Mother, if there are none, I will work for wages."
"Son, you are very delicate;
you will not be able to perform labor for wages.
"Mother, I shall go; I am able."
"Son, if you are able, go.

The brahmins and householders were hiring other laborers.
No one questioned him. Having passed the day there, he went home at the wrong hour.
He was asked by his mother: "Son,..."
"Have you finished the work for your wages?

If you must perform work for wages, [then do it in such a manner]."
"Assuming such a disguise, go to the street of laborers and stay there.
"Mother, excellent!
I shall do so."
On the following day, having assumed such a disguise, he went to the street of laborers and stood there.
Eventually, a certain householder came out from his house and went to the street for the sake of hiring laborers.
188.009. Having rejected him, he took other hired laborers.
188.010. He said, "Householder, I too will do work for wages."

He reflected, "What he says is excellent."

"Let us go," he said. He was led home by him.
Those other laborers performed their work with deceit.
He performs his work with great haste and instructs those laborers:

188.017. "If we perform this deed through deceit, what will be our destination when we pass away from here?
They said, "Nephew,"
"You are newly subdued.

He was skilled in worldly narratives.
He presented such a discourse on worldly tales that,
upon hearing it, those hired laborers were captivated.
As he walked with a very rapid pace, they followed step by step behind him,
thinking, "Lest we fail to hear the story of the world.
On that day, those hired laborers performed twice as much work as usual.
He asked the supervising man: "O man, have you taken on other laborers?
"Noble sir, none have been taken."
188.023. "Then why has twice the amount of work been done today? He reported exactly what had occurred. 188.024. Having heard this, the householder began to give the boy double wages.

When that householder’s house was completed, the boy began to calculate his wages; however, when five hundred kārṣāpaṇas were not yet reached,

"Why do you wish to deceive me?

189.007. "Lord, what [is it]?

"He is able to provide it.

"Therefore, out of compassion for me, you should have the food prepared.

Having arrived, I shall feed the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with my own hand. The householder reflected: "This house of mine has not long been established; it will be enjoyed by the community of monks, headed by the Buddha."
"I am awake.
Having understood this, he said: "Son, well done!
Set aside the kārṣāpaṇas and go."
"Invite the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow;
