applied a smooth coating of cow dung, and had seats arranged.

"Make the *purobhaktaka* offerings," [the King] said.
They replied, "We shall do so.
They then made the *purobhaktaka* offerings.
189.031. The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks in that householder’s residence.
189.032. The group of six monks also sat down in the midst of the community after having finished their morning meal.
190.001. Then, seeing that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, that foremost householder personally satisfied them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
190.002. While constantly serving food, he saw that the group of six monks was not eating with due respect.

190.003. Having seen this and knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he stood before the Blessed One and said: "Blessed One, some of the noble ones here have eaten their food without showing proper respect."
"Will I not be reborn among the gods?
The Blessed One said, "Child,
you would be reborn among the gods even by the mere use of bedding and seats, let alone by the use of food and drink."
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that householder’s son with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
In the meantime, about five hundred merchants arrived at Rājagṛha having successfully completed their voyage by sea.
Since a festival was taking place in Rājagṛha, nothing could be obtained even for purchase.
Among them was one merchant who was a regular visitor to the monks' alms-round.
He said, "Sirs,
wait and see whose house will provide a meal today for the community of monks headed by the Buddha;
there, there will certainly be something worthy of being set aside."

190.011. Searching by means of hearsay, they approached that householder and said: "Householder, today the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, has eaten here; since a festival has arrived, nothing at all can be obtained even for purchase."
190.013. "If there is anything here that is subject to being sold, let it be given for a price.
190.014. "This food is not for sale."
"Rather, this is the meal of that householder’s son;
ask him for it. They approached him and said, "Householder’s son,"
"Let us be given whatever remains from your meal;
we shall pay you its price.
He replied, "I will not give it to you for a price."
"But rather, I shall give it in this very way.

Having been fully satisfied with that food and drink, they went to the householder and said, "Householder, you have gained great profit, for in your residence the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has been fully satisfied with food and drink."
"And these five hundred merchants.
He said, "This son of a householder has gained great profit;
it is he who has satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with food and drink, not I."
They asked, "Whose son is this, householder?
[He replied,] "The son of such-and-such a caravan leader.
The caravan leader said, "Sirs,"
"This is my friend's son.
His father went down to the great ocean and met with disaster through his own misconduct.
It is possible for many to rescue one."
"But it is not that many [should give] to one. Therefore, let this cloth be spread out, and whoever has renounced anything,
let him place it upon this cloth."
190.023. Since they were already well-disposed and were further encouraged by the caravan leader, they gave him gems, pearls, and other jewels according to their means.
190.024. A great heap was formed.
The caravan leader said, "Son, take it."
He said, "Father,
I did not give it for a price.

"We do not pay you a price.
And if a price were to be calculated,

"But we have faith in you; we perform this act of faith, so please accept it.
He replied, "Father, I have fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, and thus I shall be reborn among the gods."
"Therefore, what remains has been given to you.
If I were to accept it,
there is the possibility that I would not be reborn among the gods."
The caravan leader said: "Son, do you have faith in the Blessed One?

"Go and ask the Blessed One.
He approached the place where the Blessed One was,
and having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
190.031. That householder’s son said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, after I had fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, I gave whatever food and drink remained to the *viṇikas*.
They, being pleased with me, perform acts of favor for me.”
"Is it permissible for me to accept this, or is it not permissible?
The Blessed One said, "If you are pleased and perform the act of being pleased, then take it.
[He replied,] "Blessed One, will I not then fail to be reborn among the gods?"
The Blessed One said: "Child, this is the flower;
the fruit shall be something else."
191.003. Having gained full confidence in the words of the Blessed One, he departed satisfied and took the jewels.
191.005. In the meantime, a merchant in Rājagṛha who had no son passed away.

191.006. "Which merchant should we consecrate?
Thereupon, some said, "The one who is renowned for his great merit.
Others said, "How are we to know [which one that is]?"
They said, "We shall throw seeds of various colors into a jar filled with cooked rice; whoever extracts those of a single color, him we shall consecrate as the guild-leader."
They threw seeds of various colors into a jar filled with cooked rice and announced: "Sirs,
whoever can extract seeds of a single color from this jar,"
"Let that merchant who is intended by you to hold the position of guild-leader be consecrated;
let him be raised to it."
191.011. They began to extract them. All of them extracted those of various colors, but that son of a householder extracted those of a single color.
The citizens and country-folk said, "Sirs,
this man is one who possesses great power through merit.
Let us all consecrate him as the guild-leader."
191.013. Thereupon, some said: "Sirs, this man is a hired laborer.
How can we consecrate him as the guild-president?"
Others said, "Let us investigate once more.
Thus, they extracted grains of the same color three times.
They said, "Sirs,"
Even the men addressed him with a challenge:
"Come, let us consecrate him as king!
He was then consecrated by them as the guild-leader (śreṣṭhin).
The householder reflected: "Even though he has performed work for me as a hired laborer, nevertheless, this being is one who possesses great power through merit;
I must provide him with support."
He gave him his daughter, adorned with every ornament, to be his wife;
and he gave him that house and abundant wealth.
Because he had suddenly emerged with such wealth, the householder became known by the name Sahasodgata, "Sahasodgata the Householder."
He reflected: "Whatever wealth, fortune, and excellence we possess, all of it has come from the Buddha, the Blessed One.
What if I were to again invite the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to my home and provide them with a meal?"
191.021. Having understood this, he approached the Blessed One.
191.022. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the householder Sahasodgata was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
191.024. Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he remained silent.

191.025. Then the householder Sahasodgata rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow."
191.026. The Blessed One consented to the householder Sahasodgata by remaining silent.
191.027. Then the householder Sahasodgata, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
191.028. Then, that very night, the householder Sahasodgata prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
Having prepared everything, rising early in the morning, having arranged the seats and set out the water jars, he announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger:
"It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems fit."
191.031. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a community of monks, approached the residence of the householder Sahasodgata.
191.032. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
192.001. Then the householder Sahasodgata, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, [served] with his own hands pure and excellent solid and soft foods.

He satisfied him and served him; in many ways, having personally satisfied and served him with pure and exquisite foods, both solid and soft, he knew that the Blessed One had finished eating, his hands were washed, and his bowl was removed, and [he sat] on a lower seat.
Having taken [the bowl], he sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Upon hearing it, the householder Sahasodgata shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

192.007. Having seen the truths, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Venerable Sir, what has been done for us by the Blessed One is not something that could have been done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by our beloved ones, nor by our circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by kings, nor by deities, nor by our ancestors, nor by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
192.009. The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up."
The mountains of bones have been leaped over;
the gates to the lower realms have been closed; the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened.
We have been established among gods and humans.
O Venerable One, I have gone for refuge; I have truly gone for refuge.

"I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One, and to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, as one who is devoted with all his being.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the householder Sahasodgata with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.

The monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the householder Sahasodgata, such that he performed labor for wages and yet suddenly increased in wealth?"
"And has the vision of the truth been attained?

The Blessed One said: "Monks, by the householder Sahasodgata, deeds were performed and accumulated that have gathered their requisite conditions, whose causes have matured, which stand before him like a rushing torrent, and which are inevitable.
By the householder Sahasodgata, deeds were performed and accumulated."
192.019. Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases do actions performed and accumulated— whether wholesome or unwholesome— reach their maturation.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

192.025. Once upon a time, monks, there lived in a certain mountain village a householder who was wealthy, of great fortune and great enjoyment, possessing vast and extensive holdings, and endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal status. He sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
192.027. While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
192.028. After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
192.029. A boy was born.
192.029. For him, after performing an extensive birth festival for twenty-one days—three times seven days—a name was established that accorded with his family.
192.030. He was reared and grew until he became a man.
192.031. Then, at another time, when the spring season had arrived and the flowers were in full bloom, that householder...
Accompanied by his retinue, he went out to a park grounds within a forest grove resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote lodgings and seats, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.

Meanwhile, a certain pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small town (*karvaṭaka*). Since those who frequent remote lodgings and seats do not enter [villages], he did not enter the town at all, but approached that very garden.
193.004. That householder saw that Pratyekabuddha entering the garden, his body serene and his deportment tranquil.
193.005. Having seen him, he was filled with joy and gladness and went out to meet him in great haste.
193.006. The Pratyekabuddha reflected: "This garden is crowded."
"Let me go elsewhere.
Having realized this, he began to turn back.
That householder fell at his feet and said, "Noble one,"
"Why do you turn back? Are you seeking alms? "I too am seeking merit."
"Stay in this very garden;
we shall provide you with almsfood so that you lack for nothing.
Such great beings are devoted to the welfare of others.
193.009. Having established a mind of compassion toward him, he began to dwell in that very garden. 193.010. He, too, began to provide for his sustenance with alms-food.
193.011. Then, at another time, a certain business arose for that householder in a particular market town.
193.011. He addressed his wife: "My dear lady, a certain business has arisen for me in that village; I am going there.
193.012. "I shall go there."
"You must ensure that there is no lack of food and drink for that great-souled one who has gone forth.
Having said this, he departed.
On the following day, that housewife rose early in the morning and began to prepare food and drink for his sake.
193.014. She was asked by her son: "Mother, for whose sake is this food and drink being prepared?
She replied: "Son,"
"He who stays in the park with a tranquil mind as a renunciant—for his sake this is being accomplished.
He, becoming enraged, said: "Mother!"
"Why do you perform work for wages and yet not eat?
She replied, "Son, do not speak thus."
"The ripening of this action is undesirable.
Although he was being restrained, he did not desist,
until that householder arrived.
He addressed his wife: "My dear, have you provided him with food so that he has no lack?
"Noble son, I have."
"But this boy has uttered harsh words toward him.
He said, "My lady, what is he saying?"
She related it in detail.
He reflected: "This ascetic is capable;
I shall go and ask forgiveness of that great-souled one, lest he be utterly ruined."
Having understood this, he took the boy and approached the place where the pratyekabuddha was.
That pratyekabuddha saw the householder approaching with him as his second companion.
He reflected: "Never before has this householder come accompanied by a second person."
193.024. What, then, is the reason for this?
The knowledge and vision of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not function without focused attention. 193.025. He proceeded to apply himself to such focused attention.
193.025. Having reflected upon this, he understood:
"The teaching of the Dharma by those Great-souled Ones is through the body, not through speech.
193.026. Out of compassion for him, like a king of swans with outspread wings, he rose high into the air and began to perform the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
193.027. The supernatural power of an ordinary person is quickly captivating.
193.028. Like a tree cut down at its root, he fell at his feet along with his son.
Then that boy, his hair standing on end with joy, said: "Descend, descend, O truly worthy recipient of offerings!"
"Please grant me, who am submerged in the mire of desire, a hand to pull me out.
Out of compassion for him, he descended.
Then that householder’s son, with intense resolve, fell at his feet and began to make this aspiration: "Since I have uttered harsh words toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings..."
May I not be a partaker of that karma.
But since my mind has now been inspired with serene faith, by this root of merit may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
"May I become a recipient of such qualities as these,
and may I please, and not displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one."
194.003. What do you think, monks?
That son of a householder was none other than this householder Sahasodgata.
194.004. Because he uttered harsh words toward a Pratyekabuddha, for five hundred births he was born as a hired laborer; even until now, he has performed work for wages.
194.005. Thus, even at this time, he has performed work for wages.
Furthermore, because he made a vow after having developed a mind of deep faith in that very person,
he was suddenly enriched with wealth;
and in my presence, he has realized the vision of the Truths.
"And by him, I—the Teacher who am more distinguished than hundreds of thousands of millions of Pratyekabuddhas—have been pleased and not displeased.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves."
194.010. (This, then, is the origin [of the rule], yet the Blessed Buddha had not yet laid down a training precept for his disciples in the Vinaya.
194.012. Thus spoke the Blessed One;
the monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
194.013. The twenty-first avadāna, the Account of Sahasodgata.
********** Avadāna 22 ********** 195.001. Divyāvadāna 22: The Avadāna of the Bodhisattva Cāritra of Candraprabha. 195.002. Thus have I heard:
195.002. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty.

195.003. There, the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Behold, Venerable Sir, how the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have both entered final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder even before us."
But they did not allow the death of their father to come to pass.
In this regard, monks, what is the wonder now that the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—
free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair?
Free from craving and free from grasping, with all attachment to "I-making," "mine-making," and the conceit "I am" abandoned along with their underlying tendencies,

they remained before the community of monks headed by the Buddha; yet, they passed away first into the realm of nirvana without remainder of substrate, without even having experienced the death of their father.

195.009. As for the fact that in the past Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, while still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and unliberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, purified their minds toward me, passed away,
transcended the realm of desire, and were reborn in the Brahma-world;
But they did not cause their father's death;
hear that now.

195.013. Once upon a time, monks, in the past, there was a royal capital named Bhadraśilā in the northern region. It was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
195.014. It was twelve yojanas in length and twelve yojanas in width; it was square, possessed four gates, and was well-laid out.
It was adorned with high arches, windows, lattices, and balconies; filled with various jewels; a home for merchants possessing all manner of abundant goods;

a residence for kings, ministers, householders, guild-leaders, provincial lords, and those wearing crowns; and it resounded with the music of lutes, flutes, drums, sweet-sounding instruments, harps, clay drums, kettledrums, tabors, conchs, and shells.

And in that royal capital, fragrances of agallochum, sandalwood, and powdered incense, as well as the scents of flowers that bloom in all seasons, were wafted by various winds, creating an exceedingly delightful atmosphere throughout the streets, squares, and intersections. The city was endowed with a fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; its broad and most beautiful main roads were adorned with wheeled carriages and vehicles, while colorful banners and flags were raised high, and the archways, windows, and crescent-shaped ornaments were beautifully arrayed.
It shines like the abode of the immortals (Amarālaya).
Adorned with fragrant water-born flowers such as blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-lotuses, and white lotuses; graced by ponds, lakes, wells, and springs filled with sweet, clear, and cool water;

covered with blossoms of karṇikāra, aśoka, tilaka, puṃnāga, nāgakeśara, campaka, bakula, atimuktaka, pāṭala, and other trees; and surrounded by groves and gardens resounding with flocks of sparrows, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, peacocks, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds.
And in the capital city of Bhadraśilā, there was a royal park named Maṇigarbha, adorned with various trees bearing flowers and fruits,
provided with water wells, and made exceedingly delightful by the charming songs of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds.
Thus did the capital city of Bhadraśilā become most beautiful.
In the capital city of Bhadraśilā, there was a king named Candraprabha— handsome, beautiful to behold,

and gracious; possessing divine vision, he was a universal monarch over one quarter of the world, a righteous king of dharma who, being self-luminous, exercised sovereign power and lordship over Jambudvīpa.
195.029. Indeed, as King Candraprabha proceeded, there was no darkness;
nor was a jewel, a lamp, or a torch carried before him.
Rather, from his own body, rays of light issued forth from King Candraprabha, just like rays from the orb of the moon.
For this reason, King Candraprabha came to be known by the name Candraprabha.

196.001. At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there were sixty-eight thousand cities, headed by the capital city of Bhadraśilā; they were prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
196.002. Moreover, at that time, the people of Jambudvīpa were free from taxes, free from tolls, and free from ferry-fees. 196.003. The districts became gentle and abundant in agricultural produce.
The villages, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals were so close together that a cock could fly between them.
At that time, the lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa was forty-four thousand years.
King Candraprabha was a bodhisattva who gave everything away, relinquishing all things, and renouncing everything without attachment.

He was engaged in great generosity. Therefore, having departed from the capital city of Bhadraśilā, he had four great sacrificial enclosures constructed outside each of the four city gates, with parasols, banners, sacrificial posts, and flags raised on high.
Then, having struck golden drums, gifts were distributed.
Meritorious deeds are performed,
such as giving food to those seeking food and drink to those seeking drink.
Tasteful foods, edible delicacies, garlands, ointments, garments, beds, seats, supports, dwellings, lamps, and parasols; chariots, ornaments, and decorations;
golden vessels filled with silver powder, and silver vessels filled with gold.
Cows with golden horns that yield every desire were given;
boys and girls adorned with all kinds of ornaments were presented as gifts;
and garments of various colors, raised from many lands, and of diverse patterns were bestowed.

Such as these: garments of fine silk, Chinese silk, and washed cotton cloth; beautiful clothes made of wool and *dukūla* fibers; *aparāntaka*, *phalaka*, *haryaṇika*, and *kambala* blankets; precious gold coverings; and *ākāśika*, *aṃśuka*, and *kṣaumaka* fabrics.
King Candraprabha bestowed such gifts that all the people of Jambudvīpa became wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
196.015. King Candraprabha bestowed such gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, and parasols that not even a single person in this Jambudvīpa had to travel on foot.

196.016. All the people of Jambudvīpa traveled by the backs of elephants and in chariots yoked with four horses, with parasols made of gold and silver held over them, moving from garden to garden and village to village.
They wandered through the village.

Then, this thought occurred to King Candraprabha: "What is the use of my giving away such inferior gifts? Why should I not give away those very same garments, ornaments, and decorations that I myself wear?"
"I shall bestow such gifts that all the people of Jambudvīpa may enjoy themselves with royal sports.
Then King Candraprabha bestowed upon the people of Jambudvīpa crowns, turbans, garments, ornaments, and jewelry.
That is to say, he bestowed gifts such as bracelets, armlets, necklaces, half-necklaces, and so forth.
King Candraprabha likewise gave away as many royal garments, ornaments, crowns, and turbans as there were,
by which all the people of Jambudvīpa came to wear crowns and turbans.
196.023. All the humans of Jambudvīpa came to possess exactly the same appearance as King Candraprabha.
196.024. Thereupon, King Candraprabha caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the sixty-eight thousand cities: "May all you people of Jambudvīpa enjoy yourselves with royal diversions!"
"As long as I live.
Then, having heard King Candraprabha’s proclamation by the ringing of the bell, all the people of Jambudvīpa began to engage in royal sports.
With thousands of lutes, flutes, panavas, sughoṣakas, vallaris, kettledrums, tabors, clay drums, cymbals, and conchs, and with hundreds of musical sounds, they played.
Amidst the sounding of musical instruments, they— wearing armlets, necklaces, gems, pearl ornaments, and earrings, and surrounded by throngs of women adorned with every kind of finery—
enjoyed royal splendor. At that time, among the people of Jambudvīpa who were sporting with royal grace, whoever...

The sound of lutes, flutes, panavas, sughoṣakas, vallaris, kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors, as well as the resonance of the sixty-eight types of cymbals and pipes, and the beautiful, melodious sound that issued from the golden drums being struck in the four great sacrificial enclosures of Candraprabha—

by all this, the entire Jambudvīpa was filled with a delightful sound, just as the interior of the Trāyastriṃśa gods' realm resounds with the sounds of divine dancing, singing, and instrumental music.

In this very way, at that time and on that occasion, the entire populace dwelling in Jambudvīpa was so utterly devoted to pleasure by the sound of that singing and instrumental music that they took extreme delight.
At that time, there dwelt in the royal capital of Bhadraśilā seventy-two hundred billion people.
King Candraprabha was dear and pleasing to them.
Even now, as they gazed upon the stability of his complexion, form, and marks, they could not reach satiety.
And at whatever time King Candraprabha went to the great sacrificial enclosure,
at that time hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings would look upon him.
And they said: "Ah, this King Candraprabha is surely a divine embryo (devagarbha) who exercises sovereignty here in Jambudvīpa!
Indeed, no humans possess such color and physical form as does the Lord Candraprabha.
Wherever King Candraprabha looked, [he saw...]
Thousands of women gazed upon him from here and there, thinking, "Blessed are those women whose husband is he!
This was because of their pure minds and not otherwise;
such was King Candraprabha, so beautiful to behold.
King Candraprabha had twelve thousand five hundred ministers.

Among them were two chief ministers, Mahācandra and Mahīdhara. They were distinguished, learned, and wise; they excelled all the members of the circle of ministers in their virtues. They were appointed with full authority, acting as the leaders of the king and the protectors of the kingdom.
King [Mahāsudarśana] was little concerned with all his administrative duties.
And the chief minister Mahācandra constantly exhorted the people of Jambudvīpa toward the ten paths of wholesome action, saying:
"Sirs, you people of Jambudvīpa, take up and abide by these ten paths of wholesome action."
197.014. And just as was the instruction and admonition of the universal monarch, such was the instruction and admonition of the minister Mahācandra.
197.016. King Candraprabha was beloved, dear, and pleasing to the chief minister Mahācandra.
Even now, as he gazes upon his complexion, form, characteristics, and physical proportions, he does not reach satiety.
Then, at another time, the chief minister Mahācandra saw a dream: the crown of King Candraprabha was removed by smoke-colored piśācas. Upon waking, he was seized by fear and became apprehensive.
A thrill of horror arose within him: "May no one come to beg for the head of the divine Candraprabha!
For the King is a giver of all;
in his total renunciation, there is nothing whatsoever that he has not already given away to the poor, the helpless, the wretched, the mendicants, and the beggars."
197.021. The thought occurred to him: "I must not report this dream to King Candraprabha.
Rather, having had heads made of jewels, I should have them placed inside the treasury and storehouse. 197.022–197.023.
"Should anyone indeed come as a petitioner for the king's head," he thought, [he would then present one].
"I shall entice him with these heads made of jewels.
Having realized this, he had heads made of jewels, placed them in the treasuries and storehouses, and set them aside.
At a later time, the chief minister Mahīdhara saw a dream: a ship made entirely of jewels, belonging to the family of Candraprabha, shattered into hundreds of pieces.
Upon seeing this, he became afraid, terrified, and agitated, thinking: "Could it be that King Candraprabha will suffer the loss of his kingdom, or that there will be an obstacle to his life?
He summoned the brahmins who were skilled in omens and wise in interpretation, and said to them: "Sirs, I have seen such a dream."
"Make it free from defects.
Then those brahmins, soothsayers, and scholars declared: "O King, according to the dream you have seen, before long a petitioner for King Candraprabha’s head will arrive."
"And he shall descend right here in this royal capital of Bhadraśilā.
Then the chief minister Mahīdhara, having heard the description of the dream, rested his cheek upon his hand and remained lost in thought:
"How very swift is the power of impermanence over King Candraprabha, who is so friendly by nature, compassionate, and devoted to all beings!"
"It has presented itself.

Then, at another time, a dream was seen by thirteen thousand ministers: in the four sacrificial enclosures of King Candraprabha, the *karoṭapāṇi* yakṣas had broken the parasols, banners, flags, and golden drums.

Upon seeing this, they were again terrified, trembling, and deeply agitated, thinking: "May the power of impermanence not overcome King Candraprabha, the great protector of the earth, who is compassionate by nature, merciful, and affectionate toward all beings; may there not come about for us a separation, a parting, and a dissociation from the Lord; may Jambudvīpa not become without protection and without refuge!"
King Candraprabha heard this.

Having heard it, he caused a proclamation by means of bells to be made throughout sixty-eight thousand cities: "Sirs, let all the humans of Jambudvīpa enjoy themselves with royal splendor as long as I am here. What is the use of your thoughts, which are like illusions and like dreams?"

Having heard King Candraprabha’s proclamation by the ringing of the bell, all the people of Jambudvīpa began to sport with royal splendor; they were surrounded by throngs of women adorned with every ornament— wearing armlets, necklaces, gems, pearls, earrings, and bracelets— as hundreds of musical instruments, including thousands of lutes, *vīṇās*, *paṇavas*, *sughoṣakas*, *vallarīs*, kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, and conchs, were being played.
They experienced royal splendor.
At that time, while the people of Jambudvīpa were engaged in royal pastimes,
there arose from the golden drums being struck in the four great sacrificial enclosures of King Candraprabha a sound that was beautiful and charming.
By that, all of Jambudvīpa resounded with delightful sounds.

Just as in any city of the Trāyastriṃśa gods there is the sound of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, even so at that time and on that occasion, the entire population dwelling in Jambudvīpa, enraptured by that sound of song, rejoiced exceedingly, being established in absolute happiness.
At that time, there lived on Mount Gandhamādana a brahmin named Raudrākṣa, who was an expert in the rituals of *indrajāla* (magical illusions).
The brahmin Raudrākṣa heard that in the capital city of Bhadraśilā, there was a king named Candraprabha who proclaimed himself to be "one who gives everything.
He thought, "What if I were to go and ask him for my head?"
The thought occurred to him: "If he is to be one who gives everything, he will give me his head.
However, it is difficult, impossible, and out of the question that he would thus relinquish his head—that most cherished, beloved, dear, pleasing, and supreme limb."
"This is not possible," he thought;
having realized this, he descended from Mount Gandhamādana.

Then the deity dwelling on Gandhamādana began to cry out: "Alas, what a tragedy! The power of impermanence has overcome King Candraprabha, who was of a loving nature, greatly compassionate, and affectionate toward all beings!"
At that time, all of Jambudvīpa was thrown into utter turmoil; it was shrouded in the darkness of smoke, and meteors fell.
The quarters were ablaze, and divine drums resounded in the sky.

And not far from the capital city of Bhadraśilā dwelt a seer named Viśvāmitra, possessed of the five superknowledges, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, who was benevolent in nature, compassionate, and affectionate toward all beings.

198.026. Then that seer, seeing all of Jambudvīpa in a state of turmoil, addressed the young brahmins: "O young brahmins, you should know that all of Jambudvīpa is now utterly agitated and shrouded in the darkness of smoke.
198.027. Even the sun and moon, so great in their majesty, do not shine, do not glow, and do not radiate light. 198.028. Surely the passing away of some Great Being must be occurring."

Then the Elder Upagupta entered into meditative absorption and surveyed: "In what manner was the assembly arranged by the Tathāgata?
He saw that the assembly was seated in the shape of a half-moon.
Then he surveyed further: "In what manner was the teaching of the Dharma performed by the Tathāgata?"

He perceived that after delivering the discourse on what is to be done in the past, the revelation of the truth had been accomplished. Having also delivered the discourse on what is to be done in the past, he began to perform the revelation of the truth.
And Māra released a rain of pearl necklaces upon that assembly.
The minds of those to be converted were thrown into confusion, and not even a single person attained the vision of the Truth.
Then the Elder Upagupta looked about: "By whom has this distraction been caused?"
He saw that it was Māra.
On the second day, an even greater multitude of people went forth;
Upagupta was teaching the Dharma.
And a rain of pearl necklaces was showered down.

Then, on the second day as well, after the Elder Upagupta had delivered his customary discourse and begun to reveal the Truths, Māra released a rain of gold upon that assembly and agitated the minds of those ready for conversion.
Not even a single person had seen the Truth.
Then the Elder Upagupta looked about, wondering, "By whom has this distraction been caused?
and he saw that it was by Māra, the Evil One.
222.021. When it came to the third auspicious day, a vast multitude of people went forth.
222.022. Upagupta was teaching the Dharma, and a rain of pearls and a rain of gold were falling.

When the third day arrived, the Elder Upagupta, having delivered his discourse on the duties to be performed at the beginning of the day, began to proclaim the Truths. Not far away, Māra commenced a theatrical performance,
and celestial musical instruments were played.
And divine apsarases began to dance.
As soon as the assembly of people, though free from passion, saw the divine forms and heard the divine sounds, they were drawn away by Māra.
Thus, the assembly of Upagupta was led astray by Māra.
With a joyful mind, Māra placed a garland upon the head of the Elder Upagupta.
Then the Elder Upagupta began to reflect: "Who is this?
He saw that it was Māra.
The thought occurred to him: "This Māra is causing great distraction within the Blessed One’s teaching.
Why has he not been disciplined by the Blessed One?
He sees that this one is to be disciplined by me."
"And because of his discipline and his assistance to sentient beings, I have been declared by the Blessed One to be a Buddha without marks.
Then the Elder Upagupta reflected: "Has the time for his discipline arrived, or has it not?
He saw that the time for his discipline had arrived.
Then the Elder Upagupta took up three corpses—a snake corpse, a dog corpse, and a human corpse.
By means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he manifested a garland of flowers and approached Māra.
Upon seeing him, joy arose in Māra, thinking, "Upagupta too has been drawn away by me."
Then Māra presented his own body. The Elder Upagupta bound it himself.
Thereupon, the Elder Upagupta bound the serpent carcass upon Māra.
A dog's carcass was on his neck,
and a human corpse was clinging to his ear.
Then, having touched him, he said:
"Just as you have bound this garland, which is repulsive to the people among monks,
so too have I bound this corpse for you, which is repulsive to those who lust after people."
223.007. Display whatever strength you possess, for today you have encountered the Son of the Buddha.
223.009. Even the ocean water, though surging with waves curved by the wind, turns back within the hollows of Mount Malaya. (19)
Then Māra began to remove that corpse;
however, even though he himself entered it, he was unable to remove it, just as an ant cannot move a king of mountains. Being powerless, he sprang up into the air and said:
223.013. If I cannot myself release this dog's carcass from my neck, then other gods of even greater splendor than I shall release it. 223.014. [Verse 20]
The Elder said:
"Seek refuge in Brahmā or Śatakratu, or enter the blazing fire or the ocean;
yet this corpse situated in the throat shall undergo neither moisture, nor drying up, nor dissolution here."
223.020. Having approached the gods—Indra, Rudra, Upendra, Draviṇeśvara, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, and the others—and having failed to achieve his purpose, he went to Brahmā.
223.021. He was told by him: "Forgive me, dear child; as a disciple of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, you have yourself established the boundaries of destiny through your supernatural power."
Who is able to break through that [resolve], just as it is impossible to breach the shore of the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa? //22//
223.024. Someone might even lift up Mount Himavat by binding it with lotus fibers; 223.025. but I cannot remove this dog's carcass clinging to your neck. (23)
223.026. Granted that I too possess great strength, nevertheless, I am not equal to the strength of the Son of the Tathāgata.
223.028. It is not that there is no fire among those who are radiant; however, that splendor which exists in the solar orb is not present in the sacrificial fire. (24)
224.001. Māra said: "What do you command now? To whom shall I go for refuge?
Brahmā replied:
224.002. Go quickly for refuge to that very one, by encountering whom a creature who has fallen here upon the surface of the earth rises up again, supported once more by the earth. //25//
224.006. Then Māra, perceiving the power of the Tathāgata’s disciple, reflected: 224.007.
"The teaching of even whose disciples is honored by Brahmā— 224.008.
who indeed would be able to measure the power of that Buddha? (26)
"What instruction would that one of noble vows have wished to give me?
For it was through his patience that he protected me by not inflicting it."
224.011. What need is there for much?
224.012. Today I recognize the great compassion of that Sage, whose nature is supreme loving-kindness, whose mind is liberated from all calamities, and who shines like a mountain of gold.
224.014. For though I, blinded by delusion, distressed him here and there with various arguments, even so, that powerful one did not speak anything unpleasant to me. (28)

224.016. Then Māra, the lord of the desire realm, realizing that there was no other destination for him except Upagupta, cast everything aside, approached the Elder Upagupta, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Venerable sir, is it unknown to you how hundreds of offenses against the Blessed One were committed by me, beginning from the foot of the Bodhi tree? Why is this so?
[Because] when he reached the village of Śālā, that Gautama encountered me..."
Even when deprived of food, he did nothing unpleasant to me. //29//
Having become a cow, standing like a serpent, and assuming the form of a cart-driver,
that protector was exhausted by me, yet I was not harmed by him.
But you, O hero, having abandoned me— your own natural inheritance— have today brought me to ridicule among the worlds, including the gods and asuras. (31)
The Elder said: "O Evil One, how can you, without even investigating, compare a disciple to the majesty of the Tathāgata?
Do you here equate Mount Meru with a mustard seed, the sun with a firefly, or the ocean with a puddle?"
224.028. For that compassion of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers toward living beings is indeed different; O gentle one, a disciple does not possess such great compassion. //32//
Moreover—
That for which the Blessed One endured even the obstruction [caused by us],
that very reason has been directly perceived by us. (33)
Māra said:
"Speak, speak! Tell me the state of mind of that illustrious one who has cut off attachment and whose vow is protected by patience.
He, though constantly harassed by me out of delusion, has looked upon me with nothing but loving-kindness."
The Elder said: "Listen, gentle one; for you have repeatedly stumbled before the Blessed One.
And there is no cleansing of unwholesome states that have been planted in the mind other than through faith in the Tathāgata alone."
Therefore, because that far-sighted one perceived this cause, you were not addressed with anything unpleasant here, but were instead granted only what is agreeable. (35)

225.010. By this method, devotion has been generated in your heart by that one of supreme intelligence; for even a slight amount of devotion toward this [teaching] yields the fruit of *nirvāṇa* for those possessed of wisdom.
225.012. Whatever evil you have committed here, O Sage, with a mind blinded by delusion—all of it has been washed away by the streams of the water of faith flowing within your heart. (36)

Then Māra, with the hair on his body bristling like a *kadamba* flower, prostrated himself with his whole body and said: "It was only fitting that I tormented him in many ways before he attained perfection; yet, having achieved his desires on this earth, that best of sages endured it all, as a father might with gentle persuasion endure the transgression of a son. (37)
225.019. His mind nourished by faith in the Buddha, he reflected for a very long time on the qualities of the Buddha, then prostrated at the feet of the Elder and said:

225.020. "A supreme favor has been done for me by you, in that reverence for the Buddha has been instilled within me. 225.022. But please cast off this ornament of the great seer’s anger, which hangs around my neck out of [false] compassion. (38)
The Elder said, "I shall release you on one condition. Māra asked, "What is the condition?
The Elder replied, "From this day forward, monks must not be harmed."
Māra said, "I shall not cause you harm.
What else do you command?
The Elder replied, "Such is my command regarding the work of the Teaching."
"I shall inform you regarding my own business.
Then Māra, with agitation, said: "Be gracious, Elder;
what do you command?"
The Elder said: "You understand for yourself that since I went forth into homelessness after the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa a hundred years ago, it was his Dharma-body that I beheld;
I did not see his physical body, which resembled a mountain of gold, belonging to the Lord of the Three Worlds."
226.001. <226> Thereafter, O incomparable one, manifest here an act of grace by displaying the form of a Buddha;
for there is nothing more dear to me than this, as I am indeed filled with curiosity regarding the form of the One Possessing the Ten Powers. //39//
226.005. Māra said: "In that case, listen also to my agreement.
226.006. Upon suddenly beholding him here wearing the garb of a Buddha, 226.007.
you must not offer salutation out of reverence for the qualities of an omniscient one. (40)
O Lord, if you should offer me even a slight act of worship with a mind made tender by the recollection of the Buddha, I shall be consumed.
What power do I have to endure a prostration performed by one free from passion? It is like the sprouts of an eraṇḍa tree unable to bear the touch of an elephant’s trunk.
The Elder also said, "So be it;
however, I shall not bow down to you.
Māra replied, "In that case, wait for a moment."
Meanwhile, having entered the dense forest—
[I recall] how formerly, out of a resolve to deceive Śūra, I assumed through the power of my inconceivable intellect that form of a Buddha with the luster of refined gold;
and having taken that very form which delights the eyes of living beings, here I am now eclipsing even the stainless web of the sun’s rays with my own halo.
226.018. Then the Elder, saying "So be it," removed that corpse and stood there, eager to behold the form of the Tathāgata.
226.019. And Māra, having entered the thicket of the forest and assumed the form of a Buddha—like an actor in exquisite costume—began to emerge from that forest thicket.
226.020. For it will be said:
Displaying the body of a Tathāgata, enriched with the most excellent marks and bringing peace to the eyes of men, he adorned that forest like one unveiling a costly, freshly dyed painted canvas. (43)
Then, having manifested the form of the Blessed One— adorned with a halo of light extending a fathom in length, its appearance beyond all description—

and having placed the Elder Śāradvatīputra at his right side, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana at his left side, and the Venerable Ānanda behind him holding the Buddha’s bowl in his hand, as well as the great śrāvakas such as the Elders Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, and Subhūti;
Having manifested forms and displayed himself in the guise of a Buddha, surrounded by one thousand two hundred and fifty monks in the shape of a half-moon,
Māra approached the Elder Upagupta.
And as the Elder Upagupta beheld this form of the Blessed One, thinking, "Such is his appearance," joy arose within him.
226.029. With a joyful heart, he rose quickly from his seat and, looking about, said:
227.001. <227> "Fie upon that pitiless impermanence, which destroys even such forms as these!
227.003. Indeed, the body of that great sage, having encountered impermanence, has come to destruction. (44)

227.005. Through mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, his mind became so intensely attached that he clearly approached [the Buddha], thinking, "I am seeing the Blessed Buddha. 227.006. Joining his palms like a lotus bud, he said: "Oh, how beautiful is the form of the Blessed One! What more need be said? 227.007. Why elaborate further?
227.008. For with his face he surpasses the lotus; with his eye, the blue water-lily; with his radiance, the grove of flowers; and with his loveliness, the moon of full splendor. 227.010.
He surpasses the great ocean in depth, Meru in stability, the sun in brilliance, the lion in his gait, the bull in his gaze, and gold in his complexion. (45)
227.012. His heart overflowing with even greater joy, he spoke in a resonant voice:
227.013–227.014. "Oh, how sweet is the fruit of action for those whose intentions are pure!
This form has been created by this very action, and not by sovereign power or mere chance. (46)

That which arose from speech, body, and mind over many hundreds of billions of kalpas— purified by that Arhat through the restraint of generosity, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom— by means of this,
this stainless form has been manifested, so beautiful to the eyes of living beings, seeing which even an enemy would be filled with joy, let alone one such as I.

227.019. With the Fully Awakened One as his object of focus, he forgot his own perception and established the perception of the Buddha; like a tree cut at its root, he fell with his entire body at the feet of Māra.
227.020. Then Māra, in a state of agitation, said: "Venerable sir, you ought not thus to transgress our agreement. 227.021. The Elder asked: "What is this agreement?"
Māra said: "But was it not promised by the Venerable One—'I shall not bow down before you'?

Then the Elder Upagupta, rising from the surface of the earth with a voice choked with emotion, said: 'O Evil One, it is certainly not unknown to me that he, the preeminent among disputants, has attained final peace like a fire extinguished by water.'"
Moreover, having seen his form, so pleasing to the eye, I bowed before that seer; but I do not pay you such honor.
Māra said: "Why am I not honored here, since you thus bow down to me?
The elder replied: "Listen."
"Just as you have not been worshipped by me at all,
nor has any transgression of our agreement been committed by me—
just as people [behave] toward clay images of the gods."
Disregarding the notion of death, one bows down with the notion that [the recipient] is immortal. //49//
Thus, beholding you here, who bear the form of the Lord of the World, I disregarded the notion that you were Māra and bowed down with the recognition that you were the Sugata.
228.005. Then Māra, having made his Buddha-attire disappear and paid homage to the Elder Upagupta, departed.

On the fourth day, Māra himself began to sound a bell in Mathurā, proclaiming: "Whoever among you desires the happiness of heaven and liberation, let him hear the Dharma from the presence of the Elder Upagupta."
"And those among you who have not seen the Tathāgata, let them behold the Elder Upagupta. And he said:
"Having cast aside poverty, which is the root of misfortune, whoever desires here abundant and glorious prosperity,"
228.011. And he who desires heaven and liberation should, therefore, listen to the Dharma with faith. //51//

228.013. Those by whom the foremost of bipeds, the Teacher, the Greatly Compassionate One, the Self-Existent One, has not been seen—let them behold the Elder Upagupta, who is like the Teacher himself, a radiant lamp for the three worlds. (52)
228.017. News spread throughout Mathurā that the Elder Upagupta had subdued Māra.
Upon hearing this, the majority of the people residing in Mathurā went into the presence of the Elder Upagupta.
Then, as hundreds of thousands of brahmins gathered together, the Elder Upagupta ascended the lion-throne, fearless like a lion.
And he will say:
"It is not possible for one who is ignorant to ascend my lion-throne;
for he who sits upon that lion-throne shrinks away like a deer. (53)
He who, like a lion, roars fearlessly for the sake of destroying the pride of the foremost enemies, he is said to be a fit lion worthy of ascending the lion-throne. //54//
228.024. Then, after the Elder Upagupta had delivered a discourse on what is to be done in former times, he revealed the Truths.
228.025. Upon hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation;
some attained the fruit of a non-returner.
Some attained the fruit of once-returning,
some the fruit of stream-entry, and as many as eighteen thousand went forth into homelessness.
And by all who applied themselves in this way, up to the point that they attained arhatship.
There, on Mount Corumuṇḍa, there was a cave eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width.

When they had accomplished what was to be done, the Elder Upagupta said: "Whoever, through my instruction, shall realize arhatship by the abandonment of all afflictions, he must cast into the cave a tally-stick four finger-breadths long."
228.030. Eventually, on a single day, ten thousand arhats cast their voting sticks.

228.031. A report spread throughout the earth as far as the ocean: "In Mathurā, there is one named Upagupta, whom the Blessed One has designated as the foremost of those who provide instruction—just like the great-souled Elder Upagupta, who is like a second Teacher, having conquered the lord of the desire realm."

On Mount Urumuṇḍa, he whose pair of feet is worshipped by gods, humans, great serpents, asuras, garuḍas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas, causes the sprouts of liberation to flourish for many hundreds of thousands of beings— whose continuums of seeds of merit were planted in previous buddha-fields— by the falling rain of the stream of water from the True Dharma.

"Out of necessity for our task, we shall first recall the gift of dust offered long ago to King Aśoka, whose footstool was illuminated by the rays from the crest-jewels of all his prostrating vassals.
Thus it is heard:
The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Place.
229.007. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagṛha for alms, surrounded by a host of monks and preceded by the community of monks.
229.009. And it will be said:
229.010. His body is like the peak of the Golden Mountain, resembling the lord of elephants, and he moves with graceful ease.
With a face as gentle as the full moon, the Blessed One, surrounded by a multitude of monks, proceeded on his way. //55//
229.014. When the Blessed One, with deliberate effort, set his foot upon the threshold of the city gate,
it was indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddha-Blessed Ones, with deliberate effort, place their feet upon the threshold of the city gate,
then various wonderful miracles appear.
The blind regain their sight;
the deaf become capable of hearing;
the lame become capable of walking.
The bonds of sentient beings imprisoned in stocks, fetters, and dungeons become loosened.
Sentient beings who have been bound by enmity through successive lifetimes immediately thereafter attain a state of loving-kindness.
Calves, having broken their ropes, reunite with their mothers.
The elephants trumpet, the horses neigh, and the bulls bellow.
Parrots, mynas, cuckoos, jīvañjīvakas, and peacocks warbled sweet sounds; ornaments placed in caskets emitted sweet sounds; and musical instruments, though untouched, produced sweet sounds.
The elevated regions of the earth sink down;
those that have sunk rise up; and it remains free from stones, pebbles, and potsherds.
And at that time, this earth shook in six ways:
namely, the eastern quarter rose while the western sank;
the center sank while the periphery rose.
It shook, it trembled, it quaked, it quaked violently; these and other such wonderful phenomena appeared when the Blessed One entered the city. And he will say:
Then the earth, including the ocean-dwelling [beings], the cities adorned with towns and markets, and the mountains—
pressed down by the feet of the Sage, it sank like a vessel struck by the force of the wind.

Then, drawn by the miracles manifested at the fixed time of the Buddha’s entrance, the women and men of that city made it like the great ocean agitated by waves and surging billows stirred by the force of the wind; they broke into loud cries of exultation. Indeed, no wonder equal to the entrance of a Buddha is found in the world.
229.032. Indeed, at the time of the Blessed One’s entry into the city, various wonderful and marvelous signs were seen.
And it will be said: 230.001.

<230> By the power of the Buddha, the earth—low-lying places rising up and high places sinking down—becomes level; and the ground, free from stumps, pebbles, and thorns, attains a state of flawlessness.

At that moment, men who were blind, mute, dull-witted, or impaired in their senses regained their faculties; and in the city, musical instruments resounded with joy, even though they had not been struck. //57//
And that entire city became suffused with the radiance of the Buddha, which surpassed the light of a thousand suns and was the color of golden rays. And he said:
"Indeed, having eclipsed the light of the sun, his splendor pervades the entire world, including all its forests."
And having attained [this state], he indeed delights in the most excellent discourse on the Dharma for the world—including gods, asuras, and humans—having brought them to the state of liberation.

230.011. Eventually, the Blessed One set out upon the royal highway. There, two young boys were playing with sandcastles: one was the son of a preeminent family, and the second was the son of a wealthy merchant.
The first was named Jaya and the second Vijaya.
By them the Blessed One was seen, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and beautiful to behold, never tiring the sight.
230.013. Then, thinking "I shall give some roasted flour," the boy Jaya threw a handful of dust into the Blessed One’s bowl, and Vijaya, with palms joined in reverence, expressed his approval.
230.015. And it will be said:
Having seen the Great Compassionate One, the Self-Existent, whose entire body was illuminated by a fathom-wide radiance,
he, inspired with faith by the Sage’s serene countenance, offered dust to the one who brings an end to birth and old age.

230.020. Having presented it to the Blessed One, he began to make a formal vow: "By this root of merit, may I become a king over the earth under a single umbrella, and may I perform acts of service for this very Buddha.
230.022. Then the Sage, having understood the disposition of that youth throughout the night and his perfect vow, [proceeded accordingly].
Seeing that the desired fruit was attained through the power of his resolve, he took up some dust out of compassion. (60)
By him, merit resulting in the ripening of sovereignty was projected.
Therefore, you displayed a smile.
Indeed, it is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, display a smile, [light rays issue forth].
At that time, rays of light— blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, crystal, and silver— issued forth from his mouth;
some went upward,
and some went downward.
230.029. Those who go downward, having gone to Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and as far as the Avīci hells, fall into those cold hells having become warm,
and into those hot hells having become cool.
230.031. By that, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them: "Sirs, have we passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?"
"By this, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Then, in order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One dispatched an emanation.
It occurred to them: "We have not passed away from here,"
"Nor have they been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being never seen before.
It is through his power that our particular sufferings have been stilled."

231.004. Having developed serene confidence in that emanation and having exhausted their karma to be experienced in hell, they take rebirth among gods and humans where they become vessels for the truths.
231.005. Those who go upward [to the higher realms] reach the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin.

Having gone to the gods of the Brahma-realm, the Ministers of Brahma, the Great Brahmas, the Limited Light, the Immeasurable Light, the Radiant, the Limited Purity, the Immeasurable Purity, the All-Pure, the Cloudless, the Merit-Born, the Vast Fruit, the Unclouded, the Without-Heat, the Good-Appearing, the Good-to-See, and up to the Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they spoke these two verses:
“Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut. (61)
For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end to suffering. (62)
231.014. Then those rays of light, having circled the trichiliocosm—the great three-thousandfold world system—returned toward the Blessed One.
231.015. If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma, they vanished behind him.
231.015. When he wishes to prophesy the future, [the rays] disappear in front of him. 231.016. When he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, [they disappear into his soles].
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the soles of his feet; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals,
they disappear into his heels.

231.017. If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), [the light] disappears into his big toe. 231.018. If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, [the light] disappears into his ankle.
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch,
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

231.019. If he wishes to prophesy the attainment of the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), they disappear into the palm of his right hand. 231.020. If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods, [they disappear into his navel].
If he intends to prophesy awakening as a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*),
they disappear into his mouth.
231.021. If he intends to prophesy solitary enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*), they disappear into the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft. 231.022.
If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*), [they disappear into the uṣṇīṣa].
They vanished into the crown of his head.
Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times to the right and disappeared into the palm of the Blessed One’s left hand.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, spoke this verse:
231.025. Free from rebirth, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme cause for the world.
231.027. These Jinas, who have conquered their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a reason. (36)

At this time, O Hero, having realized it for yourself through your own wisdom, O Śramaṇa, Lord of Jinas, dispel the arisen doubt of the listeners who long for it, with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words, O Bull among Sages. (64)
O you whose voice has the resonance of thundering clouds and whose eyes resemble those of a lordly bull,
O Supreme among Men, please explain the fruit of the gift of sand.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so, Ānanda.
Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Rather, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas manifest a smile with cause and with condition."
"Ānanda, do you see that boy who threw a handful of dust into the Tathāgata’s alms bowl?
"I do, Venerable Sir.

"Ānanda, by this root of merit, when the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa after a hundred years, this boy shall become a king named Aśoka in the city of Pāṭaliputra, a universal monarch ruling over one-fourth of the earth."
He shall be a righteous king of Dharma,
who will cause my relics to be widely distributed and will establish eighty-four thousand stūpas of the King of Dharma.
"He will practice for the welfare of many people. And he said:
"After I have passed away, there will be a sole ruler named Aśoka, who shall possess vast renown."
232.012. This land of Jambudvīpa, adorned with the womb of the element of passion, shall belong to those honored by men and gods. //66//
"This is his gift of merit: that a handful of dust was placed in the bowl of the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One gave them all to the Venerable Ānanda.
Having mixed them with cow dung, he smeared it on the place where the Tathāgata used to walk for his exercise.
There he offered a ball of cow dung.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having mixed it with cow dung, applied the ball of cow dung wherever the Blessed One was walking.
Now at that time, King Bimbisāra was ruling in Rājagṛha.
