In detail, it continued until the king said: "Where there are more [debtors], [the clearing shall proceed]."
And where they are fewer, there one should not give.

240.026. When the king had gone to the Kukuṭārāma and approached the Elder Yaśas, he said: "This is my heart's desire—that on a single day, in a single moment, eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stupas [be established].
The Elder replied: "So be it.
At that time, I shall cover the solar disk with my hand."
240.028. On that day, the Elder Yaśas covered the solar disc with his hand.
240.029. In a single day, during a single muhūrta, eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stupas were established.
240.030. And it will be said:
241.001. Having taken the relics of that seer from those seven previous monuments, Maurya, while ruling the world, constructed eight thousand stupas whose radiance was like autumn clouds. //87//
241.005. When King Aśoka had established eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stūpas, he became a righteous king of Dharma (*dharmarāja*).
241.006. The name Dharmāśoka arose for him.
And it will say:
"That illustrious noble Maurya, for the sake of the welfare of his subjects, caused stupas to be built throughout the entire world.
Having previously attained the state of Caṇḍāśoka on earth, he obtained the state of Dharmāśoka through that deed. (88)
241.011. The twenty-sixth avadāna, "The Gift of Dust."
Having now recently conceived faith in the teaching of the Buddha, wherever he saw followers of the Son of the Śākyas—whether in a crowd or in private—[he paid them honor].
There, having prostrated with his head at [the Blessed One's] feet, he paid homage.
Now, that king had a minister named Yaśas who was supremely faithful in the Blessed One.
He said to the king: "Your Majesty,"
"You ought not to perform prostrations before those who have gone forth from all four castes. For there are Śākya novices who have gone forth from the four castes.
The king said nothing to him.

242.005. Then, after some time, that king said to all his ministers: "I have need of the heads of various living beings. You must bring the head of such-and-such a creature; you, the head of such-and-such. 242.007. [He assigned them tasks, saying: "You, bring the head of such-and-such a creature; you, [bring the head] of such-and-such."
242.007. Furthermore, the minister Yaśas was commanded: "Bring a human head. 242.008. When the heads had been brought, he said: "Go;
sell these heads for their price."
242.009. Then all the other heads were sold;
however, no one would take that human head.
Thereupon the king said, "Give this head to anyone, even without payment."
242.010. And there was no one at all who would accept it. 242.011. Then the minister Yaśas, finding no one to receive the head, approached the king with shame and spoke these words:
242.013. "The heads of cows, donkeys, sheep, deer, and birds have been purchased by men for their prices."
242.015. "But this human head is unwholesome; it will not be accepted even for a price, O King. //1//
242.017. Then the king said to that minister, "Why is it that no one takes this human head?
The minister replied, "Because it is loathsome.
The king asked, "Is only this head loathsome, or are all human heads likewise?"
The minister said, "All human heads.
The king asked, "Is even my own head loathsome? And he, out of fear, did not wish to speak the truth of the matter.
The king said to him, "Minister,
speak the truth. He replied, "So be it."
242.021. Then the king, having established that minister in his promise, rejected him and spoke this matter: "Ho there!
You who are deluded by the intoxication born of beauty and power, is this becoming of you?"

Why do you wish to dissuade me from prostrating at the feet of the monks? Even without a price, there is no recipient on earth who is so loathsome; if merit is earned here by touching my head to them, what could be more contrary to reason than that? (2)
242.028. You perceive birth among the Śākya monks, yet you do not perceive the virtues within them.
242.030. Therefore, through the arrogance of pride in birth, you harm yourself and others out of delusion. (3)
243.001. At the time of bringing home a bride and at the time of the wedding ceremony, there is an examination of birth (*jāti*), but not at the time of performing the Dharma.
243.003. For in the performance of Dharma, virtuous qualities (*guṇa*) are the cause; and virtuous qualities do not take birth into consideration. //4//
243.005. If faults found in those of noble birth incur censure in this world, how is it that virtues found in low-born people do not deserve honor? //5//
243.007. For it is by the power of the mind that the bodies of men are either censured or honored.
243.008. And since the minds of the Śākya mendicants are pure, they are therefore worthy of honor; thus, the Śākyas [are honored]. //6//

243.009. If a twice-born man is devoid of virtues, he incurs contempt even if he is renowned as one who has fallen from his status; 243.011. but a person endowed with auspicious qualities is honored and revered, even if born into a family of low birth. (7)
Moreover:
Have you not heard these words of that compassionate bull among the Śākyas: "That which is essential should be grasped by the wise from men here who are otherwise without essence"?
If I desire to carry out the command of him whose word is never otherwise, and if you strive to obstruct it, this is not the mark of a friend. (8)

243.018. When my body, crushed like a stalk of sugarcane, shall lie upon the earth—incapable of rising, of salutation, or of the labor of joining palms in reverence—what wholesome deed will I then be able to perform with this body? Therefore, before meeting my end in the cemetery, I must grasp the essence from what is considered noble. (9)

243.022–243.023. Like those emerging from a blazing house, or like those sinking into the waters for the sake of a treasure of jewels, those who do not perceive the essence within the body—which is subject to both dissolution and destruction—[are lost]. (10)

243.024. Not seeing the essence and being unskilled in distinguishing between the essential and the non-essential, even though they are wise, 243.025. they despair at the time of entering the mouth of the crocodile of death. //11//
243.026. It would be better for a jar of cream to be broken after its essence has been extracted through the consumption of curd, ghee, fresh butter, milk, and whey.
243.028. There is not much to be lamented; just as there is no grief at the time of death regarding a body whose essence has already been taken away by one's good conduct. //12//
244.001. But when death violently shatters the jar of the body of those who are averse to good conduct and are arrogant, 244.003.
then the fire of grief burns their hearts, like a pot of curd that has been completely broken before its essence could be enjoyed. (13)
Therefore, you ought not to create an obstacle for me regarding this prostration of the body; for one who, shrouded in the darkness of delusion, reckons "I am superior" is a lack of discernment.

But the wise man who examines the body by means of the lamps of the teachings of the One Possessing the Ten Powers does not perceive any inequality between his own body and that of a king or a servant. (14)
244.009. "The elements of skin, flesh, bone, sinew, liver, and so forth are indeed common to all men; it is only through external ornaments that the body’s superiority is produced.

244.011. But that which is considered the essence here is this: that by relying upon this wretched body, the wise bring about wholesome qualities such as rising to greet and paying homage. (15)" 244.013. Then King Aśoka, having realized that the body is even more devoid of essence than the water of a crocodile, a grain of sand, a lump of clay, or a piece of castor-oil wood, [proceeded further].

Having set aside the fruit arising from prostrations and other such acts for many eons— just as one might set aside the great earths compared to Mount Sumeru— and having likewise set aside the fruit arising from [other deeds] for many eons, he perceived that the fruit of venerating the stūpa of the Blessed One was more essential than those; desiring thus to adorn himself, he went to the Kukkuṭārāma surrounded by his circle of ministers.

Standing there at the end of the assembly with palms joined in reverence, he said: "O All-Seeing One, is there anyone else who has been designated as a second [worthy recipient], just as I was designated by that wise man through the gift of dust? (16)

244.020. Thereupon, the Elder of the Saṅgha named Yaśas said: "It is so, Great King. When it was the time for the Blessed One’s final nirvāṇa, having subdued the nāga Apalāla and the nāgas Kumbhaka and Caṇḍālīgopālī, he arrived at Mathurā.
There, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: ‘Ānanda, in this Mathurā, one hundred years after the Tathāgata has passed into final nirvāṇa, there will be a perfumer named Gupta.’"
"He shall have a son named Upagupta, the foremost among instructors, a Buddha without the marks,
who will perform the work of a Buddha after I have passed into parinirvāṇa for a hundred years. Do you see, Ānanda, that dark-blue streak in the distance like a line of blue cloth?"
"So be it, Venerable One.
Ānanda, this is the mountain named Urumuṇḍa.
Here, one hundred years after the Tathāgata has attained final nirvāṇa, there will be a forest hermitage named Naṭabhaṭikā."
"Ānanda, this will be for me the foremost among resting places conducive to tranquility, namely the forest hermitage called Naṭabhaṭikā.
And he said:
"The most excellent of instructors is the highly renowned Upagupta."
244.029. The Lord of the World has prophesied that he will perform the work of a Buddha. //17//
The king asked, "Has that pure being already been born, or has he not yet been born even now?
The Elder replied, "That Great-souled One has already been born."
On Mount Urumuṇḍa, he who has conquered the afflictions dwells, surrounded by a host of Arhats, for the sake of compassion for the world.
Moreover, O King— [he] that being of pure essence, acting with the grace of the Omniscient One, proclaims the sublime Dharma before the assembly.
245.003. He leads by the thousands the gods, lords of asuras, nagas, and humans to the city of liberation. //18//
At that time, the venerable Upagupta was dwelling in the Naṭabhaṭika forest hermitage, surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats.
Having heard this, the king summoned his ministers and said:
"Prepare the body of elephants, chariots, and horses; I shall set out quickly for Mount Urumuṇḍa."
I shall behold in person the Arhat named Upagupta, who is completely liberated from all outflows. //19//
245.011. Then the ministers said to him, "Your Majesty, a messenger residing in his territory should be sent; he will come to Your Majesty of his own accord.
245.012. The king said, "He does not deserve to come to us."
But we alone are worthy to go to him.
Moreover—
I consider his body to be made of diamond, even more so than a mountain.
For that man who would disregard the command of Upagupta, who is equal to the Teacher himself. //20//
245.016. As long as the king had not yet dispatched a messenger to the presence of the Elder Upagupta with the message, "I shall come to see the Elder," 245.017.
the Elder Upagupta thought: "If the king comes, there will be distress for the great multitude of people and for the alms-round."
Then the Elder said, "I shall go there myself.
Thereupon, for the sake of the Elder Upagupta, the king had a ferry-boat established between Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra.
Then the Elder Upagupta, out of favor toward King Aśoka, boarded a boat surrounded by eighteen thousand Arhats and arrived at Pāṭaliputra.
245.021. Then the king’s men informed King Aśoka: "Your Majesty, may you prosper!
For the sake of favoring you, Sopagupta has arrived—he who is the Lord of the Mind and the helmsman of the Teaching."
Honored by those who have crossed to the further shore of the flood of existence, he has arrived here together with his two lotus-feet. //21//

Having heard this, the king, with a joyful mind, removed from his own body a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces and gave it to the messenger for bringing such pleasant news. He then summoned the bell-ringer and said, "Let the bells be sounded throughout Pāṭaliputra:
let it be announced that the Elder Upagupta is arriving."
245.028. It should be said:

245.029. He who, having cast aside poverty—the root of misfortune—desires here abundant and glorious prosperity, and who seeks the means for heaven and liberation, let him behold the compassionate Upagupta. (22)
246.001. Those who have not seen the foremost of bipeds, the Teacher, the Greatly Compassionate One, the Self-Existent One;
246.003. they behold the noble Elder Upagupta, who is like the Teacher himself and a lamp for the three realms of existence. //23//

246.005. When the king had caused a bell to be sounded in Pāṭaliputra and had the city beautified, he traveled two and a half yojanas with all kinds of musical instruments, all flowers, perfumes, and garlands, accompanied by all the citizens and all his ministers, to go out and meet the Elder Upagupta.

246.007. From afar, the king saw the Elder Upagupta, surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats in the shape of a half-moon. 246.008. At the very moment the king beheld the Elder Upagupta, he descended from the back of his elephant, approached the riverbank on foot, placed one foot upon the bank and the second upon a wooden plank in the boat, and embraced the Elder Upagupta with all his limbs.
He ferried him across from the boat. Having ferried him across, he fell at Upagupta’s feet with his entire body like a tree cut down at its root;
having rubbed Upagupta’s feet with his face, he rose, placed both kneecaps upon the surface of the earth, and—
With palms joined in reverence, he gazed at the Elder Upagupta and said:

"When I had slain the hosts of my enemies and gained this earth, adorned by the oceans and its mountains, under a single umbrella—then the joy I felt was not equal to that which I feel now upon beholding you, O Elder. (24)
246.017. By the sight of you, a twofold grace arises within me here at the forefront of this excellent teaching.
246.019. And through the very sight of you, another peerless Self-Existent One has been seen by me today with pure vision. //25//
Moreover:
When the compassionate Lord of Jinas had passed into peace, you performed the work of a Buddha throughout the three worlds;
when the world’s delusion had vanished and its eyes were closed, you became the maker of the light of knowledge, like the sun. (26)
246.026. You are like a Teacher, the unique eye of the world, the most excellent among instructors, and a refuge. 246.028.
O All-pervading Lord, speak your command to me quickly today; I, a being of pure essence, shall carry out your word. (27)

247.001. Then the Elder Upagupta, stroking the king’s head with his right hand, said: 247.002. “Exert yourself with diligence and carry out the sovereignty of your kingdom. 247.003. ‘The Three Jewels are difficult to encounter; O King, worship them constantly. (28)”

"Moreover, Great King, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—the best of charioteers for sentient beings—has entrusted the teaching to both you and me in the midst of the assembly; it must be guarded and preserved by us with great effort.
The king said, "Elder,"
Just as I have been instructed by the Blessed One, so shall it be performed. Why? Because it has already been done.

247.007. With various stupas resembling mountain peaks, adorned with raised parasols and banners variegated with jewels, my earth has been beautified on all sides, and the repositories of relics have been made extensive. (29)
Moreover:
One's own self, son, home, wife, the earth, and even the treasury—nothing whatsoever was not surrendered under the teaching of the King of Dharma. (30)
The Elder Upagupta said: "Excellent, excellent, Great King! This very thing must be carried out.
Why?"
Those who live by the essence [of their practice] and derive their livelihood from the enjoyments of the body do not grieve when time has passed; they go to the desired abode of the gods.
247.017. Then the king, with a great display of royal splendor, had the Elder Upagupta enter the palace; embracing him with his entire body, he seated him upon a prepared throne.
247.018. The body of the Elder Upagupta was soft and exceedingly tender, just like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.

247.019. Then the king, having experienced the touch of the Elder Upagupta’s body, spoke with palms joined in reverence: 247.020. “Your limbs are soft, O noble being; they are like cotton, like the finest Kāśi cloth. 247.022. But I am unfortunate, with limbs harsh and rough, my body lacking pleasant touch, and my frame coarse. (32)
The Elder said:
"I have indeed given a gift that was pleasing, most auspicious, and sublime, to one who is without equal.
But I did not give a gift of dust, such as you have offered to the Tathāgata."
The king said: "Elder, in my youth, having previously obtained this unsurpassed field, I sowed seeds of dust therein; such is the fruit that now belongs to me. (34)

248.001. Then the Elder, gladdening the king, said: "Great King, behold the great power of the field, wherein even dust grows; by means of which you have obtained royal glory and unsurpassed sovereignty. (35)
248.004. Having heard this, the king, his eyes wide with wonder, summoned his ministers and said:
248.005. "The sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch has been obtained by me through the mere gift of some dust.
248.006. By whom, sirs, should the Blessed One not be honored with diligent effort? (36)

248.007. Then the king, prostrating at the feet of the Elder Upagupta, said: "Elder, this is my wish: that I should honor those places where the Blessed Buddha dwelt, and that I should establish monuments there for the benefit of future generations."
And he said: "I shall go and pay homage to those places where the Blessed Buddha dwelt, and I shall leave marks there for the sake of compassion for future generations.
The Elder said: "Excellent, excellent, Great King!"
"Excellent is your resolve for awakening!
Now I shall show you those regions where he dwelt; with palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to them."
Having gone there, I shall undoubtedly set my marks upon them. (37)
248.014. Then the king, having arrayed his fourfold army and taken perfumes, garlands, and flowers, set out accompanied by the Elder Upagupta.
248.015. Thereupon, the Elder Upagupta, having led King Aśoka into the Lumbinī grove first of all, extended his right hand and said: "In this place, Great King, the Blessed One was born."
And he said:
"This is indeed the first shrine of the Buddha, the one with the supreme vision.
As soon as he was born here, that Sage took seven steps upon the earth. (38)
Having looked in the four directions, he spoke these words in the past: "This is my final birth; this is my last dwelling in a womb. (39)
248.021. Then the king, prostrating himself there with his entire body at [the Buddha's] feet, rose up and, with palms joined and weeping, said:
248.022. "Blessed are they, and those who have performed meritorious deeds, by whom that great sage was seen!"
And those by whom his delightful words were heard as soon as he was born. //40//
248.024. Then the Elder, in order to increase the king’s faith, said: "Great King, will you see that deity by whom the best of speakers was seen while he was being born in this forest?"
Having heard seven words from the sage as he was reciting them step by step, [he attained peace]. //41//
The king said, "But I shall see it, O Elder.
Then the Elder Upagupta, extending his right hand toward the tree branch upon which Queen Mahāmāyā had leaned while giving birth, said:

248.029. May that celestial maiden who dwells here in this Aśoka tree and has beheld the Perfectly Awakened One reveal her own body in person to King Aśoka, for the sake of increasing his clarity of faith. (42)
249.001. When that deity had stood before the Elder Upagupta in her own form, she spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Elder, what do you command?
Then the Elder said to King Aśoka: "Great King,..."
"This is that deity by whom the Blessed One was seen being born.
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that deity:

249.004. Have you seen him, whose limbs were adorned with the marks [of a great man], as he was being born, with eyes as broad as lotuses? 249.006. And have you heard the first charming words of that bull among men in this forest? (43)
The deity said: "Indeed, I saw that foremost of bipeds, golden-hued, as he was being born;
and I heard the words of that Teacher even as he took seven steps."
The king said, "Tell me, O goddess,
what kind of splendor attended the Blessed One as he was being born? The goddess replied, "It is not possible for me to describe it fully with words."
249.014. But listen briefly:
249.015. Resplendent like refined gold, white as gold, and delightful to the eyes of the three worlds including Indra;
249.017. the earth, bounded by the oceans and together with its mountains, shook like a ship situated upon the great ocean. //45//
249.019. When the king had given a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the birthplace, he established a caitya and departed.
249.020. Then the Elder Upagupta, having informed the king about Kapilavastu, extended his right hand and said: "In this place, Great King, the Bodhisattva was presented to King Śuddhodana.
Having seen him—his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and so beautiful as to be beyond description—the king fell prostrate at the Bodhisattva’s feet with his whole body.
This, Great King, is the temple of the gods named Śākyavardha."

249.023. Here, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, [people] brought him forward, thinking, "He shall worship the gods. 249.024. And all the deities prostrated themselves at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
249.024. Then King Śuddhodana, seeing that he was a god even to the gods, gave the Bodhisattva the name Devātideva, "God beyond Gods."

249.025. In this place, O Great King, the Bodhisattva was presented to the Brahmins, the fortune-tellers, and the learned scholars. 249.026. In this place, he was pointed out by the seer Asita, who declared, "A Buddha will appear in the world.
249.027. In this place, O Great King, he was reared by Mahāprajāpatī.
In this place he was taught the knowledge of scripts;

in this place he became a master of elephant-ridership, horseback riding, charioteering, the wielding of arrows and bows, the grasping of javelins, the handling of hooks, and of all branches of learning befitting his lineage.
This was the Bodhisattva’s training hall.
249.030. In this place, O Great King, the Bodhisattva, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deities and together with sixty thousand women, experienced sensual pleasure.
249.031. In this place, the Bodhisattva, distressed by the sight of an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, retired to the forest.

249.032. In this place, sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree (*jambu*), secluded from evil and unwholesome states, he attained a state accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, consisting of joy and happiness, resembling the untainted (*anāśrava*).

He had entered the first dhyāna. Then, when midday had passed and the time for the meal had elapsed, while the shadows of other trees slanted toward the east, inclined toward the east, and tended toward the east, the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave the body of the Bodhisattva.

And having seen him, King Śuddhodana fell prostrate with his whole body at the feet of the Bodhisattva. By this gate, the Bodhisattva, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deities, departed from Kapilavastu at midnight. At this spot, the Bodhisattva gave the horse and the ornaments to Chandaka and sent him back.
And he said:
"Having returned his ornaments, his horse, and [his retinue] to him, the hero has entered the forest of asceticism alone, without attendants. (46)

In this place, the Bodhisattva, having received saffron robes from the hunter in exchange for his Kāśī garments, went forth into homelessness. In this place, he was invited by Bhārgava to his hermitage.
In this place, the Bodhisattva was invited by King Bimbisāra with the offer of half the kingdom.
In this region, he approached Ārāḍa Udraka. And he said:
"In this penance grove, there are seers named Udraka-Ārāḍakas."
It was heated by that Lord of Men, who had attained the nature of a true teacher. //47//
In this place, the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years.
And it is said:
"Having indeed performed severe penance for six years, the Great Sage—"
Knowing that "this is not the path for direct knowledge," one should abandon it. //48//
In this place, sixteenfold honeyed milk-rice was accepted by the Bodhisattva from the two village daughters, Nandā and Nandabalā. And he said:
"In this place, having eaten the honeyed milk-rice of Nandā..."
The Great Hero, the best among speakers, went to the foot of the Bodhi tree. //49//
In this place, the Bodhisattva was greeted by Kālika, the king of the nāgas, as he was approaching the foot of the tree of awakening. And he said:
"The best among speakers has been greeted by Kālika, the lord of serpents."
Seeking the deathless state, he has set out for the seat of awakening by this path. (50)
Then the king, prostrating at the feet of the Elder with palms joined in reverence, said:
"May we also see the Lord of Nagas by whom the Tathāgata was seen as he traveled along this path with the majestic stride of a rutting lord of nagas?"
250.028. Then the nāga king Kālika, standing near the Elder with palms joined in reverence, said: "Elder, what do you command?

250.029. Then the Elder said to the king: "Great King, this is that very Kālika, the nāga king, by whom the Blessed One was praised as he was departing along this path toward the foot of the Bodhi tree."
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, said to Kālika, the Naga king:
"I have seen the Teacher, whose complexion is like blazing gold, who is peerless to me, and whose face is like the autumn moon.
Tell me a single portion of the virtues of the One Possessing the Ten Powers; tell me, what was it like for you at that time, O Sugata?"
251.005. Kālīka said: "It is not possible for me to explain it in full; however, hear it in brief: 251.006.
Struck by the sole of his foot, the earth together with its mountains then shook in six ways."
In the world of men, it surpasses the radiance of the sun's rays; it is as lovely as the splendor of the moon, the Sugata. //53//
251.010. When the king had established a caitya and departed, the Elder Upagupta led the king to the foot of the Bodhi tree, extended his right hand, and said:
"In this place, Great King, the Bodhisattva, aided by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), having conquered the entire host of Māra, attained unexcelled [enlightenment]."
Perfect enlightenment was fully realized.
And it is said:
"Here, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the bull among sages swiftly shattered and cast away the host of Namuci."
This sublime and supreme awakening, this nectar, has indeed been attained by that peerless person. //54//
251.017. When the king had given a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for the sake of enlightenment, he established a caitya and departed.
Then the Elder Upagupta said to King Aśoka: "In this place, the Blessed One, having received four stone bowls from the four Great Kings, [placed one...]"
In this place, alms were also accepted from the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika.
In this place, while the Blessed One was proceeding toward Vārāṇasī, he was praised by the Ājīvika Upaga.
[The Elder] went as far as King [Bimbisāra] at Ṛṣivadana.

Having approached and extended his right hand, he said: "In this place, O Great King, the Blessed One set in motion the wheel of Dharma that is righteous, characterized by three revolutions and twelve aspects.
And he said:
"The auspicious wheel consisting of Dharma turns back the cycle of saṃsāra."
In this place, the unsurpassed [teaching] was set forth by the Protector. (55)
In this place, a thousand matted-hair ascetics went forth into homelessness.
In this place, the Dharma was taught to King Bimbisāra,
and by King Bimbisāra, the Truths were seen.
And by eighty thousand deities and many thousands of Magadhan brahmins and householders [it was heard]:
"In this place, the Dharma was taught by the Blessed One to Śakra, the lord of the gods;
and by Śakra and eighty thousand deities, the truths were realized."
251.029. In this place, the Great Miracle was displayed.

251.030. In this place, the Blessed One, having taught the Dharma to his mother among the Trāyastriṃśa gods during the rainy season, descended surrounded by a host of deities. [252] In detail, up until the Elder led King Aśoka to Kuśinagarī and [offered] the right...

Extending his palm, he said: "In this place, O Great King, the Blessed One, having completed all the work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣe nirvāṇadhātau). And he further said:"

Having disciplined the world—including its gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, and nāgas—within the discipline of the inexhaustible Dharma, the wise one, that great seer of supreme compassion, whose mind was stilled due to the absence of beings to be trained, has passed into peace. //56//

Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell down. After being revived by the sprinkling of water, the king somehow regained consciousness; he gave a hundred thousand pieces of gold to the assembly, erected a stupa, and prostrating at his feet, said: "Venerable One,"
"This is my heart's desire: that I shall perform the worship of the bodies of those disciples who have been designated by the Blessed One as foremost.
The Elder said, "Excellent, excellent, Great King!"
"Excellent is your resolve!
Having led King Aśoka into the Jeta Grove, the Elder extended his right hand and said, "Great King, this is the stūpa of the Elder Śāriputra;
let worship be offered to it."
The king asked, "What were his qualities?

The Elder replied, "He was indeed a second Teacher, a commander of the army of Dharma, a turner of the wheel of Dharma, and was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.
Apart from the Tathāgata, he surpassed all the wisdom of the entire world."
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of Śāriputra’s wisdom. //57//
And it is said:
"The peerless Wheel of the True Dharma which was set in motion by the Jina—indeed, that was followed by the wise Śāriputra. (58)
252.021. Who else here, O Buddhas, is a man capable of praising that Śāradvata? 252.022. Only one who has realized him as a treasury of a multitude of virtues could speak of him exhaustively. (59)

252.023. Then the king, with a joyful mind, having offered a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the stupa of the Elder Śāradvatīputra, spoke with palms joined in reverence: 252.024. “With devotion I pay homage to Śāradvatīputra, who is liberated from the bonds of existence;
252.025. the hero of supreme wisdom, whose fame illuminates the world. (60)

252.026. Then, while showing the stūpa of the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Elder Upagupta said: "Great King, this is the stūpa of the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Let worship be offered to it. 252.027. The king asked: "What were his virtues?"

The Elder said: "For he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers (ṛddhimat), by whom, with his right big toe, the Vaijayanta palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods, was made to tremble,
and the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, were subdued."
And he said:
"O best of the twice-born, that Kolita, by whom the palace of Śakra was shaken with his big toe, is worthy of being honored with great effort. (61)
Those two formidable serpent-lords have been tamed so that they are no longer difficult to traverse;
who in this world could reach the further shore of that ocean of virtues belonging to him of pure intellect? (62)
253.005. When the king had offered a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the stūpa of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he spoke with palms joined in reverence: 253.006.
“Foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers, you who are liberated from birth, old age, sorrow, and suffering— 253.007.
To the renowned Maudgalyāyana, I pay homage, bowing down with my head. (63)
253.008. When the Elder Upagupta reached the stūpa of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, he said, "Let this [stūpa] be honored. The king asked, "What were his virtues?"

The Elder said: "For that Great-souled One was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who have few desires, who are contented, and who proclaim the virtues of purification (dhuta-guṇa);
he was invited to share half of the Buddha's seat and was clothed in a white robe."
He is the one who takes hold of the wretched and the afflicted, and he is the upholder of the teaching.
And it is said:
"The noble field of merit is the effortless one who takes hold of the wretched and the afflicted."
Wearing the robe of the Omniscient One, he is wise and a sustainer of the Teaching. //64//
253.014. What man is able to describe exhaustively the virtues of that teacher, for whom the wise person offered half of his excellent seat? (65)
Then King Aśoka, having made an offering at the stūpa of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, spoke with palms joined in reverence:

"I pay homage indeed to the Elder Kāśyapa, who dwells in mountain caves and the open air, who has turned his back on enmity, who is endowed with tranquility, and who is increased by the virtue of contentment. (66)

253.019. When the Elder Upagupta, showing the stūpa of the Elder Vatkula, said: "This, Great King, is the stūpa of the Elder Vatkula; let worship be performed," 253.020. the king asked: "What were his virtues?"
The Elder said: "That Great-souled One was designated by the Blessed One as foremost among those with few ailments. Moreover, he never recited even a single two-line verse for anyone."
The king said, "Let a farthing be given here.
When the ministers asked, "Your Majesty,
why is a farthing being given here when all [the coins] are equal?"
The king said: "Listen to my intention in this matter:

'Although the darkness residing in the house of the mind has indeed been destroyed by him with the lamp of his command, that benefit for sentient beings was accomplished by him just as it would have been by others. (67)
253.028. Being thus rejected, she fell at the feet of that very king.

253.028. When the ministers were struck with wonder, they said: "Oh, how great was the fewness of desires of that noble-souled one! Even by her he was not moved. 253.029. "He had no need for her either."

253.029. Then the Elder Upagupta, pointing out the stūpa of the Elder Ānanda, said: "This is the stūpa of the Elder Ānanda. Let its worship be performed. 253.030. The king asked: "What were his virtues?"
The Elder said: "For he was an attendant of the Blessed One, the foremost among those of great learning, and a master of the sacred teachings.
And he said:
254.001. Skilled in protecting the leaves of the Sage, firm in mindfulness, fortitude, and intelligence, he was an ocean of learning.
254.002. Possessing clear and sweet speech, honored by gods and men, he was ever joyful. (68)
Skilled in the mind of the Perfectly Awakened One, discerning in all things, a casket of virtues;
praised by the Jinas, having conquered the battle, honored by gods and men, ever joyful. (69)
254.005. Eventually, the king gave ten million [pieces of gold] to his stūpa.
254.005. Then the ministers said to him, "For what reason, O King, is this person honored more highly than all others?
The king replied, "Listen to my intention:"
That body of the best of speakers, whose nature is dharma—pure and consisting of dharma—was carried by him named Viśoka;
therefore, he is especially worthy of worship. (70)
254.011. Since today the lamp of Dharma blazes among living beings, bringing an end to the darkness of the afflictions; 254.013.
therefore, by virtue of that very power, the son of the Lord of Sugatas is especially worthy of worship. (71)
Just as no one could ever fill the ocean’s waters with a single drop from a cow’s hoofprint, so too,
having observed the nature of this Dharma, the Protector has consecrated this Elder as the upholder of the Sūtras.
254.019. Then the king, having performed worship at the stūpas of the elders and prostrating at the feet of the elder Upagupta, spoke with a joyful mind:
254.021. "Human birth has been made fruitful; the highest essence has been grasped through hundreds of sacrifices, through desired sovereignty over a kingdom, and through fleeting riches.

254.023. This world has been adorned with hundreds of shrines that shine like peaks of white clouds; what difficult task has not been accomplished for us today by this peerless one? (73) Thus he spoke.
254.025. Then the king, having prostrated himself before the Elder Upagupta, departed.
254.026. King Aśoka gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] each at the sites of the birth, the enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the final nirvāṇa.
He developed a particularly profound faith toward the site of the enlightenment, thinking: "It was here that the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
254.027. He [offered] those jewels endowed with exceptional qualities.
He sent them to Bodhi.
Then, King Aśoka had a chief queen named Tiṣyarakṣitā.
The thought occurred to her: "This king is enjoying pleasure with me."
She sent precious gems of exceptional quality toward Bodhi.
Then Mātaṅgī was addressed by her: "Are you able to kill my co-wife, Bodhi?"
She replied, "I shall be able,
but give me some kārṣāpaṇa coins.
Then the Mātaṅgī woman consecrated the Bodhi tree with mantras.
And he read the sūtra.
(254.032) Then, as the bear began to dry up, the king’s men informed the king: "Your Majesty," they said, "the bear is beginning to wither away."
"The Bodhi tree is withering. And he said:
"Seated there, the Tathāgata has awakened to this entire world exactly as it is."
O Lord of Men, having attained omniscience, that Bodhi tree shall come to its end.

255.005. Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground. 255.005. When water was sprinkled on him, he was revived. 255.005. Then, having somehow regained consciousness, the king wept and said:
255.007. Having seen that king of trees day after day, I know that today I have seen the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū) himself. 255.009.
When the Lord of Trees has gone to his destruction, my own life-breaths too shall go to their destruction. (59)
255.011. Then Tiṣyarakṣitā, seeing the king afflicted with grief, said: "Your Majesty, if Awakening (bodhi) does not come to pass, I shall produce delight for Your Majesty."
The king said, "That was not a woman;
rather, it was the Bodhi tree.
It was there that the Blessed One attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Tiṣyarakṣitā said to Mātaṅgī, "Are you able to restore the Bodhi tree to its former state?
Mātaṅgī replied, "If my life remains until then,
I shall restore it to its former state."

255.015. In detail, until the sūtra was finished, he dug around the tree and during the day fed [the boy] with a thousand jars of milk. 255.016. Within a few days, he became as he was before. Then the king’s men reported to the king: "Your Majesty,..."
"By good fortune you prosper; you have become as you were before.
Having heard this, with a joyful mind, he gazed at the Bodhi tree and said:
255.019–255.020. "That which was not performed by the lords of kings, such as Bimbisāra and others who possessed splendor—that supreme double honor, I shall perform. (76)
255.021. And I shall bathe the Bodhi tree with jars filled with fragrant water;
255.022. and I shall perform the five-year festival (pañcavārṣika) in honor of the noble Saṅgha. //77//

Then the king, having filled a thousand jars made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal with scented water, and having brought together an abundance of food and drink, prepared a collection of perfumes, garlands, and flowers; he bathed, put on new, long-fringed garments, observed the fast endowed with the eight limbs, and took up an incense burner.
Having ascended to the roof of the palace, he began to appeal to the four quarters: "May those who are disciples of the Blessed Buddha come to show me favor.
Furthermore:

Those who have rightly gone forth, the disciples of the Sugata, whose faculties are stilled and who have conquered the faults of desire—worthy of honor and worshipped by men and gods, may they come here out of compassion for me. (78)
256.001. <256> Delighting in tranquility and self-restraint, freed from attachments, these excellent sons of the Sugata, the King of Dharma; 256.003.
Honored by asuras, gods, and men, and possessing noble conduct—may they come here out of compassion for me. (79)

Those wise ones who dwell in the most beautiful city of Kaśmīra, as well as those noble ones in this Tamāsāvana, in Mahāvana, on Revataka, and at Raya— may they come to me for the sake of showing me favor.

Those sons of the Conqueror who dwell in Lake Anavatapta, in mountain rivers, and in mountain caves—may they, who are ever devoted to meditation and possess the power of compassion, assemble here today. (81)

256.013. May those sons of the best of speakers, who dwell in the preeminent Śairīṣaka celestial palaces, come here free from sorrow, their hearts imbued with compassion, for the sake of showing me favor. (82)
And those of great majesty who dwell on Mount Gandhamādana—having been invited, may they come here, having generated compassion. (83)
When the king had spoken thus, three hundred thousand monks assembled;
therein were one hundred thousand who were arhats, those still in training (śaikṣas), and virtuous ordinary persons (pṛthagjana-kalyāṇakas).
Not a single seat for the elders was left unoccupied.
The king said: "For what reason is that seat for the elders not occupied?
There is an elder named Yaśas who possesses the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
He replied: "Great King,"
"This seat is for the elder," [he said].
King [Bimbisāra] asked, "Elder, is there anyone else more aged than you?
The elder replied, "There is, Great King."
"O King, this foremost seat belongs to Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who was designated by the Best of Speakers, the Self-controlled One, as the preeminent among those who roar like lions. (84)
256.026. Then the king, his hair standing on end like a kadamba flower, said: "Is there any monk who has seen the Buddha and is still living?
The Elder replied: "There is, Great King; the one named Piṇḍolabharadvāja, who has seen the Buddha, is still living.
The king said: "Elder..."
"Is it possible for us to see him? The Elder replied, "Great King,
you shall see him now."
"This is the time for his arrival.
Then the king, with a joyful mind, said:
"It would be a supreme, incomparable gain for me here; this is great happiness and unsurpassed."
I behold that noble being, who is visibly named after the lineage of Bharadvāja. (85)
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, stood gazing fixedly at the expanse of the sky.
Thereupon, the Elder Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja—surrounded by many thousands of Arhats in the shape of a half-moon—descended from the sky like a royal swan and sat down at the head of the elders.
Upon seeing the Elder Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja, many hundreds of thousands of other monks also came forward and took their places.

King [Bimbisāra] saw Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, with his head white with grey hair, his eyebrows hanging down over his forehead, and the pupils of his eyes deeply set—possessing the physical marks of a Pratyekabuddha.
Upon seeing him, the king fell prostrate with his entire body at the feet of the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja like a tree cut down at its root.
Having wiped the elder’s feet with his face, he rose, placed both knees upon the ground, and gazed at the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja with palms joined in reverence.
When I had slain the hosts of my enemies and obtained the earth, adorned by the oceans and its mountains,
with its single son, Pṛthu— then I felt no such joy as I do now upon beholding you, O Elder.
"It is because of seeing you that this has come to pass. Today the Tathāgata has been seen;
through the attainment of compassion and from the sight of you, a twofold clarity of faith has arisen within me."
"Furthermore, Elder, have you seen my teacher, the Blessed Buddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds?
Then the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, raising his eyebrow with both hands, said to King Aśoka:
"Indeed, I have seen that peerless Great Sage many times, whose splendor is equal to molten gold."
Bearing the thirty-two marks, with a face like the autumn moon, possessing a voice superior to that of Brahmā, he indeed dwells in the state of passionlessness. //87//
The king said: "Elder,
where was the Blessed One seen by you, and how?"
The Elder said: "Great King, when the Blessed One—having conquered the host of Māra—first entered the rains retreat at Rājagṛha together with five hundred Arhats, I was present there at that time.
I beheld that one worthy of offerings with right vision."
And it is said:
When that Tathāgata, the Great Sage free from passion, dwelt in Rājagṛha during the rains retreat, he was surrounded by those who were themselves free from passion. (88)
At that time, I was there in the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One;
just as you see me now before your eyes, so was the Muni seen by me.
Furthermore, Great King, when the Blessed One performed the great miracle at Śrāvastī for the sake of defeating the non-Buddhist teachers— manifesting the Buddha-ornament up to the Akaniṣṭha realm—
I was present right there at that time.
"I have witnessed that display of the Buddha's miraculous power.
And he said:
"When the heretics who had set out upon a wrong path were indeed subdued by the Blessed One through the method of his supernatural power,"
O King, I have witnessed that noble and joy-inducing display of the One Possessing Ten Powers, which brings delight to all living beings.
Furthermore, Great King, when the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and taught the Dharma to his mother, descended at Sāṃkāśya surrounded by a host of gods,
I was right there at that time.
I witnessed that splendor of gods and humans.
And by Utpalavarṇā, the prosperity of a universal monarch was manifested.
And it is said:
"When the best of speakers had descended from the world of the gods after indeed spending the rainy season there..."
I was also present there; I saw that sage, the supreme being.

"Great King, when I was invited by Sumāgadhā, the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍada, and went to Puṇḍravardhana by means of my supernatural power together with five hundred arhats, I then took hold of Mount Parvataśaila and ascended into the expanse of the sky to reach Puṇḍravardhana.
For that reason, the Blessed One issued this command to me: 'You must not enter final nirvāṇa as long as the Dharma has not disappeared.'"
And it is said:

When the Leader, the Teacher, went by the power of his supernormal might at the invitation of Sumāgadhā, he then took up a mountain with his supernormal power and went swiftly indeed to Puṇḍravardhana. (92)
258.020. Then that compassionate one, born of the Śākya clan, gave me this command:
"258.022. You must not attain final nirvāṇa until this Dharma has disappeared. (93)

Furthermore, Great King, when formerly in your childhood you threw a handful of dust into the bowl of the Blessed One— who had entered Rājagṛha for alms with the thought, "I will give him flour"— and Rādhagupta expressed his approval,

you were not pointed out by the Blessed One as: "This boy, one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, will become a king named Aśoka in the city of Pāṭaliputra, a righteous universal monarch (caturbhāga-cakravartin)."
Whoever shall cause my relics to be widely distributed and shall establish eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Dharma King,
I will be right there at that very time.
And he said:
"When a handful of dust was placed by you in the bowl of the Buddha out of childishness and with a pure heart, it was at that very spot that I was then reborn. (94)
The king said, "Elder,
where is he being entertained now?
The elder replied:
259.002. On the northern mountain Gandhamādana, the king of lakes, 259.003. I dwell there, O Lord of Men, together with my fellow celibates. //95//
The king asked, "How large is the Elder's retinue?
The Elder replied,
"O best of men, his retinue consists of sixty thousand Arhats."
259.006. With those who are free from desire and have conquered their defilements, I dwell together. //96//
Moreover, Great King,
what is the use of this doubt?
Let the community of monks be served.
259.007. "After the community of monks has finished eating, I shall offer them my greetings.
259.008. The king said, "So be it; as the Elder commands."
"But having been awakened by the mindfulness of the Buddha, I shall first perform the ritual bathing of the Bodhi tree.

Immediately thereafter, I shall attend upon the community of monks with pleasing food. Then King Sarvamitra addressed the announcer: "I shall give a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to the noble Saṅgha."
"I shall bathe the Bodhi tree with a thousand jars, and let my name be celebrated for five years as the 'Five-Year Festival'.
At that time, Kuṇāla’s two eyes were still unimpaired.
He stood at the king's right side.
He raised two fingers, but did not speak a word.
"I shall double [the reward]," he signaled.
As soon as Kuṇāla raised his hand, the entire multitude of people burst into laughter.
Then the king, having laughed, said: "O Rādhagupta!"
"By whom has this been increased?
Rādhagupta replied: "Your Majesty, there are many living beings who seek merit."
259.016. "He who seeks merit has increased it.
The king said, "I shall give three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to the noble Saṅgha, and I shall bathe the Bodhi tree with a thousand jars."
"Let it be proclaimed in my name that there shall be a five-year festival!
Then Kuṇāla raised four fingers.
Thereupon, the king became enraged.
Rādhagupta said: "Aho! Rādhagupta, who is this ignorant man who opposes us?
And seeing the king enraged, Rādhagupta fell at the king's feet and said: "Your Majesty,"
Who would have the power to rival the lord of men?
Kuṇāla is virtuous;
he vies with his father.
Then the king, turning to the right and looking at Kuṇāla, said: "I am an elder.

Having entrusted the treasury, the kingdom, the harem, the assembly of ministers, and myself to Kuṇāla, I shall bathe the Great Bodhi tree with five thousand jars made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli, filled with various perfumes, milk, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and *vāsitra*."
I give hundreds of thousands of flowers to the noble Saṅgha, headed by the Bodhisattva;
let my name be proclaimed as the "Five-Year Festival.
And he said:

Having established my prosperous kingdom, along with the treasury, the harem, and the entire assembly of ministers, I give myself and Kuṇāla, who is endowed with virtues, to the Saṅgha, which is a vessel of merit. (97)

259.029. Then the king, having presented [the offerings] to the community of monks headed by Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja, and having fastened a curtain around the four sides of the Bodhi tree, himself ascended the curtain and performed the ceremonial bathing of the Bodhi tree with four thousand jars of water. 259.030. As soon as the bathing of the Bodhi tree was completed, the Bodhi tree became restored to its former state.
For it will be said: "As soon as the king had performed the supreme consecration of the Bodhi tree, the Bodhi tree then became tender with green shoots. (98)
260.003. Having seen it, rich with green leaves and tender with sprouts and shoots, 260.004. the king, together with his assembly of ministers and the merchants, attained supreme joy. (99)
260.005. Then, having performed the ceremonial bath for the Bodhisattva, the king began to serve the community of monks.
There was an elder named Yaśas, who said:
"Great King,..."
"This great and most worthy assembly of the Noble Sangha has gathered; you must serve them in such a way that no offense is committed.
Then the king served with his own hand until he reached the youngest member.
260.007. There, two novice monks (śrāmaṇera) lived while undertaking the practice of winning over others through affectionate conduct.
One gave them roasted grain flour (saktu), and the second also gave roasted grain flour.
260.009. One [person] had sweetmeats, and the second also had sweetmeats;
one had cakes.
The second one also played with a ball.
Seeing them, the king laughed:
"These two novices are playing with children's games."
260.010. When the king had finished serving the community of monks and had ascended to the seat of the elders, 260.011.
the Elder questioned him: "Has Your Majesty given rise to any lack of faith toward anyone?
260.011. The king replied: "No."
"However, there are two novices who are playing with children's toys.
The Elder said, "Enough, Great King; for both of them are Arhats liberated in both ways."
260.014. Upon hearing this, the king’s mind was filled with joy, and the thought occurred to him: "When those two novices arrive, I shall clothe the community of monks with cloth.
260.015. Then, understanding the king's intention, the two novices thought, "We must further manifest our own virtues.
Thereupon, one of them prepared cooking pots.
The second one brought forth the pigments.
When the king saw the two novices, he asked,
"What has this been undertaken?"
They said to him, "Your Majesty, having understood our situation, desires to clothe the community of monks with cloth.
We shall dye those cloths.
Upon hearing this, the thought occurred to the king: "It was only by me that this was conceived."
But no word was uttered.
"These two great-souled ones are readers of others' minds.
Then, prostrating with his entire body at their feet and joining his palms in reverence, he said:
260.021. The Mauryan king, together with his ministers, his people, and his citizens, has well obtained gains and wealth and has performed sacrifices most excellently.
260.023. Such is his favor toward virtuous people; likewise, at the proper time, he has been diligent and has bestowed gifts. (100)
260.025. Then the king declared, "Upon your arrival, I shall clothe the community of monks with the three robes.

260.026. Thereupon, King Aśoka, having completed the five-year festival, clothed all the monks in the three robes, gave four hundred thousand [pieces] as a gift for the community's clothing, and [offered] the earth, the inner apartments, the assembly of ministers, and himself.
And he ransomed Kuṇāla;
furthermore, having attained faith in the teaching of the Blessed One, he established eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Dharma King.
On the very same day that King Aśoka established eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stūpas,
on that very day Queen Padmāvatī gave birth to a son for King Aśoka; he was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
And his eyes were exceedingly beautiful. Then it was reported to King Aśoka: "Your Majesty, by good fortune there is an increase [of prosperity]."
"A son has been born to the Lord.
Hearing this, the king was delighted and said:
"I have attained supreme joy; indeed, a vast prosperity has come to the Maurya lineage."
Since I have indeed ruled the kingdom according to the Dharma, may this son be one who causes the Dharma to increase. //101//
He was given the name Dharmavivardhana. When the boy was presented to King Aśoka,
the king, having gazed upon the boy with a joyful mind, said:
261.007. My son’s excellent eyes are most meritorious, resembling well-grown blue lotuses;
his face, adorned and shining, appears like the full moon. (102)
261.011. When the king said to his ministers, "Have you seen such eyes as these belonging to anyone?
the ministers replied, "Your Majesty, we have not seen them in any human being."
Moreover, Your Majesty, there dwells on the Himalaya, the king of mountains, a bird named Kuṇāla;
his eyes are like those of yours.
And he said:

"On a mountain peak belonging to Himendra, the king of mountains, rich in water and abounding in sprouts, flowers, and blossoms—the bird named Kuṇāla dwells there; therefore, these eyes of his are equal to [those of] his father. (103)
Then the king said, "Let the bird Kuṇāla be brought here.
Yakṣas hear him from a league above, and Nāgas from a league below.
Thereupon, the Yakṣas brought the bird Kuṇāla at that very moment.

261.019. Then the king, having gazed at Kuṇāla’s eyes for a very long time, perceived no difference [between them]. 261.020. Thereupon the king said: "The prince's eyes are like those of Kuṇāla. Let the prince's name be Kuṇāla."
For it will be said:
"Because of his affection for [his] mother, that lord of kings then spoke of his son as 'Kuṇāla';
thus the name of that noble being, the prince, became renowned throughout the earth. (104)
261.026. In detail, until the prince had grown up;
then a girl named Kāñcanamālā was brought to be his wife.
261.027. Eventually, King Aśoka went with Kuṇāla to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.

261.027. There, an elder of the Saṅgha named Yaśas was an arhat endowed with the six superknowledges (ṣaḍabhijña). He perceived that Kuṇāla’s eyes would soon be destroyed. He said to the king: "For what reason is Kuṇāla not employed in his own duty?"
Then the king said to him, "Kuṇāla,
whatever the Elder of the Saṅgha commands must be carried out.
Thereupon, Kuṇāla prostrated at the feet of the Elder and said, "Elder,"
"What do you command?

Oppressed by physical and mental sufferings, they perceive the aggregates as executioners,

274.005. Indeed, for one who constantly perceives with the mind objects that are pleasing to the mind. //8//

Where is there need for assistance for the moon as it wanders through the sky, or for the powerful lord of beasts by the strength of its fangs? 297.029.
Where is there need for assistance for fire in a forest conflagration? And what would be the use of the strength of assistance for one such as I? //41//
298.001. <298> "O sir, is the water of the great ocean not to be plunged into? Is one bitten by a snake not to be treated at all?"

298.003. "One should cultivate great vigor as witnessed by those of heroic character; if success is not achieved despite effort being made, what fault is there in this? (42). 298.005. Thereupon, Prince Sudhana set out according to the instructions given by Manoharā. In due course, having overcome mountains, rivers, caves, precipices, and other obstacles through the application of medicinal herbs, mantras, and antidotes, he arrived near the palace of Druma, the king of the kinnaras.

298.007. Not far from the city, the prince saw a magnificent grove adorned with various flowers and fruits, frequented by diverse birds, and surrounded by ponds, long lakes, and pools filled with *kiṃnaras*.
298.008. There he saw *kiṃnarīs* who had approached for the sake of water.
Then Sudhana Kumāra asked them, "What is to be done with this abundant water?"
They said, "There is a daughter of Drum, the king of the kinnaras, named Manoharā.
She has fallen into the hands of a human;
that human odor of hers must be removed."
Prince Sudhana asked, "Are all these jars to be dropped upon her all at once,
or rather in succession?
They replied, "In succession."
He reflected: "This is an excellent stratagem.
I shall place this finger-ring into one of the jars.
Thereupon, he secretly dropped it into the jar belonging to one of the kinnarīs.
And that kinnarī was told: "With this jar, you must bathe Manoharā first of all.
She reflected, "Surely there must be some purpose in this.
Then she poured that jar first upon the head of Manoharā, until the finger-ring fell into her lap.
She was recognized by Manoharā.
Then she asked the kinnarī, "Did any human being come there? She replied, "One did come."
298.017. "Go, and bring him in secretly.
298.018. He was brought in by her and placed in a well-concealed spot.
298.018. Then Manoharā, prostrating at her father’s feet, said: "Father, if that Prince Sudhana, by whom I was abducted, should come here,"
"What would you do to him?
He replied, "I would cut him into hundreds of pieces and throw them into the four oceans.
He is but a human being; what is he to me?"
298.020. Manoharā said: "Father, how could one who has become a human being come here? I speak thus."
298.021. Then the agitation of Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*, subsided.

298.022. With his agitation gone, he said: "If that prince should come here, I will give you to him as a wife, adorned with all ornaments, surrounded by a thousand *kiṃnarī*s, and provided with many various articles."
298.024. Then, Manoharā, thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, presented Prince Sudhana—adorned with divine ornaments—to Druma, the king of the kinnaras.
298.025. Thereupon, Druma, the king of the kinnaras, beheld Prince Sudhana, who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of auspicious complexion.
298.026. Having seen him, he was again struck with supreme wonder.
298.027. Then, desiring to test him, golden pillars were erected,
along with seven palm trees and seven drums.
There were seven boars. And he said:
"By your beauty, these young kiṃnaras have already been surpassed."
Since your power has been demonstrated, you ought to accept this divine alliance.
Having made the reed-thicket exceedingly long and having extracted the reed in an instant,
gather up the scattered seeds without omission and give back a full measure of sesame.
299.001. Display your skill in the science of archery, such as hitting a fixed mark and other feats.
299.002. Then this captivating banner of fame shall be within your grasp.
Sudhana Kumāra was a bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas are skilled in those various fields of arts and fields of work.
Furthermore, the deities will apply themselves with zeal to ensure that there are no obstacles for them.

Then the Bodhisattva was surrounded on all sides by many thousands of *kiṃnaras*, amidst a variety of musical instruments— such as dancing, singing, the *vīṇā*, the *paṇava*, the *sughoṣaka*, the *vallarī*, and the *mṛdaṅga*— which had been brought forth by the gods;
he was also accompanied by *yakṣas* in the form of boars, commanded by Śatakratu.
When the thicket of reeds had been uprooted and leveled, a measure of sesame seeds was sown there.
Having gathered and unified them with the ants created by Śakra,
the prince presented them to the astonished king of the Kinnaras.

Having taken up a sword with the hue of a blue lotus petal, while the *kinnara* king Druma looked on, he went to the vicinity of the golden pillars and, like the cutting of a plantain tree, shattered those pillars into pieces.
Then, having scattered them into bits as small as sesame seeds, he pierced seven palm trees, seven drums, and seven boars with a single arrow and stood unshakable like Mount Sumeru.
Thereupon, the deities stationed in the expanse of the sky and hundreds of thousands of *kinnaras* let out a loud cry of "Hā hā! and a tumultuous sound of joyful shouting.
Upon seeing this, the king of the kinnaras was filled with great wonder.
Then, having placed Manoharā in the midst of a thousand kinnarīs whose forms were equal to hers, he said to Prince Sudhana: "Come, prince;
do you recognize Manoharā?"
Then Prince Sudhana, having recognized her, spoke with a song of verses:
"Since you are Manoharā, the daughter of Druma, right here before me—by this truth, O Manoharā, quickly step forward! (48)
Then she stepped forward with quickened pace.
The *kinnaras* said, "Your Majesty, this Prince Sudhana is endowed with strength, heroism, and prowess; he is a worthy match for Manoharā."
"For what purpose do you deceive us?
Let Manoharā be given to him.
Then Druma, the king of the kinnaras, being praised by the host of kinnaras, [gave] Sudhana to the kinnara maiden Manoharā.
Honoring him with great ceremony, he took the heart-stealing Manoharā— adorned with divine ornaments— in his left hand,
and holding a golden water-pitcher in his right, addressed Prince Sudhana: "Prince, here is Manoharā, the Kinnarī, accompanied by her husband, given to you as a wife."
"Human beings are strangers;
act in such a way that they will not abandon her.

Having assented to the Kinnara king Druma, saying "Very well, father," Prince Sudhana remained in the Kinnara abode and sported with Manoharā to the accompaniment of instrumental music performed by women alone.
He took his pleasure and enjoyed himself.

After some time, remembering his own country and being deeply afflicted by the suffering born of separation from his parents, he informed Manoharā: "The suffering born of separation from my parents oppresses me.
Thereupon, Manoharā related this account in detail to her father.
He said, "Go with the prince;
you must escape.
Men are deceivers."
Then Druma, the king of the kiṃnaras, having given him abundant jewels, pearls, gold, and other riches, sent him away.
Together with Manoharā, he set out through the sky above by way of the path of the kiṃnara birds.
In due course, he arrived at the city of Hastināpura.
300.001. Then the city of Hastināpura was made fragrant in every direction by various delightful and sweet-smelling perfumes.
300.002. Upon hearing this, King Dhana had the drums of joy beaten, and he had that entire city cleared of stones, gravel, and pebbles.

300.003. It was sprinkled with sandalwood water, adorned with bundles of hanging silk ribbons, with banners and flags raised aloft, fitted with censers of fragrant incense, and made beautiful by being strewn with various flowers.
300.004. Then the prince, surrounded by many thousands of excellent men, entered the city of Hastināpura together with Manoharā.
300.005. Having dispelled the fatigue of the journey and taken up various jewels, he approached his father.
300.006. He was embraced around the neck by his father and seated upon the royal throne at his side. Then, the journey to and from the city of the Kinnaras was related in detail.
300.007. Then, King Dhana, recognizing that he possessed exceeding strength, heroism, and prowess, consecrated him with the royal inauguration.
300.008. Prince Sudhana reflected: "That my reunion with Manoharā has come to pass, and that I have attained the royal inauguration, is due to the particularity of causes previously performed."
300.009. "What if I were now to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds?
300.010. Thereupon, in the city of Hastināpura, he performed a twelve-year sacrifice as a renunciant.
"Great King, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the prince Sudhana was someone else.
But you should not view it in this way.
Rather, it was I myself who, at that time and on that occasion, while engaged in the conduct of a bodhisattva, was the king named Sudhana."
300.013. "The strength, vigor, and prowess that I displayed for the sake of Manoharā, and the twelve-year sacrifice I performed without interruption—
even by that, I did not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
However, that generosity and that vigor are merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
And all those people, with uplifted minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
300.017. Thus ends the Sudhanakumāra-avadāna.
Divyāvadāna 31: The Great Avadāna of Toyikā.
301.002. There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Śrāvastī."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī. Eventually, in a certain place along the way, a brahmin who had already finished his meal was plowing with a plow.
For his sake, a girl went carrying a gruel-pot.
And the Blessed One arrived at that place.
That brahmin saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

His body was adorned with the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), radiant and graced by a fathom-wide halo; his splendor exceeded that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing him, faith in the Blessed One arose within him.
301.008. Even *śamatha* practiced for twelve years does not produce such fitness of mind as the attainment of a son by one who has no son,
or the discovery of a treasure by a poor man.

Just as the consecration to kingship is the joy of sovereignty, so too is the first sight of a Buddha for a being who has accumulated roots of merit. Taking that rice-gruel, he approached the Blessed One with great speed.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "O Gautama, here is the rice-gruel.
If you have compassion for me, may the Blessed Gautama drink the rice-gruel."
Then the Blessed One showed the old well to the brahmin, saying, "If you have renounced them, O brahmin, throw them into this old well. He threw them into that old well.
301.013. That dilapidated well began to fill up until it was full of broth, through the power of the Buddhas and the power of the deities.
301.014. Then the Blessed One said to that brahmin, "Distribute the broth, great brahmin."
He began to distribute it.
The Blessed One empowered it in such a way that the entire Saṅgha drank from it; and as that old well was being replenished, it remained filled with the gruel just as before.
301.017. Thereupon, that brahmin, with even greater devotion, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
301.018. Having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One gave him a teaching on the Dharma such that he penetrated the four noble truths.
As before, having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated over beginningless time with the thunderbolt of knowledge, he realized the fruit of stream-entry.
"Venerable sir, I have transgressed; I have indeed transgressed!
I now go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Buddha, and to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of monks."
"And accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) from this day forward for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge with his very life and is full of faith.

Then that brahmin, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken.

Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he departed from the presence of the Blessed One and went to the field. Upon reaching that field, he saw golden barley growing there in abundance.
Having seen this, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke this verse:
301.027. Oh! This field is composed of virtues and is entirely free from all defects.
301.028. Sown this very day, the seed yields fruit this very day. (1)

301.029. Thereupon, that brahmin went very quickly into the presence of the king. Having approached and greeted him with wishes for victory and long life, he said to the king: "Your Majesty, barley has been scattered by me."
They became made of gold. [The king said: "Let the superintendent show his favor. Thereupon, the king dispatched an official as superintendent.
301.031. The brahmin gathered them into a heap and divided them. 301.031. The king’s share turned out to be natural barley.
301.032. The supervisor informed the king.
301.032. The king commanded, "Divide it again!
302.001. They divided it again;
in that very same way, the king's share became natural barley.
302.001. In this manner, it was divided up to seven times. 302.002. It was exactly so. 302.002. The king, filled with curiosity, looked for himself—and it was exactly so.
Then he said to that brahmin: "Brahmin, this has been produced by your own merit.
Enough with the king's share."
"Give me that according to my wish.
Then, whatever was given by that satisfied brahmin turned into gold.
Then the Blessed One set out.
Eventually, in a certain place, he saw five hundred plowmen who were pale and sallow, with cracked hands and feet, and clad in hempen garments, as they were driving their plows.
Those oxen, too, with their bodies wounded and mangled by the bound goads and whips of their drivers, were pulling along while sighing again and again.

Then those farmers saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as described previously, until: for the first time, for a being who had accumulated roots of merit, [they beheld him].
Then they approached the place where the Blessed One was.
The Blessed One saw those farmers from afar.
Having seen them, and out of consideration for those to be trained, he stepped down from the path and sat upon the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then those farmers bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, having understood their intentions, underlying tendencies, dispositions, and natures, delivered a teaching on the Dharma such that it led to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
As before, up until having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time with the vajra of knowledge, they realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, they approached the Blessed One; having bowed to the Blessed One, they said this to him: "Venerable Sir, please teach!"
"May we go forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the status of monks; may we practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One.
They were ordained by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikṣukā*), as described previously, until they stood there fulfilling the aspirations of the Buddha.
The Blessed One gave them instruction. As they applied themselves to practice, they became as worthy of salutation as before.
Those oxen, too, having broken their yokes, thongs, and straps, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, they stood surrounding the Blessed One on all sides.

The Blessed One taught them the Dharma through three points, as previously described, just as at the descent of the Gaṅgā for the geese, fish, and tortoises, until they had seen the truths and returned to their own abodes. The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "What karma was performed by those monks who were formerly farmers, by which..."
"How did they become farmers, and how, having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, did they realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions?
What karma was performed by those sons of gods who were formerly oxen?"
"How is it that they were reborn as oxen and yet attained the vision of the Truth?
The Blessed One said: "Monks, these very deeds were performed and accumulated by them; having reached their necessary conditions, as previously described, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings."
302.026. Monks, in the past, during this very Fortunate Eon (*bhadrakalpa*), when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world.
302.027. As before.
302.027. He dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana (the Abode of Sages).
Under his teaching, these five hundred farmers went forth as monastics.
There, they neither studied nor recited, nor did they apply their minds to meditation;
rather, having repeatedly consumed what was given out of faith, they were devoted to socializing and succumbed to laziness.
303.001. "What do you think, monks? Those five hundred monks were none other than these five hundred farmers.
He who was the owner of the monastery—"
This is that very householder to whom these field-laborers belong.
Since they have consumed the offerings given out of faith belonging to the master of the monastery, yet neither recited nor studied, nor even applied their minds to meditation,
but instead— delighting in socializing— were overcome by laziness;
By that karma, for five hundred births he became the farmers of that very monastery owner;
even now, he has been born as their farmer once more.
As for the fact that these men went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and practiced the holy life, [it was because of that merit].
Therefore, having now gone forth in my teaching, he has realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Those sons of the gods who were formerly oxen had previously gone forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa;
there, they violated the minor and lesser rules of training.
By that karma, they were reborn among oxen;
because they had developed a serene and confident mind toward me,
they were reborn among the gods.

"Because they practiced the holy life under Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, they have now, having become sons of gods, realized the vision of the Truths. Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black."
As before, up to the point where application of effort must be made.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.

There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda, let us go to Toyikā. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One arrived at Toyikā.
And in that place, a brahmin was plowing with a plow.
Then he saw the Blessed Buddha, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as described previously, up until the words "auspicious in every way.
Having seen him, he reflected: "If I approach the Blessed Gautama and pay him homage..."
"If I go,
my merit will decline; but if I do not go to greet him, my spiritual practice will decline."
303.018. "What means might there be by which there would be for me neither a falling away from my duty nor a falling away from merit?
The thought occurred to him: "I shall perform my salutation while remaining right here.
In this way, there will be neither a falling away from my duty nor a falling away from merit."
303.020. Standing there with the goad-stick exactly as he had grasped it, he offered this salutation: "I pay homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One. 303.021.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this is the opportune moment for this brahmin.
If such a right knowledge and vision were to arise within him regarding his own self," 303.022. [he would attain liberation.]
"In this place, the undisturbed collection of bone-relics of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa remains. Then, having approached it, he would pay homage;
in this way, he would have paid homage to two perfectly enlightened ones.
303.024. For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, in this very spot remains the undisturbed collection of the bone-relics of Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one.
303.025. Then the venerable Ānanda quickly spread out his upper robe folded fourfold and said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One sit upon the seat that has been prepared."
303.027. Thus, this spot of earth will have been used by two perfectly enlightened Buddhas: both by the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa and by the Blessed One here and now.
