303.028. The Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, do you wish to see the unbroken mass of the relics of Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
"Now is the time for this, Blessed One."
"O Sugata, now is the time for this:
may the Blessed One show the monks the undisturbed collection of the bodily remains of the Perfectly Enlightened Kāśyapa; having seen them, the monks will develop serene faith in their hearts."
303.032. The Blessed One generated a worldly thought.

It is indeed the nature of things that at whatever time the Buddha-Blessed Ones generate a worldly thought, at that very time even living beings such as ants and termites understand the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
304.002. The nāgas reflected: "For what reason has the Blessed One generated a worldly thought?
The Blessed One desires to see the unbroken mass of the bodily remains of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa.
304.003. Thereupon, they raised up the unbroken mass of the bodily remains of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, take note of this sign;
it is about to vanish.
And so it vanished.
304.006. King Prasenajit heard that the Blessed One had raised up the undisturbed body-relics of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kāśyapa, for the disciples to behold.
304.007. Having heard this, filled with curiosity, he set out together with the women of the inner court, the princes, the ministers, the army officers, and the merchants and countryfolk to see it.
304.008. Likewise did Virūḍhaka and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The seer Ṛṣidatta, the ancient chief architect,
Viśākhā the mother of Mṛgāra,
and many hundreds of thousands of living beings, filled with curiosity, set out to see [the display], being impelled by their previous roots of merit.
304.010. When he had disappeared, they heard that the collection of the bodily relics of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had vanished. 304.011–012.
Upon hearing this, sorrow and dejection arose within them, and they thought, "Our journey has become in vain."
Then a certain lay follower circumambulated that place and formed this thought in his mind: "How much merit will arise for me from this act of walking about?
Then the Blessed One, having understood the thought in that lay follower's mind, and in order to generate a state of freedom from regret in that great multitude of people, spoke this verse:

Even a hundred thousand gold *niṣkas* of Jāmbūnada gold would not equal the merit of that wise person who, with a mind full of faith, takes a single step toward the reliquaries (*caityas*) of the Buddha. (2)
A certain lay follower also offered a lump of clay in that place, forming this thought: "The Blessed One has declared that such is the merit for merely taking a step;
how much merit, then, will there be from this lump of clay?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing his mind as well, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand lumps of gold made of Jāmbūnada [gold] would not equal it, for one who, with a devout mind, places even a single lump of clay upon the stūpas of the Buddha. (3)

304.028. Having heard that, many hundreds of thousands of living beings performed the rite of depositing lumps of clay. Others scattered loose flowers there and formed this mental resolve: "The Blessed One has declared that such is the merit of even a single step taken or a single lump of clay deposited."
"But as for us, who have offered these loose flowers, how much merit will there be?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts as well, spoke this verse:
"Even a hundred thousand measures of gold from the Jāmbūnada river would not be equal to this."

305.003. "Whoever, with a devout mind, should place a heap of loose flowers upon the shrines of the Buddha... (4) // 305.005. Others there constructed flower garlands and formed this mental resolve: "The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of loose flowers."
305.006. "How much merit will there be for our Mālāvihāra?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts as well, spoke this verse:
305.008. "Hundreds of thousands of loads of Jāmbūnada gold would not equal it."
305.010. "The wise person who, with a mind full of faith, constructs a flower-garland pavilion at the shrines of the Buddha.
(5) 305.012. Others there offered rows of lamps and formed this mental resolve: "The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of constructing a flower-garland pavilion."
305.013. "How much merit will there be from our gift of lamps?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
305.015. "Even hundreds of thousands of millions of gold pieces made of Jāmbūnada gold would not equal it."
305.017. “The wise person who, with a mind full of faith, offers a lamp at the shrines of the Buddha [attains great merit].
(6) 305.019. Others there offered a consecration of perfumes and formed this thought: “The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of offering a lamp.”
"305.020. How much merit will there be from our perfumed consecration?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse: "305.022.
Even hundreds of thousands of gold coins from the Jambū river would not equal it."
305.024. "The wise person who, with a devout mind, performs the sprinkling of perfumes at the shrines of the Buddha [attains great merit].
(7) 305.026. Others there raised banners and flags and formed a resolute intention regarding the act of walking [around the shrine] and the offering of lumps of clay.
"The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of offering loose flowers, of walking with flower garlands, of giving lamps, and of perfumed ablutions;
but how much merit will there be for us from raising parasols, banners, and flags?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts, spoke this verse:

306.001. Even hundreds of thousands of golden mountains equal to Mount Meru do not equal [the merit of] one who, with a devout mind, offers umbrellas, banners, and flags at the shrines of the Buddha. (8)
"For this is said to be the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) for these Tathāgatas who are immeasurable, for the Perfectly Awakened One who is like the ocean, the unsurpassed Caravan Leader.

(9) Then, this thought occurred to them: "Regarding the Blessed One who has now entered parinirvāṇa, there is the merit spoken of by the Blessed One concerning the performance of worship and so forth."
"How much merit will there be for those who remain?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"One should worship him while he remains, and also when he has entered final nirvāṇa."
306.010. There is no distinction in merit equal to the clarity of the mind; 306.011. for thus are the Buddhas inconceivable, and the qualities of a Buddha are also inconceivable. (10)
"11. It is not possible to reach the limit of the qualities of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, who are inconceivable, who inspire faith, and who set in motion the unimpeded wheel of Dharma.
Then, the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma to that great multitude of people.
By many hundreds of thousands of living beings, a great distinction was attained:
some resolved their minds upon the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvaka-bodhi), and some upon the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (pratyeka-bodhi).
Some have attained the stages of heat;
some, the summits;
and some, the patiences that accord with the truths.
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning,
and some the fruit of non-returning.
Some realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
For the most part, that assembly became established as inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
Together with the brahmins and householders there, a great festival was established in that place; it became known by the name "Toyikā Festival," or simply "Toyikā."
306.021. Thus ends the thirty-first great narrative, the Toyikā-avadāna.
********** Avadāna 32 ********** 307.001. Divyāvadāna 32: The Legend of Rūpāvatī. 307.002. Thus have I heard:
307.002. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.

307.003. The Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by kings and royal ministers; by various merchants, śramaṇas, brahmins, wandering mendicants, and people from towns and countryside; and by nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
307.005. The Blessed One was a recipient of abundant and exquisite robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, both divine and human;
yet the Blessed One remained unsullied by them, like a lotus by water.
307.007. At that time, moreover, there arose this fitting, sublime, and auspicious report concerning the Blessed One’s fame.

The verse was recited: "Thus indeed is that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Having personally realized, directly witnessed, and fully attained this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, he dwells therein."
307.011. He taught the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end.
307.012. He fully proclaimed the holy life (*brahmacarya*) which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine.

307.013. Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, it would be well if beings were to understand in this way: [the nature of] giving, the fruit of giving, and the maturation of the distribution of gifts."

Even now, they would not consume even that final morsel, that last mouthful, without sharing it with others, nor would the thought of stinginess arise and persist in them, taking possession of their minds.

307.016. Therefore, monks, because beings do not know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts, for that reason, beings— even regarding that which is the final morsel, the very last mouthful— [do not give it away].
Without giving that very thing away or sharing it with others, they consume it themselves;
and the stain of stinginess, having arisen, persists by completely overwhelming their minds.

307.020. The monks, having conceived every kind of doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that even now there are beggars for the Blessed One.
307.021. "Monks, it is not only now that beggars are dear to me; even in the past, they were likewise dear."
307.022. Listen to that.
307.023. Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the northern regions, there was a royal capital named Utpalāvatī, which was prosperous, flourishing, secure, and crowded with many people.

307.024. Then, at a later time, a famine occurred in the royal capital of Utpalāvatī; it was difficult to live in, alms were hard to obtain, and it was not easy to maintain one's life by gathering or collecting food.

At that time, in the royal capital of Utpalāvatī, there was a woman named Rūpāvatī who was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with a most excellent complexion. Then, the woman Rūpāvatī, having departed from her own residence, began walking about the royal capital of Utpalāvatī and entered a certain chamber.
At that very time, in that inner chamber, a woman gave birth;
she had brought forth a boy who was handsome, pleasing, and endowed with a magnificent, beautiful complexion.
Overcome by hunger and with a mind intent on devouring him, that woman took hold of the boy.
And she wished to beg for her own son’s flesh.
Seeing her, the woman Rūpāvatī said this: "Sister, what is it that you wish to do?
She replied: "I am hungry, sister."
307.032. "I wish to eat my own son's flesh.
308.001. Rūpāvatī said, "Sister, is there anything in the house—be it food, drink, a meal, or something savory?
The word 'son' is rare for people in this world."
"Sister, there is nothing at all in my house—neither food, nor drink, nor solid food, nor soft food, nor anything to be tasted, nor anything to be licked.
"Life in this world is difficult to obtain," said Rūpāvatī. "In that case, sister, wait for a moment."
"As soon as I have gone home, I will bring food for your sake.
She said, "Sister, you should know that my belly seems to burst and the earth itself seems to split apart."
"My heart is smoking; the directions are no longer clear to me.
You shall not have emerged from the gatehouse until my vital breaths have departed."
308.007. It occurred to Rūpāvatī: "If I take the boy and go, this woman, overcome by hunger and emaciation, will die.
But if I leave the boy behind and go..."
"He will certainly devour the boy.
"But how can both of us obtain life while I am acting thus?

This thought occurred to her: "In this cycle of existence, which is characterized by an innocent disposition, many sufferings have been experienced by me—repeatedly in the hells, repeatedly among animals, and repeatedly [among other beings]."

In the world of Yama and repeatedly in the worlds of humans, I have experienced the cutting off of hands, the cutting off of feet, the cutting off of ears, the cutting off of ears and noses, the cutting off of limbs and minor members, as well as many other various sufferings. What purpose has been achieved by me through that, when I could have generated my own stability, strength, and vigor, and satisfied this woman with my own blood and flesh?
"I shall deliver this boy.
Rūpāvatī asked, "Sister, is there a weapon in your house?
The woman replied, "There is."
"In that case, show me where it is.
She showed him that place.
Then Rūpāvatī herself took a sharp weapon and, having cut off those two breasts, she satisfied that woman with her own flesh and blood.
Having satisfied the woman, she said this to her: "Sister, you should know that this boy has been purchased by me with my own flesh and blood.
I am giving him to you as a deposit; do not eat the boy anymore."
"As soon as I have gone home, I will bring food for your sake.
She replied, "For now, let it be more than that.
Then the woman Rūpāvatī, covered in blood, went toward her own residence.
308.021. The husband of the woman Rūpāvatī saw Rūpāvatī from afar, being dragged along and torn apart by blood, as she was departing.
308.022. Having seen her, he spoke thus to Rūpāvatī: "Rūpāvatī, who has inflicted such a cruel treatment upon you?"
He related the matter of Sautā’s nature in detail.
Having related it, he said this: "Noble son, prepare a meal for that woman.
He replied: "Noble daughter, prepare a meal for her."
"Moreover, I shall first utter a word of truth:
Noble daughter, by this truth, by this word of truth— that such a marvelous and extraordinary phenomenon as this has never before been seen or heard—
by that truth, by that word of truth, may both your breasts appear just as they were before."
308.026. By means of this truthful declaration thus made together, at that very moment both her breasts reappeared just as they were before.

Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "What extraordinary generosity and what extraordinary reverence for generosity has been shown by the woman Rūpāvatī! Lest that woman Rūpāvatī cause me to fall from this abode of Śakra; therefore, let me investigate her."

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having transformed himself into the form of a noble brahmin and taking up a golden staff and water-pot, while being fanned with a jeweled yak-tail whisk by a golden handle— just as a strong man might extend his contracted arm or contract his extended arm— [disappeared from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, Śakra, the lord of the gods, vanished from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and appeared in the royal capital of Utpalāvatī.

Then, as Śakra, the lord of the gods, was wandering for alms in the royal capital of Utpalāvatī, he approached the residence of the woman Rūpāvatī and stood at her door. Thereupon, the woman Rūpāvatī, taking some alms-food, went toward Śakra, who was wearing the guise of a brahmin.
Having approached him, she offered him alms.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the woman Rūpāvatī: "Is it true, O Rūpāvatī, that you have sacrificed both breasts for the sake of the boy?
She replied, "Noble Brahmin, it is true."
309.005. He said to her, "Rūpāvatī, when you were giving up both breasts, did you feel any regret in your mind as you were giving them up, or after you had given them up?
She replied, "No, as I was giving up both breasts, there was no regret in my mind.
Śakra said, "Who would believe this?"
Rūpāvatī said: "In that case, O Brahmin, I shall utter a word of truth.
By that truth, O Brahmin, by that word of truth, may there be no alteration of mind and no regret in my mind as I cast off both breasts, or having already cast them off."
Moreover, O Brahmin, by that truth that I have renounced both breasts for the sake of this child—

not for the sake of a kingdom, nor for the sake of enjoyments, nor for the sake of Śakra, nor for the sake of the sensory realms of universal monarchs (cakravartin), but solely so that, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, I might tame those who are untamed and liberate those who are unliberated— by that truth...
"May I encourage those who have not yet found encouragement, and may I lead to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it;
by that truth, by that word of truth, may my female organ disappear and a male organ appear."
At that very moment, her female organ disappeared and a male organ appeared.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, being satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer, rose into the air by means of his supernatural power from that very spot and uttered this exclamation regarding Rūpāvatī:
The male organ appeared,
and for the woman Rūpāvatī, the name "Prince Rūpāvata" was established.

Then, at another time, King Upālāvatī passed away in the capital city of Upālāvatī without a son. Thereupon, it occurred to the high ministers of the Piṇḍata clan: "What if we were to install Rūpāvata as king in the capital city of Upālāvatī?
Then it occurred to them: "There is no one other than Prince Rūpāvata, who has performed merit and practiced virtue."
309.020. They installed Prince Rūpāvanta as king in the royal capital of Utpalāvatī.
309.021. Then he ruled the kingdom for sixty years.
Having ruled the kingdom righteously, he passed away.
309.022. Upon the dissolution of his body, he was reborn in that very capital city of Utpalāvatī, in the womb of the principal queen of a certain wealthy merchant-householder.
309.023. When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with an abundance of radiant complexion.
309.024. As soon as he was born, such a light was emitted from his body.
By that radiance, the splendor of the moon was rendered lusterless.
Then, a certain woman approached the merchant householder.

Having approached him, she said this to the merchant householder: "Householder, you should know that a son has been born to you—one who is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with a magnificent and auspicious complexion."
309.027. As soon as he was born, such a radiance was emitted from his body that it eclipsed the radiance of the moon.
309.028. Then that merchant-householder, satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness, [regarding] her...

When the night had passed, those who were experts in the characteristics of Brahmins—namely, the Naibhittikas and Vaipañcikās, who were skilled in the mantras of the earth and the intermediate space, and who knew the movements of the constellations, Venus, and the planets—having assembled them, he showed the boy to them, saying: "O Brahmins, you should know that this boy has been born to the chief queen; he is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and possesses a magnificent excellence of complexion."
309.032. As soon as he was born, such a radiance was emitted from his body that the light of the moon was rendered lusterless.
309.033. Therefore, having examined the marks of this boy, the brahmins established his name.

310.001. Then those brahmins—interpreters of marks and omens, expounders of the Vedas, experts in the mantras of the earth and the atmosphere, and skilled in the constellations, Venus, the planets, and eclipses—approached the boy.
310.002. Having observed him, they said: "Householder, this boy who has been born is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with a magnificent excellence of complexion.
310.003. As soon as he was born, such a radiance was emitted from his body that it rendered the light of the moon lusterless."
310.004. "Therefore, let his name be Candraprabha.
310.005. Then the merchant householder, having fed those brahmins and dismissed them, provided four nurses for the boy Candraprabha: a lap-nurse, a bath-nurse, a breast-nurse, and a playmate nurse.

310.006. She who carries the child on her hip is called the lap-nurse (*aṅkadhātrī*), for she draws the child about on her hip and positions his limbs. 310.007. She who bathes the child is called the dirt-nurse (*maladhātrī*).
She removes dirt from the robes.
She who suckles the child with breast milk is called the wet-nurse (*stanyadhātrī*).
She who provides playthings for children—those things which serve as toys for children who are clever and young—is called the plaything-provider nurse (*krīḍāpanikā dhātrī*).

For example— those without bodies, those with bodies, those who leap about, those who carry baskets, those who carry bamboo flutes, those who run along, those in the form of elephants, those in the form of horses, those in the form of oxen, and those holding bows, arrows, water-vessels, brooms, brushes, medicine-cases, and bags—
are dragged along in front [of the chariot].
310.012. He was raised and nurtured with great splendor and good fortune.

When the boy Candraprabha reached the age of eight years, his parents, having bathed him well, anointed him, and adorned him with all kinds of ornaments, sent him to learn writing, surrounded by many other boys.
At that time, about five hundred boys were learning writing in that schoolroom.
Then the boy Candraprabha said this to those boys: "Boys, let us all generate the mind set upon awakening for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
They asked: "Candraprabha, what is to be done by a bodhisattva?"

He said: "The six perfections (pāramitās) are to be fulfilled. Which six? Namely: the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom."
310.018. "Therefore, I shall give this gift;
what if I were to give gifts even to those who have gone into the animal realm?
310.19. Taking up a sharp weapon and honey and ghee, he went toward a certain great cemetery.
310.020. Having wounded his own body with a weapon and smeared it with honey and ghee, he cast himself into that great cemetery to die.
310.021. At that time, a bird named Uccangama lived in that great cemetery.
310.022. Perching upon the body of the boy Candraprabha, it seized his right eye and plucked it out.
Again he released him.
A second and even a third time, the bird Uccaiḥśravas seized the right eye of the boy Candraprabha, plucked it out, and then released it again.
Then the boy Candraprabha said this to the bird Uccaiḥśravas: "What is this, bird? Having seized my eye and plucked it out again and again, why do you release it?"
He said: "O Candraprabha, I do not desire even the slightest thing from you, such as a human eye.
Do you think, O Candraprabha, that you will ward me off?"
Candraprabha said: "Even if that bird were to seize my eye and pluck it out a thousand times, and then release it again, I would certainly not prevent him."
Having said this, that many birds gathered together;
by them, Candraprabha was stripped of his flesh and reduced to a mere skeleton,
and he passed away.
In that very capital city of Utpalāvatī, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of a certain eminent and wealthy Brahmin.
After the completion of nine full months, she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with a magnificent and radiant complexion.
310.032. His parents gave him the name Brāhmaprabha.
310.033. When the young brahmin named Brāhmaprabha reached the age of eight years, he had mastered all the brahminical mantras.
311.001. When the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha reached the age of twelve years, he himself taught the mantras to about five other young Brahmins.
311.002. When the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha had reached the age of sixteen years,
Then his parents said to him, "Brahmaprabha,
we shall build a residence for you.
He replied, "Mother, Father,"
"I have no need for a dwelling at this time.
They both asked, "But what will you do, O Brahmaprabha?
He replied, "I desire to perform austerities for the sake of sentient beings and to practice what is difficult to do."
The two of them said, "O Brahmaprabha, do whatever you now deem to be the right time.

Then the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha, having bowed his head at the feet of his parents and circumambulated them three times, departed from the capital city of Utpalāvatī and went toward a certain forest grove.
At that time, two brahmin seers were living in that forest grove.
311.008. The two brahmin seers saw the young man Brahmaprabha approaching from afar.
311.009. Having seen him, they said this to the young man Brahmaprabha: "Come, Brahmaprabha; welcome."
"Do not be weary; do not be exhausted.
For what purpose have you come to this forest grove?
He replied, "I desire to perform austerities for the sake of all sentient beings and to practice what is difficult to do."
The two of them said, "So be it; let it be so;
may our intentions be fulfilled."
May all your heart's desires be fulfilled.
311.012. Then the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha, having had a hut built in a certain place and established a walking path, practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings.
311.013. Then, at another time, a tigress pregnant with young took up residence not far from the hut of Brahmaprabha;
the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha saw her.
Having seen her, he went back to where those two brahman-sages were.
Having approached them, he said this to the two brahman-sages: "O sages, you should know that not far from my hut here, a pregnant tigress has taken up residence.
Who is able to give her food?"
The two of them said, "We shall give her food.
Then, at another time, the tigress gave birth; overcome by hunger and emaciation, she desired to eat her own two cubs. She seized one cub and released the second.
He did not eat it.
Then the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha saw her;
having seen her, he approached where those two brahmin seers were.

311.019. Having approached, he went again to where those two brahman-sages were. 311.020. Having approached, he said this to the two brahman-sages: "O brahmans, you should know this: that tigress has given birth; overcome by hunger and emaciated, she desires to devour her own cubs. She takes hold of one cub and lets go of the second, yet she does not devour it. 311.021. [She takes] one cub and releases the second, but she does not eat him.]
"Who would venture to give her food?
The two replied, "We two shall give her food.
Then those two brahmin seers approached the place where that tigress was.
311.023. The tigress saw the two brahmin seers approaching from afar.
311.024. Having seen them, she was overcome by hunger and wished to spring upon them.
Then this thought occurred to her: "Who would venture to sacrifice their life for the sake of one belonging to the animal realm?"
Then, by means of their supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the two of them rose up into the air from that very spot.
The young Brahmin Brahmaprabha saw them;
having seen them, he spoke thus to those two brahmin seers (*brahmarṣi*): "Are these not brahmins?"
"You two have said this: 'We shall give her food.
Is this indeed true, O brahmins, for you who belong to the brahmin caste?
They both replied: "Who would venture to sacrifice their own life for the sake of one belonging to the animal realm?"
The young Brahmin Brahmaprabha said, "I am willing to sacrifice my life for the sake of one who has fallen into the womb of an animal.
Then the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha approached where the tigress was and threw himself down before her.
The young Brahmin Brahmaprabha had become one who dwelt in loving-kindness (*maitrīvihārī*).
She was unable to devour him.
Then, this thought occurred to the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha: "This tigress does not devour my body because it is devoid of consciousness."
311.032. He looked here and there;

then, taking a sharp bamboo splinter and a sharp [blade], he made this kind of declaration of truth: "May those noble gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas who dwell in this forest grove attend to me!"
May they all likewise attend to me:
"I shall now perform a renunciation— a renunciation beyond renunciation, a renunciation that transcends renunciation— the voluntary relinquishing of my own throat."
"Moreover, by that truth, by that word of truth, which I renounce—

not for the sake of a kingdom, not for the sake of enjoyments, not for the sake of Śakra, nor for the sake of the domain of a universal monarch (cakravartin), but solely so that, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, I may tame those who are untamed— "
May I ferry across those who have not crossed over; may I liberate those who are not liberated;
may I bring comfort to those who are not comforted.
"May I bring those who have not attained final nirvāṇa to final nirvāṇa;
by this truth, by this word of truth, may my sacrifice not be in vain. Having thus resolved, he cut his own throat and placed it before the tigress.
For a moment, her chest, being torn away by the playful movements of the rows of the tigress's claws, appeared as if she were looking on.
With her body covered in horripilation, she was as white as the moon, appearing as if filled with sprouts of radiant rays. //1//
As he watched, the tigress, intoxicated by her consumption of flesh and blood, devoured the thousand [deer];
meanwhile, his own life-force, distressed by the long duration of his absence, found a momentary sustenance by clinging to his neck.
Monks, as soon as the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha had relinquished his own throat,
this trichiliocosm shook, trembled,
and quaked; it moved and was set in motion.
It quivers, it trembles, it shakes violently; the eastern quarter rises while the western sinks,
and the western quarter rises while the eastern sinks.
The southern direction rises and the northern direction sinks; the northern direction rises and the southern direction sinks;
the center rises.
One end sinks down, the other end rises up; the middle sinks down.
The sun and moon do not shine, do not gleam, and do not radiate splendor.
312.021. "It might occur to you, monks, that at that time the capital city named Utpalāvatī in the northern regions was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, it was Puṣkalāvatī that was the capital city named Utpalāvatī."
"Monks, you might have some doubt or uncertainty, thinking that at that time, on that occasion, the woman named Rūpāvatī in the capital city of Utpalāvatī was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I myself was the woman named Rūpāvatī."
"Monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty that at that time, on that occasion, it was some other woman who gave birth in the inner chamber.
It should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, it was the young girl Candraprabhā who gave birth in the inner chamber."
312.027. O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty [thinking] that the boy at that time, on that occasion, was someone else.
312.028. It should not be viewed in this way.
Prince Rāhula was the boy at that time, on that occasion.
312.029. "O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty, thinking that the boy named Candraprabha at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
At that time and on that occasion, I myself was the boy named Candraprabha."
312.031. Monks, you might have some doubt or uncertainty that at that time, on that occasion, those five hundred boys were someone else.
312.032. It should not be viewed in this way.
312.033. These very five hundred Bhadrikas were, at that time, on that occasion, those five hundred boys.
313.001. "O monks, you might have some doubt or uncertainty, thinking that at that time, on that occasion, the bird named Uccaṅgama in that great cemetery was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way.
The monk Kauṇḍinya was, at that time and on that occasion, the bird named Uccaṅgama."
313.003. "O monks, you might have some doubt or uncertainty, thinking that the young brahmin named Brahmaprabha at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
313.004. It should not be viewed in this way.
313.005. I myself was that young brahmin named Brahmaprabha at that time and on that occasion."
313.005. "O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty, thinking that at that time, on that occasion, those who were the parents of the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha were someone else.
313.007. It should not be viewed in this way.
King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyādevī were, at that time, on that occasion, the parents of the young Brahmin Brahmaprabha."
313.008. "O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty [thinking]: 'Was that forest at that time and on that occasion someone else?
313.009. ... O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty [thinking]: 'Were those two at that time and on that occasion two different brahmin seers? 313.010. It should not be viewed in this way."
313.010. At that time, at that period, the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the Buddha Suprabha were two brahmin seers in that forest grove.
313.011. O monks, you may have some doubt or uncertainty [thinking] that she who was the tigress at that time, at that period, was someone else.
313.012. It should not be viewed in this way.
313.012. The monk Kauṇḍinya was those two tiger cubs at that time, on that occasion.
313.015. It should not be viewed in this way;
rather, the monks Nanda and Rāhula were the two tiger cubs at that time, on that occasion.
"Monks, at that time Maitreya Bodhisattva, who had been set forth for forty kalpas, was turned back by my single gift of my own throat.
Monks, it should be understood by this method:
if all sentient beings knew the fruit of giving and the ripening of the distribution of gifts as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the distribution of gifts,"

Even that final morsel, the very last mouthful, they would not consume themselves without first giving it away and sharing it with others; nor would a mind of stinginess arise and persist in them, taking possession of their hearts.

313.020. Therefore, monks, because beings do not know the fruit of giving nor the ripening of the distribution of gifts, they consume even that which is their very last morsel, their final mouthful, by themselves, without having given it away or shared it with others.
And once it has arisen, this stain of stinginess remains, having completely taken possession of their minds.
Furthermore, he does not see what is unwholesome, nor the auspicious or inauspicious, nor that which has been practiced;
he does not see it among wise people, nor does it perish within the assembly of the noble ones. //3//
313.025. What has been done, whether good or evil, never perishes among those who are mindful of what has been done.
313.026–27. A well-performed deed is beautiful, and a badly performed one is ugly;
there is indeed the ripening of both, for their fruit will inevitably be given. //4//
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen were uplifted in mind; and the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and the entire assembly rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
313.030. The Thirty-second Avadāna: The Story of Rūpāvatī.
********** Avadāna 33 ********** 314.001. Divyāvadāna 33: The Story of Śārdūlakarṇa/ 314.002.
Thus have I heard.
314.002. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
314.003. Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered the great city of Śrāvastī for alms.
314.004. Then the venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Śrāvastī and finished his meal, approached a certain well.
At that time, a Mātaṅga girl named Prakṛti was drawing water from that well.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti: "Sister, give me some water; I shall drink.
When this was said, the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, I am a Mātaṅga girl."
"Sister, I do not ask about your family or your birth;
rather, if this water has been relinquished by you, give it, for I shall drink."
314.009. Then Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, gave water to the Venerable Ānanda.
314.010. Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, having drunk the water, departed.

Then the maiden Prakṛti, having carefully and thoroughly observed the signs on the body, face, and voice of the venerable Ānanda, was overcome by wise reflection and conceived a mind of passion, thinking: "May the noble Ānanda be my husband."
"And my mother is a great vidyādhara;
she will be able to bring the noble Ānanda.
Then Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, taking a water jar, approached the house of the Caṇḍāla.
Having set down his water-jar in a secluded spot, he said this to his mother: "O Mother, you should know this: there is a śramaṇa named Ānanda, an attendant and disciple of the Great Śramaṇa Gautama;
I desire him as my master."
"Mother, will you be able to bring him back?
She said to her, "Daughter, I am able to bring back Ānanda, with the exception of one who is dead or one who is free from passion (vītarāga).
Furthermore:
King Prasenajit of Kośala serves, honors, and attends upon the ascetic Gautama excessively.
If he were to find out,
he would act to the detriment of this Caṇḍāla family.
"It is heard that the ascetic Gautama is free from passion (*vītarāga*).
Furthermore, the spells (*mantra*) of one who is free from passion overcome all other spells.
Having been told this, the maiden Prakṛti, the daughter of Mātaṅga, said this to her mother: "If, Mother, the ascetic Gautama is indeed free from passion..."
If I do not obtain the monk Ānanda from his presence,
I shall give up my life;
if I do obtain him, I shall live.
"O daughter, do not abandon your life!
I shall bring the ascetic Ānanda."

314.024. Then Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅga, smeared the middle of the house courtyard with cow dung, anointed the altar, spread darbha grass, and kindled a fire. Taking eight hundred arka flowers and reciting mantras, she consecrated each arka flower one by one with the mantra and cast it into the fire.
In this regard, the spell is as follows:
"O stainless one, O pure one, O saffron-colored one, O flower-like one!
By whom you, the lightning, have been bound."
314.027. By his will, the god rains, flashes lightning, and thunders.

314.028. To increase the wonder of the Great King, from among the gods, humans, and gandharvas, I offer to the Śikhigraha gods and the Viśikhigraha gods for the sake of Ānanda’s arrival, his gathering, his advancing, and his grasping: *svāhā*!
315.001. Then the mind of the Venerable Ānanda was unsettled.
He went out from the monastery and approached the house of the Caṇḍāla. 315.002.
And the Caṇḍāla woman saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar.
Having seen him, she spoke thus to her daughter Prakṛti: "Daughter, here comes this ascetic Ānanda.
Prepare a bed.
Then Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, joyful, satisfied, and delighted in mind, prepared a bed for the venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the house of the Caṇḍāla. Having approached, he stood leaning against the sacrificial altar.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda wept once more.
Shedding tears, he spoke thus: "I have fallen into calamity, yet the Blessed One does not take heed of me.
Then the Blessed One took heed of the venerable Ānanda.
315.008. Having focused his mind, he countered the Caṇḍāla mantras with the mantras of the Perfectly Awakened One.
315.008–009. In this regard, the vidyā is as follows: "Stability, non-falling, and excellent guidance."
May there be well-being for all living beings.
The lake is clear, faultless, tranquil, and entirely free from fear;
therein calamities are stilled and all perils are dispelled. (1)
The gods, all the siddhas, and the yogis indeed pay homage to that.
By this word of truth, may there be well-being and bliss for this monk.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, his mantra having frustrated the Caṇḍāla’s spell, emerged from the Caṇḍāla’s house and began to proceed toward his own monastery.
315.016. The Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti saw the Venerable Ānanda returning.
Upon seeing him, she said this to her mother: "Mother, here is that śramaṇa Ānanda returning.
Her mother said to her: "Surely, daughter, he must have been attended to by the śramaṇa Gautama."
"Because of that, my mantras will be thwarted.
Prakṛti said, "But mother, are the mantras of the ascetic Gautama more powerful than ours?
Her mother replied to her, "The mantras of the ascetic Gautama are more powerful; ours are not."
"Daughter, those mantras by which one has power over the entire world,
the ascetic Gautama, desiring them, thwarts. But the world, in turn, does not have the power to thwart the mantras of the ascetic Gautama."
315.022. Thus, the mantras of the ascetic Gautama are more powerful.
Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;

having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. As the venerable Ānanda was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: "Ānanda, receive this six-syllable vidyā."
315.025. Retain it, recite it, and master it for your own benefit and happiness, and for the benefit and happiness of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
315.026. Ānanda, this six-syllable vidyā has been spoken by the six perfectly enlightened Buddhas and by the four Great Kings.
It was spoken by Śakra, the lord of the gods, and by Brahmā, the lord of the Sahā world; and now it has been spoken by me, Śākyamuni, the perfectly awakened Buddha.
315.028. You too, Ānanda, should now recite and master that *dhāraṇī*.
That is to say: 315.030. Aṇḍare, pāṇḍare, kāraṇḍe, keyūre, arcihaste, kharagrīve, bandhumati, vīramati, dhara, vidha, cilimile, viloḥ.
These are the poisons in the world:
*viṣa cala cala*.
*Golamati gaṇḍavile cilimile sātiniṃne yathāsaṃvibhakte golamati gaṇḍavilāyai svāhā!*
316.001. <316> Ānanda, whoever shall provide protection and auspiciousness through this six-syllable vidyā,
if that person should be liable to execution, they shall be released from punishment.
One deserving a staff should be struck;
one deserving a blow should be censured.
One who deserves reprimand is released by Romaharṣaṇa, and one who deserves Romaharṣaṇa is likewise released.
Ānanda, I do not perceive anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas... [who could do so].

Among all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras, whoever is able to overcome one for whom this six-syllabled vidyā has been made into a protection, for whom a protective thread has been bound on the arm, and for whom a rite of well-being has been performed— excepting only the ripening of past karma.

316.007. Then, at the end of that very night, Māraṅga’s daughter Prakṛti, having bathed her head, clothed herself in unwashed fine garments, and adorned with pearl necklaces and ornaments, went toward the city of Śrāvastī. Arriving there, she stood leaning against the base of the gate-panel at the city entrance, waiting for the Venerable Ānanda, thinking:
"Surely the monk Ānanda will come along this path."
The venerable Ānanda saw the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti following closely behind him.
Upon seeing her, appearing ashamed and lacking confidence, distressed and dejected, he departed quickly from Śrāvastī and approached the Jeta Grove.
Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.

316.012. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this daughter of the Mātaṅgas, my companion by nature, follows closely behind me as I go and stands close behind me as I stay.
Whatever family I enter for alms, she follows right after me. 316.014. "Whatever family I enter for alms..."
She stands silently at each and every door.
"Save me, Blessed One! Save me, Sugata!"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "What business do you have with the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti, Ānanda, the monk?
Prakṛti replied: "Venerable sir, I desire the venerable Ānanda as my husband. The Blessed One asked: "Prakṛti, have you been permitted by your parents to [marry] Ānanda?"
"I have been permitted, Blessed One;
I have been permitted, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, then, seek my permission in my presence."

316.019. Then Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅga, having given her word to the Blessed One, bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
316.020. She approached her own parents; having approached, she bowed her head at the feet of her parents and stood to one side.
316.021. Having approached, she bowed her head at the feet of her parents and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, she said this to her own parents: "Mother and father, bestow Ānanda upon the ascetic Gautama in my presence.
Then Prakṛti’s parents, taking Prakṛti with them, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, she said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those two, her mother and father, have arrived.
Then the Blessed One said this to the parents of the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti: "Has the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti been permitted by you both to go to Ānanda?
They replied: "She has been permitted, Blessed One."
"Permitted by the Sugata,
you may now depart for your own homes, leaving Prakṛti behind.
Then the parents of the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from his presence.
316.031. Then, perceiving that Prakṛti’s parents had departed not long before, the Blessed One said this to Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅgas: "Prakṛti, do you have a desire for Ānanda?
Prakṛti replied: "I have a desire for him, Blessed One; I have a desire for him, Sugata."
317.001. "Therefore, you must maintain that very same appearance which Ānanda currently possesses.
She said, "I shall maintain it, Blessed One."
"I shall uphold it, Sugata!
May the Sugata grant me the going-forth;
may the Blessed One grant me the going-forth."
317.002. Then the Blessed One said this to Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl: "Come, bhikṣuṇī; lead the holy life.
317.003. When this was said, Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, had her head shaved and was clothed in saffron robes by the Blessed One.

317.004. Then the Blessed One, having caused the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti to go forth with the designation of "bhikṣuṇī," instructed her, exhorted her, inspired her, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dharma.
He gladdened them.
This discourse—which for a long time has been disagreeable to hear for those immersed in *saṃsāra*—is as follows:
the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical conduct, the discourse on heaven; [and] the danger in sensual pleasures, the escape from them, fear, and defilement and purification.
The Blessed One thoroughly taught those factors conducive to enlightenment to the nun Prakṛti.

Then, the nun Prakṛti, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dharma, became joyful in heart, virtuous in heart, delighted in heart, free from hindrances in heart, upright in heart, and unblemished in heart.
They were capable of understanding the teaching of the Dharma.

And when the Blessed One knew that the bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti was joyful in heart, with a virtuous mind, a glad mind, a mind free from hindrances, and capable and competent, then the Blessed One delivered that supreme teaching of the Dharma which penetrates the four noble truths, as is the way of all Blessed Buddhas.
Namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
the Blessed One elucidated these in detail for the nun Prakṛti.
Then, while seated on that very seat, the nun Prakṛti directly realized the four noble truths.
[She realized] suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a cloth that has been cleared of black stains and prepared for dyeing would properly take the color when thrown into the dye-vat,
even so, while seated on that very seat, the bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti attained the clear realization of the Four Noble Truths.
Namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Then the bhikṣuṇī Prabhāvatī had seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, realized the unshakable Dharma, and reached the culmination of the Dharma; she had achieved the gain of her goal, crossed over doubt and perplexity, been freed from indecision, attained self-confidence, and became independent of others and not led by others in the Teacher’s teaching; she was a follower of the true Dharma and was one who had become well-trained.
Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One regarding the Dharma, he said this to the Blessed One: "I have transgressed, O Blessed One;
I have transgressed, O Sugata!
Like one who is childish, like one who is deluded, like one who is unrefined, like one who is unskilled, and of a nature characterized by wicked ignorance."
"Venerable Sir, I addressed the bhikṣu Ānanda with the address 'master. I see that transgression as a transgression;
having seen it as a transgression, I confess it."
"I confess my transgression as a transgression. I undertake restraint for the future.
Therefore, O Blessed One, please acknowledge my transgression as a transgression and accept it out of compassion."

The Blessed One said: "Abiding in restraint for the future, you have acknowledged your transgression as a transgression before Prakṛti. Just as one who is childish, foolish, unrefined, unskilled, and of a nature lacking wisdom, you addressed the monk Ānanda with the address used for a master.
Since you recognize your transgression before Prakṛti,"
Since you perceive your transgression and undertake restraint for the future, I too accept your transgression as a transgression.
"317.028. Only an increase in wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) is to be expected for you, Prakṛti, not a decline.

317.029. Then the nun Prakṛti, having been gladdened and instructed by the Blessed One, dwelt alone in seclusion, diligent, ardent, mindful, and clearly comprehending, with her senses withdrawn and living in solitude.
317.031. For this purpose, daughters of noble family shave off their hair, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home to the homeless life out of right faith."
Having personally realized, witnessed, and attained that unsurpassed holy life which culminates in this very world, he declared: "Birth is exhausted for me;
the holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished."
"I know no further existence beyond this."

318.002. The brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī heard that the Blessed One had indeed ordained a Caṇḍāla girl. Upon hearing this, they spoke with contempt: "How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl practice the right conduct of the monks?
How can she practice the right conduct of the nuns, the laymen, or the laywomen?"

"How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl enter the families of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and great Śākyan householders? King Prasenajit of Kośala heard that the Blessed One had ordained a Caṇḍāla girl. Upon hearing this, he spoke with reproach: "How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl practice the right conduct of the monks?"
"How will he practice the right conduct of the bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās?
How will he enter the families of the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and great householders?
Having reflected thus, he had a fine carriage harnessed, mounted that fine carriage, and departed from Śrāvastī, surrounded and escorted by a great many brahmin householders of Śrāvastī.
He proceeded toward the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Indeed, he went as far as the ground was passable for a vehicle.
Having traveled by carriage for some distance, he alighted from the vehicle and, surrounded and preceded by a body of foot-soldiers, entered the monastery on foot.
Having entered, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

318.014. Those many brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders from Śrāvastī also bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. 318.016. Some, having exchanged various greetings with the Blessed One in his presence—conversations that were friendly and pleasing—sat down to one side. 318.017. Others, having announced their respective names and lineages, including those of their mothers and fathers, in the presence of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Some, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, sat down to one side;
others, remaining silent, sat down to one side.

318.020. Then the Blessed One, having understood with his own mind the thoughts in the minds of King Prasenajit of Kosala and those many brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders of Śrāvastī concerning King Prasenajit, and further concerning the former lives of the nun Prakṛti, addressed the monks: "Monks, do you wish to hear of the Tathāgata’s..."
"Would the bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti like to hear a discourse on the Dharma from the Blessed One, beginning with [her] previous lives?
The bhikṣus said to the Blessed One: "Now is the time for this, O Blessed One; now is the occasion for this, O Sugata."
"Since the Blessed One would deliver a discourse on the Dharma concerning the former lives of the nun Prakṛti,
which the monks, having heard from the Blessed One, will remember," the Blessed One said: "Therefore, monks, listen."
"Pay close and careful attention; I shall speak.
"So be it, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then said this to them:

318.027. Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there lived on the bank of the Ganges, in a region dense with groves of *atimuktaka*, plantain, *pāṭala*, and *āmalakī* trees, a king of the Mātaṅgas named Triśaṅku, together with many thousands of Mātaṅgas.

318.028. Furthermore, monks, that king of the Mātaṅgas, Triśaṅku, recollected the Vedas studied in his previous births—complete with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), along with the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), the glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), the *Kaṭha-bhāṣya*, the various divisions of phonemes, and history as the fifth.
He was proficient and free from doubt in other treatises, in the lexicon, in grammar, in the Lokāyata, in sacrificial mantras, and in the characteristics of the Great Man (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa).
He spoke the commentary in accordance with the Dharma, and he recited the Vedic vows and the words as they had been heard in tradition.
To that king of the Mātaṅgas, Triśaṅku, a prince named Śārdūlakarṇa was born.

He was endowed with beauty, noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and all excellent qualities; he was handsome, pleasing to behold, inspiring confidence, and possessed of the highest excellence of complexion and physical perfection.

Then, the king of the Mātaṅgas, Triśaṅku, had the prince Śārdūlakarṇa study the Vedas learned in his previous births—namely, the Vedas together with their limbs (aṅga) and sub-limbs (upāṅga), along with the secret doctrines (rahasya), the glossaries (nighaṇṭu), and the ritual manuals (kaṭha).
And other treatises, as well as commentaries, the Vedic vows, and the words of the Dharma, according to the law.

319.005. Then this thought occurred to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas: "This son of mine, the prince named Śārdūlakarṇa, is endowed with excellence in terms of appearance, lineage, conduct, and virtue;
he is possessed of all good qualities, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest perfection of complexion."
319.007. "He has fulfilled his vows, mastered the mantras, and reached the further shore of the Vedas.
This is the proper time for me to perform the marriage rite for him.
But from where shall I obtain a wife for my son Śārdūlakarṇa—one who is virtuous, endowed with good qualities, beautiful, suitable, and capable of bearing offspring?"
At that time, there was a brahmin named Puṣkarasārī who enjoyed the district of Droṇamukha called Utkūṭa, together with its seven outlying villages, its grass, wood, water, and grain;

it had been granted as a *brahmadeya* by King Agnidatta. Furthermore, the brahmin Puṣkarasārī was pure on both his mother’s and father’s side, unblemished in his family and lineage, and untainted by accusations regarding birth or clan, extending back through seven generations of maternal and paternal ancestors.

319.013. At that time, the preceptor was a teacher, a master of mantras, one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas—along with their auxiliary branches (*aṅga*) and sub-branches (*upāṅga*), their secret doctrines (*rahasya*), their glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), their *kaiṭabha* commentaries, and their phonetic analyses—as well as the histories (*itihāsa*) as the fifth, and the lexicons and grammar.
319.015. He had reached the further shore of the Lokāyata system, the sacrificial mantras, and the characteristics of the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
He governed the district town named Sphītamutkūṭa.
The Brahmin Puṣkarasārin had a daughter named Prakṛti;
she was endowed with excellence in terms of beauty, lineage, conduct, and virtue.
She was endowed with all virtues, beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing; she was possessed of the highest excellence of complexion, virtuous, and full of merit.

Then this thought occurred to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas: "To the northeast there is a village headquarter named Utkūṭa. There dwells a brahmin named Puṣkarasāra, who is well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side, and so forth, being fully versed in the three Vedas and their expositions."

And he enjoyed the district of Utkūṭa-droṇamukha, together with its seven outlying areas, its grass, timber, and water, along with the revenues from grain—a royal gift (*brahmadeya*) bestowed by King Agnidatta.

That Brahmin Puṣkarasārin had a daughter named Prakṛti, who was endowed with beauty, noble lineage, and virtuous conduct; she possessed all excellent qualities, was handsome, lovely to behold, pleasing, and possessed the highest excellence of complexion.
"She is endowed with virtue, possessed of moral conduct and excellent qualities; she will be a fitting wife for my son Śārdūlakarṇa.

Then Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, having reflected and deliberated extensively upon this very matter during the night, at the end of that same night, at the time of dawn, mounted a chariot drawn by mares that were entirely white and set out with a great [retinue].
Surrounded by a host of outcastes (śvapāka) and a host of ministers, he departed from the city of the Caṇḍālas and proceeded northward toward Utkūṭa Droṇamukha.

Then Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, approached the garden named Sumanaska to the northeast of Utkūṭa— a place covered with various trees, filled with the blossoms of various trees, resounding with the warbling of various birds, like the Nandana grove of the gods.
Having approached, he stood waiting for the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, thinking, "The brahmin Puṣkarasārin will come here to have the young students recite the mantras."
319.031. Then, at the end of that night, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin mounted a chariot drawn by white mares and,
surrounded by a host of disciples and preceded by five hundred young brahmins, set out from Utkūṭa to have the brahmins recite the mantras.
320.001. Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, saw the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, radiant with splendor like the rising sun,
blazing like a sacrificial fire,
and surrounded by brahmins like a sacrifice.
Like Śakra surrounded by hosts of gods,
like the Himalayas with their medicinal herbs,
and like the ocean with its jewels.
He was resplendent, surrounded by [his followers] as the moon is by the stars, Vaiśravaṇa by hosts of yakṣas, and Brahmā by hosts of celestial sages.
Seeing him approaching from afar, he went out to meet him, performed the proper rites according to the Dharma, and said this: "O Puṣkarasārin, welcome! Come here.
I shall tell you what needs to be done."
"Let that be heard.

When this was said, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin spoke thus to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas: "Indeed, my dear Triśaṅku, it is not possible for a brahmin to address another with the word 'bhoḥ' (sir).
But I, my dear Puṣkarasārin, am able to address you with the word 'bhoḥ'."
320.007. "That which is possible for me to do, that is certainly not possible for you to do.

However, O Puṣkarasārin, there are four kinds of undertakings for a person that have been previously initiated, namely: for one's own sake, for the sake of others, for one's own possessions, or [for the sake of both]."
Or for the sake of gathering all beings together.
And in this regard, there is this even greater task,
which I shall explain to you.
Listen to this:
"Give your daughter Prakṛti to my son Śārdūlakarṇa as his wife.
Whatever you consider to be a suitable family dowry, [offer that]."
I shall give as much as that.

Furthermore, upon hearing these words of Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin was deeply incensed; he became fierce and displeased, and on that account, giving rise to anger, hatred, and malice,
he knit his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead, gnashed his teeth, and glared with his eyes.
Turning his gaze, which was tawny like a mongoose, toward Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, he said this: "Fie upon you, vulgar outcaste!
This speech of yours is not fit for a dog-cooker (śvapāka), you who, being born of a lowly outcaste womb, desire to insult a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas."
320.017. O you of evil mind—320.018. You do not know the nature of things, yet you imagine yourself to be the self.
320.019. Do not, O sir, place a mustard seed on the tip of a hair; do not bring suffering upon yourself.
Do not long for that which is not to be desired; do not bind the wind with a noose.
320.021. For gold, O fool, can never become ashes;
320.022. whether in light or in darkness, is no difference perceived? //4//
"You are indeed born from the womb of a Caṇḍāla, while I am a twice-born man.
O fool, how can you, being inferior, seek a connection with one who is superior? (5)
"You have been born from a *caṇḍāla* womb, while I am born of the twice-born (*dvijāti*).
For one who is superior does not wish to form a connection with one who is inferior;
indeed, in this world, the superior twice-born form connections only with those who are superior. (6)

But those who are perfected in knowledge and purified in conduct, who are not disparaged on account of their birth, and who have attained the supreme state through mantras—[they are truly brahmins]. (7)
320.030. Teachers who uphold the mantras and have mastered the three Vedas; 320.031. those Brahmins who study the Vedas along with the Nighaṇṭus and the Kaṭhas; 320.032.
it is with such as these that the twice-born form connections here in this world. (8)

321.001. For one who is superior does not desire to form a connection with one who is inferior. 321.002. You seek to bind the wind with a noose—something that ought not to be sought. 321.003. That you wish to enter into a relationship here with us [is as impossible]. (9)
321.004. Despised by the whole world, wretched, the lowest of men— 321.005. Go away quickly, you outcaste! Why do you insult us? (10)
321.006. Caṇḍālas form alliances with Caṇḍālas, and Pukkasas with Pukkasas; 321.007. in this very world, they establish connections only with those of their own kind. //11//
321.008. Brahmins together with Brahmins, Kṣatriyas with Kṣatriyas, 321.009. likewise Vaiśyas with Vaiśyas, and Śūdras with Śūdras. (12)
321.010. Like people associate with their equals; they bring about mutual relations among those who are similar.
321.011. For indeed, Caṇḍālas do not form alliances with Brāhmaṇas. (13)
321.012. You are devoid of all noble birth and despised by all castes.
321.013. How can you, being so lowly, desire to form a connection with one who is supreme? (14)
321.014. Having heard these words again from the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, said this:
321.015–321.016. "Just as no distinction is perceived between gold and ashes, so indeed there is no distinction whatsoever between a brahmin and one of another caste. (15)
Just as a distinction is perceived between light and darkness,
so indeed there is no distinction whatsoever between a Brahmin and one of another caste.
For indeed, O Brahmin, the fire (jātavedas) has not arisen from the sky or from the winds; nor was it born by piercing through the earth, but rather [it arises] from the fire-drill (araṇi). //17//
321.021. Brāhmaṇas are born from a womb, and even Caṇḍālas are born from a womb. 321.022. What cause do you see for superiority or for being a low-born person? (18)

321.023. Even among Brahmins, one who has died and been abandoned is called loathsome and impure; 321.024. it is exactly the same for other castes as well—what then is the distinction in this matter? (19)
Whatever evil action, defilement, and strife there may be that leads to the injury of sentient beings— all that has been proclaimed by the Brahmins.
321.027. Thus these actions have been proclaimed by the Brahmins;
321.028. yet through even these cruel deeds, the twice-born say, "I am meritorious. //21//
Desiring to eat meat, the brahmins prepared it;
for they believed that goats and sheep, once consecrated with mantras, would go to heaven.
322.001. "O noble one, since this is the path [to heaven], why do these brahmins not [use it]? Or rather, why do they indeed consecrate themselves or their kinsmen with mantras?
322.002. [They] truly sprinkle themselves and their relatives with sacred formulas.
322.003. These twice-born ones do not sprinkle their mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or wife [with water]. 322.004. //24//
Whether they be friends, kinsmen, companions, or even those who dwell in the same realm—
if they are consecrated with these mantras, they all shall go to a happy rebirth.
322.007. All those summoned by sacrifices shall go to the destination of the virtuous. 322.008. O sir, what is the use of sacrificing with animals? Why do you not sacrifice yourself? (26)
322.009. Goats do not go to heaven by means of sprinkling or mantras.
322.010. For this is not the path to heaven; false sprinkling is what is called [this practice]. //27//
322.011. This very method was devised by brahmins of fierce intent; 322.012.
desiring to eat meat, they prescribed the ritual sprinkling of the animal. (28)
Furthermore, I shall declare that which has been formulated by the Brahmins:
indeed, four kinds of sins are proclaimed among the Brahmins. (29)
322.015. Stealing gold, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s wife, and killing a Brahmin—these four are the mortal sins (*pātaka*) among Brahmins. //30//
The theft of gold must be avoided; no other theft is [so] significant. That Brahmin who steals gold thereby ceases to be a Brahmin. (31)
322.019. One must not drink liquor; food and drink may be taken according to one's desire.
322.020. But that brahmin who drinks liquor, by that act he becomes a non-brahmin. //3//
322.021. One must not approach the wife of a guru, nor the wives of others at will.
322.022. But he who approaches the wife of a guru would thereby cease to be a Brahmin. //33//
One should not kill a single Brāhmaṇa, for by killing him one might kill many others;
indeed, he who would kill a Brāhmaṇa thereby ceases to be a Brāhmaṇa himself.
322.025. Thus, these four kinds of heinous sins (pātaka) have been declared among Brāhmaṇas; 322.026.
by which one becomes a non-Brāhmaṇa, whereas others are recorded as minor sins (apātaka). //35//

Having committed even one of these four [offenses], he would no longer be a Brahmin; he does not receive the proper courtesy in the assembly of Brahmins, nor is he entitled to a seat, water, or the ritual rising [in his honor]. (36)
322.030. But the escape for one who has fallen was seen by the brahmins:
322.031. By undertaking the vow, he shall indeed return to the state of a brahmin once again. //37//
323.001. Having worn a rough antelope skin for twelve years, he raised aloft a skull-topped staff and carried the heads of the dead as his insignia. 323.002. //38//
Having undertaken this vow with firm resolve and without interruption,
after twelve years are complete, one shall again attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
323.005. Thus has the way of escape been seen by the Brahmins who practice austerities.
323.007. Therefore, O Brahmin, I tell you this: that which is called a "Brahmin," a "Kṣatriya," a "Vaiśya," or a "Śūdra" in this world is merely a designation.
323.008. Having realized that all this is indeed one and the same, give my daughter Prakṛti, a young woman, to my son Śārdūlakarṇa to be his wife.
"I shall give you whatever bride-price you deem appropriate."

323.010. Furthermore, having heard these words of Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, the brahmin Puṣkarasārī became resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased; giving rise to wrath and hatred on that account, he knit his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead, gnashed his teeth, rolled his eyes, which were as tawny as a mongoose’s, and—
Having formed this view, he said this to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas:
"Indeed, this notion was formed by you without due reflection.
In this world, there is but one single birth that is common to all; it is not of different kinds. (41)
323.015. How is it that you, born of the outcaste Śvapāka class and of low origin, desire here to assault a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas? 323.016. [42]
"Indeed, O Vṛṣala, kings are those who discern the proper distribution [of duties].

That is to say, whether it concerns the law of the country, the law of the city, the law of the village, the law of the market town, the law of customs duties, the law of marriage by capture, the law of formal marriage, or matters of prior legal actions.
O Vṛṣala, there are these four castes."
Namely: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Regarding their laws of marriage, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives:
namely, a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrī.
323.020. A Kṣatriya has three wives:
a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, and a Śūdra woman. 323.021. A Vaiśya has two wives.
323.021. [These are] the Vaiśya woman and the Śūdra woman.
323.022. But for a Śūdra, there is only one wife, who is a Śūdra woman alone.
323.022. Thus, O Vṛṣala, a Brāhmaṇa has four sons.
323.023. Namely: the brahmin, the kṣatriya, the vaiśya, and the śūdra.
323.023. The kṣatriya had three sons: a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, and a śūdra.
A Vaiśya has two sons:
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra.
A Śūdra, however, has only one son, namely, a Śūdra.
323.024. Furthermore, O Vṛṣala, those Brāhmaṇas are the sons of the Brāhmaṇa; they were born from his breast and from his mouth. From his chest and from his arms, the Kṣatriyas [were born].
From the navel, the Vaiśyas;
from the feet, the Śūdras. Indeed, O low-born one, this world and all living beings were created by Brahman.
323.027. "We are his eldest sons, the Kṣatriyas immediately after them;
the Vaiśyas are the third caste, and the fourth is named Śūdra. (43) Thus it is said.
"O low-born man, you do not even appear to belong to the fourth caste.
And yet, I belong to the foremost caste, the best caste, the supreme caste, the most excellent caste;
and you desire a union with me for the sake of the ultimate goal."
Perish quickly, you low-born one!
Do not hold us in contempt.
Having heard these words of the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, said this: "O brahmin, listen here to what I say.
This world belongs to Brahmā;
all beings were created by him."
324.001. "The eldest of his sons were the Kṣatriyas; immediately after them, 324.002.
the Vaiśyas were the third caste, and the fourth was named Śūdra. (44) Thus it is said.
324.003. Men have shanks that are [well-proportioned] with a quarter-measure, along with nails, flesh, and sides and backs.
324.005. Since there is no distinction from one side, the four castes do not exist on this basis. //45//
324.007. "Furthermore, if there is some superior distinction, tell me what that is and how you approve of it. 324.009.
Or, if indeed no superior distinction exists, then these four castes do not exist apart from this [human condition]. //46//
"Just as young children playing on the great highway gather heaps of dust and themselves assign names to them. (47)
"This is milk, this is curd, this is meat, this is ghee.
Yet, merely by the words of a child, dust does not become food.
324.015. O Brāhmaṇa, just as you have spoken, there are likewise four castes (varṇas).
324.016. Under the designation of "heaps of dust," no such connection whatsoever exists. (49)
Not by the hair, nor by the two ears, nor by the head, nor by the eyes;
not by the mouth, nor by the nose, nor by the neck, nor by the arm. (50)
Nor from the sides, nor from the back, nor from the belly; nor from the thighs, nor from the shanks, nor from the nails of the hands and feet.
Neither by voice, nor by complexion, nor by all [physical] features, nor by sexual characteristics,
is there any distinction found among all human beings.
324.023. Just as in other births the gender and the womb are each distinct, 324.024.
what do you consider to be the common cause therein among those births? //53//
Furthermore, human skeletons complete with heads, skin, sense organs, and internal cavities cannot be described as possessing the four [Brahmin] castes. (54)
324.029. For this fault would indeed be improper here, regarding that which has been stated by you as the cause.
324.031. But having heard from me, O gentle one, and having understood it, listen now to what I consider to be the objection raised herein. (55)
325.001. Whatever here is logical—whether it be uneven or even—that I shall declare to you as I am exhorted.
325.003. Furthermore, whatever fault there may be in what is illogical, I shall explain to you with successive responses.
325.005. Having heard from me, O gentle one, and having understood that human beings arise through the sovereign power of karma, [you should act accordingly]. (56)

325.007. Furthermore, O Brahmin, if inference is also a valid means of knowledge for you, then as for what you say—that Brahmā is one—therefore the progeny must also be of a single birth. We, too, are of a single birth.

325.008. And as for what you say—that this world and all living beings were created by Brahmā—if this, O Brahmin, is your authority, then it is improper for you, O Brahmin, to say that there are four castes: Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
"Moreover, O Brahmin, my words would be false if, through comparison with humans, a distinction were perceived in the human species—
whether by way of the head, the face, the ears, the nose, the eyebrows, the form, the configuration, the color, the shape, the birth, or the food."
Or rather, a distinction is recognized according to their occurrence.

325.014. For example, O Puṣkarasārin, a distinction is perceived among cows, horses, donkeys, camels, deer, birds, goats, and sheep—whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation.
325.015. That is to say, a distinction is perceived in terms of their feet, their faces, their color, their shape, their food, and their mode of birth.
325.016. Yet, no such distinction is perceived among those four castes.
Therefore, all this is one.

Moreover, O Brahmin, a distinction is perceived among these inferior trees— such as the *āmrātaka*, *jambu*, *kharjūra*, *panasa*, *dāla*, *vanatinduka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *bījapūraka*, *kapittha*, *akṣoda*, *nārikela*, *tiniśa*, *karañja*, and so forth; that is to say,
a distinction is perceived from their roots, from their trunks, from the portion of their bark, from their pith, from their leaves, from their flowers, and from their fruits.
And thus, no distinction between the four castes is perceived.

"325.022. For example, O Brahmin, among these land-growing trees—such as the *sāra*, *tāla*, *naktamāla*, *karṇikāra*, *saptaparṇa*, *śirīṣa*, *kovidāra*, *syandana*, *candana*, *śiṃśapā*, *eraṇḍa*, *khadira*, and others—a distinction is perceived. 325.023. That is to say, a difference is observed from their roots, from their trunks, from the bark, from the branches, from the heartwood, from the leaves, and from the fruits."
And thus, no distinction among the four castes is perceived.
325.026. For example, O Puṣkarasārin, among these milk-exuding trees—such as the udumbara, plakṣa, aśvattha, nyagrodha, and valguka—a distinction is perceived.
325.027. That is to say, a distinction is perceived by way of their roots, trunks, bark, heartwood, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
But indeed, no distinction between the four castes is perceived.

325.029. For example, Puṣkarasārin, even among these medicinal fruit trees such as the *āmalaka*, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, and *pharasaka*, as well as various other medicinal herbs— whether growing in villages or on mountains—
their distinct differences are discerned.
That is to say, a distinction arises from the roots, the trunks, the stems, the pith, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruits;
however, no such distinction is perceived among the four castes.
326.001. Just as the distinction between land-growing flowering trees—such as the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *dhanuṣkārika*, and so forth—is perceived;
326.002. that is to say, their distinction is perceived by way of form, color, fragrance, and shape;
326.003. yet no such distinction among the four castes is perceived.
326.004. "For example, O Brahmin, even among these water-born flowers—such as the lotus, the blue lotus, the fragrant one, the soft-scented one, and so forth—a distinction is perceived.
That is to say, a distinction is perceived in terms of their form, their scent, their shape, and their color.
But no such distinction is perceived among the four castes."
