409.028. A certain man came and touched the ninth mandala;
409.029. he further touched his thigh, and the contemplation of the Dharma was contemplated. //899//
409.030. In that place, sounds are indeed to be heard; of this there is no doubt. 409.031. For the sacrificer, the officiating priest, and likewise the patron of the sacrifice— 409.032.
having heard such sounds as these, one should direct one's thoughts toward the sacrifice. //900//
410.001. Some man might come and touch the tenth mandala.
410.002. Having reflected upon the thought of karma, there is no doubt that it concerns household affairs. //901//
410.003. If he touches his knees, one should indicate that he is contemplating past actions (karma).
410.004. In that case, these sounds will arise and must be heard; of this there is no doubt. //902//
410.005. The work on the ground, the field, and likewise the work pertaining to the field—having observed such an omen as this, one should declare the consideration of the karma. //903//
If some man comes and touches the eleventh [digit],
and then touches the shanks again, one should predict the acquisition of wealth.
410.009. Therefore, these sounds will certainly be heard here; of this there is no doubt: 410.010.
[The sounds of] cowries, gold, garments, grain, and earrings with gems. //905//
410.011. Having heard such a sound, one should indicate gold for him. 410.012. Or else, whatever the sound may be, one should predict a result corresponding to that.
A certain man came and touched the twelfth mandala;
he touched my feet and asked about my mind, though it was free from worldly desire.
But that object which has been contemplated, as well as whatever adventitious hope there may be,
or rather, the sounds that are to be heard by those who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of signs— [these should be understood].
410.017. One should indicate that Ghoṣa is indeed hopeless and that he is without hope.
410.018. Or rather, whatever the sound may be, such is what he has contemplated. //909//
410.019. This, O Puṣkarasārin, is the chapter named "The Twelve Zodiacal Signs."
410.020. Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter titled "The Characteristics of Maidens.
Listen to that. 410.021.
"Very well," [he replied].
410.021. May the Blessed One speak of Triśaṅku— 410.022. the characteristics of a maiden; 410.023.
by which the truth is understood and by which auspiciousness is attained.
I shall describe the characteristics of women, both those that are censured and those that are praised.
One should examine father and mother, as well as maternal uncle and brother, just like one image from another, according to the words of Triśaṅku.
When the hour is auspicious, the lunar day is perfect, and the asterism is honored,
the knower of the scriptures, having consulted with those who are learned in that matter, should examine the girl.
410.029. Examine the hands and feet, as well as the nails and the fingers;
410.030. likewise the lines on the palms, the calves, the hips, the navel, and the thighs.
411.001. <411> The lips, the tongue, and the teeth, as well as the cheeks and the nose;
411.002. the eyes, the eyebrows, and the forehead, and likewise the ears and the hair. //914//
One who is skilled in the scriptures should examine the hair-line, the voice, the complexion, the recitation of mantras, and the singing of girls, as well as their intellect and character; therein,
the wise man should first examine them himself.
A woman with a voice like a swan, the complexion of a cloud,
and sweet eyes shall give birth to eight sons and be surrounded by male and female servants.
She whose four hair-tufts all curl to the right and whose limbs are well-proportioned will give birth to eight sons.
A woman who has a frog in her womb attains sovereignty;
she shall give birth to blessed sons and enjoy their affection.
She on whose palm the tortoise, the svastika, the banner, the goad,
the earring, and the garland are clearly and firmly visible shall give birth to one son, and he shall be designated as a king.
She in whose hand a granary with its arched gateway appears shall become the wife of a king, even if she is born in the family of a slave.
She who has thirty-two teeth, all as white as cow’s milk, with even peaks and a glossy luster, gives birth to a king.
With a smooth, languid gaze like that of a *kāraṇḍava* duck, her eyes like those of a doe and her skin delicate,
she with red lips and tongue and a beautiful face approaches the king.
She has a delicate and prominent nose, a face free from redness, beautiful eyebrows, and lovely hair; such a maiden will indeed have many offspring.
Her fingers are joined together beautifully, her nails resemble lotuses, and her feet are very straight and red; that girl prospers in happiness.
She whose two curls are symmetrical and glossy, and both sides of whose body are well-proportioned,
shall indeed become a queen.
411.027. One should walk around her clockwise and look at her while moving clockwise. 411.028. One should take as a wife a maiden whose conduct is clockwise. //926//
411.029. Her thighs, shanks, and sides are well-proportioned, and her gait is firm.
411.030. With large eyes and reddish corners, that girl prospers in happiness.
411.031. She with the eyes of a deer, the shanks of a deer, the neck of a deer, and the belly of a deer—411.032.
that woman whose name is truly fitting attends upon the king. //928//
She whose hair is beautifully arranged at the crown and whose face is perfectly round,
and whose navel spirals to the right— that maiden increases the prosperity of her family.
Neither too long nor too short, well-settled with thin skin, and with hair-ends that are pleasant to the touch—one does not transcend good fortune. (930)
But a woman who has lovely lips, red lips, and speaks pleasantly—a wise man should choose such a woman for the sake of the household, as one who brings happiness to the home. //931//
She who has the luster of a blue lotus and the soles of her feet with long toes shall become the mistress of many thousands.
Having obtained a daughter endowed with auspicious marks, a man prospers, being possessed of wealth, grain, long life, fame, and splendor.
412.011. I have already described the auspicious characteristics of fortunate women. 412.012. Now I shall explain the unfavorable characteristics according to their respective categories. //934//
One who looks upward, one who looks downward, and one who looks sideways;
one who is bewildered and one with wide eyes—these should be avoided by the wise. (935)
She whose long, coarse hair has split ends,
who possesses variegated streaks and a spotted body, is a woman who acts according to her own desires.
412.017. A woman who is lustful, tawny-eyed, fair-skinned, or excessively dark;
412.018. one who is too tall or too short—these should be avoided by the wise. //937//
She whose forehead, belly, and buttocks hang down excessively—she slays three men: her husband's younger brother, her father-in-law, and her own husband.
If there is a line of hair on the side [of the abdomen] and the waist is sunken,
one attains a long life but remains miserable for a long time.
And that woman who has legs like a crow’s, red eyes, and a gurgling voice;
who is devoid of happiness and hope, and abandoned by her lost kinsmen. (940)
A woman whose belly is excessively large and hangs down like a deep pit will be utterly lacking in self-control, will have many sons, and will be deeply afflicted by suffering.
But she who possesses all proper conduct, has delicate limbs, and has attained evenness,
being endowed with all equal virtues, should be known as one who acts according to her will.
She whose shanks are covered with hair and whose face is perfectly round—
such a woman desires either a son, a brother, or even a lover.
She whose two forearms and wrists are covered with a line of hair,
and who has hair upon her upper lip, devours her husband.
413.001. She whose hands and feet have gaps between the digits, and whose teeth have gaps between them—413.002.
the wealth acquired by her husband does not find pleasure in her home. //945//
But she whose joints crack as she walks should be known as one who experiences much suffering and never attains happiness.
She whose little toe does not touch the ground shall abandon her husband from her youth and do what pleases herself.
The toe of her foot does not touch the ground;
she finds no pleasure in youth and lives as a courtesan.
413.009. That maiden whose second toe extends beyond the big toe will, once she reaches youth, especially take a lover. //949//
She whose back has a whorl and whose navel is deeply recessed does not enjoy her youth; she obtains a second husband.
Deformed, with a webbed hand, and having coarse hair on her cheeks and head—
even if born in a royal family, she falls into servitude.
But she who, while laughing, develops a depression on her cheek,
will go even to a fire ritual and quickly bring about misfortune.
A woman with beautiful eyebrows that meet at the center, who has whorls on her cheeks,
and whose lips hang down excessively, does not delight in one man for long.
413.019. With a protruding belly, a thick head, red eyes, and a tawny face, she devours eight heroes; at the ninth, she remains for a long time. //954//
413.021. Neither a *devikā*, nor a *nadikā*, nor one named after a deity; 413.022. nor one bearing the name of a tree or a shrub—these should be avoided by the wise. //955//
A woman who bears the name of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or one who bears the same name as her *gotra*, even if she is well-concealed or guarded, might still commit evil in her mind. (956)
413.025. One should avoid these wives whom I have described; however, a man should always take one such as those previously praised. 413.026. [957]

413.027. Maidens who possess the lotus, the goad, the svastika, the vardhamāna, the wheel, the banner, and the pitcher in their hands; 413.029. and who bear the excellent marks of the conch and the parasol—such maidens lead to prosperity. //958//
413.031. This, O Puṣkarasārin, is the chapter entitled "The Characteristics of Maidens."
414.001. Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter on garments;
let that be heard. "Very well."
414.002. Let the Blessed One speak concerning Triśaṅku—414.003.
the chapter on garments.
414.004. Under Kṛttikā, fire burns; under Rohiṇī, there is the gain of wealth.
Mṛgaśirā brings rats and gadflies; Ārdrā is destructive to life. //959//
Under Punarvasu one shall be fortunate; under Puṣya, one shall indeed possess clothing. Under Āśleṣā there shall be theft; one should go to the cremation ground under Maghā.

If it occurs under the Phālgunī stars, one will possess knowledge; under the Uttarā-phalgunīs, one will be well-clothed; under Hastā, one will perform manual labor; and under Citrā, travel is certain.
Under Svāti, one obtains beautiful clothing; under Viśākhā, that which is pleasing to behold;
Anurādhā brings many garments; and Jyeṣṭhā is the destroyer of clothing.
If it falls under Mūla, one's clothing will become damp; under Āṣāḍhā, there will be the onset of disease.
Under Uttarā, one will be a consumer of refined food; under Śravaṇā, there will be pain in the eyes.

414.014. One should know that Dhaniṣṭhā brings an abundance of grain; there is danger in Śatabhiṣaj. 414.015. There is water in Pūrvabhādrapadā, and Uttara [Bhādrapadā] leads to the gain of a son. //964//
Revatī brings the acquisition of wealth; Aśvinī bestows the gain of clothing.
Bharaṇī is filled with fear, and it may be frequented by thieves.
414.018. This, O Puṣkarasārin, is the chapter on garments.
414.019. Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall proclaim the chapter on the *luṅga* (mango);
let it be heard. 414.019.
"Very well," [he replied].
414.020. May the Blessed One speak concerning Triśaṅku—414.021. the chapter on the *luṅga*—414.022.
where did these seeds originate?
And among grains, there are barley and the like—
those by which this entire universe, both stationary and moving, is sustained.
How should one sow the seed, and how should one employ the plough? Under which conjunctions of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and under which conjunctions of lunar days (*tithi*) should this be done?
414.026. Should one sow [the seeds] in autumn or in summer? In which month, indeed, should one sow them? 414.027. How many signs are praised, and which ones should one avoid?
414.028. To whom should one cause incense to be offered, and with what mantra should one cause it to be offered? //968//
If the *luṅgā* plant grows with its coils turning clockwise,
then that *luṅgā* with the face of a serpent burns even one who has a variegated countenance.
415.001. Or even the darbha-grass needle-point—what could be the cause for that? 415.002. How many types of prosperity are there, and how many types of misfortune are recorded?
415.003. How many colors are fully described, and how many colors are demonstrated? //970//
If Vāsava sends rain upon one whose seeds have been lost or destroyed,
or if there is a violent thunderclap, or even if the earth should quake— 971.
415.006. What is the cause for the grain and its fruit to be perceived there?
415.007. I wish to hear all of this in brief, according to the truth. //972//
415.008. Having heard the words of the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the lord of the Mātaṅgas, spoke these words:
415.009–010. "In the past, by the gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras, the nectar was seen when it arose from the ocean during its churning. (973)
415.011. While the nectar was being consumed, the twice-born one requested a share.
415.012. Thereupon, ten drops of nectar were granted as shares by the gods.
Then these seeds were produced upon the earth, bringing happiness to the world:
barley, rice, sesame, wheat, mung beans, and black gram.
Śyāmaka is known as the seventh, and Ādiksudhā is recorded as the eighth;
the remaining many varieties of grain were produced together in abundance.
415.017. Among all the *harītaka* fruits and whatever other species of beings there were, 415.018.
a ninth drop fell everywhere upon their bodies and became nectar (*amṛta*). 415.019. And likewise, upon all the roots, a single drop was cast down. //977//
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should sow rice and other grains; likewise, all autumnal crops and the like should be sown in the month of Bhādrapada.
In the month of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, one should sow the summer grains on the fifth,
the seventh of the bright fortnight, the sixth, and on the eleventh days.
On the thirteenth, the second, and likewise on the ninth days,
one should especially sow all seeds in low-lying places.
In the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Puṣya, Mūla, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Maghā,
and especially in Kṛttikā and Viśākhā, [the rain] is particularly abundant in autumn.
415.028. Under the Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Maitra (Anurādhā), Anurādhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śravaṇa constellations, 415.029.
the sowing of all seeds is recommended during the northern course [of the sun].
415.030. One should avoid one's birth constellation, and one should also avoid the Saṃgraha constellation. //982//
Whatever seed is in the village field and whatever household deity is in the home—
one should observe these as auspicious signs and favorable omens.
A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a maiden, and a blazing fire;
or a lordly elephant, a bull, or a horse well-adorned.
A full water-jar, a banner, an umbrella, raw meat, liquor,
as well as an extracted *dhāraṇī*, a bound single animal, and curd.
If one sees a cart mounted with wheels or a sow mounted with crows,
and observes someone being placed upon another, one should predict an abundance of grain.
416.007. All [omens] on the right are auspicious, as are beasts and birds appearing in front;
416.008. the sight of white flowers and fruits is likewise commended. //987//
416.009. A goat or a ram on the left is praiseworthy, as is a jackal;
likewise, one who is deformed, hunchbacked, afflicted with leprosy, or has a face covered in a beard [is so]. //988//

Having seen a man who is reviled, dejected, afflicted by grief, or tormented by disease; or a herd of boars, a snake, or a donkey freed from its burden— one should turn back the seed and enter the village again.
416.014. Likewise, there may be the sowing of a jar completely full of sesame seeds.
416.015. Indeed, having heard these [omens], one should predict an abundance of crops for those who are traveling. //990//

416.016. "Heaped," "strung together," "washed," "resting in its own state," "sprouted," and likewise "cleansed by hearing"—those who know these [terms] are known as those who have acted with speed. //991//
Having heard [the sound], one should predict that it will be withered, parched, and of scanty rain.
Having heard [it], one should turn back the seed and enter the village again.
Even if Indra sends down rain upon a seed that is being carried away,
that grain itself will surely be enjoyed by its owner in due time.
If the seed being carried along makes the earth tremble,
and the farmer is spun around from his place, it is not possible to sow it.
If there is a violent crash while the seed is being carried away,
it indicates that the death of the master or the grain-guard will soon occur.
416.026. Or else, it may cause confusion and cut short the king's punishment.
416.027. Having seen this, one should withdraw the seed and settle it again in the village. //996//
Having given to the brahmins according to his ability, he should then proceed;
having constructed a very large altar and strewn darbha grass all over it.
416.030. Having kindled the fire with sacrificial fuel, one should offer oblations of ghee and mustard seeds.
416.031. One should first recite the Veda-śānti, and thereafter the Śasya-śānti. //998//
First, one should recite the *Pārāśara* [text] and have the twice-born recite the *Priyā* [hymn].
Then, one should first cast the seed-syllable facing east, or alternatively, toward the north.
When ants store grain in the field,
there will be good rain, abundance of food, and a harvest of all crops.
If they carry away seeds from the grass, they are thieves of the grain;
for they harm one another, and the crop shall go to ruin.
417.006. Seeing an accumulation [of clouds] over high ground, one should predict a great rain.
417.007. But seeing an accumulation over low ground, one should predict a drought. //1002//
But when the seed that has been sown sprouts within seven nights,
there will be excellent rain, abundance of food, and a harvest of all crops.
But when the sown seed sprouts within half a month,
the grain produced is meager and a famine arises therein.
If a mango fruit falls within three or four nights, there will be excessive rain in that region; the wise know this to be a danger from a foreign army.
If the feet of Luṅga are five, seven, or nine,
there will be good rain, abundance of food, and a bountiful harvest of all crops.
If the stalks of the *luṅga* plant have four or eight nodes,
one should predict that the grain harvest will be meager and that there will be famine.
417.018. If twelve feet of the *luṅga* are seen anywhere, 417.019.
in some places the crop will flourish, while in others one should predict famine.
417.020. If they are seen turning to the left, one should indicate that there will be famine there. //1008//
417.021. When the *luṅgā* faces east, it indicates safety and rain. 417.022. When the *luṅgā* faces west, it indicates excessive rain. //1009//
When Luṅgottarāmukhī appears here with the luster of yellow orpiment and gold, shining like a rising auspicious light, there will be security and abundance of food.
417.025. And wherever a needle-mouthed blade of *darbha* grass is seen, 417.026. or where grain fails to grow, one should predict famine there. //1011//
417.027. Whenever the *luṅgā* plant with a serpent-like face (*nāgamukhī*) is seen anywhere, 417.028. or wherever grain fails to grow, one should predict famine there. 417.029.
Furthermore, there will be fear of lightning and fear from the clouds; of this there is no doubt. (1012)
"This entire triple world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, has agriculture as its root.
There is no means of livelihood equal to agriculture," so it was said by the Self-Existent One himself.
418.001. One does not obtain dharma through lack of cultivation, nor does one obtain happiness through lack of cultivation.
418.002. Through cultivation, the farmer obtains everything: dharma, wealth, and likewise pleasure. //1014//
418.003. Thus ends the chapter on the Lunga.
418.004. Again, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin said this to Triśaṅku, the lord of the Mātaṅgas: 418.005.
"How is it that there are *nāgas* upon the earth, and by whom are they restrained? 418.006.
From what does their fundamental origin arise, and where do thunderclaps (*nirghāta*) originate? (1015)
418.007. From where do the clouds arise, displaying various colors across the ten directions?
418.008. Whose is this great sound that is heard, like the resonance of a drum? //1016//
418.009. For who indeed creates famine and prosperity for living beings?
418.010. Who is that one there called the Best of Sages? Tell me his name and lineage.
And tell me of the deities and the ordinances of the Self-Existent One; also of the sacrifice, the sacrificial portions, and how the oblation is to be offered.
Tell me, who is the deity upon the earth? Tell me, who is the deity in the hermitage?
Tell me, who is the deity among the gods; by whom was that goddess fashioned?
418.015. Tell me the deity of the alms-bowl; tell me the deity of the full water-jar. 418.016. Tell me the deity of the water-pot, and likewise the deity of the cooking-pot. (1020)
418.017. Tell me the deity of the grain, and the deity of the guardian of the grain.
418.018. And through how many masses of wind does Śukra release his velocity? (1021)
418.019. Then Triśaṅku, the lord of the Mātaṅgas, said this to the brahmin Puṣkarasārin:
418.020. "Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth— 418.021. therein the mass is formed; from that, the cloud proceeds. (1022)
418.022. This [cloud] pervades the sky and is produced by the wind; 418.023.
the rays of the sun draw water from the ocean into the vault of the heavens. (1023)
That water was withdrawn by the Nāgas, and from that, Varuṇa’s domain was withdrawn;
the wind roared through the sky, fire blazed, and the quarters of the world shone.
418.026. A clod of earth is thrown by the wind, and there is a thundering crash.
418.027. Furthermore, there is a conflict between the wind, the fire, and the air. (1025)
The celestial sphere remains in the sky and subsequently falls to the earth;
that which is the sovereign of the planets and even of the stellar luminaries,
through its conjunction with the wind, causes Parjanya to rain as well.

While Mahāpanthaka says very little and grasps much, when this Panthaka is told 'sī', he forgets 'dham'."
The brahmin reflected: "All brahmins are skilled in the scripts and letters;
this one must be a Vedic brahmin.
He was then entrusted to a teacher to have him taught the Vedas.
When he says "Oṃ," he forgets "Bhūḥ"; when he says "Bhūḥ," he forgets "Oṃ.
The teacher said, "I have many young students whom I must teach."
428.019. "I am unable to teach Panthaka.
When he says 'om,' he forgets 'bhūḥ'; when he says 'bhūḥ,' he forgets 'om'."
The brahmin reflected: "Not all brahmins are masters of the Vedas;
this man must be a brahmin by birth alone. Whenever he went to a place where he was invited, [he would behave accordingly].
Taking that very Panthaka with him, he departed.
At that time, the brahmin had fallen ill;
although he was attended to with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, and fruits, he continued to decline.
He said to Mahāpanthaka, "Son,
you are not to be mourned after my passing;
however, you must provide for Panthaka's livelihood."
Having said this:
"All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation; and life ends in death. (1)
Thus, he was joined with the law of time.
They decorated his bier with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths, and after cremating him in the cemetery with great honor and dispelling their grief, they remained there.
428.029. The venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, while wandering on tour through the Kosala countryside, arrived at Śrāvastī.

428.030. The people of Śrāvastī heard that the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, while wandering on tour through the Kosala countryside, had arrived at Śrāvastī. 428.031. Having heard this, the multitude of people began to go out of the city.
428.032. Mahāpanthaka, too, was outside Śrāvastī at the foot of a certain tree, teaching the Vedic mantras to about five hundred young brahmins.
He saw that crowd of people departing from Śrāvastī and asked those young men: "Sirs,..."
"Who is this great multitude of people going out?
They said to him, "Preceptor,
the two venerable ones, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having traveled on a journey through the Kosala country with a retinue of five hundred, have now arrived here at Śrāvastī."
He approached in order to see them.
"Why indeed should those two be seen,
they who have now abandoned that supreme excellence and gone forth into homelessness in the presence of the second-rate ascetic Gautama?"
429.005. Among them, there was one young brahmin who was faithful.
429.006. He said, "Teacher, do not speak thus."
Those two possess great majesty.
If their preceptor were to hear the Dharma from them, it is possible that even the preceptor would find it pleasing.
429.007. It was the custom of those young brahmins that whenever they had no lessons,
they would sometimes go for a sightseeing tour of the city,
and sometimes go to bathe at sacred fords.
429.009. Sometimes they go to gather firewood.
At another time, they all became unlearned in the scriptures.
Those who were gathering firewood set out [on their way].
Mahāpanthaka also stood engaged in walking meditation at the foot of a certain tree. There he saw a monk;
having approached him, he said this: "O monk!"
"Let some word of the Buddha be spoken. Then, he explained the ten paths of wholesome action to him in detail. Having gained faith, he said: "O Bhikṣu!"
"Tell me again in detail," he said,
and having spoken thus, he departed.
At a later time, those [students] became even more unlearned.
429.014. Having gathered firewood, they set out.
Mahāpanthaka also approached the presence of a certain monk. That monk extensively explained to him the twelvefold dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in both forward and reverse order.
Having gained faith, he said: "O Bhikṣu, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a Bhikṣu in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya?
May I practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Śramaṇa Gautama."
That monk reflected: "I shall ordain him in the teaching; thus he will lift up the burden.
He said to that brahmin: "Brahmin,"
"Do so.
Mahāpanthaka said, "Bhikṣu,
we are renowned brahmins."
"I shall not be able to go forth right here. Let us go to the countryside and go forth there.
Having been led by him to the countryside, he went forth and was fully ordained; and he was told:
"There are two duties for a monk: meditation and study.
What will you do?
"I shall do both."

By reciting [the scriptures] during the day, cultivating them through systematic reflection (*yoniśo bhāvanā*), and by contemplating, weighing, and examining them at night, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions (*sarvakleśaprahāṇa*).
He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, and possessing a mind like space or the palm of a hand.

He was like one for whom an axe and sandalwood are equal; he had split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge; he had attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights; he had turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor;
and he became one to be honored, worshipped, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
429.026. When Panthaka’s wealth had become diminished, exhausted, and completely spent, he began to struggle to make a living.
429.027. Then this thought occurred to Panthaka: "Whatever was to be attained by me through learning, that has been attained by me."
"What if I were to go to Śrāvastī and attend upon the Blessed One?
Then the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī.
Traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived at Śrāvastī.

429.029. In Śrāvastī, the populace heard that the noble Mahāpanthaka, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, while wandering on tour through the Kosala country, had arrived at Śrāvastī. 429.031. Having heard this, they began to go out [to meet him]. He was seen by Panthaka.
He asked, "Sirs, where is this great multitude of people going?
They replied, "The noble Mahāpanthaka, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, while wandering on tour through the Kosala country, has arrived at Śrāvastī."
430.001. A great multitude of people approached him in order to see him.
430.002. Panthaka reflected: "He is neither a brother nor a kinsman to them;
but he is my brother."
430.002. "Why do I not go to see him? He too has come to see me. 430.003. He saw him and asked: "Panthaka!"
"How do you sustain yourself?
Do you sustain yourself with difficulty? Why do you not go forth?"
He said, "I am Cūḍa, the most excellent Cūḍa; Dhanva, the most excellent Dhanva.
Who will ordain me?
The Venerable Mahāpanthaka reflected, "Does he possess any roots of merit? He saw that he did.
430.006. "Why is he not fit [for ordination]? Come, I shall ordain you. 430.007. He was then ordained and received full admission.
430.007. He gave him this instruction: 430.008. "One should not commit any evil in the entire world, whether by mind, speech, or body. 430.010.
Empty of desires, mindful and clearly comprehending, one shall not experience suffering that brings harm. (1)
This verse of his had not been recited even after three months;
however, having heard it from other cowherds and shepherds, it became current.
With reverence and respect, he approached them and began to inquire about it.
430.013. They gathered together. It is indeed the nature of things that for the Blessed Buddhas there are two assemblies of disciples:
one on the full moon of Āṣāḍha at the commencement of the rainy season retreat, and one on the full moon of Kārttika.
In the same way, it is also for the great śrāvakas.

Among them, those who approach at the time of the invitation at the end of the month of Āṣāḍha take up various specific mental orientations and enter the rains retreat in various villages, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
430.017. Those who approach on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika request instruction and inquiry,
and they report what they have understood.

430.018. The monks who were co-residents and pupils of the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, having spent the rains retreat in the countryside, also approached the Venerable Mahāpanthaka on the full moon day of Kārttika.
There, some of them requested [the opportunity] for recitation.
Some questioned, while others reported what they had realized.
Among them were those who were Cūḍās, supreme Cūḍās, Dhanvas, and supreme Dhanvas.
They served, honored, and attended upon the group of six monks.
The venerable Panthaka served, honored, and attended upon the group of six monks.
He was addressed by the group of six monks: "Venerable Panthaka,"

"Your fellow students are requesting from their own preceptor a lesson for private recitation and an opportunity for questioning. Go; you too should request from your own preceptor a lesson for private recitation and an opportunity for questioning.
He replied, "I have not studied anything at all during these three months."
"But not even a single verse has been composed by me;
why should I ask for instruction? They replied, "Has it not been said by the Blessed One: 'Those who do not recite [the teachings] are intoxicated'?"
"430.026. What will come of your reciting verses while you are not studying?
Go and beg for them!
430.027. He went and said, "Preceptor,"
"First, give me some instruction for my private recitation.
The Venerable Mahāpanthaka reflected: "Is this his own inspired eloquence, or has he been prompted by someone else? He saw that he had indeed been prompted.

The Venerable Mahāpanthaka reflected: "Is this person to be converted through encouragement, or is he to be converted through discouragement? He saw that he was one to be converted through discouragement. Taking him by the neck, he led him outside the monastery.
"You are indeed Cūḍa, the most excellent Cūḍa; Dhanva, the most excellent Dhanva.
What will you do under this teaching?
He began to weep.
"430.032. Now I am neither a householder nor a renunciant.
431.001. The Blessed One saw the venerable Pathaka wandering outside the monastery.
Seeing him as he was returning, he said this: "Why, Pathaka, do you weep outside the monastery?"
"Why do you shed tears?
"Venerable sir, I have been expelled by my preceptor;
now I am neither a householder nor a renunciant."

The Blessed One said: "My son, this word of the Lord of Sages was not acquired by your preceptor; rather, after fulfilling the six perfections through three incalculable eons and many hundreds of thousands of difficult feats, this teaching of the Lord of Sages was fully realized and brought forth by me.
Are you not able to recite it from the presence of the Tathāgata?"
"Venerable sir, I am Cūḍa, the most excellent Cūḍa; Dhanva, the most excellent Dhanva.
Then, on this occasion, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"He who is a fool by virtue of his foolishness is, for that reason, a wise man in that regard."
But the fool who considers himself wise is indeed called a fool here. //2//
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would teach the Dharma word by word; such a thing cannot occur.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have Paṇṭaka recite this.
The Venerable Ānanda began to make him recite it.
431.013. He was unable to teach him.
The Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I must first attend upon the Teacher and master what has been heard."
"The assembly must be recited.
The Dharma must be taught to the Brahmins and householders who come and go.
I am not able to teach Panthaka."
The Blessed One gave him two steps: "I remove the dust," and "I remove the stain. He did not obtain these two steps.
The Blessed One reflected:
"The removal of his karma must be performed.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, will you be able to wipe the soles of the monks' sandals from their very bases?"
"Very well, venerable sir, I shall be able to do so.
"Go, wipe it clean.
He then set about wiping the sandals and the soles of the feet of the monks.
The monks did not grant it to him.
The Blessed One said, "Grant it;
his removal from the offense must be performed."
"431.020. Grant me a pair of sandals for the purpose of recitation.
431.021. He wipes the soles and the edges of the monks' sandals."
431.021. Those monks gave him the instruction for the recitation of those two lines.
431.022. As he was reciting those two lines, after some time they became familiar to him.
431.023. Then, at the time of dawn during the night, this thought occurred to the venerable Panthaka: "The Blessed One has said thus: 'I remove the dust.'"
"I am removing the stain.
"Does the Blessed One speak with reference to internal dust, or rather to external [dust]?
As he was reflecting thus, at that moment three verses never heard before appeared and occurred to him:

431.026. Here, "dust" refers to passion, for this is not mere soil; "dust" is a designation for passion, not for soil. 431.028. The wise who are not heedless in the teaching of the Sugata dispel this dust. (3)

431.030. Here, "dust" is hatred, for this is not the dust of the earth; "dust" is a designation for hatred, not for soil. 432.001. The wise who are not heedless in the teaching of the Sugata dispel this dust. //4//

432.003. Here, "dust" is delusion; it is not the physical particle of dust. "Dust" is a designation for delusion, not for physical dust. 432.005. The wise who are not heedless in the teaching of the Sugata dispel this dust. //5//
By striving, exerting himself, and applying effort, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings, and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became one to be honored, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Śakra and Upendra.
While he was seated in meditation, he was seen by the Venerable Mahāpanthaka. However, the knowledge and vision of Arhats does not function without focused attention.
432.011. He took him by the arm and said, "Come, first practice recitation;
after that, you may practice meditation.
432.012. Then, through the abandonment of all defilements, the Venerable Panthaka realized arhatship.
An arm resembling the trunk of an elephant was extended.
The Venerable Mahāpanthaka, looking back over his shoulder, saw it and said,
"Venerable Panthaka,"
"Have these multitudes of qualities been attained by you in this way? "They have been attained."
432.016. When the Venerable Panthaka had realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements, the followers of other sects reviled, censured, and spoke ill of him.
432.017. "The ascetic Gautama says thus: 'My Dharma is profound, appearing profound; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond logic, and not within the sphere of logic.'"
It is subtle, to be experienced by those who are skillful, wise, and discerning. What is so profound about it now,
that even Panthaka and others— who were once the crest-jewels, the supreme crest-jewels, the archers, and the supreme archers— have now gone forth as renunciants?
The Blessed One reflected: "A great multitude of people is gaining faith in this great disciple who resembles Mount Sumeru.
His virtues must be proclaimed.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda."
"Tell Panthaka: 'The bhikṣuṇīs are to be instructed by you.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the venerable Panthaka.
Having approached him, he said this to the venerable Panthaka: "The Teacher, venerable Panthaka, says this to you: 'The bhikṣuṇīs are to be instructed by you.'"
The Venerable Panthaka said: "For what reason does the Blessed One, setting aside the elder monks, appoint me as the instructor of the nuns?
I shall fulfill the Teacher’s wish by manifesting my own virtues. The nuns [were concerned about] the loss of their *chanda*.
Having arrived at the Jeta Grove,
they asked the monks, "Who has been appointed by the Blessed One as our instructor?
They replied, "The Venerable Panthaka."
They said, "Sisters,
look how this woman has been humiliated!
While she has recited but a single verse in three months,"
She, too, did not proceed.
The bhikṣuṇīs were masters of the Tripiṭaka, preachers of the Dharma, and possessed of ready and eloquent intelligence;
it was said that he would instruct these bhikṣuṇīs.
When they had assembled in that gathering, they were asked by the bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters, who will come to instruct us?
They replied: "The noble Panthaka."
"Is this the noble Mahāpanthaka?
"No, this is not he; rather, it is another, Cūḍapanthaka.
This was heard by the group of twelve nuns.
432.032. For that long they were reproaching him.
433.001. "Sisters, look! How has this assembly of women been insulted?"
Since one single verse was not mastered by him even after reciting it for three months, [he thought:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are masters of the Tripitaka, preachers of the Dharma, and possessed of logical, fluent, and inspired eloquence."
He, it is said, wondered, "What will he teach them?
They replied, "Sisters,
prepare a lion-throne with twelve elephant-lengths of cords."

433.004. Let the six young men, having entered Śrāvastī, proclaim it in every street, lane, crossroads, and square: "Such a teacher will come to us who will not perceive our subtle truths; by that, we shall have to dwell in saṃsāra for a long time.
433.005. [They replied: "By that, he will have to dwell in saṃsāra for a long time."
433.006. No one—not even a son of a *moṭika*—who is of little learning, dares to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. 433.007.
For them, a seat was prepared with six women and twelve elephant-ropes.
Six bhikṣuṇīs, having entered Śrāvastī, announced it in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions: "Such an instructor as that will come for us."
"He who shall not perceive our subtle truths will have to dwell for a long time in saṃsāra.
Then the Venerable Panthaka, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms.
433.011. Having finished his meal and returned from his alms-round with his bowl, he put away his bowl and robes, washed his feet, and entered the monastery for seclusion.
433.012. Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Panthaka rose from his seclusion, took up his outer robe, and set out accompanied by another monk as a junior attendant.
433.013. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings—some filled with curiosity—[followed].
Some were being impelled by their former roots of merit.
Then that assembly saw the Venerable Panthaka from afar;
having seen him, they asked one another, "Which of these is the instructor of the nuns?"
"Is he a forerunner-ascetic (puraḥśramaṇa), or rather a follower-ascetic (paścācchramaṇa)?
Regarding this, some say: "He is a forerunner-ascetic."
433.016. They began to murmur, "Look, Venerable One! We have been intentionally harassed by the bhikṣuṇīs.
By him who has recited a single verse in three months..."
She too has not set out; how then will she instruct the nuns or cause them to recite the Dharma? Let us go.
Others said, "We shall stay if he will teach the Dharma; otherwise, we shall depart. Thus that assembly remained poised.

When the Venerable Panthaka saw the lion-throne prepared, he reflected: "Was this prepared by those who have conceived a spirit of faith, or rather by those with the intention to cause harm? He perceived that it was indeed by those with the intention to cause harm. Having seen this, he reflected again: "Was this prepared by those who have conceived a spirit of faith, or rather by those with the intention to cause harm?"
He saw that they were all intent on causing harm.
Then, the Venerable Panthaka extended his arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, and placed that lion-throne back in its proper position.
The Venerable Panthaka sat down there.

As he sat there, some saw him while others did not. Then, remaining right there, the venerable Panthaka entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from his own seat, rose into the air in the eastern direction, and—just as before—displayed various miraculous feats of supernatural power. Having withdrawn those manifestations of psychic power, he reappeared upon his very seat.

Having sat down, the Venerable Panthaka addressed those bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters, in three months I have recited a single verse. Would you be willing to listen for seven days and nights as I analyze its meaning through other words, syllables, and phrases?"
"One should not commit any evil in the entire world, whether by mind, speech, or body.

Empty of desires, mindful and clearly comprehending, one shall not experience suffering that brings about harm. (6) Thus spoke the Blessed One regarding the cause of all evil—so much so that as one studies the meaning of the verse, it leads to the realization of its true purpose.
At that time, twelve thousand living beings perceived the truths;
some realized the fruit of stream-entry, and some the fruit of once-returning.
Some attained the fruit of non-returning; some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions; and some generated the resolve for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha.

Then the venerable Panthaka, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that assembly with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed. As he was coming along, he was seen by the monks, who reflected: "Today, the venerable Panthaka must have inspired faith in a great multitude of people."
434.008. They were unable to ask the venerable Panthaka unpleasant things to his face.
434.008–009. They subsequently asked a junior monk:
"Venerable sir, today, was the great multitude of people won over by the venerable Panthaka, or not?"
By the Venerable One, no one has been left without faith.

By the Blessed One, at Ṛṣivadana, the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, the Dharma wheel—threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects—was set in motion; that very wheel has now been set in motion by the Venerable Panthaka.
434.011. Before he had even analyzed the meaning of the verse, twelve thousand living beings perceived the truths.
434.013. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples, who are skilled in the transformation of the mind—namely, the monk Panthaka.
434.014. The monks asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Behold, Venerable Sir, by the group of twelve, thinking 'we shall do harm to the venerable Panthaka,' they have done exactly that.
434.015. The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, thinking 'we shall do him harm,' they did exactly that."
434.016. Let that be heard.
434.017. Once upon a time, monks, there lived a brahmin in a certain village. He took a wife from a family of equal status. He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.

While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, he sported, enjoyed himself, and diverted himself further until twelve sons were born. He provided them with wives. At a later time, his wife passed away.
That brahmin, too, had reached an advanced age.
Having become blind, his daughters-in-law were of immoral conduct.
Whenever their husbands went outside, they would act accordingly.
Then they were sporting with other men.
That brahmin was skilled in the art of sound;
he recognized it, thinking, "This is the voice of my son."
"This is another man!
Hearing the sound of men's footsteps, she roared at her daughters-in-law.
They reflected, "This brahmin has set out for our ruin."
434.024. They gave him a meal of *cakaṭī* rice and sour gruel.
434.026. They were asked by those [others]: "For what reason do you give your father a meal of *cakaṭī* rice and sour gruel?
They replied: "His merits have been exhausted."
For its sake, leadfish are thrown into the cauldron,
and wheaten porridge is being stirred.
When curd was poured into the sour gruel (*kāñjika*), it turned back into its original state.
They asked, "How can this be so?
They replied, "We shall demonstrate it to you."
They said, "We have made a vow that must now be fulfilled.
They spoke to the potter: "Friend, will you be able to make two pots with a single opening?
He replied, "I shall be able to do so."
434.031. Therefore, two pots with a single opening were made.
Into one of those pots, husked rice was poured; into the second, sour gruel.
434.032. They placed rice in one vessel and curd in another before their masters. 435.001.
When these were prepared, they asked: "Noble son, shall your father eat first, or shall you?"
They said, "Father has already eaten.
Then, in their presence, they drew some rice from one pot and gave it to them, while drawing buttermilk from the second pot and giving that to them.
Then again, having drawn rice from one pot, they gave it to them, and drew curd from the second pot and gave that to them.
They said to him, "Father,
your merits are exhausted;
for when śāli rice was poured into a single pot,"
On the second day, there was curd;
that same rice with ghee and sour gruel had been transformed. The brahmin reflected: "By raising my hands hundreds of times, I have acquired these enjoyments."

435.007. "What is the reason that my merits have been exhausted? Thinking thus, he entered the kitchen while they were not looking on; searching with his hands, he felt with his touch and found two pots with a single opening. He hid them away.
435.009. He showed this to his sons who had arrived: "Look, my merits have been exhausted!
435.010. Go and see for yourselves that single-mouthed pot right here in our house."
"Little son, in other houses there are two kinds of rice with their husks removed, but for us unfortunate ones, there is none. They beat their wives with sticks.
The wives reflected: "This brahmin has set out to bring us misfortune."
"Let us kill them," they said. At that spot, a snake-charmer arrived. They asked him, "Is there a snake here?"
He asked, "What kind of snake are you seeking—is it alive or dead?
They replied, "Dead.
He reflected, "What will they do with this dead snake?"
"Surely these women must intend to kill this old man.
Now, it is the nature of an angry snake that its venom is concentrated in two places: at the head and at the tail.
Therefore, having become enraged, he himself cut off his own head and tail and gave the snake to them in their midst.
435.017. Having prepared the *joma* broth, those women said to the brahmin, "Father, will you drink the *hilima-joma*?
The brahmin reflected, "Will they give me this *hilima-joma*?"
"Surely some non-medicine must have been administered.
He reflected, "I shall drink it;
as it is, so shall I die."
435.019. They gave him *hilimā* and *joma*.
435.020. He drank it, and by its vapor, his cataracts burst open.
435.020. He began to look [at him]. 435.020. He fell down and remained there.
435.021. And he said: "I am dying! I am dying!"
They said, "Drink quickly!
They said, "Father,
will you drink more?"
He said, "I shall drink.
They gave him more *hilima* and *joma*,
and he drank it again.
435.023. By that shedding of tears, his film was split open to a greater degree, and he began to see more clearly. 435.024.
Those women, just as they had previously roamed about with confidence toward him while he was blind, began to roam about in that very same way.
435.025. Taking up his staff, he stood up and said: "Do you think that even now I do not see?
I see now!"
435.026. Full of shame, they fled away.
"What do you think, monks?
That brahmin at that time and on that occasion was none other than this very Panthaka."
Those who were his twelve daughters-in-law are none other than these twelve members of the group. Even then, they intended to bring him harm, and indeed they did so.
Even now, thinking, "We shall cause harm to this man," they have done exactly that.

435.030. The monks asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Behold, venerable sir, how the Blessed One, having exhorted the venerable Panthaka with a brief instruction, has drawn him out from the wilderness of saṃsāra and established him in the ultimate, unsurpassed security of nirvāṇa."

"We shall provoke his pride so that he will meet with disaster through such misconduct, just as one who would enter the great ocean [only to perish] right there.

There is musāragalva, red gems, and right-spiraling conch shells.

and to establish offerings from time to time for ascetics and brahmins on behalf of his mother and father, his children and wife, his female and male slaves, laborers and servants, and his friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations— [let him do so].
May he descend into the great ocean— an act that leads to the summit [of existence], brings forth splendor, results in happiness, and conduces to rebirth in heaven in the future—
for the world desires prosperity.
A great multitude of people had boarded [the ship], so that the vessel became unmanageable.

438.018. Lest you feel regret later when you have returned to Jambudvīpa.

"You must not consume those.

438.023. After the passing of seven days, they released such a wind that the ship was carried away, as if its purpose had not yet been accomplished. 438.024. Having heard this, those merchants remained attentive, vigilant, and steadfast.

438.025. They reached Jambudvīpa by means of a favorable wind. 438.026. In this manner, it happened up to seven times that he returned with the vessel successfully filled.
His mother said to him: "Son,"
"Let a house be built here.

after that, I shall build a house."

He replied: "Mother,"
"I alone know.
438.029. He had four mice made out of the four precious gems.

not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;

"What do you think, monks?
He who was a monk learned in the Tripitaka during the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa, and who later became a butcher— [is he anyone else?]"
This very person is the monk Panthaka.
Because of his stinginess, he did not teach even a single four-line verse to anyone;
and because he slaughtered pigs, he was reborn here from among the non-percipient beings.
As the ripening of that karma, Cūḍa became Paramacūḍa and Dhanva became Paramadhanva.

"Jīvaka, act in such a way that there may be an increase in your wholesome qualities.

"Venerable Ānanda, so that there may be an increase in his wholesome qualities:

He announced the time: "It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems fit.
Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went to the residence of Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya.

446.002. The Buddha, the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kuru country, arrived at Kalmāṣadamya.
