Shake off the army of death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut. //1//
466.025. He who shall indeed practice vigilantly within this Dharma and Vinaya, 466.026.
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end to suffering. //2//
If he asks, "What is this?", one should say:
"This is assistance; this is training; this is worldly convention; this is extreme enthusiasm.
They recorded everything exactly as they were instructed.
The Blessed One said to King Bimbisāra: "Great King, send a letter to Rudrāyaṇa: 'Dear friend, this gift, which surpasses all that exists in the three worlds, has been sent to you by me.'"
"You must prepare the beauty of the road for two and a half *yojanas* of his journey. You yourself, with a fourfold army, must go out to meet him.
Having stationed him in a spacious location and having performed great worship and honor, you must open [the city]."
"Therefore, there will be the attainment of great merit for you.
King Bimbisāra, having written a letter according to these instructions, dispatched it.
The letter was presented to King Rudrāyaṇa.
He read it;
he was filled with indignation.
He said to the ministers: "Sirs," he said.
"What kind of gift has been sent by him for me, for which I must perform a formal reception?
Prepare the fourfold army!
We shall inflict a crushing defeat upon his kingdom."
The ministers said, "Your Majesty,
that king is renowned as a great-souled one;
it is not possible for him to send back just any ordinary gift."
"Let the proceedings be conducted in due order.
If Your Majesty’s mind is not satisfied,
we shall know the proper time for that."
"Let it be done thus.
Thereupon, he prepared the adornment of the road for two and a half *yojanas*.
Then, having gone out himself to meet him with his fourfold army, he escorted him inside.
Having placed it in a spacious location and performed a great worship, [the casket] was opened.
Then, merchants from the Middle Country arrived there bringing their merchandise.
Upon seeing the image of the Buddha, they raised a cry with one voice: "Homage to the Buddha!"
467.009. Upon hearing that sound, "Buddha"—a term he had never heard before—all the hairs on his body stood on end.
He asked, "Sirs, who is this called 'Buddha'?
They replied, "Your Majesty,..."

"A prince has been born among the Śākyas on the slopes of the Himalayas, on the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī, not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila. He has been prophesied by brahmins who are skilled in omens and learned in the sciences:
if he dwells at home as a householder,"
He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror by means of the fourfold army, righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven treasures.

These are his seven treasures of such a nature, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
"And he shall have a full thousand sons—heroes, warriors, of excellent form and appearance, who crush the armies of adversaries.

Having completely conquered this great earth, bounded by the ocean, free from thorns, rid of stains, and without oppression, by means of righteousness, peace, and without punishment or weapons, he will dwell as its sovereign.
If, however, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life, [he will become a Buddha]."
"He will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame shall resound throughout the world.
He is this one called 'Buddha';
this is his inspired eloquence."
"What is this? "It is acceptance. "What is this? "It is the training rule (śikṣāpada).
"What is this? "It is the engagement with and withdrawal from the world."
"What is this? "It is extreme enthusiasm.
Consequently, he has correctly grasped dependent origination in both its forward and reverse orders.

467.021. Then King Rudrāyaṇa, together with his ministers, at the time of dawn, having brought all affairs and all undertakings to a halt, sat down cross-legged, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. 467.022.
He contemplated this very twelvefold dependent origination in both its forward and reverse orders.
That is to say: "When this exists, that comes to be;
from the arising of this, that arises"—namely, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations, up to the point where there is both origination and cessation.

By thus contemplating this twelvefold dependent origination in its forward and reverse order, he shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with twenty peaks.
He realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, he spoke this verse:
"By the Buddha, the jewel of the earth, the eye of wisdom has been purified."
Homage to that excellent physician whose medical treatment is indeed such as this. //3//

467.029. He sent a message to King Bimbisāra: "Dear friend, it is because of you that my foot has been drawn out from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and established among gods and humans."
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed over;
and having shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, the fruit of stream-entry has been realized.
"I desire to see a monk;
therefore, you ought to send a monk.
Then King Bimbisāra approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, King Rudrāyaṇa has seen the truths.
He has sent me word, saying: 'I desire to see the monks.'"
The Blessed One reflected: "Which monk is capable of converting King Rudrāyaṇa along with his retinue, as well as the populace residing in Rauruka? [He saw that] it was the monk Kātyāyana.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Apply your attention, Kātyāyana, to King Rudrāyaṇa along with his retinue and the inhabitants of the city of Rauruka."
And [he addressed] the assembly of people.
The venerable Mahākātyāyana consented;
having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
468.007. Then, when that very night had passed, the venerable Mahākātyāyana dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.

468.008. Having walked for alms in Rājagṛha and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after the meal; having rested at his lodging and packed away his bowl and robe, he set out for Rauruka with a retinue of five hundred.
He set out on his journey. King Bimbisāra then sent a letter to King Rudrāyaṇa:
"Dear friend," [he wrote].
"I have sent this monk to you, a great disciple who is like a teacher himself. You must prepare the road for him for two and a half yojanas and decorate the city.
Furthermore, you yourself must go out to meet him with a fourfold army."
500 monasteries are to be constructed; 500 sets consisting of couches, stools, small seats, high seats, pillows, bolsters, and square mats are to be provided;
and 500 portions of alms-food are to be designated.
"Therefore, you shall obtain a great accumulation of merit.
Consequently, he beautified the road for two and a half yojanas and beautified the city."
Five hundred monasteries were built,
and accompanied by a retinue of one thousand people, he himself went out to meet him and, with great honor, led him into the city of Roruka;
outside the city, five hundred monasteries were constructed.
Five hundred sets of beds, stools, small seats, high seats, cushions, pillows, and square mats were provided;
five hundred portions of alms-food were prepared;
and on a wide expanse of ground, the arrangement of seats was caused to be made.
The venerable Mahākātyāyana sat down on the seat prepared for him at the head of the community of monks.
Many hundreds of thousands of living beings had assembled;
some were filled with curiosity.
Some were being impelled by their former roots of merit.

Then, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having understood the intentions, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of that assembly, delivered such a teaching of the Dharma that upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained a great distinction.
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of non-returning,
and some, having abandoned all defilements through renunciation, realized arhatship.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka,
some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha.
In the city of Rauruka, there lived two householders named Tiṣya and Puṣya.
They approached the Venerable Mahākātyāyana;
having approached him, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana and sat down to one side.

The householders Tiṣya and Puṣya said this to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Venerable Mahākātyāyana, may we receive the going forth and full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Venerable Mahākātyāyana, may we lead the holy life under you. They were both granted the going forth and full ordination by the Venerable Kātyāyana.
Instruction was given.

As the two of them applied themselves, exerted themselves, and strove, they understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and shifting; they [understood] all conditioned states by way of their nature to be broken, fallen, scattered, and destroyed in hundreds of ways.

Having struck down all afflictions through their abandonment, they realized arhatship. They became two arhats, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with minds like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights, and turned away from gain, loss, greed, and honor.
They became objects of worship, honor, and salutation for the gods, including Śakra and Upendra.
Having performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing light, they passed away into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
Their kinsmen, having performed the funeral rites for their bodies, erected two stupas—one for Tiṣya and [one for Puṣya].
The second [is the fruit] of merit.

King Rudrāyaṇa, having heard the Dharma day after day from the venerable Mahākātyāyana, announced it to his harem: "The noble Mahākātyāyana teaches the Dharma most sweetly; like honey, it is sweet and brings great delight."
They said, "The appearance of a Buddha has borne fruit for Your Majesty.
How so? Because you hear the Dharma. [He asked:
"If that is so, why do you not listen?"
"Your Majesty, we are modest women.
How could we go there and listen to the Dharma?
If the noble Mahākātyāyana would come here and teach the Dharma, [we would do so]."
"In this way, may we too hear it.
King Rudrāyaṇa said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, "Noble sir, my inner apartments wish to hear it.
He replied, "Great King,"
"Monks do not enter the inner apartments to teach the Dharma;
entry into the inner apartments has been forbidden by the Blessed One. Noble sir, who is it here that teaches the Dharma to the inner apartments?"
"Your Majesty, the bhikṣuṇīs.
King Rudrāyaṇa has sent a letter to King Bimbisāra: 'Dear friend, he desires that the women of the inner apartments hear the Dharma.'"
"Therefore, you ought to send some bhikṣuṇī.
King Bimbisāra, having read that letter, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Bimbisāra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, King Rudrāyaṇa has sent a letter stating that he wishes his harem to hear the Dharma;
therefore, it would be fitting for you to send some bhikṣuṇīs. “In this matter, how should we proceed?”
The Blessed One reflected: "Which nun is capable of converting the retinue of King Rudrāyaṇa’s harem and the women residing in Rauruka?
He saw that it was the nun Śailā.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the nun Śailā: "Apply your mindfulness, Śailā, toward the people of King Rudrāyaṇa’s harem and the women residing in the city of Rauruka."
"So be it, Venerable One," the nun Śailā replied to the Blessed One. Having bowed her head at his feet, she departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Then, when that very night had passed, in the forenoon, the nun Śailā dressed herself, took her bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having finished her meal and returned from her alms-round after the meal, she [set aside] what she had eaten.
Having prepared his lodgings and taken up his bowl and robes, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, he set out on a journey toward the city of Rauruka.
King Bimbisāra then sent a letter to King Rudrāyaṇa, saying: "Dear friend,"
"I have sent this great female disciple of mine, who follows the Teacher, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred.
You must prepare the adornment of the road for three and a half *yojanas* and the adornment of the city for her arrival. Furthermore, you yourself must go out to meet her with a fourfold army."
Within the city, five hundred monasteries are to be built;
five hundred beds and stools are to be provided; and five hundred sets of small cushions, large pillows, bolsters, and square mats are to be given.
"Five hundred alms-offerings should be prepared;
from this, you will obtain merit.
Having read the letter, King Rudrāyaṇa, filled with joy, had the road beautified for two and a half yojanas.

Accompanied by a retinue of many thousands of people, he himself went out to meet them and, with great honor, led them into the city of Rauruka. Within the city, he had five hundred monasteries constructed and provided five hundred sets of couches, stools, mats, pillows, bolsters, and square cushions.
Five hundred alms-offerings were prepared.
The nun Śailā entered King Rudrāyaṇa’s harem and taught the Dharma day after day.
King Rudrāyaṇa was skilled at playing the lute.
Queen Candraprabhā was dancing. Then, at another time, King Rudrāyaṇa played the lute while Queen Candraprabhā danced.
470.005. As she was dancing, he perceived the signs of her impending death.
470.006. Observing her from this side and that, he reflected: "After seven days have passed, she will die.
470.007. The lute slipped from his hand.
She fell to the ground.
Queen Candraprabhā said, "My Lord,
did I perform a bad dance?"
"O Queen, you have not danced poorly;
rather, while you were dancing, I perceived the signs of your destruction—that on the seventh day, your time will come.
Queen Candraprabhā fell at his feet and said, "Your Majesty, if it is so,"
"I have performed service for Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty would grant permission,
I would go forth into the religious life."
He said, "Candraprabhā,
I grant you permission on this condition:
if, having gone forth, you realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions."
"This indeed is the end of your suffering.
Now, having passed away with some fetters remaining, you will be reborn among the gods;
once you have become a god, you must show yourself to me."
She replied, "Your Majesty, let it be so.

King Rudrāyaṇa then entrusted Queen Āryacandraprabhā to the nun Śailā, saying, "The noble Queen Āryacandraprabhā desires the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
"Therefore, you ought to let her go forth and grant her full ordination.
The nun Śailā replied, "So be it;
I shall let her go forth."
She was ordained by her and received full admission.
Having reflected upon this, she gave her instruction: "Cultivate the perception of death.
Queen Candraprabhā then began to cultivate the perception of death.
On the seventh day, she passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Now, it is the natural law that when a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has been reborn for but a short time, three thoughts arise: "From where have I passed away?"...
"Where has she been reborn, and by what karma?
The celestial maiden Candraprabhā reflected: "Have I already passed away?"
From among humans,
where were they reborn?
Among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
"By what karma?
"By having practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) under the teaching of the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to her: "It would be improper for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my period of residence is still incomplete."
"What if I were to approach the Blessed One for an audience before my period of probation has expired?
Then the celestial maiden Candraprabhā, wearing shimmering, stainless earrings and her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces,
that very night filled the lap of her carriage with divine blue lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and *māndārava* flowers, and [arrived] with all...
Having illuminated the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, with a sublime radiance and having scattered flowers over the Blessed One,
she sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Knowing her disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma that it led to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard this, the divine maiden Candraprabhā shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us by the Blessed One was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved ones, nor by our circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by those who have passed away before, nor by recluses and brahmins."
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed;
and the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
The gates to heaven and liberation have been opened, and [the Dharma] has been established among gods and humans. And he said:
471.001. Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with manifold sufferings, has been closed;
471.003. the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the path to Nirvana has been found by me. (4)
471.005. Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure, faultless, and perfectly purified eye;
471.007. I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering. (5)
O Sage, worshipped by Daityas, humans, and gods in this world; free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
whose sight is so difficult to obtain even in thousands of lifetimes—today your vision has become fruitful for me. (6)
Then, bowing down with joy at the sight of her lover, she whose long necklace was swaying paid homage to both his feet;
having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies clockwise, she departed for heaven, facing the world of the gods.
Then the divine maiden Candraprabhā was like a merchant who had gained profit,
like a farmer whose crops had ripened,
and like a hero who had won the battle.
Like a patient freed from all diseases, she set out for her own palace with the very same splendor with which she had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to her: "I promised King Rudrāyaṇa that I would show him [the Blessed One]."
Then the celestial maiden Candraprabhā approached King Rudrāyaṇa.
At that time, King Rudrāyaṇa was lying alone on the upper floor of his palace.
She illuminated the area with a sublime radiance and awakened him with the sound of a snap of her fingers.
471.022. With eyes heavy from drowsiness and his words indistinct, he spoke without recognizing her: "Who are you? She replied: "I am Candraprabhā.
The king said: "Come here."
"Let us enjoy ourselves," they said.
She replied, "Your Majesty, I have passed away and died; I have been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."

471.024. "If you desire union with me, go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One. 471.025. If you do so, you will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements in this very life."
"That indeed is the end of your suffering. Furthermore, if you have some fetters remaining,
after passing away, you will be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
"There you shall have a meeting with me.
Having said this, she vanished right there.
King Rudrāyaṇa, reflecting upon the life of renunciation throughout the entire night, rose early in the morning and addressed his ministers: "Look, sirs!"
"Where does Queen Candraprabhā reside? They replied, "Your Majesty, she has passed away."

471.029. Rudrāyaṇa reflected: "It would not be fitting for me, having been impelled by the gods, to continue dwelling in the midst of a household; nor should I enjoy sensual pleasures through the accumulation of wealth or the passing of time. What if I were to consecrate Prince Śikhaṇḍin in the kingdom, shave off my hair and beard, don saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith go forth from the home to the homeless state?"
471.032. He then summoned his two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhiru, by messenger and said to them:
"Sirs, just as my son, Prince Śikhaṇḍin, is to me, so too are you both."
472.001. "This very person must be restrained from what is unwholesome by you two and established in what is wholesome.
'I am going forth into the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,'" he said.
472.002. These two stood there with throats choked with tears.
Prince Śikhaṇḍin was also addressed: "Son,

just as you consider my word to be worthy of being heard and carried out, so too should you consider the word of these two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhūru, to be worthy of being heard and carried out."
"I am going forth into homelessness in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Having heard this, he too stood there with his throat choked with tears.
Then King Rudrāyaṇa had a proclamation made by the sounding of a bell in the city of Rauruka: "Listen, O citizens residing in Rauruka and the multitude of people arrived from various lands!"
"472.007. Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith.
472.008. Furthermore, he said to his son: 'Son, while you are ruling the kingdom, you must not forgive anyone for their offense.'"
472.009. That king was beloved by his citizens and rural folk.
472.009. Upon hearing this, the entire populace residing in Rauruka, as well as others who had arrived from various lands, stood with their throats choked with tears.
472.010. Then King Rudrāyaṇa, having installed Prince Śikhaṇḍin on the throne and having asked his kinsmen for forgiveness, [departed].
Having given gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars, and having made his merchandise ready, he set out toward Rājagṛha with a single man as his attendant.
Then King Śikhaṇḍin, along with his harem, ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, as well as a multitude of people who had come from various lands, followed closely behind him.

Followed by many hundreds of thousands of living beings, he departed from the city of Rauruka and, after staying for a moment in a certain park adorned with various groves of trees, abundant with diverse flowers and water, and resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds, he looked back toward the city of Rauruka and addressed King Śikhaṇḍin: "Son," he said.
"I have ruled the kingdom according to the Dharma,
by which these hundreds of thousands of living beings have followed behind me.
Therefore, you too must rule the kingdom according to the Dharma."
He also comforted that body of people and said, "Sirs, this king of yours has been interrogated by me. He is now returning; you shall dwell in peace."
Having spoken thus, he set out.

King Śikhaṇḍī, together with his harem, princes, ministers, citizens, and people of the countryside, returned toward the city of Rauruka with eyes clouded by tears, turning back again and again to gaze after him.
Then King Rudrāyaṇa, traveling by stages, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
472.021. Having stayed in the park, he said to that man: "Go, my good man, go to King Bimbisāra and inform him: 'A man named Rudrāyaṇa is staying in the park.
472.022. That man went and informed King Bimbisāra: "Your Majesty," he said.
"King Rudrāyaṇa is staying in the park.
Upon hearing this, the king rose up suddenly and addressed his men: "Sirs, King Mahāsādhana has arrived without even being announced."
"Has this not been understood by any of you?
He replied, "Your Majesty,
how could there be any means of proof for this?"
"He has arrived with himself as his only companion.
King Bimbisāra reflected, "It would not be fitting for me to allow the Kṣatriya Rāhula, who has been consecrated on the head, to enter in such a manner.
I shall have him enter with great honor. Having understood this, and having caused the road and the city to be adorned, he went out to meet him with a fourfold army.
Embracing him around the neck and mounting him upon the back of an elephant, he was brought into the great city of Rājagṛha. He was bathed with water perfumed with various fragrances;
having been adorned with garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments worthy of a king, he was fed.

When the fatigue of the journey had been dispelled, he was addressed: "Dear friend, having abandoned a prosperous kingdom, the harem, the princes, the ministers, and the people of the city and countryside—what is the purpose of your coming here?
Has some neighboring king caused an invasion of your realm?"
"Or was it attempted by some prince who, instigated by wicked ministers and longing for the kingdom, has exerted himself? He replied, "Friend,
I desire the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
473.001. Having heard this, King Bimbisāra, with a joyful mind, raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this inspired exclamation: "O, the Buddha! O, the Dharma!
O, the Saṅgha! O, the well-expounded nature of the Dharma!"

"Since even men such as these, having now abandoned a flourishing kingdom, a vast harem, a wide circle of kinsmen and relatives, and abundant treasuries and granaries, desire to go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Having said this, he took King Rudrāyaṇa with him and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma.
The Blessed One saw King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha from afar.
Having seen him, he addressed the monks: "Monks, King Bimbisāra is approaching with a gift."
"There is no such gift for a Tathāgata as the gift of those to be converted.
Having said this, he remained silent.
King Bimbisāra, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Bimbisāra said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, this King Rudrāyaṇa desires the going-forth and the full ordination within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
May the Blessed One, out of compassion, grant him the going-forth and the full ordination."
The Blessed One addressed him with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monk; lead the holy life.

At the conclusion of the Blessed One's words, he became shaven-headed, clad in the saṃghāṭī robe, with bowl and water-strainer in hand, and stood possessed of the deportment of a monk ordained for a hundred years.

When addressed by the Tathāgata with the words "Come," he stood there with shaven head and his body wrapped in the saṃghāṭī robe, his senses immediately calmed; thus did he stand according to the Buddha's wish. (8)
473.019. In the forenoon, the venerable Rudrāyaṇa, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
473.020. He was seen by a great multitude of people, and this report spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha: "King Rudrāyaṇa has gone forth into homelessness under the Blessed One."
He entered Rājagṛha seeking alms.
Upon hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered together.
Even the women moving about within the palace began to look out, stationed at the windows, the lattice-panels, and the balconies.
The ministers informed King Bimbisāra:
"Your Majesty, King Rudrāyaṇa has entered Rājagṛha for alms and stands there surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of living beings.
Upon hearing this, King Bimbisāra approached the place where the monk Rudrāyaṇa was.
Having approached, he said this to the monk Rudrāyaṇa:
"O lord of men, having enjoyed thousands of villages and Rauruka itself, do you not feel remorse now that you have cast them aside and are seeking alms? (9)

while those who had faith experienced wonder;

King Śikhaṇḍī reflected: "If there are truly no Arhats in the world, for what purpose do I provide almsfood to the noble Kātyāyana of the Kāśyapa clan with his retinue of five hundred, and to the nun Śailā with her retinue of five hundred?

He was seen by King Śikhaṇḍin standing at one side.

Practicing with difficulty, he goes;
karma is performed;
the bowl and robes will be covered with dust.
The king remained silent.
Then, as the venerable Mahākātyāyana was leaving Rauruka after walking for alms,

Even now,
what is the reason for this?
Behind him, those two wicked ministers were following.

485.004. Having heard this, he became agitated.
485.005. He said: "Sirs, for whomsoever I am dear,"
"Let everyone throw a handful of dust upon this shaveling ascetic!

485.006. With each handful of dust thrown, a great mound of dust was piled up upon the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.

485.011. With throats choked with tears and faces weeping, they began to clear away the dust along with the cowherds and shepherds.
485.011. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana emerged.
485.012. They fell at his feet and asked: "Noble One,..."
"What is this? He replied, "What else could it be?
They both said, "Noble sir,"
"What will become of this deed performed by Śikhaṇḍin, with Mahākātyāyana and the body of people as his assistants? [The answer was:
"On the seventh day from now, the city of Rauruka shall be buried under dust."
"Venerable sir, what will our future course be?
"Venerable ones,
on the first day, a great wind will arise and clear the city of Rauruka of stones, pebbles, and potsherds."
On the second day, a rain of flowers will fall;
on the third, a rain of garments;
and on the fourth, a rain of gold.
In the fifth year, there will be a rain of gold;
subsequently, those inhabitants living on the borders of Rauruka will perform a collective action,
and they will destroy the city of Rauruka.
"When they have entered those [cities], on the sixth day a rain of jewels will fall,
and on the seventh day a rain of dust. They said, "Noble sir,"
"Are we two to partake in the fruit of this action?
"Noble sirs, you two are not partakers in the fruit of this action."
"Noble sir, if it is thus, how are we to depart from this city?
He replied, "The two of you should have a tunnel dug between your house and the river; then, having stationed a boat near the house, wait.
When the rain of jewels falls,"
"Then, having filled a ship with jewels, you must flee.
Having prostrated at his feet, the two entered Rauruka. Upon entering the presence of the king, they said, "Did Your Majesty say anything to the noble Mahākātyāyana, that he was buried under sand?"
He said, "Sirs, is he alive?
"Your Majesty, he lives."
"What does he say? "Your Majesty, he says this: 'On the seventh day from now, the city of Rauruka shall be buried under dust.
"What is the sequence of events? He replied, "Your Majesty," and continued:
He spoke thus:
"First, on the first day, a great wind will come and clear the city of Rauruka of stones, pebbles, and potsherds;
on the second day, a rain of flowers will fall."
On the third day there was a rain of garments; on the fourth, a rain of silver;
on the fifth, a rain of gold.
"Afterwards, those who dwell in the vicinity of Rauruka shall perform a collective action; they will enter the city of Rauruka,
and once they have entered, on the sixth day a rain of jewels will fall,
and on the seventh day a rain of dust."
The two of them said, "Noble sir,
are we also partakers in this deed?
"O fair-faced ones," [he replied].
"You two are not sharers in this deed.
"Noble sir, if that is so, how are we to escape from this house? He replied, "Dig a tunnel from the house to the river; once it is finished, stay near the house and wait for a boat."

"When the rain of jewels falls, you must fill a boat with those jewels and flee. Those two wicked ministers said, "With his alms-begging completely cut off and overwhelmed by a rain of dust, what else could he possibly say?"
"Or he speaks thus: 'Is this a deity, or is it a wicked man?
King Śikhaṇḍī reflected, "It must be so."
486.004. The two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhiruka, having disfigured their faces and twisted their hands, departed.
486.005. There, Hituka had a son, a boy named Śyāmāka;
486.006. Bhiruka had a daughter, a girl named Śyāmāvatī.
486.006. Hituka gave the boy Śyāmāka to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, saying, "Noble sir,
if he possesses any roots of merit,
you should let him go forth."
"If this attendant does not belong to you," [the girl said].
Then, out of fear, the girl Śyāmāvatī was given by Bhiruka to the nun Śailā: "Noble Lady, if she possesses any roots of merit..."
"You should let him go forth [into the religious life].
If not, you must hand him over to the householder named Ghoṣila, who is my friend in Kauśāmbī. She consented.
Then the nun Śailā, taking Śyāmāvatī with her, departed from the city of Rauruka by means of her supernatural power.
At that time, she was given to the householder Ghoṣila in Kauśāmbī,
exactly as had been instructed and communicated.

The venerable Mahākātyāyana remained right there. Hiru and Bhiruka, the two chief ministers, had a tunnel dug between their house and the river, and they stationed a boat near the house. Then, on a certain day, a great wind arose.
By which that city of Rauruka was established, cleared of stones, pebbles, and potsherds.
On the second day, a rain of flowers fell.
Those two wicked ministers said: "Your Majesty,..."
"It is heard that for King Māndhātṛ, a rain of gold fell for seven days.
This rain of flowers has fallen for Your Majesty;
before long, a rain of garments will fall."
On the third day, a rain of garments fell.
Those two wicked ministers said, "This rain of garments has fallen for the king;
before long, a rain of gold will fall."
On the fourth day, a rain of gold fell.
Those two wicked ministers said, "This rain of gold has fallen for the King;
before long, a rain of gold will surely fall again."
On the fifth day, a rain of gold fell.
Those two wicked ministers said, "This rain of gold has fallen for the King;

486.022. The two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhiruka, having filled a ship with jewels, fled away.

486.024. In a certain region, Bhiruka had a city built named Bhiruka. It became known by the name Bhirukaccha.
On the seventh day, a rain of dust began to fall.
486.026. The gates were blocked by non-human beings.
Śyāmāka asked, "Noble sir, what is this loud and great noise?"

take the Kāśika cloth out through the window.
He took the Kāśika cloth out through that window.
It was not covered with dust.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana reflected: "The range of her activity still remains.

Pūrṇā had become one whose hair was bound in a topknot.

486.030. Then the deity residing in Rauruka approached the venerable Mahākātyāyana. Having approached and paid homage at his feet, she said: "Noble one, I too am coming."
"I shall perform service for the Noble One.
Then the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to Śyāmāka, "Son, take hold of the corner of my robe."
