he set out through the air above by means of his supernatural power, carrying the boy Śyāmaka with him.
A deity dwelling in Rauruka was also following behind him with her own supernatural power.
The city of Rauruka was likewise buried under dust.
They eventually arrived in succession at my small village of Khara.
487.004. Therefore, they remained there at the threshing floor.
487.005. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having placed the boy Śyāmāka at the threshing floor, entered for alms.
487.006. Through the power of the deity, the grain in that threshing floor began to increase.
The man who was stationed there,
seeing the boy, approached him and said: "O boy,
it is indeed through your power that the grain increases in what is called the threshing floor."
He said, "It is not by my power that grain grows in the threshing floor;
rather, a deity residing in Rauruka has come here and stays in this spot,
and it is by her power that grain grows in the threshing floor."
487.010. Having gone to her presence and fallen at her feet, he said: "O goddess, please hold this key and the lock for as long as it takes me to go to the village and return."
"And you must not give it to anyone else except me. He, too, went to the mountain village and assembled the body of people residing there, and said to them: "Sirs,"
A deity residing in Rauruka has come here and stays at the place called Khalabhidhāna. By her power, grain increases in Khalabhidhāna.
I have placed a key and a lock in her hand.
And he said: "O deity, hold onto this lock and key until I return from going to the village;
and you must not give them to anyone else except me."
"I declare this condition: if you consecrate my son as the guild-president, I shall deprive myself of life.
Because of this condition, the deity will not go anywhere else."
"Your wealth shall increase, and all calamities shall be pacified. 487.019.
His son, the guild-leader, was then deprived of life by him.
Then, taking all that—having adorned the entire settlement with perfumes and flowers, and beautified it with parasols, banners, and flags—they approached the place where the deity was.
Having approached and prostrated at her feet, they said: "O deity, be our protector!"
"Stay right here. "I have no place to stay here; I am an attendant to the noble Mahākātyāyana."
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said: "O goddess, attend to this: from whom were the staff and the key taken?
She began to reflect and saw [the truth].
When he had passed away,
she addressed the body of people residing in that district: "Sirs,
I shall remain here for a fixed period."
487.025. A sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) was prepared for that deity exactly as it was for the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
487.027. Taking the lamp that had been placed at the shrine of that deity, he set it upon the sacrificial ground of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
487.028. A certain man standing on the top of the wall saw her going along carrying a lamp.
487.029. He reflected: "This is a goddess going as a messenger for the noble Mahākātyāyana.
487.030. She perceived his thought.
She became enraged: "This populace dwelling in Karvaṭaka has a wicked disposition;
they are leveling slander against the noble Mahākātyāyana, who is free from the stench of worldly desires and insatiable in his merit.
Therefore, she unleashed a pestilence upon that Karvaṭaka.
487.032. A great plague broke out among the people.
As the deceased were being carried out from bed to bed, a loud clamor arose.
The multitude of people living in that settlement summoned the fortune-tellers and asked them, "What is this?"
They replied, "It is due to the wrath of a deity.
They then began to ask for her forgiveness.
She said, "Is it that you are showing disrespect toward the noble Mahākātyāyana, who is free from the scent of impurity?"
They spoke further: "Forgive us, O goddess;
no one shall show you disrespect. She replied: "If you will do exactly as you did for the noble Mahākātyāyana."
They said, "O goddess, forgive us;
we shall do something even more distinguished.
She granted them her forgiveness.
They also rendered the Venerable Mahākātyāyana even more distinguished honor.
Having spent the rainy season retreat there, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana took the boy Śyāmāka, addressed a deity, and set out on his journey.
She said, "Noble sir,"
"Give me some token so that I may remain there, having made a memorial," he said.
He gave her a garment from Kāśī.
Having cast it there, she established a stūpa and inaugurated a festival; thus, the name "Kāśīmaha, Kāśīmaha" came to be known.
Even today, monks who pay homage to the caityas venerate it.
Meanwhile, the boy Śyāmāka, clinging to the corner of a robe and hanging down, was seen by cowherds and shepherds.
They let out a loud cry, "He hangs! He hangs!
In that district, the people came to be known by the name Lambakapāla.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana arrived at a certain small town.
There, having placed the boy Śyāmāka at the foot of a tree, he entered [the town] for alms.
Now, in that small town, the king, who was childless, had passed away.
The citizens and countryfolk gathered together and said: "Sirs,..."
"Which king shall we consecrate?
Thereupon, some said, "He who is renowned for his great merit.
Others said, "How is he to be identified?"
Others said, "Let experts be employed. They were then employed by them, and those experts began to search here and there.
488.017. They saw that he had fallen asleep beneath the tree.

488.017. They began to observe his physical signs, and as they looked, they saw that the shadows of the other trees were slanting toward the east and leaning toward the east. 488.018. [But] the shadow of this tree remained directly beneath it.
"The shadow of that tree does not leave the body of this boy Śyāmaka. Having seen this, they began to speak among themselves: "Sirs, this is a being of great power through merit."
"Let us consecrate him," they said.
Having been awakened by them, he was told: "Child, accept the kingdom."
He said, "I do not desire the kingdom;
I am an attendant to the noble Mahākātyāyana.
This was heard by the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
He began to reflect:
"Does this boy possess the karmic actions conducive to becoming a king, or not?
He saw that they do exist.
He said, "Son,
accept the kingdom;
however, you must administer it according to the Dharma."
He accepted it; he was consecrated in the kingdom by them,
and thus the kingdom was ruled by the boy Śyāmāka.
The designation "Kingdom of Śyāmāka, Kingdom of Śyāmāka" came into being.
The venerable Mahākātyāyana arrived at Vokkāṇa.
In Vokkāṇa, the mother of the venerable Mahākātyāyana had been reborn.
Upon seeing the venerable Mahākātyāyana, she said: "After a long time, I see my dear son."
"Ah, after such a long time, I behold my little son!
At that moment, streams of milk flowed from her breasts.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana comforted her, calling out, "Mother! Mother!"
She fed the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Having understood her disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the venerable Mahākātyāyana gave her a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, she shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truths, she uttered this inspired utterance three times: "Venerable Sir, what has been done for us by you is not something that could have been done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins.
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up."
The mountains of bones have been leaped over;
the gates to the states of woe have been closed; the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened.
"We have been established among the Devamauṣyas. And he said:
"That which must be done by a good son who performs difficult deeds for his mother,"
By that act, you have caused my mind to be intent upon liberation.
"Having rescued you from the miserable states of existence and established you in heaven with great effort, O son, you have done well; your deed was virtuous."
Then the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having established that noble maiden in the truths, said: "Mother, look upon me with favor;
I am going."
She said, "Son,
if that is so, give me something with which I may perform worship and remain."
He gave her a staff.
She erected a stūpa and placed that [image] upon it;
thus, it became known as the Yaṣṭistūpa (Staff Stūpa).
Even now, the monks who worship the caityas continue to pay their respects.
Then the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, desiring to go to the Middle Country, arrived at the Indus River.
Then the deity who dwelt in the Northern Region said this to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Noble One,..."
"Give me also some token, so that I may remain here having performed worship to it.
He reflected: "The Blessed One has stated that in the Middle Country, images (pula) are not to be maintained."
489.015. "Therefore, I shall give these to you.
He gave them to her. Having had an altar constructed by her, they were installed there; thus, the name Itacarasaṃtisā came into being.
The venerable Mahākātyāyana arrived at Śrāvastī in due course.
When he was seen by the monks, they said to him, "Welcome, welcome, venerable sir! Is all well with your practice of virtue?"
He said, "Venerable ones, there is the practice of ease and there is the practice of hardship.
The monks asked, "What is the practice of ease? What is the practice of hardship?"
He said: "That which was done for the sake of sentient beings is a practice of happiness;
that King Śikhaṇḍī, the people residing in Rauruka, and I were all buried under dust."
The two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhiruka, escaped with great difficulty,
saying, "This is a life of suffering.
Then, O monks, the Pāṭhas, speaking reproachfully, said, "He is a slayer of his father!"
By that [means], the Venerable Rudrāyaṇa attained arhatship.
As for the statement that "one who commits an act of violence is executed," this is merely a figurative expression regarding him.
"There will be another fruit."

The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Rudrāyaṇa, such that he was reborn into a wealthy family of great riches and great enjoyments;
and having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, how did he realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions?"
"And yet, having attained arhatship, he was killed by a weapon?

The Blessed One said: "By the monk Rudrāyaṇa, actions were performed and accumulated; their conditions have been met, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
By Rudrāyaṇa, actions were performed and accumulated."
489.028. Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.

Actions performed and accumulated— whether wholesome or unwholesome— do not ripen in the fire element nor in the wind element; rather, they ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
"Karmas do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.

Having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. Thus it was said. "Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during the appearance of Blessed Buddhas, there were Pratyekabuddhas."

There arise those who are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, who are like the horn of a rhinoceros, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world. 490.005. Now, in a certain small town (karvaṭaka) there lived a man named Labdha. Not far from that town was a well, which served as a dwelling place for many deer.

There, that hunter day after day set down numerous snares and poisoned traps for the purpose of destroying, killing, and bringing ruin through misconduct upon many deer. And those snares and poisoned traps of his were unfailing.
Now, a certain *pratyekabuddha*, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small town and stayed overnight in a temple.
490.009. Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he arrived at that market town (*karvaṭaka*). He entered that market town for alms.
Then, having wandered for alms, he reflected: "This temple of the gods is crowded during the day."
"I shall take my alms at a quiet spot outside the village.
Having departed from the village, thinking, "This is quiet, this is quiet," he approached that well.
Having approached it, he set aside his bowl-washing basin in a secluded spot, washed his feet, and rinsed his hands.

Having strained the drinking water, gathered withered leaves, sat down, and made a determination regarding his meal, he washed his hands, his face, and his bowl; having set aside the bowl-rinsing water in its proper place and washed his feet, he took recourse at the foot of a certain tree, assumed the cross-legged posture— coiled like the body of the sleeping king of serpents— and sat down with a tranquil deportment.
On that day, not even a single deer was caught due to the human scent. Then, that hunter rose early in the morning and approached the well. He began to inspect those snares and traps.
He did not see even a single deer.
This thought occurred to him: "These snares, traps, and glue-pastes of mine have never failed;
what is the reason that not even a single deer has been caught today?"
He began to search the vicinity of that well.
He saw human footprints. Following those footprints, he went along.
He saw that Pratyekabuddha sitting with a peaceful deportment. He reflected: "These renunciants, having tranquil selves, take delight in such places as these.
If I do not deprive him of his life this very day,"
"He will certainly bring about the destruction of my livelihood;
in every way, he must be killed.

With this thought, that man of merciless heart, having abandoned all concern for the next world, drew his bow back to his ear in the shape of a hand and struck him in a vital spot with a poisoned arrow.
That great-souled Pratyekabuddha reflected: "Lest this poor man, being greedy, should become utterly wounded and ruined. Thinking, "I shall grant him a lift for his hand," he acted accordingly.
Like a king of swans with outstretched wings, he rose high into the air and began to perform the miracles of blazing, scorching, raining, and flashing lightning.
The supernatural power of an ordinary person is quickly captivating;
like a tree cut at its roots, he fell at his feet and said, "Descend, descend, O truly worthy recipient of offerings!"
"Please grant me, who am submerged in the mire of the afflictions, a hand to pull me out.
Out of compassion for him, he descended;
then, he was made free from the arrow by him.
He harbored resentment and said, "Noble sir,
let us go to our home."
"If even a single gold coin must be given here, I shall provide it.
He reflected: "Whatever was to be attained by me with this putrid body, that I shall now attain by entering the peaceful realm of nirvana without remainder."
490.031. Having risen once more into the expanse of the sky before him and displayed various miraculous feats, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).
490.032. He was found to be wealthy;
therefore, [the king] had a funeral pyre constructed with all kinds of fragrant wood and cremated him.
That funeral pyre was extinguished with milk.
Those bones were placed in a new jar, and a reliquary stupa for the body was established.
Canopies, banners, and flags were raised.

491.002. Having placed perfumes, garlands, and incense upon the water-jar and prostrating at his feet, he made this aspiration: "Since I have committed an injury toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may I not be a partaker of the result of this karma.
But as for the service that was performed..."
"By this root of merit, may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; may I become a possessor of such qualities as these,
and may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him."
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the hunter, is none other than this monk Rudrāyaṇa.
Because he struck a Pratyekabuddha in a vital spot with a poisoned arrow,"
As the ripening of that karma, he was boiled in the hells for many hundreds of years and many thousands of years;
even there, he was struck in a vital organ with a poisoned arrow in that very well.
By the remainder of that same karma, even now, though he had attained arhatship, he was slain by a weapon.

491.011. Again, monks, having become filled with doubt, they questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Śikhaṇḍin, the body of people residing in Rauruka, and the venerable Mahākātyāyana, by which they were buried under dust?"
"Did Hiru and Bhiru, the two ministers, flee?

The Blessed One said, "Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by them."
491.015. Who else shall experience [the result]? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the air element,
but rather in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases alone do performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
491.020. Long ago, monks, a householder lived in a certain small town.
He took a wife from a family of equal status. He played, delighted, and enjoyed himself with her.
491.021. While he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him.
491.022. Again, while he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a daughter was born to him.
Eventually, a certain *pratyekabuddha*, wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small town.
491.023. Suitor-boys come to those girls who are marriageable, but no one comes to her.
491.024. No one at all comes to her.

491.024. When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, dwelling in remote lodgings, and are the sole objects of offerings for the world.
491.025. Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small village.
491.026. Meanwhile, after that girl had swept the house, she threw the refuse over the top of the enclosure wall.
As that Pratyekabuddha was walking for alms, it fell upon his head. That girl saw it falling,
yet no thought of regret arose within her.
"No, it was not so.
On that very same day, a beggar arrived.
She was asked by her brother: 'What did you do today, that no beggars came to you?'"
She replied, "I applied a consecrated powder upon it, and because of that,
it blossomed.
Then the girl informed another girl.
She too developed this evil view regarding this world:
"Whosoever comes as a petitioner,
let her throw refuse upon that Pratyekabuddha."

"All those great-souled Pratyekabuddhas are afraid of being treated with disrespect. Having said this, he departed from that mountain retreat and began to cast insults upon the sages who possessed the five superknowledges.
They also departed.
Then they began to cast [the blame] upon their parents.
In that small town, two householders lived who were equals.
She was told by them: "Sirs, this false dharma is spreading; desist from it!"
492.004. Having been dissuaded by those two, they desisted.
"What do you think, monks? That girl who threw refuse upon the pratyekabuddha was none other than this Śikhaṇḍin.
And that body of people residing in the Karvaṭaka village..."
This very group of people residing in Rauruka is that same body of people.
Because they conceived and harbored evil, poisonous views toward the Pratyekabuddhas, as the ripening of that karma, they have been buried under dust.
The householder who was prevented by those two is none other than these two chief ministers, Hiru and Bhiru.
It was as the ripening of that karma that they fled.

He who was the brother of that girl by whom it was covered with dust is none other than this monk Kātyāyana. Because of the ripening of that karma of having covered it with dust, he has been buried under sand.
492.011. If his mind had not been scattered by that, nor overwhelmed by dust;
492.011. if an evil view had not arisen within him.
"Even the monk Kātyāyana would have met with disaster through misconduct, being overwhelmed by the dust.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those who are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned entirely black actions and those that are mixed, you should apply yourself exclusively to entirely white actions.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The monks rejoiced at the words spoken by the Blessed One.
492.017. Thus ends the Rudrāyaṇa-avadāna in the glorious Divyāvadāna.

********** Avadāna 38 ********** 493.001. Divyāvadāna 38: The Story of Maitrakanyaka/ 493.002. Living beings who commit harm against their mothers fall here itself into the abyss of calamity; therefore, by virtuous persons whose minds are constantly filled with love, faith, and great respect, mothers [should be honored].

493.003. Thus it is heard: there was once a caravan leader named Mitra, adorned with a multitude of virtues like a garland of blooming white water-lilies, moons, and kunda flowers; one who had accumulated in previous lives an immeasurable, faultless, and vast store of all the requisites for enlightenment; a treasury of jewels equal to Kubera, the god of wealth; and a mass of noble riches and essentials enjoyed by his own kin, the poor, and beggars.
The vast riches of that noble being became even more abundant, delightful solely in their essence of benefiting others;
like the rays of the new moon on a clear autumn night, they were as pure as white water-lilies.
The minds of those possessed by hope had been burnt in many ways by the winds of craving and the fierce flames of grief;
he extinguished them with the sprinkling of the water of generosity, which was delightful through its affectionate nature.

493.015. Having seen this world—its festive joy of giving abandoned out of fear for the loss of wealth, its noble intentions corrupted by being under the sway of the demoness of worldly affliction—he gave wealth out of compassion to the protectorless, the wretched, the weak, and the sick; and he considered his own life to be exceedingly fickle, like the waves of a turbulent ocean. (3)

493.019–493.021. Those objects in which the minds of others become entangled—objects as terrifying as the coils of the wives of the best of serpents, which plunge those who have acquired them into a pit of sin whose interior cavities are formidable with the flames of blazing fire;

objects that flicker like the lashes on the eyes of the finest women of men dancing to the force of the wind—the King bestowed these through gifts that were skilled in pacifying the suffering of supplicants. //4//

493.023. Therefore, because of the nature of sons as wealth, whenever the glories of sons— longed for by those desiring offspring and repeatedly manifested through hundreds of desires— are forcibly brought to an end by the great fire of all-consuming death, which has its fuel in the most intense flames of enmity and possesses a terrible power that admits of no remedy, they become solely intent upon their final dissolution.

When he, having set out upon the path by means of mere worldly rumor, began to petition specific deities— such as Dhanada, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śaṅkara, Janārdana, and Pitāmaha— for the sake of a son; in whichever lake of a son, filled with clear water, there arose growth for the lotus of the glory of his great lineage that had emerged in the forest.
493.029. Each of those things of his turns into intense bitterness; I think it is like the sun drying up water with its clusters of sharp rays—the orb of fortune being like the sun's disk. //5//

Seeking a son, he went for refuge to Rudra—who bears a crown of many skulls, who holds the discus as his weapon, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the creator, the one whose banner is the sea-monster, the son of the Mountain’s Daughter, and whose seat is the peacock—as well as to those various gods whose waters are as white as the conch-shell petals of the Gaṅgā; furthermore, he gave abundant gifts to the twice-born.
Whatever auspicious teachings people followed, and whatever hardships they underwent through vows and fasts—
with their minds immersed in the desire to achieve success in obtaining sons and wealth— they cast aside their weariness and performed those various acts.

494.009. When, despite these auspicious vows and fasts that caused manifold physical and mental exhaustion, his sons never at any time returned to life, then a certain virtuous man spoke to him as he was sinking into the waters of a vast and deep river of grief: 494.012. "It is karma alone that sustains all the prosperity of embodied beings."
But for living beings, a fall from a lofty peak does not lead to well-being.
494.014. Many have fallen into affliction because their minds were tormented by longing for a son. 494.015. Yet they do not live even now; why, then, do you distress yourself? (9)
494.016. Having been liberated from their karmas, how could the inhabitants of heaven abandon their births out of mere satisfaction?
494.018. Those who cannot obtain an individual existence without certain [causes], how could they undergo birth without those very causes? (10)

494.020. Those who are embraced by the creeping vines of the blazing flames of the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra generally seek the happiness of humans, gods, and nāgas through means such as generosity.
494.022. By whom are you, dull-witted man, being mocked? You are like one crazed with the hope for a son who desires to reach heaven by relying on a flight of stairs that are far too large! //12//
494.024. I shall instruct you in another rite for the sake of success; you too should perform it at some point for the sake of complete accomplishment.
494.026. If a daughter is born to you, proclaim her name throughout this entire realm for the sake of renown. (13)
Then, after some time, she gave birth to a son who, like the sun-girt orb, illuminated the vault of heaven with his own mass of rays, and who was the glory of his own lineage.
And he—whose radiant splendor was as white as a slice from the peak of a mountain of pure, refined gold; whose broad and brilliant head was like the perfectly full and stainless orb of the moon.

Furthermore, his form shone with the marks that were delightful and as brilliant as a clearly manifest, quivering rainbow—marks produced by the power of great merit accumulated over many thousands of eons; it was like a beautiful golden peak fallen from the earth, entwined by sprouts of jewels emitting a dense mass of their own rays.
With hair as lovely and dark as rows of bees and yaks' tails, a broad and even forehead, and a beautiful,
prominent nose— the father, with a joyful heart, announced to the world ten days later that his son was named Maitrakanya.
With various foods and drinks that promote the growth of embodied beings, abundant and of superior quality,
she attained prosperity like the shore of the ocean under the moonbeams as white as nectar.
Reared by nurses with milk and the cream of clarified butter,
he caused his beautiful body to grow like a lotus situated in a lake.
Then his father, the caravan leader Mitra, having loaded goods onto a ship with the merchants, entered the great ocean with joy.

In the ocean whose waves were increased by the agitation caused by the *timiṃgila* fish, where vessels were destroyed by sea monsters, when his father had passed away, he said to his mother: "What deed did my father perform? (20)
Then his mother, her heart withered by the grief of separation from her husband, fell into deep reflection:
"Drawn by hundreds of snares of hope, one does not see death, just like an elephant; one who is wretched for the taste of sense-objects does not see their bondage, just like an elephant. (21)
"Even though I speak of my father as being on a ship, he too,
due to my own dullness, will meet his destruction in the ocean."

As long as this entire world does not ask him about the true nature of livelihood in this realm and does not explain it to him, it is right for me to restrain this son of mine while he is still within the jaws of death, caught in the thickets of various sufferings and calamities, and afflicted by disease. (23)

496.001. <496> Even another person who, having abandoned the path frequented by virtuous people, resorts to a wrong path, should be restrained from his own misguided opinion by others with great effort; how much more so, then, one's own son? //24//
Then his mother said:
"Son, your father supported me by means of the pig-herding trade. If I am to be made happy, you should perform the ornamentation of the pigs. (25)
496.008. Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having bowed his head to his mother’s words as if they were a garland of flowers, set out on another day for the butcher’s shop.
496.010–011. For that great being, who possessed a vast store of merit and was compassionate toward all creatures, on that first day, four kārṣāpaṇas’ worth of wealth was acquired. (26)
496.012. Rejoicing, he gave that wealth to his mother, who was suffering from the burden of carrying him in her womb;
496.014. wealth that cuts through the calamity of the suffering of poverty and brings forth the fruit of great enjoyment. (27)

496.016. Now, those who were long-established butchers in that excellent city, their minds won over by his increasing success through the principle of impartial commercial conduct and by his natural kindness and charm, saw that Great Being approaching for the sake of business and [withdrew] him from that trade.
To turn him back, they said:
"In former times, there was a merchant-guild leader in this city who was a perfumer;
you were he. Why do you abandon that livelihood and resort to another with such a mindset? (28)
496.021. Then the Bodhisattva, having abandoned even that livelihood, established a perfumer’s shop.
496.022. On the very day that the virtuous man established the perfumer’s shop, 496.023.
eight kārṣāpaṇas were produced for him on that very same day. (29)
He gave that too to his mother.
Then the men who were perfume shopkeepers gathered together and approached the Great Being, attempting to dissuade him:
"The perfume shop was indeed not established by our father in this city; it has been taken over by eunuchs."
Having become a goldsmith right there, O virtuous one, he acquired vast amounts of wealth.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having abandoned even that livelihood, established a goldsmith's shop.
By means of that trade, he surpassed all those other goldsmiths in business practice;
on his very first day, he obtained sixteen highly valuable *kārṣāpaṇas* and gave them away.
On the second day, having earned thirty-two kārṣāpaṇas,
he gave those as well to his mother for the sake of a distinguished recipient of offerings.
Then, a group of men who were goldsmiths and money-changers gathered together and approached him, speaking in order to turn him away from that work:
"Having been born into a family as white as the rays of the autumn moon, how is it that you have resorted to this wretched livelihood for the sake of a living? (33)
In a fire made terrifying by flames fanned by the wind, with sparks flying about, it is far more praiseworthy for men to turn away from it than to fall away from their own proper conduct. (34)
Your father plunged into the turbulent ocean, its waves violently churned by the hissing of great serpents, and having reached its bottomless depths, he acquired this wealth for you. (35)

Since you, a clever man who follows the ways of the world, have now undertaken this action out of a desire for wealth, how could you not attain a full measure of good fortune and the vast prosperity of your father once he has passed away? (36)

Even the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) could not sustain his hopes for true purpose through the vast expansion of his riches before her, whose fame is as pure as that of Mahendra; how is it that you, the son of such a woman, do not feel shame? (37)
497.024. Those who do not count death, who do not swallow calamity as their prey, O sinless one, who are diligent and whose hearts are free from attachment to home, kinsmen, and sons;

497.026. those wise ones who, having crossed oceans of unfathomable waters terrifying with whirlpools, and having attained their goals, pervade the world with fame white as the tusks of an elephant. (38)

497.028. Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, having understood that their speech was likewise appropriate, resolved to embark upon the ocean and approached his mother, saying: "Mother, our father was formerly a caravan leader; therefore, grant me your permission. 497.029. "Grant me your leave."
"When even I am about to embark upon the great ocean," she thought.

Previously, her hope for life had already departed due to the sorrow of her husband’s death; now, as if her heart were being violently torn apart by the weapon of grief at the separation from her son—a separation so cruel it was not even anticipated—she cried out:
"My child, who has told you this, without cause, as if he were an enemy?"
Whose life is undesirable to you? Who is playing with you? (39)
"By some stroke of fate, you have today somehow restored one eye to me;
yet now, you are being carried away by death, which has made me a sharer in the suffering of losing a son."
498.003. "As long as this thorn of my suffering has not been destroyed by tearing through my grief, 498.005.
how can a second one be cast upon me by enemies consisting of evil? (41)
Those whose minds are unshakable by various bitter labors and sufferings, yet who—possessing pitiable hearts and greedy for enjoyments—have abandoned their lives;
they, having abandoned their relatives whose faces are wet with streams of tears falling from their eyes, go to destruction through death in the abode of Makara, the ocean.

Therefore, how can you make the effort to depart, abandoning me—me who am without a protector, who must be cared for, and whose life is bound solely to the hope of your survival? Let not such a thought arise; let not my words be disregarded.
"498.015. One cannot achieve absolute happiness by entering a state that puts one's own life at risk.
498.017. Since this is how the wealth of merchants is acquired, my son, I dissuade you from it in this manner."

498.019. For her benefit, he cast aside even those flower-like words, though sweet, as if they were mere straw; and with boldness, he uttered this somewhat boastful reply: 498.021. "It would be better indeed if those people who are born were never born at all—those people who are destitute.
If there must be suffering for one who is born, death is better than life. (45)
498.023–498.024. Having come to my house with hope, these wretched and miserable ascetics, seeking wealth from me, a sinner, depart sighing and dejected in mind. (46)
498.025. Those embodied beings who lack the power to acquire wealth and the like endure hundreds of sufferings.
498.027. Furthermore, I cannot bear to watch for long as this world is tormented by hundreds of miseries. (47)
"Therefore, I shall disregard your words; I will go there, so you must abandon your grief.
I shall either meet my death right there in the ocean, or I shall sever the calamity of these people."
499.001. Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, disregarding his mother, departed from his home and proclaimed himself a caravan leader in the city of Vārāṇasī:
499.003. "In this very city, which rivals the city of Indra, there once lived a merchant named Mitra, whose banner of fame was celebrated among both gods and men.
499.005. 'On this very day, his son shall set out for the great ocean. Let those merchants who have prepared their equipment be ready to depart. (49)

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka set forth, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants who had gathered various provisions and equipment, who were auspicious for their departure on a chosen day, and who had presented various auspicious offerings.
When his mother heard that he was going, she said, "My only son," and so on.

"Where will you go? she cried, her voice reduced to nothing but the most piteous of lamentations; with her lotus-like hands—tender, stainless, and languidly graceful like the petals of a lotus—she struck her chest, which was radiant with beautiful breasts as large as jars fashioned from fine gold and with thighs of equal splendor.
Her throat was choked by the continuous flow of streams of tears, and the mass of her hair was darkened by the rows of water-laden clouds scattered by the force of the wind.
Hurrying with great speed, he approached and embraced the feet of the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, saying: "Do not, do not abandon me, my son, as you depart!
For men whose intellects are deluded by the grasp of harmful passion see only what is not beneficial.
Even the words of those who speak the truth, whose minds are intent on performing what is beneficial for the virtuous, are not heard [by the wicked]. //50//
499.018. Maitrakanyaka, his mind filled with rage, struck his mother—who was prostrate on the ground and overcome by grief—on the head with the thunderbolt of his foot.
499.021. His sorrow having been repeatedly intensified, driven by his own karma, he became quick-witted and set out to travel with the merchants. (51)
Then his mother rose up and said: "My son, since I am now intent on stopping your journey, let there be no further accumulation of demerit for me from the striking of my head.
May you never again suffer the infinite fruit of such an act; do not transgress the words of your guru even in a dream."

499.028. Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, wandering through various delightful monasteries, abodes, mountains, groves, thickets, rivers, ponds, gardens, and many cities, market towns, and forest villages, eventually reached the seashore and prepared his ship.

He descended into the ocean—a sea whose vast, pure waters were agitated by the powerful winds issuing from the mouths of the lords of serpents; whose surface was colored by the red hue of the radiance of clusters of rubies as beautiful as the mass of rays of the young morning sun; whose waves were fierce with the breaking of lofty surges tossed up by the waters struck against the peaks of mountains that had crouched down in fear of the falling thunderbolt, which was terrifying with the rows of flames of fire flickering from the palms of the hands of the Lord of Asuras wielding his sword; a sea that seemed to leap into the sky with its shimmering, towering waves tossed up by great gales.
It was as if being seized by the playful movements of its arms—the rushing currents of the waters of a thousand rivers.
500.005–007. The mass of waters was tossed and turned by the terrifying coils of agitated hooded serpents;
upon their heads, the clusters of waves were drenched by masses of rays emerging from jewels and by a multitude of flames.
500.009–500.011. [He saw] the conch shell, terrifying from the burning of the fierce fire of poison released by the bite of the lord of serpents;
and that mountain, its peaks split by the thunderbolt-like claws of the *timi* fish, with its masses of aquatic creatures struck down by the waters falling from its base. //55//
Its shores were raised by towering waves, where swans settled and uttered soft cries;
its fish were fierce, wounded by the claws of swans, and the shoreline trembled as the fish turned over.
The conch is radiant, covered by jewel-vines, its whiteness increased by the rays of the moon;
it is fierce with the great terror of aged serpents, and its wheel is struck by a fierce, great makara.
500.021. With the thunderbolt-like claws of the Lord of Birds playfully striking and tearing open the root-holes of the trees, [the forest] appeared as follows.

500.025. Perceiving that very place, which was marked by lines reaching to the shore, and where circles of schools of fish and serpents were whirling about in the interior of deep and formidable pits, he—whose body was as vast as a mountain peak—crossed over that abode of waters, which possessed manifold wonders and extraordinary excellence.

As the ship of Makarakaripati was being overwhelmed by great masses of water— rising up with forms as formidable as mountains and terrifying with the clamor of released shrieks— the vessel, along with its crew whose limbs were failing from the despair of fear for death and who were intent solely on wretched weeping and crying out,
began to sink together into the depths of the ocean.

500.030–500.032. With fierce waves as high as mountains, possessing the violent force of the winds at the end of an eon, that ship was battered by the surging masses of water in the ocean and torn asunder in its midst.
501.001. <501> In the mouth-cavity of the fish, terrifying with its fangs, a certain ascetic died, crying out in distress.
501.003. Others, their throats constricted by the surging water, passed away from lack of breath, their voices silenced. (60)

501.005. Even after traveling some distance, some, looking toward the shore of the ocean with great planks, were afflicted by the exhaustion of the long journey through the waters; agitated by fear, they raised a loud cry. //61//

501.009. Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, despite that great onset of calamity, his mind undisturbed by fear, despondency, dejection, or exhaustion, summoned a great measure of fortitude and prowess;
and taking up a plank with haste, he set out.
501.010. Thereupon, by means of those water-floats, which moved with a graceful motion produced by the speed of the steady wind, he drifted here and there.

Being tossed about and with his lotus-like eyes and face fading from lack of food, after many other days and nights, he somehow reached the southern shore of that great ocean whose waters were so difficult to fathom.
Having crossed that bottomless sea and reached the shore, he cast away the plank.
501.016. Recalling his mother’s words, he pressed his head against her hands and spoke as follows: //62//

Those men who do not listen to the words of their teachers—which are for their own welfare, aimed at the arising of benefit, and conducive to auspicious action—these calamities bring upon them and prevail over their heads. (63)

By those very same wise ones who honor the words of their teachers in this world, the fruit of the tree of birth—which yields manifold misfortunes and is as fragile as the reflection of the moon in water—has been attained. (64)
For me, a doer of evil deeds, who has transgressed the words of my mother—who is ever-striving for my very welfare—when will this flower, so heavy with sin and terrible, reach its final fruit? (65)

501.030–032. How is it that I, a wicked man, who bears upon my heavy head the thunderbolt of your feet—a thunderbolt more terrifying than the extreme edges of a fire-scorched line, more fierce than one fallen in its course, and more utterly formidable than a bolt of lightning—did not shatter the earth and fall into the abyss of a chasm? (66)

502.001. <502> Those virtuous ones who, with clear intellect, carry out the words of those who speak for their welfare, will certainly attain the highest good, just as [the inhabitants] did in the city of the flesh-eaters.

502.003. But those who, having abandoned speech that is beloved for its great meaning and essence, resort to other [words], fall into an ocean of calamity difficult to cross; they grieve just as I do.
Then, proceeding by degrees, he followed along the edge of a dense forest thicket consisting of *khadira*, *sarala*, *nicula*, *bakula*, *tamāla*, *tāla*, and coconut trees;

a place difficult to traverse due to various thickets of *mālula* creepers that had been trampled and crushed by the tusks of excellent elephants, boars, yak-cows, *śarabhas*, *śambaras*, and buffaloes;

a place where the feet of forest-dwelling creatures were startled by the fear of the roars of agitated lions; and a place whose borders were, with great difficulty, untrodden by the feet of Śabara men.
Stopping at one point, he spoke thus:
"These monkeys, their faces as red as pomegranate blossoms, have let out a great clamor; they are fearless, displaying rows of teeth with their laughter and appearing loathsome.
Having struck down snakes—terrible with the fierce flames flickering from their poisonous fire—with their palms, they now move about helpless, surely terrified by their own hissing."

502.013–502.015. At the base of lovely sandalwood trees—cool with a thick carpet of shade, covered in soft blue grass, and strewn with clusters of clearly visible blossoms—these delighted *kiṃnaras*, their hearts captivated by the music, sing joyfully to the accompaniment of flutes and the sweet sounds of cymbals that provide rhythmic interludes. (69)
Then, having traveled not very far, he saw a mountain with the form of a preeminent lord of the earth.
In some places, it was filled with the movement of terrifying caves made fragrant by the intensely beautiful luster of jewels;
in other places, it resounded with the songs of soaring *kiṃnaras*, awakening the families of *nāgas* in their agitation. (70)
502.022. With flowering trees swaying in the restless wind atop its temple-like summit, and with bees hovering there;
502.024. Its mountain caves filled with the humming of bees, and its hollows inhabited by a multitude of fierce serpents. (71)

The mountain peak was adorned with birds, and upon its rocky plateaus sat perfected beings (siddhas); its lovely groves were frequented by the wives of the siddhas, and intoxicated birds dwelt within those thickets.
Delightful with the sweet, soft cries of intoxicated peacocks, with lions emerging from the mouths of lovely caves,
with elephants agitated by fear at the roar of the lions, and with breezes fragrant with the rut-fluid of elephants— 73.
In some places, its slopes were scarred by thunderbolts that struck the tips of the tusks of elephants gathered there, while forests of *śikhāguru* trees grew in full splendor;

in other places, its beautiful banks were variegated by the plumages displayed by flocks of peacocks, who were colored by the sounds of thunder vibrating through the weight of the clouds above; and in yet other places, its peaks and ridges were perfumed by the abundance of flowers, as fragrant blossoms fell from trees shaken by the wind.
503.004. Furthermore, he saw another— 503.005.
painting the sky with a network of formidable peaks, casting away the darkness of oceans with his rays; 503.007.
bearing a mountain as heavy as a cloud-clad garment, and in some places shedding streams of golden water. (75)

May the mountain—its peaks and ridges adorned with groves of trees, its slopes graced by the wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees laden with ripe *āmalaka* fruits, and its summits where pairs of celestial nymphs sport sweetly with their mates—protect you. (76)

In some places, it possessed a multitude of many great jewel-sprouts, made terrifying by the mass of rays shattered by the falling wheels of the great chariot of the sun; in other places, it bore a bearer of the blazing vajra, who was bowed down and raised up by the weight of crowns.

In some places, its rocks were washed by the waters of the celestial river, where swarms of trembling kalahaṃsa geese—like pearl necklaces—were tossed about by the waves of Indra’s lordly elephant as he trampled through them.

In other places, it bore the coils of serpents drawn forth from the surface of the ocean waters, which had been split open by the vajra-like arms of the great yakṣas raised in the playful sport of the king of the egg-born (the Garuda).
In some places, there were great circular moats with waves of blood flowing from the great asuras who had fled after being struck down by weapons in the battle between the gods and the asuras. //77//
Having seen this, he spoke as follows:

"These lions, whose beauty is like the glow of the sun's fresh red rays and who have gathered on the ground beneath the shade of trees and mountain peaks, are out of pride looking at an elephant whose temples are being licked by bees restless with ichor, as they tear it apart with great force. (78)

503.026. Thus, wandering through that most formidable wilderness, subsisting solely on water and fruit, he beheld a city named Ramaṇaka—the Lord of the Three Worlds having arisen from the mire of saṃsāra—appearing as if the world were veiled by the thick darkness of ignorance.
503.028. [It was adorned] with lofty, towering, and fluttering banners, resounding with the cries of birds swooping down.
503.030. With houses shaped like mountains, featuring golden walls and peaks of jewels and gold, and well-guarded; //79//

In some places, it was exceedingly captivating with massive trees whose branches were entwined by creepers of gems and gold; where lotuses, marked by bees and swarms of bees resting upon them, were tinged yellow by the pollen of blooming lotuses; where the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) seemed to rival the trunks of celestial elephants; and where emerald grasses were as blue as the feathers of parrots.

With golden palaces as white as blooming *navakarnikāra* flowers, variegated with many jeweled peaks, it bore the entire splendor of the Lord of Mountains, whose broad jewel-summit was radiant with its own rays of light. (82)
In one place, it was delightful with the sounds of great drums struck by the fingertips of celestial nymphs.
Then, having gained hope for life from that sight, he approached the city of Ramaṇa.
Emerging from that city, four *apsarases* appeared, their forms as pure and radiant as the hue of molten, fresh gold.

The daughters of Maitraka possessed the playful charm of a pair of lotus-eyes with the luster of blooming water-lilies; their slow and graceful gait was accentuated by the radiance of various beautiful jeweled girdles that tinkled as they moved;

their slender waists were bent under the weight of broad hips resembling golden jars; the sprout-like lips on their faces were radiant like the petals of a lotus awakened from its withered state by the touch of the sun’s rays;
they were adorned with hundreds of diverse ornaments, possessed a flawless appearance, and held lotus-blossoms joined as cupped hands upon their heads.

As he placed his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva, they said: "Welcome, O you whose face is like the moon, who increase the joy of the womenfolk; welcome, O you whose mind is refreshed by the nectar of compassion, and who have long been firmly resolved upon awakening. (84)
This very day our sufferings have come to rest; this very day our life has attained its essence. This very day, auspicious joys characterized by a special and unerring love stand before us. (85)
504.029. These minds of ours, mangled by the goad of suffering and scarred by grief, have now blossomed upon encountering you, like the interiors of forests in the spring season. (86)
505.001. Whatever white deeds, resulting in auspicious outcomes, were accumulated by you in other previous existences—505.003.
the mere sight of them is sufficient for their fruit; why then do you prolong this attachment to me? //87//
505.005. Even today, for whom do there not exist the calamities consisting of talk about the grief of separation from kinsmen and friends?
505.007. We four are your celestial nymphs (apsaras); we are like your shadows, and you are not able to transgress us. //88//
505.009. There are jewels, radiant garments, most excellent beds and dwellings, and we ourselves; 505.011. there are husbands worthy of the king of the gods. O Vidhi, enjoy happiness here! //89//
Moreover:

Those who endure for a long time while remaining amidst great suffering that is terrible and beyond remedy, being bewildered by the onset of the burden of misery, go swiftly to their destruction right there. (90)
505.018. While permanent separation stands before them in the form of death, they grieve over separations caused by distance;
deluded by the onset of disease, they have fallen into a calamity resulting from the blows of desire. //91//

505.022–505.024. As he entered that city—which resembled a peak of the Golden Mountain, where the dwellings were being pointed out by excellent *apsarases* with their beautiful, tinkling anklets and girdles—many people there bowed with palms joined in reverence.
And others again thought:
"Is this the sun with its blazing rays, or is it the sun with its rays concealed? Is it the god of love, Puṣpaketu, who has suddenly descended?
Alas! Having cast down the sharp-pointed thunderbolt, what has become of the Lord of the Gods? Thus did they speculate. (93)
505.031. With faces like drawings in thick darkness, their eyelashes dark and fine, wearing bright golden necklaces and limbs radiant with set jewels;
506.001. standing at the lattice windows of the vast rows of palaces, others, their minds full of joy, cast down their loosened girdles. (94)

He entered the abode of those apsarases—a palace whose darkness was dispelled by jewel-lamps, whose floors were radiant with pearls, and where the clouds were pierced by the tips of fluttering banners. (95)
Playing with their graceful movements, playful gait, smiles, sidelong glances, and sweet chatter, his mind entirely overcome by passion, he did not perceive that time had passed. (96)
And every day they tried to prevent him from going toward the south. Yet, the more he was restrained,
the more his mind became eager to travel in that direction.
Wherever this world is restrained by a person of beneficial intent,
there the person with perverted intellect runs about in confusion.
506.015. If one were to act upon the beneficial advice of friends in this world, 506.016. one would go to heaven or to the netherworld (pātāla), and not even to a pit—even in a dream. (98)
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, his purpose for going unknown to those apsarases, set out upon the path toward the southern direction. As he traveled, he reached a city named Sadāmattaka.
From that city as well, eight apsarases emerged in great haste and led the Great Being inside.

Having experienced intense delight there for a very long time, and having had his actions of staying and departing forbidden by them, he continued on that same southern path and beheld a city named Nandana.
Therefore, sixteen *apsarases* approached him, paid him honor, and led him inside.
Having enjoyed amusements there for a long time, he departed from that place as well and proceeded to the city named Brahmottara.
There too, having enjoyed the pleasures of the senses with great hospitality provided by thirty-two *apsarases*, he said to them:
506.023. "I wish to go; therefore, ladies, do not lie in the lake of sorrow on my account.
For who indeed in this world does not possess miseries of separation, even when their successes are auspicious? (99)
"Even though we have remained together for so long, at the time of our end, there will surely be separation from you, who are like the enemy Death himself.
Therefore, with my cheeks still moistened by the tears from my eyes, I wish to depart today, leaving you behind. (100)
In this world of living beings, which is as turbulent as waves in an ocean struck by the wind and is terrifying with its manifold sufferings,
those who find delight in the pain of separation possess a mind more utterly deluded than any other.

Then all those apsarases, their hearts tormented by the grief of separation from him, hurriedly joined their palms like lotuses and water-lilies in full bloom upon their heads, as if they were lotus-pools. "How could he, whose form was to be grasped by none other, have taken our youth by surrendering his own body—he who was so dear to us, offered to us with devotion and affection? (102)
"O Lord, having gone to those three cities, you have now returned here as well; for a long time you have enjoyed the sweet pleasures of the senses and attained prosperity.
But you must not go back—what is the use of saying much more? If you go, you will remember our words when you have fallen into the ocean of calamity and are suffering. (103)
The Bodhisattva said:
"Since the rise of prosperity for men is stable through the power of habituation, how could they be prevented from it, or how indeed could they turn back from it? (104)
507.016. Those who are to be employed by enemies in whatever beneficial task is always at hand—those who provide restraint therein are enemies who exist in the guise of friends. //105//
Having obtained divine happiness in the city of Ramaṇaka, I was impelled by my karma and came here to enjoy supreme bliss, the realm of Sadāmattaka.
Having then reached the desired city of Nandana through the skill of my own actions, you have now been uprooted from your ground because of my arrival.
"Therefore, ladies, do not prevent my departure; for there is no misfortune for us.
Thinking, 'I shall obtain superior pleasures from this,' I have set out today.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, with disdain, treated even the beneficial words of those apsarases as if they were harmful.

Having disregarded him, he proceeded along that same southern path and beheld an iron city, formidable with four gates whose panels were fastened by massive bolts; it was encircled by high, broad walls of iron that could not be breached even by the Lord of the Gods; it was deep and terrifying, filled with the resounding roar of "da-ma-da-mā" emitted from the sight of the revolving circles of wheels turning within.
He then approached its gateway.
But as soon as he had arrived, at that very moment, the door burst open along with its heavy panels,
like the slope and hollow of the Vindhya mountain when its peaks are split apart by the edge of a thunderbolt.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka entered there. As soon as he had entered, at that very moment, the door— its panels and mechanisms firmly fixed—
was struck shut in an instant by the great winds produced by his own karma, as if by the tips of mighty arms.
508.010. And he heard a most terrifying roar, capable of striking fear into all people, rising from within the inner enclosure of the man whose heart was overwhelmed by intense agony.
508.011. Having heard it, the quick-witted one hurried to the gateway.
508.012. As soon as he had entered, a second door was slammed shut, blocking his way.
It was like the gate of the gods, as firm as a diamond, struck by the force of the winds at the end of time.
Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka entered. As soon as he had entered, however, the third door was found to have its panels and bolts secured.
In an instant, that entire city became agitated; terrified, he beheld it all in total turmoil.

Then the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka saw him— of immense and most dreadful appearance, embraced by a cruel garland of flames, his head being split asunder like wood by a great, revolving iron wheel that was terrifying to behold with its rows of flickering sparks and a dark, stormy mass of smoke scattered by a powerful, swift wind; his remaining life sustained only by the nourishment of the blood and marrow dripping from his own severed head.
Approaching him, he asked:

"Are you a nāga, a deva, a supreme kinnara, a yakṣa, or a human? Are you a soldier of the vidyādharas, or are you a daitya, or perhaps a piśāca? What extremely cruel deed did you yourself commit in previous lives, that you must now experience this fruit—a calamity so difficult to overcome that it makes one cry out? (112)
The man said:
"I am neither a *nāga*, nor a *yakṣa*, nor a god, nor a *daitya*; I am not even a king of the *gandharvas*.
I am neither a *rākṣasa* nor a *vidyādhara*. Know that our birth is equal to yours. (113)
The Bodhisattva said:
"What deed was committed by you, a person of evil mind wandering in the difficult prison of *saṃsāra*, such that this iron wheel, blazing like fire, revolves upon your head?
The man replied:

The Blessed Lady, who performs various difficult deeds and reveals the nature of saṃsāra, is intent upon producing the highest welfare and happiness therein; her disposition is bound by love for me. (114)

509.009. That which those of virtuous mind in the world proclaim as the supreme field for living beings, and by whose power even one burdened with unworthy acts becomes great—that mother of mine, O holy man, I, evil-minded as I was, struck on the head with my foot. Because of that, this iron wheel, blazing with fire, revolves upon my head. (115)
509.013. Then the Bodhisattva, his heart goaded by the whip of that man’s speech, beholding within himself that same contempt for others, said:
509.015. "I, of little intelligence, who am ignorant, have today censured myself whom I ought to despise.
How can I, being myself submerged in faults and virtues, mark out the world with those very same things? (116)"
509.019. Even by me, the lowest of men, an offense was committed against my mother, who was worthy of offerings;
509.021. it is to experience the fruits of that very sin that I have come here, having crossed over the expanse of water. //117//

509.023. Then, immediately after those words, from the expanse of the sky—which was as pure as the petals of a freshly blossomed blue lotus—there arose a deep and steady sound, resonant like the thundering of a water-laden cloud:
509.025–026. "Do you not see that the karmas of embodied beings are powerful?
Though one may dwell in the space between the worlds, one is dragged along as if by a rope. (118)

509.027. Those who are bound by the objects of the senses—that painful shackle consisting of strenuous labor—and who, having abandoned the words of their teachers, being blind in intellect, take refuge in evil;

509.029. Though released from those very actions by means of auspicious deeds, which are heroic in severing the painful shackles, these dull-witted beings, having attained human birth, remain far removed from liberation. //119//

509.031. Then, immediately after those words were spoken, that wheel—driven as if by the force of the winds of karma, fierce with the emission of a mass of crackling sparks of fire—rose up from his head and began to whirl, splitting open the head of the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka.
509.034. In an instant, he shone, his entire body bathed by streams of blood falling from his head.
510.001. <510> Like the body of Airāvaṇa falling down, its head split by the tip of a shattered discus. //120//
Then that man, crying out "Alas! Alas!", addressed the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, whose body was being overwhelmed by the intense agony born of the burning of his head:

"Having abandoned those other deeds which were charming with the songs of celestial maidens and which brought about the arising of joy in the mind, you have now reached this place of endless suffering. (121)
Who indeed, having attained a divine abode with incomparable auspicious enjoyments of celestial bliss,
would ever long for the terrifying pit of ruin, which is constantly filled with the flames of blazing fire?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Leaving behind forests crowded with the clamor of living beings and topped with blazing flowers, I have gone by that same desire-nature through which the *nāgas* endure calamity. (123)
Having abandoned kingdoms resplendent with vast wealth and the lotus-faces of women, many lords of men have died in battle; by that very same desire, I have gone forth. (124)

In the great ocean, fierce with its leaping and towering waves and filled with the roar released by swirling whirlpools of water— just as men go to their destruction therein, so too did I go by that same fickle will.

By that same unrestrained will, through which they cast aside the vows of the Lords of Sages— the path that accomplishes faultless and ultimate happiness, and the way to the attainment of the glory and bliss of gods and men— I have gone forth.
How can the dust from the feet of those sages, who are free from all suffering, be placed upon one's head—
those by whom the steep precipices of the directions, fierce with potent poison and terrifying with manifold miseries, have been crossed?

511.001. What could that suffering be so exceedingly intense, or what calamity such a source of manifold misery, that it should remain far away from one whose mental state is wounded by the poisonous fire of craving? (128)
Moreover, O virtuous one,
though I am far away, I am dragged by my past actions;
for karma drags living beings toward that very place where it yields its fruit.
Moreover:
"For how many thousands of years, and for how many hundreds of years, shall this blazing iron wheel revolve upon my head? (130)
The man said:
"For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
a blazing iron wheel shall revolve upon your head."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Who else, having cut through this mass blazing with a cluster of flames from a brilliant fire tawny like a crest of flame, would go astray and then return?
The man replied:
"Whoever comes here with the intention of doing harm to his mother, this [wheel] shall revolve upon his head; furthermore, it shall fall from your own head. (132)

Then the Bodhisattva, although his heart was agitated by that intense pain born from the burning of his head, gave rise to a profound resolve of compassion for infinite sentient beings and addressed that man: "Those yogins who have extinguished the entire darkness of the web of passion and afflictions and dwell in the expanse of the sky are worthy of homage. Furthermore, let those virtuous ones—the hosts of immortals with their armlets and necklaces shimmering and their crowns blazing—also listen. (133)

Even if, having committed an evil deed against my own mother, I were to carry this entire world upon my head—a wheel blazing with the red glow of fire—for ten thousand aeons, each as long as an aeon itself; though I may endure this for a long time, my mind, as it proceeds toward the welfare of sentient beings, does not waver.

511.030. Then, immediately after the words of that Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka, the Beloved of All Beings, that wheel—seemingly torn from his head and tossed upward—leaped from its height of seven palm trees into the expanse of the sky and came to rest there.
511.032. That wheel, blazing with clusters of flames flickering as they were struck by the restless wind, shone as it revolved in the air, repeatedly emitting a terrifying roar.
It was like the rising orb of the sun, with its entire mass of rays fully released, hanging down by means of pure jewels and other gems supported by walls of vaidūrya.
Then, the mountains— whose waters flowed from cascading torrents, whose flowering branches were stirred by the breeze,
and whose long horn-like arms seemed to kiss the sky— trembled as if they had been struck.

The ocean-dwellers, whose waves were stirred up by the agitation of sea-monsters and who resounded with deep roars like the thundering of clouds, were then overwhelmed by the waters that overstepped their shores; they dwelt within the crests of the jewels [upon the mountains].
512.009. The orb of the sun, radiant with its rays emitted without exception, shone in the sky.
512.011. From every direction, the quarters of the world were seen to possess manifest splendor, their interiors bristling with the sprout-like rays of the sun.
With their chests resplendent with streaks of flashing lightning and their arms bound by bracelets of Indra’s bow,
those clouds, shedding a little water, shone in the sky like a canopy.
512.017. Variegated garlands fell from the sky, and the gods, exceedingly joyful, offered hymns of praise.
512.019. Many who had long been immersed in deep affliction and were struck by suffering became, in an instant, free from ailment. (140)
While the uneven wheel was blazing and his body was split open at the extremities with the upper part raised, and all his limbs were drenched by streams of flowing blood,
that practitioner, having composed his own mind toward the Blessed One, the mass of virtues, departed for his own home in that very instant as if in a moment.
In the great ford of the water of generosity, perfectly pure through the cleanliness of ethical conduct;
fragrant with patience, cool and clear, with the unfathomable current of vigor.

512.027. Standing at that great ford of awakening, which is profound and tranquilized by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and awakens the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*), he remained eager for the city of awakening. 512.028. [143]
He washed away his remaining sins and went joyfully to Tuṣita;
even while staying there, filled with compassion upon seeing the world, he rejoiced for no long time.
512.031. What, then, is this being brought forward?

For indeed, living beings who act with malice toward their mother fall here itself into the abyss of calamity; therefore, mothers should be served by virtuous persons whose hearts are constantly filled with love, faith, respect, and affection.
512.033. Thus ends the Maitrakanyakā-avadāna in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
== End of the Divyāvadāna ==
